title: From Concepts to Actual Causes: Toward Closing the Concept-Malfunction Gap in Robot Foundation Models
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop at CoRL 2026
summary: Post-incident analysis of a robot foundation model poses a singular causal question: which internal components caused this failure, and to what degree? Mechanistic interpretability (MI), however, establishes general causal claims by decoding the concepts a policy has learned, yet knowing which concepts are encoded is insufficient for identifying the actual cause of a specific incident. In this position paper, we analyze this concept-malfunction gap by posing fault isolation in the framework of actual causality. Specifically, we formalize a fault-isolation query as a tuple of intervened internal components, counterfactual values, contingencies, and read-outs, and lay out conditions for it to be well-specified. Through this lens, we identify shortcomings of current MI approaches: they assume fixed contingencies and read out only immediate effects, letting backups obscure actual causes. We demonstrate on a toy example that these shortcomings can lead to conflicting verdicts. Lastly, based on the well-specification conditions, we outline four open research tasks toward closing the gap.

Mechanistic interpretability (MI), however, establishes general causal claims by decoding the concepts a policy has learned, yet knowing which concepts are encoded is insufficient for identifying the actual cause of a specific incident. Through this lens, we identify shortcomings of current MI approaches: they assume fixed contingencies and read out only immediate effects, letting backups obscure actual causes. Lastly, based on the well-specification conditions, we outline four open research tasks toward closing the gap. Introduction sec:intro As robot foundation models (RFMs)---e.g., vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0 and world action models (WAMs)~ ye2026wam ---enter spaces shared with humans, their failures can become serious incidents. Recent legislation such as the EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems, which can include autonomous robots, to investigate and report such incidents and implement corrective actions~ euaiact2024 . Since retraining the entire model is costly and may not even resolve the underlying fault, efficient compliance requires localizing the fault for targeted repair, which comes down to one question: which internal components actually caused the failure, and to what degree? The closest toolkit for analyzing the inner workings of a foundation model is mechanistic interpretability (MI)~ zhang2026embodied,mai2026beyond,swann2026saevla . However, MI is primarily designed to establish general causal claims across a distribution~ geiger2025abstraction , whereas an individual incident calls for a singular one. This discrepancy creates a concept--malfunction gap: MI reveals which concepts a policy encodes, not which components caused the malfunction. The closed loop of RFMs widens this gap: unlike in language models, internal errors propagate through the environment and compound over time. In this position paper, we argue that the concept--malfunction gap stems primarily from misspecified causal queries rather than deficient methods. To re-pose these queries, we ground fault isolation in the framework of actual causality~ halpern2005causes,halpern2016actual , assuming that the incident can be replayed in a deterministic simulator to compute the counterfactuals it requires. Our contributions are threefold: we (1)~formally define a fault-isolation query (Section~ sec:setting ); (2)~diagnose how existing MI methods instantiate via a toy example (Section~ sec:gap ); and (3)~outline four open research tasks toward fault isolation in RFMs (Section~ sec:agenda ). Fault Isolation as Actual Causation sec:setting In this section, we formalize fault isolation with actual causality~ halpern2016actual by treating an RFM's closed-loop rollout as a structural causal model and introducing the fault-isolation query~ . Robot foundation models. We model an RFM (VLA or WAM) as a policy that maps an observation history (e.g., images and proprioception) and an instruction to an action chunk consisting of future -dimensional actions (either discrete~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla or continuous~ black2025pi0 ), and additional future states for WAMs. We decompose the computation of at step into components , the intermediate units an investigator can intervene on and blame, e.g., attention-head outputs, MLP neurons, dictionary latents, or a WAM's predicted-state latents. Incidents and fault isolation. The exogenous context (initial state, seed, instruction), a deterministic simulator, and determine the rollout . A failure predicate encodes the incident, e.g., the gripper coming within a safety distance of a human hand, or a grasped knife being dropped. Since each action shapes later observations, a component affects directly through its action and indirectly through the environment. With collecting all components, fault isolation asks which subset caused in this rollout, not how the policy behaves on average. Counterfactuals and contingencies. Actual causality builds on but-for dependence: had taken another value, would the failure have been averted? To make this precise, we treat the unrolled rollout as a structural causal model ~ halpern2005causes over and , with equations given by and the simulator. Yet a genuine cause may fail to be a but-for cause when a backup component would have produced the failure anyway (e.g., the Hydra effect~ mcgrath2023hydra ). Actual causality therefore also tests dependence under a contingency, which holds such backups at their observed values. Definition 1 (actual cause). We call well-specified for an RFM incident if all four conditions hold, and misspecified otherwise: [label=WS ,leftmargin=*,nosep] (temporal scope) may include components at any step; (realizability) can be induced by some observation history; (searched contingency) is searched per incident, not fixed in advance; (rollout outcome) is evaluated on the counterfactual rollout. A misspecified can reach a wrong verdict: a single-step misses faults that accumulate over steps (WS1); an unrealizable may avert merely by driving the policy off-manifold (WS2; cf.\ normality~ halpern2015graded ); a fixed may hide causes that have backups, or misgrade them (WS3); and a per-step read-out can miss effects mediated by the environment (WS4). Handling backups in RFMs. (i)~Loop backups and realizability: in RFMs, the policy itself can undo a repair at later steps (e.g., a gripper stopped short of its goal simply moves toward it again), so a witness must also freeze such later reactions. A cause revealed this way is a persistent fault: repairing it alone will not prevent the failure. Such witnesses, however, may force combinations the policy would never produce (e.g., a slowed robot whose drive stays idle), so their verdicts weaken as the counterfactual drifts from the factual rollout. (ii)~Granularity and responsibility: responsibility (Definition~2) counts how many components must be frozen, which is meaningful only if each backup is one component; sparse autoencoder latents~ huben2024sae approximate this better than individual neurons. Existing MI methods as instantiations of . We examine six MI method families and summarize in Table~ tab:gap how each instantiates . None yields a well-specified query. Violating only WS1 or WS3 would merely miss causes, but every intervening family also violates WS2, so even its reported causes may be spurious. Specifically, they violate temporal scope (WS1) by intervening within a single step or only on the input (except steering); realizability (WS2) by using counterfactual values that the incident may never produce, such as masked images, other inputs~ zhang2024patching , or steered states; searched contingency (WS3) by fixing in advance or averaging it over inputs, thus ignoring the incident's backups; and rollout outcome (WS4) by reading out a per-step surrogate such as the action (except visual attribution and steering), which misses what the loop does next. title: AuroraWorld: Structured 4D World Modeling for Exo-to-Ego Video Generation in Robot Manipulation
summary: Egocentric observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation processes, capturing contact interactions and object-state changes that are important for visuomotor policy learning but difficult to observe from external cameras. However, collecting such data at scale remains expensive due to additional hardware requirements and platform-specific deployment costs. Synthesizing egocentric observations from large-scale exocentric manipulation videos provides a scalable alternative. However, existing methods struggle to synthesize physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric videos under substantial viewpoint transformations, severe occlusions, complex object interactions, and inherently sparse observations from available exocentric viewpoints.
full_text: Egocentric observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation processes, capturing contact interactions and object-state changes that are important for visuomotor policy learning but difficult to observe from external cameras. However, collecting such data at scale remains expensive due to additional hardware requirements and platform-specific deployment costs. Synthesizing egocentric observations from large-scale exocentric manipulation videos provides a scalable alternative. However, existing methods struggle to synthesize physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric videos under substantial viewpoint transformations, severe occlusions, complex object interactions, and inherently sparse observations from available exocentric viewpoints. To address these challenges, we propose , a 4D world model that infers a structured 4D embodied world state from sparse exocentric observations to enable unobserved egocentric video generation. characterizes the underlying embodied environment through complementary spatial, temporal, and motion components, capturing scene structure, temporal evolution, and motion dynamics from 3D scene geometry, temporal keyframes, and motion trajectories, respectively. These components provide structured world priors for diffusion generation, enabling geometrically consistent, temporally coherent, and dynamically plausible egocentric videos. We evaluate the proposed method on visual generation and downstream embodied policy learning tasks in both simulated and real robotic environments, demonstrating consistent improvements over existing methods across multiple benchmarks. Introduction Embodied intelligence seeks to develop intelligent agents that can perceive, reason about, and interact with the physical world, representing an important direction toward more capable artificial intelligence systems zhang2025step,jiang2026wsa . A fundamental challenge in embodied intelligence is learning generalizable robot policies that can transform sensory observations into reliable actions under diverse and complex physical interactions. Recent advances in large-scale robot learning, particularly vision-language-action models brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,khazatsky2025droid,zhang2026dreamvla,zhong2026acot , have demonstrated the potential of data-driven approaches for acquiring increasingly generalizable manipulation skills. However, scaling embodied policy learning remains limited by the availability of diverse and high-quality robot interaction data, which is costly and time-consuming to collect in real-world environments. A critical aspect of this data bottleneck is the limited availability of egocentric observations in robot manipulation, such as those captured by wrist-mounted cameras. These observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation and reveal fine-grained cues, including gripper-object contact and object states, that are valuable for precise control grauman2022ego4d,khazatsky2025droid . However, egocentric videos remain less consistently available across robot platforms and tasks, as they require additional sensing setups and dedicated data collection efforts qian2025wristworld,liu2024exo2ego . This limited availability of robot-centric observations can hinder the learning of robust and generalizable embodied policies. To alleviate this data bottleneck, researchers have explored synthesizing egocentric videos from exocentric manipulation ones. First, some works perform frame-based view synthesis to infer egocentric observations from exocentric views mildenhall2020nerf,wang2024dust3r,leroy2024mastr,wang2025vggt,szymanowicz2026lagernvs,park2026egoworld,hu2025cascaded . However, these approaches mainly synthesize individual observations, without capturing temporal evolution and robot-object interaction dynamics. Consequently, they are insufficient for generating temporally coherent manipulation videos involving evolving object states and interactions. Second, recent advances in video generation models enable the synthesis of temporally coherent videos from exocentric observations liu2024exo2ego,xu2025egoexogen,mahdi2025exo2egosyn,kang2025egox . Nevertheless, these approaches primarily focus on visual appearance generation, while lacking explicit modeling of the underlying embodied world state required for physically grounded manipulation. Recently, emerging robotic world models qian2025wristworld aim to model latent embodied states and the underlying dynamics of physical environments for predicting robot-centric observations. However, most video generation approaches and world models often require additional observational constraints, such as an initial egocentric frame or rich exocentric observations, and do not explicitly model the underlying embodied dynamics xu2025egoexogen,mahdi2025exo2egosyn,liu2024exo2ego,qian2025wristworld , to resolve viewpoint ambiguity. However, under sparse exocentric observations, they struggle with large viewpoint changes, severe occlusions, and complex robot-object interactions, making it difficult to generate physically plausible egocentric observations. To address this challenge, we formulate exo-to-ego synthesis as structured inference of the hidden 4D embodied world representation from sparse exocentric observations. To this end, we propose , a 4D world model that infers and models the evolving embodied environment through complementary spatial, temporal, and motion components (Figure fig:pipeline ). Specifically, captures spatial structures through 3D geometric scene representations, temporal evolution through motion-stabilized keyframes, and interaction dynamics through motion trajectories. These components characterize different aspects of the underlying embodied world and serve as structured world priors for egocentric video generation. By conditioning generation on the inferred 4D representation rather than appearance-level correlations alone, enables physically consistent and temporally coherent egocentric video synthesis. We evaluate on visual generation and downstream embodied policy learning tasks in simulated and real robotic environments, demonstrating improved generation quality and policy performance under sparse exocentric observations. Related Work -view Generation. Cross-view generation aims to synthesize observations from unseen viewpoints given available visual inputs. For static scenarios, recent approaches model scene structures from visual inputs to enable consistent generation from unseen viewpoints, including 3D reconstruction wang2024dust3r,leroy2024mastr,wang2025vggt,liu2025vggtx,huang2026nas3r,szymanowicz2026lagernvs , and diffusion-based synthesis park2026egoworld . Extending to dynamic scenarios, recent exo-to-ego approaches liu2024exo2ego,xu2025egoexogen,mahdi2025exo2egosyn,kang2025egox,song2025worldwander,mahdi2026synchrony,luo2024put leverage conditional video generation models with multi-view, pose-aware, and other forms of conditioning. However, these approaches are primarily developed for general visual scenarios, and perceptual realism is the dominant objective. In contrast, robotic manipulation requires physically grounded egocentric videos that preserve fine-grained geometric relationships, contact interactions, and object-state transitions essential for downstream policy learning. Qian et al. qian2025wristworld represent an initial effort toward egocentric video synthesis by exploring geometric information. However, their method lacks explicit modeling of key manipulation states or motion dynamics, limiting its applicability under sparse exocentric observations. Generation and Embodied World Models. Recent advances in large-scale video generation have achieved significant progress in synthesizing temporally coherent and realistic videos. Latent diffusion models and Transformer-based architectures have become widely adopted paradigms blattmann2023svd,wan2025wan,kong2024hunyuanvideo,hacohen2025ltxvideo,li2026skyreelsv3,yang2026omnivideo2 . To improve controllability, conditional video generation methods incorporate auxiliary visual signals, such as reference images, depth, camera poses, and geometric structures, to enhance consistency across generated sequences lee2024videoinpainter,bian2025videopainter,cai2025videocanvas,chen2026depthdirector,cao2026freeorbit4d,hu2026svor . Building upon the advances, video-generation-based embodied world models are proposed to learn latent environment dynamics and predict future states conditioned on actions hu2025vpp,zhen2025tesseract,jang2025dreamgen,dharmarajan2025dream2flow,ye2026robodream . While conventional video generation models primarily optimize visual plausibility and temporal consistency, embodied world models seek to capture latent physical states and action-conditioned dynamics. Recent studies explore strategies, including geometric modeling zhen2025tesseract,dharmarajan2025dream2flow , memory mechanisms guo2025ctrl , and action conditioning zhu2025irasim to improve physical plausibility, consistency, and long-horizon prediction. Embodied world models have been explored as simulators for generating interactive training environments agarwal2026cosmos,guo2025ctrl , data engines for scalable synthetic video generation jang2025dreamgen,ye2026robodream , and planners for decision making agarwal2026cosmos,bi2026motus . Policy Learning and Vision-Language-Action Models. Embodied policy learning aims to learn generalizable policies that enable robots to perform diverse tasks from sensory observations chi2025diffusion,kim2026cosmos,khazatsky2025droid,yin2026mivla . Vision-language-action models have emerged as a promising paradigm by jointly modeling visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions, enabling scalable learning of manipulation policies from heterogeneous datasets brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,khazatsky2025droid,yin2026mivla,zhang2026dreamvla,zhong2026acot . However, the performance and generalization of these models remain strongly dependent on the availability and diversity of robot interaction data, particularly egocentric observations that capture contact-rich manipulation processes. Collecting such videos at scale remains challenging, motivating approaches that can synthesize policy-relevant egocentric videos from more readily available exocentric observations. title: Behavioral Steering of Vision-Language-Action Models in the Low-Parameter Regime
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to adapt pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs). We investigate the problem of behavioral steering: adapting a VLA's execution style to preferences such as carrying objects higher. To investigate how little trainable capacity such steering requires and how much pretrained capability can be retained, we freeze an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and optimize TinyLoRA adapters with 8 to 384 trainable parameters using either policy-gradient RL (GRPO) or evolutionary search (CMA-ES). With just 256 trainable parameters, we raise carry height by 120 mm on trained tasks at 92% success and by 74 mm on a held-out task at 80% success. By rescaling the learned update, we can tune the trade-off between style gains and capability retention without retraining. Increasing adapter capacity generally improves this trade-off, retaining more pretrained capability at comparable style gains. The choice of optimizer also depends on capacity, with CMA-ES being competitive at low parameter counts, while GRPO offers better trade-offs as capacity grows. These findings show that extremely low-dimensional updates can steer pretrained VLA behavior, with adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling offering practical control over adaptation and retention.

To investigate how little trainable capacity such steering requires and how much pretrained capability can be retained, we freeze an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and optimize TinyLoRA adapters with to trainable parameters using either policy-gradient RL (GRPO) or evolutionary search (CMA-ES). Introduction sec:intro The usefulness of a robot depends on both task completion and execution style. Policies that achieve the same goal may differ in speed, trajectory, or smoothness, with consequences for safety, efficiency, and user preference lasota2017survey,dragan2013legibility,story2022speed . Vision-language-action models (VLAs) achieve strong manipulation performance and generalize to new objects, scenes, and instructions openvla,brohan2023rt2,oneill2023openx . Yet adapting their execution style while retaining their pretrained capabilities remains underexplored. As a case study, we steer carry height, following haon , to measure how style gain and retention of those capabilities scale with the number of trainable parameters. Prior work adapts VLA execution style through training-free activation steering, which shifts hidden activations along directions associated with a concept actadd, caa and can alter end-effector speed and carry height haon . Since these directions are not optimized for the target behavior, neither the style change nor task success is guaranteed, and activation-level interventions in VLAs range from catastrophic to negligible across architectures and features grant2026 . We find that the activation baseline based on haon 's method does not consistently increase carry height and can disrupt task success, motivating a learned weight-space direction that directly targets the desired behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL), increasingly used for VLA post-training rlinfvla, guo2025improvingvisionlanguageactionmodelonline, li2025simplevlarlscalingvlatraining , is a natural way to learn such a direction. Many execution styles, such as carry height, speed, and smoothness, can be expressed as rewards without requiring style demonstrations. As the pretrained VLA already performs the task well, such adaptation may also need little capacity: in language models, RL with TinyLoRA improves math reasoning with only 13 trainable parameters, while supervised fine-tuning needs 100--1000 larger updates to match it tinylora . We therefore study whether similarly small adapters suffice for VLA steering, and how adapter capacity and optimizer choice affect the trade-off between style gain and capability retention. We study these questions empirically by steering a frozen OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy openvlaoft to carry objects higher on LIBERO-Goal libero . We train TinyLoRA adapters ranging from to parameters using a carry-height rollout reward subject to a task-success constraint, and compare two optimizers: GRPO grpo , a policy-gradient method common in VLA post-training rlinfvla, li2025simplevlarlscalingvlatraining , and CMA-ES cmaes , a derivative-free evolution strategy increasingly explored for LLM post-training essa, esalternative, esgeometry . We find that learned updates of a few hundred parameters steer carry height where prompting and activation intervention do not, and rescaling them recovers most of the held-out success they cost. As capacity grows, GRPO gives a better style--retention trade-off than CMA-ES. Contributions: 1.5em Controlled study of VLA behavioral steering in the low-parameter regime. We vary parameter count and optimizer independently, and evaluate every update on the full LIBERO-Goal suite alongside prompting and activation-intervention baselines ( sec:steer ). Matched-retention comparison of learned updates. We use weight interpolation to trace each update's style--retention tradeoff curve, and compare updates at equal held-out success. This gives practitioners a way to tune the trade-off without retraining ( sec:distance , sec:dial ). Analysis of how parameter count and optimizer shape steering. For each optimizer, we identify how style at a fixed weight change scales with parameter count, separating the effect of added parameters from update size and training budget. We then compare the update directions GRPO and CMA-ES learn across parameter counts to understand why they differ ( sec:optimizer_diff ). Related Work sec:related Behavioral steering of VLAs. Closest to our work, haon steer VLAs without training by identifying FFN neurons whose value vectors project onto tokens expressing concepts such as fast, slow, and up, and overwriting their activations with fixed strength coefficients. They evaluate on OpenVLA in LIBERO simulation and on a physical UR5 robot controlled by -FAST but do not report task success. CTRL-STEER ctrlsteer builds on this approach by adjusting the intervention strength during the rollout with a PID or RL controller. Both methods select neurons based on their association with concept words rather than the target behavior itself, and such interventions can also break task execution: grant2026 finds that modifying even a single sparse-autoencoder feature can substantially reduce task success. Beyond activation steering, TempoVLA tempovla trains speed control into by fine-tuning on demonstrations re-timed by merging or splitting actions, but re-timing does not readily extend to other behavioral styles. We instead learn weight updates directly from a behavioral rollout reward without demonstrations, comparing them against haon 's activation steering and reporting how much held-out task success they retain. Extremely parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The intrinsic-dimensionality view of fine-tuning suggests that useful downstream adaptation of large pretrained models can lie in a much lower-dimensional subspace intrinsic . LoRA lora learns additive low-rank weight updates while keeping the pretrained weights frozen. Motivated by evidence that the pretrained weights' top singular directions provide an effective basis for fine-tuning, LoRA-XS loraxs learns only a small matrix between fixed SVD factors. To further reduce trainable capacity, TinyLoRA tinylora parameterizes this matrix through fixed random projections and parameter sharing, allowing as few as one trainable parameter. Trained with RL, it improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's GSM8K accuracy from to using only 13 trainable parameters, which the authors suggest reflects a change in output style rather than new task knowledge. We investigate whether similarly small adapters can steer a VLA's existing skills toward different execution styles. Post-training with RL and ES. Recent VLA systems use RL algorithms such as PPO ppo and GRPO grpo to fine-tune pretrained policies on task rewards, and report higher task success and better out-of-distribution performance than SFT-only baselines in simulation rlinfvla, li2025simplevlarlscalingvlatraining . We similarly use GRPO, but optimize execution style under a task-success constraint. Evolution strategies (ES) offer a backpropagation-free alternative, and have scaled to full-parameter fine-tuning of billion-parameter LLMs esatscale . While ES can match GRPO's task accuracy, studies report larger weight changes, broader off-task drift esgeometry , and greater forgetting of prior capabilities esforgetting . We investigate whether the choice between ES and GRPO matters in the same way at our extremely small parameter counts, comparing both on style and on held-out task success. Method sec:method We study stylistic adaptation of a frozen pretrained VLA policy by post-training only a small low-rank TinyLoRA adapter tinylora . Following haon , we focus on carry height: how high the robot holds an object while carrying it. To examine the effect of trainable capacity, we vary the adapter's parameter count from a handful to a few hundred and compare optimization with CMA-ES and GRPO. Our experiments use the discrete-token OpenVLA-OFT policy from RLinf openvlaoft,rlinfvla , based on the 7B OpenVLA model openvla, haon, ctrlsteer . This checkpoint was trained on all 130 LIBERO tasks libero through supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations followed by GRPO with task-success rewards. Low-rank adaptation with TinyLoRA sec:param We adapt the frozen model with TinyLoRA tinylora , an extremely parameter-efficient variant of low-rank adaptation lora . title: Selective Positional Allocation for Noise-Robust Query Retrieval in Small-Object Detection
summary: In aerial and remote-sensing imagery, detecting tiny targets is frequently hampered less by the representational capacity of the backbone network than by the manner in which positional priors are distributed across ill-defined foreground and background regions. We introduce SPAR (Selective Positional Allocation and Retrieval), a detection framework that re-conceptualizes positional cues as an allocatable resource: they are intensified at semantically meaningful locations while responses driven by scene clutter are actively attenuated. At the heart of SPAR lies Selective Positional Embedding (SPE), an interpretable embedding mechanism paired with an activation-bar visualization that facilitates direct inspection and hyper-parameter tuning. The encoder branch, termed MOHFE, fuses heatmap-modulated positional signals with category-specific and box-level evidence to yield more compact multi-scale features; the decoder branch, termed HIDQ, employs a foreground gating operation to discard background-dominated candidates prior to query decoding. To cope with the extreme sparsity of small-object evidence, we additionally design DPSConv (Dual-Path Sampling Convolution), which augments retrieval-oriented representations through two geometrically complementary sampling routes. Notably, all heatmap supervision is derived from existing detection objectives and consumed exclusively during training, requiring no auxiliary heatmap annotations and leaving inference as an ordinary forward pass with no additional gradient overhead. Comprehensive evaluations on DOTA, DIOR, VisDrone, PASCAL VOC, NWPU VHR-10, and AITOD demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed design: relative to the baseline, SPAR attains an improvement of up to 9.1 percentage points, shortens the decoder from eight layers to three, and reduces model parameters by 59.4% (66.3M versus 163M).
full_text: Selective Positional Allocation for Noise-Robust Query Retrieval in Small-Object Detection Yangchen Zeng In aerial and remote-sensing imagery, detecting tiny targets is frequently hampered less by the representational capacity of the backbone network than by the manner in which positional priors are distributed across ill-defined foreground and background regions. We introduce SPAR (Selective Positional Allocation and Retrieval), a detection framework that re-conceptualizes positional cues as an allocatable resource: they are intensified at semantically meaningful locations while responses driven by scene clutter are actively attenuated. At the heart of SPAR lies Selective Positional Embedding (SPE), an interpretable embedding mechanism paired with an activation-bar visualization that facilitates direct inspection and hyper-parameter tuning. The encoder branch, termed MOHFE, fuses heatmap-modulated positional signals with category-specific and box-level evidence to yield more compact multi-scale features; the decoder branch, termed HIDQ, employs a foreground gating operation to discard background-dominated candidates prior to query decoding. To cope with the extreme sparsity of small-object evidence, we additionally design DPSConv (Dual-Path Sampling Convolution), which augments retrieval-oriented representations through two geometrically complementary sampling routes. Notably, all heatmap supervision is derived from existing detection objectives and consumed exclusively during training, requiring no auxiliary heatmap annotations and leaving inference as an ordinary forward pass with no additional gradient overhead. Comprehensive evaluations on DOTA, DIOR, VisDrone, PASCAL VOC, NWPU VHR-10, and AITOD demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed design: relative to the baseline, SPAR attains an improvement of up to 9.1 percentage points, shortens the decoder from eight layers to three, and reduces model parameters by 59.4 (66.3M versus 163M). Introduction sec:intro Detecting objects that occupy only a handful of pixels remains one of the most stubborn challenges in computer vision, and the difficulty is amplified in aerial and remote-sensing imagery where tiny targets are readily submerged in complex background textures. Such imagery is typified by wide scale disparities, highly congested instance layouts, and a drastic imbalance between foreground and background pixels, each of which independently complicates localization and classification~ wei2024review, yang2022scrdet++, li2025efficient, hou2020mdpcaps . Meanwhile, real-world deployment scenarios increasingly demand detectors whose accuracy does not collapse when imaging conditions or scene densities vary~ cheng2023towards, cui2025efficient, akyon2022sahi . Query-based detectors built upon the Transformer architecture have gained considerable traction in the small-object regime, owing to their global receptive fields and set-prediction paradigm that obviates dense anchor design and heuristic post-processing~ zhao2024detrs, zhang2022dino,zeng2025hmpe . Nevertheless, their effectiveness in clutter-heavy aerial scenes is fundamentally gated by the caliber of queries fed into the decoder. A considerable number of existing query-construction pipelines fail to fully exploit readily available detection signals---spatial coordinates, category confidences, and box regression gradients---particularly when annotated data are scarce. The consequence is a misalignment between positional encodings and detection semantics, whereby regions carrying useful information are not sufficiently emphasized for precise small-object localization~ meng2021conditional, li2022dn . A complementary shortcoming arises from the overwhelming background-to-foreground ratio: queries are readily polluted by activations originating from background regions. Areas of low semantic quality can nevertheless produce non-negligible embeddings, yet few detectors explicitly intervene to suppress this background-borne noise prior to decoding, thereby degrading both localization fidelity and classification accuracy~ zhang2022dino, li2022dn, zhang2026center . This phenomenon also engenders an efficiency bottleneck, since the decoder is compelled to allocate multiple layers to rectifying suboptimal queries, inflating both training and inference costs as self-attention complexity scales with token count and stack depth~ zhao2024detrs . The predicament is especially acute for small objects, whose discriminative features are inherently sparse and fine-grained. In the absence of a mechanism dedicated to amplifying such sparse discriminative patterns, query-relevant representations stay brittle under clutter and fail to generalize across domains~ wei2024review, di2025toward . Motivated by these observations, we put forward SPAR (Selective Positional Allocation and Retrieval), a framework that investigates a foundational question in query-based detection: where should positional cues be placed? Instead of uniformly broadcasting positional encodings across every spatial location, SPAR concentrates them in foreground-salient regions while actively dampening them in background-dominated zones. This selective distribution tightly couples positional priors with semantic and geometric evidence, elevating the quality of decoder inputs and endowing the detector with greater resilience to scene clutter. A cornerstone of SPAR is Selective Positional Embedding (SPE), complemented by an activation-bar visualization that renders the embedding behavior directly inspectable and tunable. Leveraging SPE as a shared allocation signal, we devise two synergistic modules: MOHFE (Multi-Scale ObjectBox-Heatmap Fusion Encoder) and HIDQ (Heatmap-Induced Discriminative Query retrieval). MOHFE produces more refined multi-scale encoder features by interweaving category and geometric cues with selectively gated positional embeddings, thereby sharpening the correspondence between spatial priors and detection semantics. HIDQ subsequently assembles a compact set of discriminative queries and employs a foreground gate to eliminate background-dominated candidates, which diminishes the necessity for iterative query refinement and permits a substantially shallower decoder. The net effect is a simultaneous gain in efficiency and robustness. To confront the extreme feature sparsity exhibited by intricate small targets, we additionally devise DPSConv (Dual-Path Sampling Convolution), which captures sparse yet informative local patterns and feeds them into the retrieval pipeline, thereby enriching the representational basis upon which high-quality queries are constructed. The principal contributions of this work are enumerated below: We introduce SPE, an interpretable selective positional embedding mechanism accompanied by an activation-bar visualization for transparent analysis and convenient tuning of the allocation behavior. We design MOHFE and HIDQ to attain cleaner encoder representations and more discriminative query retrieval, collectively enabling a reduction of decoder depth from eight layers to three. We incorporate DPSConv to reinforce sparse feature extraction, achieving a 59.4 parameter reduction (66.3M versus 163M) while accelerating both training and inference. We conduct thorough empirical validation on five primary benchmarks plus an additional AITOD ablation configuration, demonstrating consistent performance gains and favorable scalability. Related Work Small-object detection can be viewed from two complementary angles: strengthening the visual features that describe tiny targets, and improving the decision process that turns those features into predictions. In aerial scenes, both are difficult at the same time because objects occupy few pixels, scene context is cluttered, and background responses often dominate the signal. Existing work therefore tends to focus either on more discriminative backbone features or on more reliable query/decoder design. CNN-based Small Object Detection CNN detectors remain a standard choice because pyramid-shaped representations naturally encode spatial detail at multiple scales. One-stage methods such as SSD~ liu2016ssd , RetinaNet~ lin2017focal , and the YOLO family~ redmon2018yolov3,zyc2022behavior emphasize efficiency, whereas two-stage systems such as Faster R-CNN~ ren2015faster and Mask R-CNN~ he2017mask refine proposals for stronger localization. For aerial imagery, many variants add extra machinery to recover tiny targets, including super-resolution enhancement~ zhang2023superyolo and comparative feature learning~ cao2023pcnet . Despite these improvements, CNN pipelines still rely heavily on dense candidate generation and NMS-style selection~ hosang2017learning . That design is vulnerable to scene-dependent thresholds and introduces redundancy when a high-resolution image contains many background patches but only a few useful targets~ cai2018cascade, cui2025detection, ren2015faster, hou2025fedc . In practice, the bottleneck is not only feature extraction, but also how to avoid spending computation on regions that are unlikely to matter. Vision Transformer in Object Detection Transformer detectors recast detection as set prediction, so the model learns a fixed number of queries instead of scanning dense candidate grids~ carion2020end . DETR and its successors, including Deformable DETR~ zhu2020deformable , Conditional DETR~ meng2021conditional , DINO~ zhang2022dino , and RT-DETR~ zhao2024detrs , combine convolutional feature extraction with transformer encoding and query-driven decoding. The main advantage is cleaner post-processing; the main weakness is that attention and query refinement become expensive when the input is large or the target is small. Recent work has therefore focused on reducing that cost or making the queries more informative. DynamicViT~ rao2021dynamicvit prunes tokens to save computation, CAM-based supervision has been used to assist localization under imbalance~ ma2024coarse , and sparse-attention designs target wide-field imagery by focusing on target-relevant regions~ li2024sparseformer . Related efficiency strategies include window attention~ liu2021swin , hierarchical or downsampling architectures~ wang2021pyramid,wu2021cvt,zeng2026deepinterestgr,dong6413179hmpe , and low-rank approximations~ xiong2021nystromformer . Even with these advances, query-based detectors remain fragile in cluttered small-object scenes: useful cues are sparse, background responses are strong, and the model may still devote too much decoding effort to poor queries. That observation motivates SPAR, which treats positional cues as something to allocate selectively rather than inject uniformly. Positional Encoding and Heatmap-guided Query Construction Positional encoding constitutes a foundational component in transformer-based detectors, as it supplies the spatial awareness that self-attention alone cannot capture. Early designs relied on fixed sinusoidal encodings~ carion2020end , while subsequent work explored learnable positional embeddings and conditionally generated spatial priors~ meng2021conditional . A particularly relevant line of research investigates heatmap-guided positional embedding, where detection-derived saliency maps are leveraged to modulate how positional cues are distributed across spatial locations. HMPE~ zeng2025hmpe demonstrates that heatmap-conditioned embeddings can substantially improve the efficiency of transformer-based small-object detection by aligning positional priors with object-centric regions. Building upon this insight, recent work further introduces noise-aware positional embedding for query retrieval~ zeng2026learning , which explicitly accounts for background interference when allocating positional resources. These studies collectively establish that the manner in which positional information is assigned---rather than merely whether it is present---plays a decisive role in query-based detection, a principle that SPA

title: CalVLA: Shaping Native Confidence in Vision-Language-Action Policies with Outcome Supervision

summary: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.

Introduction and related work sec:introduction A robot can keep issuing confident actions after a missed grasp or an unsuccessful placement. For vision-language-action (VLA) policies, this is a training mismatch: imitating demonstrated actions does not explicitly teach the model whether its behavior will ultimately succeed. OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla already produces probabilities over discrete action tokens. We call a summary of these probabilities native confidence, because it comes from the action-producing policy itself. Confidence and temporal information. Raw action probabilities need not predict task outcomes~ zollo2025confidence . Shifting Uncertainty aggregates signals across time and action dimensions~ tang2026shifting , while temporal-difference calibration learns sequential success confidence through value estimation~ francismeretzki2026td . These approaches motivate studying what confidence reveals over an unfolding attempt; our objective instead changes the native action probabilities through outcome-supervised policy adaptation. Learned monitors and recovery. SAFE and SAFECAST learn failure predictors from policy features~ gu2025safe,rajaprakash2026safecast ; Hide-and-Seek uses rollout labels~ park2026hide ; and ActProbe and INSIGHT exploit action chunks or token uncertainty~ huang2026actprobe,karli2026insight . Other work studies consistency-based monitors~ agia2025unpacking , success-only examples~ xu2025faildetect , or recovery~ ma2026cyclevla . Our contribution instead modifies the policy's native action-token confidence through outcome supervision. Frozen-feature probes isolate the detector-versus-controller choice; they are not reproductions of those prior systems. ranks confidence for successful versus failed attempts of the same task at similar normalized elapsed times, not verified equivalent physical stages. We measure failure discrimination (ranking eventual failures above successes) and task-success rate (TSR). Discrimination is distinct from probability calibration~ guo2017calibration and does not establish the benefit of a recovery intervention. This study tests whether the confidence signal can improve without an extra detector, and whether adapting the controller changes its task performance. Method sec:method Native confidence. An observation contains the current image and instruction. OpenVLA generates seven action tokens autoregressively, one per action dimension. Write for the probability of bin in dimension , suppressing the preceding tokens. We train the mean top-token confidence With deterministic decoding, each maximum is the probability of the selected token. The score is differentiable almost everywhere; a high value indicates concentrated action probabilities, not a known probability of task success. Learning from outcomes. For a rollout of steps indexed , define normalized elapsed time . We pair observations from successful and failed rollouts of the same task when . Different durations or termination conditions mean that paired observations may represent different physical task stages. The loss is This squared hinge-style ranking objective vanishes when success-associated confidence exceeds failure-associated confidence by at least the margin. Same-task, relative-time pairing reduces task-identity and timing shortcuts, but does not match physical states or identify the failed action; a failed rollout may include correct early actions. Adaptation and scoring. We update rank-16 LoRA adapters~ hu2022lora in attention and , keeping pretrained weights frozen. Validation compares candidate strengths of a forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) penalty toward the original policy and selects zero; the reported models therefore optimize Equation~ alone. At an evaluation step , failure risk is the negative observed-prefix mean, This can be updated online without future observations. We evaluate ranking, without selecting an alarm threshold or executing a recovery action. Experimental protocol sec:experiments Data and training. We evaluate the prescribed grid of ten LIBERO-10 tasks with 50 initial states each~ liu2023libero . An outcome-blind rule fixes 350 training, 50 validation, and 100 test configurations, with 35/5/10 per task. Frozen OpenVLA succeeds on 243 of all 500 configurations and 58 test configurations. Training uses 11,378 same-task pairs, with failed observations restricted to the final 130 steps and at most 128 pairs per source episode. This selects ; only its three seeds are evaluated on the locked test set. Appendices~ app:split -- app:selection give the split and training details. Controls. The predefined frozen-native baseline uses the least confident action dimension, . Because trains mean-top confidence, we also evaluate both policies with the same min-top summary. Three outcome-supervised probes on frozen 4096-dimensional representations preserve the controller: P-LINEAR (sigmoid linear readout, 4,097 parameters), P-STATIC (width-128 MLP), and P-TEMPORAL (width-128 MLP with a trailing 25-step representation mean). These controlled probes do not reimplement prior monitoring systems. Evaluation. AUROC ranks failures above successes (0.5 is chance). Joint AUROC averages landmark scores at 130 and 260 steps; at 260 only still-active trajectories are evaluated, so landmark populations differ. We report TSR and means and sample SD across adaptation seeds. Paired, task-stratified bootstrap intervals resample held-out configurations within task, preserving comparator pairing. They quantify resampling uncertainty on this deterministic test grid, not real-robot variability. Results and discussion sec:results Confidence can be shaped. Frozen min-top confidence obtains joint AUROC 0.4485, and supervised frozen-feature probes obtain 0.6146--0.6436 (Table~ tab:main_results ). reaches . Its unchanged controller makes it an important practical comparator. Full intervals and seed results appear in Appendices~ app:seed_results and~ app:uncertainty . title: Learning from an Imitable Teacher: Competition Solution for the MetaFine Challenge
comment: 2026 CoRL MetaFine Open Competition 2nd place solution
summary: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.
full_text: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher imitable raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32 more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 are large pretrained policies that follow varied instructions and can be fine-tuned to new tasks, but precision remains hard: the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, a fine-tuned VLA, reports clumsy manipulation as its dominant failure~ larchenko2025task . Precise imitation is sensitive to the demonstrations: errors compound into unseen states~ ross2011reduction , and policies may copy spurious cues~ de2019causal,geirhos2020shortcut . Noise injection~ laskey2017dart and interactive corrections~ kelly2019hg widen the states covered, yet successful demonstrations still differ in how well a policy learns from them~ mandlekar2021matters,belkhale2023data . The MetaFine Open Competition provides a diagnostic benchmark for this problem along the three dimensions of MetaFine~ xu2026beyond : understanding, perception and controlled behavior~ xu2026beyond . In a ManiSkill3-based simulator~ tao2025demonstrating , a Franka arm with a base and a hand camera follows instructions to grasp a bottle by its cap or body (T1), move a mug left, right or forward (T2), toggle the red or blue switch (T3), put one cube into the left box and the rest into the right (T4), or insert a letter peg (C, o, R, L) into its slot with about 4\,mm of clearance (T5). A task's score averages Perception (P: area under the success curve over camera and lighting perturbations), Understanding (U: success rate over 20 fixed seeds per instruction variant) and Behavior (B: success or stage progress). The organizers' baseline~ black2024pi_0 , fine-tuned per task on 200--400 planner demonstrations, scores 0.430 (Table~ tab:main ). In this report, we examine how far small task-specific policies (Sec.~ sec:arch ) can go when the effort goes into the data. All training data come from a privileged scripted teacher and its corrections of the student (Sec.~ sec:data ). We made this teacher imitable, since one that always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly through pauses, fixed habits and abrupt moves. This took T5 from 0.44 to 0.88 and T3 from 0.92 to 1.00 officially, and we placed second among 16 teams with 0.947 (Sec.~ sec:exp ). Architecture sec:arch As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview (bottom), our system separates reading the instruction from acting on it. A sentence encoder Instruction classifier (all-MiniLM-L6-v2~ wang2020minilm, reimers2019sentence ) with a linear head per task maps the instruction to a variant index, so the control networks see no language. Each task has one action-chunking transformer (ACT)~ zhao2023learning (Visuomotor policy) without the CVAE, following the standard design: an ImageNet-initialized ResNet-18~ he2016deep , with FiLM~ perez2018film on the variant, turns the hand image into tokens, and a transformer (4+4 layers, ) maps them, with joint-position and variant tokens, to 32 actions (7 joint deltas, gripper), executing 8. Fine-tuned on paraphrases from a small grammar per task with negations (``not the cap''), distractors, attribute binding and typos, the classifier reads all 14 official instructions and 226 held-out paraphrases correctly. For training, two extra heads (dashed box in Fig.~ fig:overview ) help the policy use the variant: one regresses object states, and the other predicts the instructed object's position and feeds the decoder. For 30 of the samples we feed another variant code and supervise only this goal head, with that variant's object position. Without the goal head, our T3 policy ignored the variant (blue episodes pushed the red switch) and solved 30 of 40 clean episodes, against 78 of 80 with it on the same data. Dataset sec:data Teacher and Student Model Consider a memoryless student that observes , the hand image, the joint positions and the variant, and executes 8 of its 32 predicted actions before observing again (Sec.~ sec:arch ). Its training data come from a privileged teacher that runs scripted routines (motion primitives with inverse kinematics) with perception answered from the simulator state , keeping its survey pose and close looks so that the target stays in the hand camera's view, a requirement shared with image-based visual servoing~ zhang2023occlusion . The teacher provides two kinds of data. Plain demonstrations randomize the ambient light, inject DART noise~ laskey2017dart into the executed actions while recording clean labels, continue briefly after success so that the student learns to stay put, and cover every seed under every variant. The teacher can also stage an error, such as a misaligned descent, whose frames are masked from the loss, followed by a labelled recovery. Takeovers follow HG-DAgger~ kelly2019hg, ross2011reduction : a trained student drives until a trigger fires (it stalls, closes on nothing, nears the board, ), after which the teacher resumes and only its steps are recorded. We keep only successful episodes, and training seeds are disjoint from evaluation seeds. Making the Teacher Imitable sec:imitable Success alone does not make a teacher imitable. We call the teacher imitable if (i) its action is a stable function of , so that states the student cannot tell apart receive the same action, and (ii) its margins exceed the student's errors, so that its behavior still succeeds from the states the student reaches. We traced each student failure to a violated condition and fixed it in the teacher, never at run time. Pauses become stalls. The teacher's settling waits lasted up to 13--25 steps, longer than the student's 8-step horizon. A student stopped in such a state sees a frame labelled ``hold'', predicts ``hold'' again and never leaves, which violates condition~(i). Action chunking was introduced partly to cope with such pauses~ zhao2023learning , and single-step policies are known to get stuck on idle actions~ chi2025diffusion . Here, chunking did not prevent it. One T5 network scored 0 of 240, typically holding the seated peg until the time limit, as the teacher held a seated peg still for 10--15 steps before opening. Capping waits at 3 steps, releasing as soon as the peg is home and closing the fingers while moving removed the stalls, which also caused about a third of the T3 failures and 10 of 400 T1 episodes. Fixed habits become shortcuts. The T3 teacher always began its push 4\,cm above the contact point. On the teacher's own states, a 4\,cm stroke and a push to the switch are indistinguishable, so the student learned the stroke, a case of causal confusion~ de2019causal or shortcut learning~ geirhos2020shortcut . It then turned a 10\,mm hover error into an 11\,mm push error and missed the official contact gate, which the teacher itself cleared by only 4\,mm (condition~(ii)). Drawing the pre-push distance from 2.5--7\,cm, with up to 4\,mm of lateral jitter, made the student read the push height from the image. Together with capped waits, this raised T3 from 439 to 497 of 500 paired local episodes (McNemar ) and from 0.919 to 1.000 officially, although the new data set was also twice as large. Unseen errors leave no recovery. The T5 teacher grasped exactly where it planned and never showed a peg held off-centre, whereas the student's grasps landed a few millimetres along the stroke, so it pressed the peg 6--13\,mm off a slot with 4\,mm of clearance (condition~(ii)). The revised teacher jitters its grasp by up to 6\,mm, seats the peg from its true in-hand pose and stages misaligned descents with recoveries, and takeovers add the errors the student actually makes. These corrections must agree with the plain demonstrations (condition~(i)): our takeovers first rose 2\,cm above the grasp, whereas demonstrations descend directly, and t5 f hovered 1.5--2\,cm above the grasp, where the two balance, in 48 of its 83 failures on fresh seeds. Resuming from the current height, with one more takeover round, cut never-grasped failures from 88 to 11 in 480 fresh episodes. Abrupt transitions amplify errors. The teacher opened the gripper at once, but the student released a step early and slightly off, so the jolt turned the o by 12--15 , beyond the 10 tolerance (condition~(ii)). Opening over 8 steps raised local o success from 0.81 to 0.92, but not the official score (Sec.~ sec:eval ). Experiments sec:exp Implementation Details We train all networks with AdamW (learning rate , for the backbone) and batch size 64. Arm actions use an L1 loss and the gripper cross-entropy, except in T5, where the teacher pre-shapes the fingers and the gripper is regressed with L1. We augment images with random shifts of up to 8\,px~ kostrikov2020image and use weight averaging. At test time only the two networks run on the allowed observations. The teacher, simulator state and motion primitives serve only to generate data, and the only external weights are ImageNet and MiniLM initializations. Main Results sec:eval Table~ tab:main compares our official results with the organizers' baseline. The gap grows with the precision a task requires: on T2, moving a mug, the baseline already reaches 0.93, whereas we raise T4 from 0.33 to 0.99 and T5, the hardest task, from 0.04 to 0.88. Table~ tab:t5 traces how T5 got there. The first network, trained on 1,541 plain demonstrations, solved only 13 of 80 local episodes. Each later version changed what the teacher showed (Sec.~ sec:imitable ) and added takeovers from the latest student, and the gains followed these changes rather than the amount of data: t5 f was trained on 6 fewer episodes than t5 c yet solved 61 instead of 34, and from t5 c to t5 g the official score nearly doubled (0.442 to 0.817) with 32 more episodes and the same network. Local and official numbers differ, however. Official scores were typically 0.03--0.08 below our local estimates, and with 20 fixed seeds per variant one T1 episode moves the overall score by 0.003; even identical T1 weights scored 0.894 and then 0.888, as T1 rendering is not bit-reproducible. Two changes that won paired local tests, a T1 network (45 vs.\ 19 discordant episodes, ) and the T5 release fix (69 vs.\ 47, ), scored slightly lower officially (0.867 vs.\ 0.894 and 0.869 vs.\ 0.875), so our final submission keeps the earlier networks. Conclusion sec:conclusion In this report, we presented our solution to the MetaFine Open Competition: one small policy per task, trained entirely on data from a privileged scripted teacher. The difficulty lay in millimetre-scale execution rather than in language or perception, and it responded to the data rather than the network: making the teacher imitable raised T5 from 0.44 to 0.88 and T3 from 0.92 to 1.00 officially. title: PREM: Prediction-Regulated Memory for Robot Manipulation
summary: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.

[1] [WEIDI: #1] Introduction sec:introduction Robot manipulation often takes place under partial observability, where the current observation may not contain all information needed for action selection. Visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive readings can be insufficient when relevant motion or task state must be inferred from earlier interaction. The appropriate action can therefore depend on what the robot observed and did previously. This motivates integrating current observations with task-relevant interaction history. For example, intercepting a moving object requires information about its recent motion, even when the object's current position is visible. Similarly, restoring an earlier arrangement requires remembering where objects were previously located, even when the current scene looks similar to another state. In both cases, similar current observations may require different actions because they correspond to different visual histories. A manipulation policy therefore needs to combine current observations with task-relevant visual history. illustrates these complementary requirements. Existing approaches provide access to visual history in different ways. Multi-frame models process a window of recent observations li2023roboflamingo,li2025cronusvla , while memory-based policies store or summarize earlier evidence fang2025sam2act,shi2025memoryvla,huang2026chainvla . We focus on a recurrent visual-memory architecture that carries a fixed-size visual state across action decisions. However, retaining history alone is not sufficient. The visual state must preserve information relevant to future action generation, while incorporating new observations without discarding useful history. These requirements concern both what the visual state represents and how it is updated during interaction. Future prediction has been used to learn visual representations through self-supervised objectives~ han2019video,han2020memory . Recent VLA methods combine future prediction with action generation and memory~ sun2026vlajepa,shi2026memoryvlapp,yuan2026fastwam . Related video-understanding work also studies recognizing, localizing, and anticipating unintentional actions~ epstein2020oops . Future prediction provides a natural way to address both requirements. During training, predicting subsequent visual features encourages the visual state to retain information useful for anticipating interaction dynamics. The prediction targets come directly from future observations, providing temporal supervision without additional annotations. During execution, the discrepancy between predicted and observed visual features can reveal where the current visual state is insufficient. This motivates using action-conditioned future prediction not only to supervise memory learning, but also to guide visual-state updating. This leads to our central question: how can action-conditioned future prediction guide both memory learning and visual-state updating for robot manipulation? We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and visual-state updating in VLA policies. PREM couples a recurrent visual-memory (RVM) architecture with an action-conditioned predictor. The RVM architecture maintains a fixed-size visual state across action decisions. The policy, RVM architecture, and predictor are jointly trained with action and prediction objectives. The prediction objective provides temporal supervision for memory learning, while the discrepancy between prediction and observation provides feedback for visual-state updating. At each replanning decision, PREM compares the current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision. The spatially normalized prediction discrepancy regulates how much of the candidate visual-state update is incorporated at each spatial location. The updated visual state is then used as temporal context for action generation together with the current observation. The policy's latent action representation is also provided to the predictor, which predicts the visual features of the next replanning observation. During training, the prediction objective supervises memory learning through the predictor's visual-state input. During execution, the prediction is cached until the corresponding observation arrives and then provides the reference for the next visual-state update. In this way, PREM uses the same future-prediction mechanism to learn the visual state and to regulate how it changes over time. Our evaluation follows the two temporal requirements in . We test dynamic manipulation on DOMINO and memory-dependent manipulation on RMBench M(1). Built on , PREM improves average success rate from 9.63 to 20.74 on DOMINO and from 14.4 to 83.8 on RMBench M(1). Component ablations on DOMINO show performance gains from both predictive supervision for memory learning and prediction-regulated visual-state updating. Additional evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7\,ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU. Method sec:method PREM couples an action-conditioned predictor with a recurrent visual-memory (RVM) architecture.
