title: STEER: Route-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-language action (VLA) models excel for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet their tendency to over-invoke chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning mirrors a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as deliberate reasoning can slow or mislead human judgment in routine tasks, excessive CoT in VLA incurs unnecessary compute overhead and can paradoxically degrade planning performance. Recent research tackles this via adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity by selectively triggering CoT for complex scenes while responding directly to routine ones. While prior adaptive methods rely on implicit adaptation, recent work shows that explicitly optimizing the route between CoT and direct responses yields superior performance, assuming scene-difficulty annotations which are labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity. We explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved without any scene-difficulty labeling. We introduce STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring two key components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 demonstrate that STEER is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in both planning quality and the Pareto front of inference efficiency.
full_text: Vision-language action (VLA) models excel for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet their tendency to over-invoke chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning mirrors a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as deliberate reasoning can slow or mislead human judgment in routine tasks, excessive CoT in VLA incurs unnecessary compute overhead and can paradoxically degrade planning performance. Recent research tackles this via adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity by selectively triggering CoT for complex scenes while responding directly to routine ones. While prior adaptive methods rely on implicit adaptation, recent work shows that explicitly optimizing the route between CoT and direct responses yields superior performance, assuming scene-difficulty annotations which are labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity. We explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved without any scene-difficulty labeling. We introduce STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring two key components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 demonstrate that STEER is in both planning quality and the Pareto front of inference efficiency. Introduction End-to-end autonomous driving has been significantly advanced by vision-language action (VLA) models, which directly map multimodal observations to driving behaviors~ hu2023planning,jiang2023vad,hwang2024emma,zhou2025autovla . With large-scale multimodal pretraining, these models introduce stronger semantic grounding and language-based scene understanding into trajectory generation, making it natural to incorporate explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning into the driving-planning process~ hwang2024emma,yuan2025autodrive,zhang2026minddriverintroducingprogressivemultimodal,zeng2025futuresightdrive . Such reasoning is particularly valuable in scenarios that require multi-step inference, such as negotiating unprotected intersections, handling dense merges, or reacting to partially occluded hazards. However, applying CoT reasoning uniformly to every driving scene is far from ideal, a pattern reminiscent of a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as an experienced driver does not consciously deliberate at every familiar junction, forcing explicit reasoning in routine situations can slow down responses, incur unnecessary compute overhead, and paradoxically degrade planning performance~ luo2025adathinkdrive,yang2025r . These costs are especially concerning in safety-critical autonomous driving, where both decision quality and response efficiency are essential. The key challenge, therefore, is not merely how to reason, but when explicit reasoning should be invoked. Recent research has begun to address this challenge through adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity. Existing approaches, however, differ substantially in how route selection is handled. AutoVLA~ zhou2025autovla is the first work to integrate CoT into autonomous driving, but it does not explicitly optimize the route between reasoning and direct response. AdaThinkDrive~ luo2025adathinkdrive further shows that explicitly optimizing this route yields superior performance, suggesting that route selection itself is a critical ingredient for adaptive CoT. However, current explicit-routing approaches typically rely on scene-difficulty annotations to supervise route selection. Such supervision is labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity; more importantly, perceived scene difficulty is not always aligned with the actual utility of reasoning. A scene that appears visually crowded may still admit a direct response, while a seemingly simple scene may require nontrivial inference before a safe action can be made. Motivated by this insight, we explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved entirely without scene-difficulty labeling. We propose STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation approach , built within the VLA paradigm. STEER optimizes the routing policy through two key reinforcement learning (RL) components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. By contrasting the outcomes across different routes under the same prompt, STEER encourages the model to select the route that yields the highest reward. To prevent the model from prematurely collapsing into the shorter direct response, we introduce route-balanced supervised fine-tuning to preserve a balanced dual-route prior. Our contributions are: (i) We identify overthinking as a key challenge in VLA-based autonomous driving and, for the first time, explore whether , without any scene-difficulty annotations. (ii) We propose STEER , a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring route-balanced supervised fine-tuning to preserve dual-route capabilities, routing uncertainty-aware rollout to align sampling diversity with model uncertainty, and cross-route advantage credit assignment to reinforce optimal routing decisions directly from environmental rewards, eliminating the reliance on scene-difficulty labels. (iii) We achieve on NAVSIM v1/v2, consistently improving planning quality, routing quality, and pushing the Pareto front of inference efficiency over both fixed-routing and previous adaptive reasoning alternatives. Related work sec:related Vision-language action models for autonomous driving. End-to-end autonomous driving has evolved significantly from modular pipelines~ hu2023planning,jiang2023vad to unified architectures. Recently, Vision-language Models (VLMs) have been introduced to bridge the gap between semantic reasoning and physical actions~ radford2021learning,bai2025qwen25vltechnicalreport . Current VLM-based driving approaches broadly fall into two paradigms. The first paradigm utilizes VLMs for scene understanding or high-level reasoning to produce meta-actions that guide downstream planners~ tian2024drivevlm,liao2025diffusiondrive,li2026sgdrivescenetogoalhierarchicalworld . Although this facilitates semantic integration, it prevents full end-to-end optimization. The second paradigm, VLA models, directly integrates VLMs with action generation to predict final driving trajectories autoregressively~ hwang2024emma,zhou2025autovla,li2026mtdrive . Our work builds upon this end-to-end VLA paradigm. However, rather than solely focusing on how to generate trajectories, we address a critical internal decision process: optimizing when the model should invoke explicit reasoning before committing to an action. Adaptive reasoning in autonomous driving. With the rise of long CoT reasoning in large language models, such as DeepSeek-R1~ guo2025deepseek and OpenAI o1~ jaech2024openai , explicit reasoning has become an effective tool for complex decision-making. In autonomous driving, methods such as EMMA~ hwang2024emma show that domain-specific CoT can improve trajectory prediction. However, reasoning is not universally beneficial: in routine driving scenes, forcing CoT can increase latency, introduce unnecessary verbosity, and even degrade planning quality~ luo2025adathinkdrive,yang2025r . This has motivated adaptive reasoning, where the core challenge is to decide when explicit deliberation is needed. AutoVLA~ zhou2025autovla addresses this through implicit adaptation: it mainly optimizes trajectory quality with sequence-level reinforcement learning, where supervision is applied to the overall response rather than to route selection itself. AdaThinkDrive~ luo2025adathinkdrive moves one step further by explicitly supervising routing: it defines scene complexity for route selection and adds a dedicated routing reward to directly optimize the choice between CoT reasoning and direct response. It further shows that explicit route optimization outperforms implicit adaptation. The limitation, however, is that such supervision depends on scene-complexity annotation, which is labor-intensive, difficult to scale, and inherently subjective. Our work addresses this limitation by studying explicit adaptive reasoning for autonomous driving. Method sec:method Model formulation. To address overthinking in VLA-based autonomous driving, we propose STEER, an adaptive reasoning framework that learns explicit routing between CoT reasoning and direct response from comparative task outcomes without scene-complexity labels. We instantiate STEER on top of an autoregressive vision-language model for end-to-end driving, e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-8B~ bai2025qwen25vltechnicalreport . Given a multimodal driving prompt , the model generates a textual response that specifies the future ego trajectory. To explicitly model whether the model should deliberate or respond immediately, we formulate the first step as a discrete routing decision , corresponding to two valid response formats: [leftmargin=*] Reasoning: <think> reasoning </think> <answer> trajectory </answer> Direct responding: <answer> trajectory </answer> The response distribution is then factorized accordingly as The first term determines which route to take, serving as an explicit routing policy, while the second factor generates the driving trajectories conditioned on the selected route. Model training. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:main_figure , STEER follows a three-stage training pipeline: (1) driving-centric pretraining to adapt the base model to driving tasks (see Appendix~ app:pretrain for details), (2) route-balanced supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preserve the model's prior to execute both responding routes (Section~ sec:sft ), and (3) route-aware policy optimization to optimize the routing policy (Section~ sec:route_aware_po ). Stage 2: Route-balanced supervised fine-tuning sec:sft Before RL can discover when explicit reasoning is beneficial, the model must first retain the capacity to execute both valid response routes. However, a vanilla SFT~ ouyang2022training objective is insufficient for this purpose. Because the direct route is substantially shorter than the reasoning route, standard teacher forcing introduces a strong optimization bias toward the shorter sequence. This length imbalance causes the model to prematurely collapse into the direct response, suppressing its reasoning ability before policy optimization even begins. To prevent this early collapse, we introduce route-balanced supervised fine-tuning. For each prompt , we provide both a reasoning-route target and a direct-route target , and optimize the model using a unified loss function: Here, denotes the route-indicating initial token corresponding to route , and balances the two routes ( , ). The sequence denotes the continuation after , which remains in the autoregressive prefix for every continuation token. This objective addresses the pitfalls of vanilla SFT through two key designs: (1) Routing calibration: The first term explicitly regularizes the initial decision step toward a uniform distribution, ensuring the model maintains non-trivial support for both routes. (2) Length normalization: The second term divides the next-token loss by the route-specific length . This prevents the optimization gradients from being skewed by the massive length disparity, ensuring the shorter direct route is not treated as an optimization shortcut. title: SparseWAM: Driving World-Action Models are Worth 16 Register Tokens
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) transfer scene-dynamics priors to planning by jointly forecasting future scenes and ego trajectories. However, WAMs built on video generators must generate dense future videos at inference, incurring prohibitive latency, while efficient variants discard the world branch at deployment and thus forgo test-time imagination. Even when dense video latents are replaced with patch-level DINO or JEPA features, these representations still involve long token sequences and encode decision-irrelevant information. We therefore propose SparseWAM, which forecasts in a sparse register space of only 16 tokens per frame, compressed from frozen DINOv2 features and shaped by joint planning-and-scoring pretraining to concentrate decision-relevant information. Within this space, SparseWAM employs a modality-decoupled Mixture-of-Transformers with a causal attention mask that lets action tokens condition on imagined future registers, retaining explicit imagine-then-act reasoning at deployment. Its compactness further enables low-cost multimodal sampling. As a result, our SparseWAM achieves 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 39.6 on NavHard at only 164 ms latency, roughly 1/5 that of DriveVA, demonstrating the efficiency of the sparse register space. Code will be released upon acceptance.
full_text: Introduction Autonomous driving is inherently interactive, requiring not only perception and understanding of the current scene but also anticipation of surrounding agents' behavior for safe and efficient planning. This requirement has motivated a growing family of World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly model future scene evolution and trajectory planning pwm, epona, eponav2, driveva, simwam, metis, drivelaw . Because future-frame prediction provides dense, annotation-free supervision that scales with raw driving logs, these models can transfer scene-dynamics priors to planning, improving interactive reasoning and generalization, and therefore offer a compelling alternative to conventional end-to-end methods uniad, vad, transfuser, hydra-mdp, diffusiondrive and Vision-Language-Action models emma, opendrivevla . Yet realizing this promise through explicit future prediction introduces a fundamental tension between imagination and efficiency. Inspired by the success of DreamZero in embodied intelligence dreamzero , recent driving WAMs build upon pretrained video generators such as Wan2.2-5B wan . They jointly denoise future video latents and action tokens within a unified generative process, thereby transferring the scene-dynamics priors acquired during video pretraining to trajectory planning driveva, drivewam . While this design achieves strong performance in single-trajectory planning, it requires future videos to be explicitly generated at inference time, resulting in substantial latency that hinders practical on-vehicle deployment. More recent approaches, including SimWAM simwam and Metis metis , improve efficiency by using structured attention masks to decouple action prediction from future-video generation. This allows the video-generation branch to be removed during inference. Their efficiency design, however, fundamentally changes the role of the world model. Rather than enabling the deployed policy to imagine possible futures before acting, it serves primarily as a source of representation shaping and auxiliary supervision during training. The key may therefore lie not in abandoning test-time forecasting, but in reconsidering what the model is asked to predict. When anticipating how a traffic scene may evolve, human drivers do not reason equally about every visible region. Static background elements such as the sky and roadside buildings generally receive little attention, whereas vehicles, pedestrians, and other entities that may affect the driving decision become the focus of anticipation. Dense future-video prediction does not make this distinction. It requires the model to reconstruct the entire visual scene, devoting substantial capacity and computation to appearance details that have limited relevance to planning. As a result, the dynamics most consequential for decision-making must compete with largely irrelevant visual content for modeling capacity and learning signals. Recent WAMs attempt to reduce this redundancy by predicting future representations alongside action trajectories in semantic latent spaces learned by models such as DINO and JEPA dinov2, vjepa2 . These representations offer more semantically meaningful prediction targets than pixels or VAE latents~ wan , but they do not fully resolve the underlying problem. Their patch-level token sequences can be comparable to, or even longer than, those of VAE latents, so forecasting them at inference time remains computationally demanding. More fundamentally, representations learned through generic visual pretraining are optimized to capture broadly useful visual semantics rather than the particular aspects of a scene that matter for driving decisions. They may therefore continue to encode background appearance and other variations that are visually salient but behaviorally irrelevant. These limitations point to a more fundamental question. r 0.42 SparseWAM achieves the best PDMS with the lowest latency compared to WAM planners on NAVSIM. fig:pdms-latency We address this challenge by learning a decision-aligned sparse register space with only 16 tokens per frame. Learnable register tokens registers compress the dense feature maps produced by a frozen DINOv2 encoder dinov2 into a compact representation, which is further shaped through joint planning-and-scoring pretraining. The planning objective encourages the registers to retain scene information that informs trajectory prediction, while the scoring objective complements it by preserving safety-critical cues that may not directly determine the nominal trajectory but remain essential for evaluating its consequences. The resulting registers therefore serve not merely as a compressed visual representation, but as a compact decision-oriented abstraction of the driving scene. We examine this property through counterfactual scene-editing probes that remove lead vehicles, insert pedestrians, or alter weather and illumination. The learned representation responds strongly to interventions that change driving decisions while remaining comparatively insensitive to appearance variations that leave those decisions unchanged. This compact representation makes it possible to preserve explicit test-time imagination without incurring the cost of dense video or feature prediction. Building on it, we introduce SparseWAM, a lightweight Mixture-of-Transformers denoiser mot that uses rectified flow rectflow, flow_matching to model future registers together with ego trajectories. Its modality-specific transformer branches reduce interference between world prediction and action generation while still allowing the two processes to exchange information. More importantly, we impose a causal attention structure that prevents future registers from attending to action tokens, while allowing action tokens to condition on denoised future registers. SparseWAM consequently learns a directed generative process in which it first anticipates how the scene may evolve and then plans in light of that imagined future. Unlike approaches that remove world prediction for efficiency, SparseWAM retains explicit imagine-then-act reasoning in the deployed policy. This efficiency extends naturally to multimodal planning. With only 16 tokens per future frame, SparseWAM can efficiently generate diverse future–trajectory pairs by denoising multiple independent noise samples. As shown in Fig.~ fig:pdms-latency , it achieves a state-of-the-art PDMS of 92.6 with only 164 ms latency, outperforming the recent DriveVA (90.9 PDMS, 829 ms) with 1/5 inference latency. Even under single-mode inference, SparseWAM delivers performance comparable to or better than many existing single-trajectory WAMs, with a latency of just 122 ms. Rather than trading imagination for efficiency, SparseWAM makes explicit future reasoning both multimodal and practical. Our contributions are: (i) We construct a driving-oriented sparse register space obtained through joint planning-and-scoring pretraining, and design counterfactual scene-editing probes that verify its sensitivity is concentrated on decision-relevant scene elements rather than appearance-related nuisance factors. (ii) We develop a WAM framework operating in the proposed sparse register latent space, which adopts an MoT architecture that prevents cross-modal contamination and employs a causal attention mask. (iii) Experiments across multiple NAVSIM benchmarks show that SparseWAM attains PDMS at lower latency, surpassing state-of-the-art WAMs, and remains highly competitive even under the single-mode setting, demonstrating the efficiency of the method. Related Work End-to-End Autonomous Driving End-to-end autonomous driving has progressed along two complementary lines. Classical sensor-to-planner pipelines map multi-sensor observations to trajectories through unified differentiable stacks~ transfuser, ST-P3,uniad,vad,hydra-mdp,vadv2,UAD, diffusiondrive,goalflow,flowad , typically optimizing planning with auxiliary perception or scoring objectives. In parallel, vision--language--action (VLA) models incorporate language instructions and semantic scene understanding before producing actions~ emma,DriveVLM,drivegpt4,lmdrive,Senna,omnidrive,opendrivevla . Both paradigms have substantially advanced closed-loop planning by mapping current observations or semantic instructions directly to actions. However, these approaches mainly infer actions from current observations, leaving future scene evolution implicitly modeled. This motivates WAMs, which explicitly incorporate predictive world dynamics into end-to-end planning. World-Action Models for Autonomous Driving WAMs jointly model future scene evolution and ego actions, and their effectiveness depends heavily on the choice of future representation. Video-based WAMs inherit dynamics priors from large-scale video models by coupling future visual prediction with action generation~ drivinggpt,epona,driveva,drivewam, drivelaw . These methods demonstrate the value of predictive world dynamics, but their dense video prediction objective inevitably requires modeling substantial visual details beyond those required for driving decisions. To reduce inference cost, SimWAM~ simwam and Metis~ metis use structured attention masks to decouple action prediction from generated futures, and DriveVLA-W0~ drivevlaw0 uses future-image prediction as training-time supervision with a lightweight action expert. These designs preserve representation learning during training but forgo test-time imagination. However, these approaches mainly reduce computation by avoiding future generation, rather than reconsidering what future information is necessary for planning. Latent-space WAMs instead forecast future scene states in a learned latent space~ latentwam,worlddrive,wajepa . These methods improve semantic abstraction, yet they still rely on visual representations that are not explicitly optimized for driving decisions. This motivates SparseWAM, which forecasts future dynamics in a driving-oriented latent space. Visual Representations for Autonomous Driving Self-supervised encoders such as DINOv2, V-JEPA, and MAE learn semantically rich features that transfer across vision tasks~ dinov2,vjepa2,mae . Driving-oriented methods further tailor such representations to the driving domain. Drive-JEPA adapts JEPA-style latent prediction to driving videos~ drivejepa , and DrivoR compresses multi-camera features into a small set of register tokens for trajectory generation and scoring~ drivor . However, these representations mainly serve as inputs to a current-timestep planner rather than as a space for forecasting future scene evolution. SparseWAM instead takes this compressed and driving-adapted space as the prediction target of future scene evolution. Preliminaries sec:preliminary Problem Formulation. title: A Reproducible Reconstruction and Evaluation Framework for Photorealistic Lunar Analog Scene Reconstruction Toward Digital Twins
summary: In this paper, we present a reconstruction pipeline that empirically quantifies the photorealistic scene reconstruction accuracy from both human-controlled and rover mast camera monocular feeds against physical ground truth as a function of Lunar traversal effects (e.g., motion blur, haze due to lofted regolith, trajectory bias, and sparse views). First, we benchmark six variants of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) across three Lunar analog scenes on held-out test sets using standard photometric metrics. We then establish how under traversal effects, this test-set-specific Novel View Synthesis (NVS) performance does not proportionally scale to the same photometric metrics in the reconstructed DTs. Our results quantify that splat training metrics alone are insufficient predictors of Cross-Reconstruction Photorealistic NVS Fidelity (CRPNVS), and that factors such as rover trajectory bias and geometric scene coverage play a critical role in determining the photorealistic quality of the reconstructed scenes targeting Lunar analog Digital Twins. Additionally, we pilot study Coverage Score ($S_c$), a geometry-based diagnostic derived from COLMAP poses and point cloud structure that provides a meaningful heuristic about the highest achievable CRPNVS structural fidelity, independently of splat training performance in the absence of a human-controlled reference. These findings establish a standardized, human control-referenced evaluation pipeline for photorealistic scene reconstruction for Lunar-analog Digital Twin development and future planetary exploration. Code and project page: https://rose-lab-admin.github.io/rose-lunar-dt-rec

Introduction Collecting robot point-of-view (PoV) data from the target or extremely similar environments is crucial for training and validating vision-based algorithms or policies. However, doing so for extraterrestrial missions poses significant challenges as the target venues such as Lunar terrains are simply not as accessible as their terrestrial counterparts. Contemporary methods prevalent in large volumes of literature indicate three approaches for addressing this obstacle via: (1) natural analog environments vayugundla2018datasets,arm2023scientific , (2) artificial surface simulator testbed facilities knapmeyer2025first and (3) high fidelity virtual testbeds, such as Digital Twins (DTs) richard2024omnilrs . Disregarding the sim2real gap momentarily, DTs have recently emerged as a potential alternative in circumventing the challenges of physical analog environments and testbed facilities (e.g., the replication and manipulation of environmental variables such as gravity, lighting, wind speed, and granular media, and the requirement of a physical robot). Such advantages have made DTs a convenient source of synthetic training data for image-based algorithms. However, considering the sim2real gap, purely synthetic data might relate very poorly to real-world scenes hao2024synthetic,karoly2023increasing . Therefore, photorealistic Lunar-analog scene reconstructions targeting Digital Twins need to have a strong basis from the target physical environment (the input fidelity criterion), which dictates photorealism of the synthetic data derived from these reconstructions (the output fidelity criterion). Furthermore, these criteria need to be not only qualified but also quantified by relevant metrics such as Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) to provide insight into the reliability of the DT in question for developing robust vision algorithms. However, this reconstruction and validation practice that quantifies ground truth vs photorealistic scene reconstruction toward Lunar-analog Digital Twins using direct photometric metrics under Lunar traversal effects remains largely absent in available research, as will be discussed in Related Works. Related Works A significant volume of literature is aimed at collecting Lunar-analog data without pursuing photorealistic reconstruction. For example, in vayugundla2018datasets , the authors only collect and present visual and sensor data on Mount Etna (Natural Lunar analog). From artificial testbeds, the POLAR dataset wong2017polar provides stereo imagery from NASA Ames, SPICE-HL3 rodriguez2026spice covers stereo, monochrome, and single‑photon avalanche diode modalities from LunaLab at the University of Luxembourg. The authors in martens2024synthetic offer RGB and event-camera streams from Exterres Lab. None of these expands toward photorealistic reconstruction or reports a photometric assessment of their visual data. Another prominent group addresses scene reconstruction but stops short of direct photometric evaluation. For instance, the authors in hansen2024polar extend the POLAR dataset to COLMAP-based colmap dense reconstruction under simulated Lunar light but report only pixel-level reconstruction error, not photometric metrics. POLAR-Sim chen2025polar generates high-fidelity meshes with photometric texturing, yet only qualitatively claims visual consistency. OmniLRS richard2024omnilrs evaluates photorealism through a downstream rock segmentation performance, which is not a direct photometric measurement. Additionally, some textures are sourced outside the target environment, potentially reducing true environmental accuracy. There has been a very recent surge in photorealistic Lunar scene reconstruction using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233d and its variations, most of which do report photometric metrics. For example, the authors in zhang20253d benchmark Gaussian Splat variants on SPICE-HL3 in terms of SSIM, PSNR and LPIPS on held-out test sets. In prosvetov2025illuminating , the authors compare photogrammetry, NeRF, and Gaussian Splatting across SPICE-HL3, NASA LOLA, and synthetic data in terms of similar photometric metrics. The study in casadesus2026semantic pursues large-scale Lunar mapping via real-time 3DGS fused with stereo depth on synthetic LuPNT data. However, these approaches have three distinct flaws: (1) leveraging held-out test-set metrics that might inflate with trajectory bias, resulting in poor generalization across the entire reconstruction; (2) not discussing change in method rankings under Lunar-traversal effects; and (3) not quantifying coverage sparsity affecting photorealistic performance. Research Gaps From the explored literature, five gaps are identified: Most works either omit photorealistic Lunar-scene reconstruction for DTs entirely or claim photorealism without direct photometric measurement against a physical ground truth (GT). Surveyed studies using photometric metrics depend solely on held-out test images during training. However, under traversal effects these metrics do not relate to Novel-View-Synthesis (NVS) quality at all viewpoints (Fig. fig1:nvs_issue ). For example, if the camera trajectory is mostly linear (i.e. trajectory bias), most images are zoomed in/out versions of each other, which causes model overfitting. In such cases, training metrics alone are unreliable indicators of true photorealistic reconstruction fidelity. Although standard practice of terrestrial DT reconstruction involves human-controlled data, in frontier space exploration where this control is limited, rover data (autonomous or teleoperated) might be the only source to quantify for photoreal scene reconstruction. No work in the surveyed literature quantifies the photorealistic reconstruction gap between human-controlled input and rover-derived imagery which undergoes traversal effects against a physical ground truth. Studies acknowledging coverage sparsity as a degradation factor in Lunar scene reconstruction do not quantify coverage levels affecting the metrics, making it difficult to pre-diagnose reconstruction fidelity from a given dataset. No reproducible reconstruction and evaluation framework exists in the surveyed literature that discusses reconstruction fidelity as a function of the nuances identified above. Contributions The primary contribution of this paper is a reproducible, highly photorealistic scene reconstruction and validation pipeline that guides the readers from data collection to obtaining simulation-ready Isaac Sim 5 assets for Lunar-analog DTs using only handheld monocular image captures. In addition, it replicates the same pipeline from rover-derived imagery and uses a cross-reconstruction photorealistic novel view synthesis (CRPNVS) assessment method to: (1) establish why under Lunar-traversal effects (trajectory bias, sparsity, dusty PoVs, and motion blur), training metrics from held-out test-sets are flawed fidelity indicators, (2) properly quantify scene-specific fidelity loss under the traversal effects, and (3) highlight expected and realistic rover-based fidelity loss against the proposed human-controlled reconstruction and ground truth. To compensate for datasets that have traversal effects but not a controlled or ground truth baseline, this work proposes, evaluates and justifies a Coverage Score, , derived purely from COLMAP~ colmap poses and point cloud geometry as a pre-diagnostic tool for expected photorealism from a given set of images. Method This section discusses the experimental settings, data collection pipelines, Gaussian Splat variants explored, the proposed coverage score, alignment methods and how they all come together to form a cross-reconstruction evaluation framework. Testbed and Sensors Testbed Experiments are conducted on the Mines Lunar Surface Simulator (MLSS) at the Colorado School of Mines. It is a Lunar-regolith simulant testbed designed to simulate Lunar highland regions using CSM-LHT-T type simulant~ jehn2025implications . The testbed supports configurable terrain features including mounds, craters, and rocks with a set of ArUco markers fixed to its walls. Within the MLSS, each experiment is conducted over a defined test zone, the area of which vary between experimental configurations. For highly dusty scenes (Rover-Scene 3), four additional AprilTags are placed closer to the test zone. These fiducial markers are used for splat alignment across modalities, rover localization, and scale error estimation. Sensors Data Collection Two sensors are used for collecting image data: human-control uses a stabilized GoPro Hero~8 camera that captures images at 4K resolution and 60~FPS. It follows a ``N-shaped'' sweep motion around the test zone to achieve optimal vertical and horizontal coverage, with significant emphasis on ground-level viewpoints. The camera experiences minimal to no rotation around its axes and always faces the front direction. For easier intuition, readers are encouraged to consider an imaginary wall surrounding the test-zone, where the camera trajectory paints a chain of the letter ``N'' on the outer surfaces of the wall. The bottom edge of ``N'' touches the ground plane as close as possible. This trajectory ensures good scene overlap while minimizing duplicate frames by avoiding forward-linear motion. The second sensor is an Intel RealSense D456 RGB-D camera, which serves as a fixed front-facing Mast Camera mounted on a rover, RoSey, based on Astrobotic's 6U CubeRover specification~ astrobotic_cuberover . The derived feed is pixels with an 8-bit color depth obtained at roughly 12 FPS. It is not confined to any fixed trajectory, rather teleoperated to get close inspections of regions of interest, such as craters and rocks. Scenes Three pairs of different Lunar scenarios are simulated. Scene~1 contains a diffused light environment relevant to indoor Lunar bases or construction sites. Scene~2 features low-horizon Lunar south-pole-like lighting with rocks and craters. Scene~3 shares the same lighting but introduces variation in crater locations. For the human-control, each scene is scanned as-is to provide clean physical ground truth PoVs. The reconstructions from the human-controlled scans are denoted as , where . title: Flap like a bat: Soft pneumatic wings for biomimetic ornithopters
summary: This paper describes the development of a bio-inspired ornithopter wing mechanism that uses soft pneumatic actuators, such as PneuNet structures, in place of revolute joints, inspired by the complicated kinematics of bat flight. The proposed design employs pneumatically driven air pockets within a flexible wing skeleton to achieve smooth, lifelike flapping motion. The actuation system is controlled by 3/2-way solenoid valves and an air pump, which manipulate airflow and actuator deformation. We demonstrate, using ANSYS FEA software, the bending behavior of the PneuNet actuators under varying pressures to inform the wing's structural design. The implementation of soft robotics in the flapping-wing system offers potential advantages over traditional mechanisms, such as reduced mechanical complexity, lower acoustic signatures, enhanced adaptability, and wing morphing. This work demonstrates the feasibility of replacing rigid revolute joints with compliant pneumatic actuators, enabling more agile, silent, and biomimetic aerial robots.
full_text: Flap like a bat: Soft pneumatic wings for biomimetic ornithopters , , , , , , The evolution of ornithopters, flying machines that mimic the flapping-wing motion of birds and bats, has spanned centuries due to the curiosity of how birds and bats fly. Early conceptualizations on the biomechanical understandings of bird wings can be traced back to Leonardo da Vinci's 15th-century sketch (Fig.~ fig:daVinci ), where he envisioned flying wings powered by humans ~ daVinciCodex . Although never realized in his time, these ideas laid the philosophical foundation for biomimetic flight. The 19th and early 20th centuries saw many attempts at building mechanically flapping aircraft using wood, fabric, and crank mechanisms (Fig.~ fig:edwardFrost ). These models were large, inefficient, and incapable of long flight. Small-scale ornithopters could be made with the introduction of lightweight materials and electric motors in the mid-20th century. Researchers began using rotary motors with cam-driven or kinematic linkage-based flapping mechanisms, enabling basic yet repeatable wing motion (Fig.~ fig:batRetraction )~ batRetraction . Modern designs were further advanced with servo motors and microcontrollers, to make programmable wing kinematics much easier and improve flight stability~ wood2008insect . Despite these technological advances, traditional ornithopters relied solely on rigid mechanical components, such as revolute joints and fixed kinematic linkages. These systems introduce several issues: they produce significant mechanical noise due to oscillations and an unstable center of mass, are mechanically complex, and lack the compliance and adaptability seen in biological flyers~ majidi2013perspective . Among biological flyers, bats stand out due to their highly articulated wings supported by flexible membranes and independently actuated joints. This allows for better morphing of wing shape, surface area, and curvature during flight; these characteristics contribute to their exceptional maneuverability and energy efficiency~ ramezani2017bat,miyashita2021aerobat . To achieve these features, this study proposes a soft robotic approach: the use of PneuNet actuators~ shepherd2011multigait . These flexible pneumatic networks bend if we change the internal air pressure (Fig.~ fig:PneuNetdesign ), to replace traditional revolute mechanisms~ kumar2022towards . These actuators are lightweight, compliant, and silent, making them ideal candidates for any aerial vehicle with revolute mechanisms~ kumar2022towards . The flapping mechanism is actuated by a pneumatic control system comprising 3/2-way solenoid valves and an air pump that draws air from the external atmosphere. We used ANSYS to perform the FEA simulations to understand the deformation behavior of the actuators under different pressure conditions. The design and initial modeling are performed using open-source PneuNet tools from MIT's Soft Robotics Toolkit~ softroboticsMIT . The primary goals of this study are outlined below: To design a bat-inspired flapping wing integrated with soft pneumatic actuators To simulate actuator performance using FEA, and To evaluate the feasibility and advantages of soft actuation in flapping-wing flight systems. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Sec.~ Sec:LitR provides a state-of-the-art of the topic. The design and methodology are provided in Sec.~ Sec:DesignMethodlogy . Sec.~ Sec:SimulTest provides the ANSYS simulation steps and results. Lastly, closing remarks are noted in Sec.~ Sec:Closing . Literature Review Sec:LitR Recent advances in soft robotics and biomimetic design have enabled innovative approaches to the design of flapping-wing mechanisms. Traditional ornithopters mostly use rigid kinematic linkages and servo motors, which, while effective for basic flapping motion, lack the flexibility and lifelike articulation seen in bats. Key research by Ilievski et al.~ ilievski2011soft and Polygerinos et al.~ polygerinos2015modeling introduced and refined PneuNet actuators, showing that PneuNets can generate controlled, compliant motion using pneumatic inflation. These actuators have been widely used in soft grippers and walking robots, but have seen limited use in aerial systems. Soft robotics literature, such as Laschi and Cianchetti~ laschi2014soft and Chiang et al.~ chiang2021flapping , highlights the potential of soft actuated joints in adaptable, low-noise locomotion—principles that are perfect for winged mechanisms like ornithopter flight. In the study of bat-inspired aerial robots, notable examples include Bat Bot~ ramezani2017biomimetic (Fig.~ fig:bat-bot ) and AeroBat~ miyashita2021aerobat . These designs attempted to replicate bat wing motion using articulated mechanical systems, but still rely heavily on servo motors and rigid kinematic linkages (Fig.~ fig:bat-bot ). Bat wings have long arms and fingers attached to a flexible skin membrane (patagium). This helps achieve multiple degrees of freedom, allowing independent joint control and active wing morphing during flight. Bats extend their wings fully to generate lift during the downstroke, and then retract them close to their body during the upstroke to reduce drag (Fig.~ fig:batRetraction ). This improves agility, fine maneuvering, and aerodynamic efficiency in restricted environments with many obstacles. Despite these advantages, limited studies have been conducted on the morphing wing mechanism using pneumatic actuators. This study aims to assess the feasibility of using PneuNets in winged mechanisms to enhance realism, stealth, and maneuverability in aerial robotics. Design and Methodology Sec:DesignMethodlogy This section presents the design and methodology of the proposed pneumatically actuated air pockets integrated within a flexible wing skeleton for bat-inspired flight. Skeleton Structure The structural design of the ornithopter is based on the anatomy of a bat's wing. The upper parts of Fig.~ fig:Skelt are the arms and fingers of the wing. The lower links are the bat's legs, and a flexible material is used to connect the ends of the fingers and legs to the body, similar to the patagium in bats. This helps in increasing the area of the wing used to generate lift. All these joints in the structure are replaced with PneuNet actuators. These actuators independently control every angle between the joints. During the upstroke, all angles between the linkages will be minimized to reduce drag force, and during the downstroke, angles will be returned to normal to maximize the wing's area and increase lift by pushing more air. The manufacturing process is also designed to be practical. The skin can be produced using either the rolling or calendering method. The actuators themselves are made using stereolithography printing with silicone materials. The bones can be 3D-printed or manufactured using subtractive techniques, providing flexibility in the structure's design. PneuNet Actuator The PneuNet actuator is a soft robotic component that replicates biological joint movements by combining pneumatic actuation with hyper-elastic materials. The CAD model of the PneuNet actuator, as shown in Fig.~ fig:ourPrototype , consists of a series of cuboidal chambers aligned along a compliant base. In this design, the cuboidal chambers are hollow, allowing pressurized air to be injected. These chambers are fabricated using Silicone 40A, a hyper-elastic elastomer known for its high elasticity, low stiffness, and excellent flexibility. When air is introduced into the chambers, the silicone walls expand, enabling the structure to deform and perform mechanical work through pneumatic inflation. The actuator is equipped with a base layer fabricated from nylon fabric to direct this expansion into a predictable bending motion. This material, which is bio-compatible and optimized for medical and soft robotics applications, exhibits a moderate Young's modulus (1-2 GPa), significantly higher than that of Silicone 40A, but still flexible enough to allow bending while restricting in-plane stretch. Unlike rigid plastics, nylon fabric maintains compliance while acting as an inextensible constraint layer, preventing the base from elongating axially during pressurization. When the chambers are inflated, the silicone 40A walls tend to expand omnidirectionally due to their hyper-elastic nature. However, because the nylon fabric base resists axial elongation, the deformation is forced to propagate as a curved bending motion. This mechanism converts uniform chamber expansion into a directional bending of the entire actuator. The degree of bending can be finely controlled by regulating the input pressure, providing an adjustable actuation system well-suited for soft robotics. In this research, the PneuNet actuator serves as a replacement for conventional revolute joints in an ornithopter-inspired flapping mechanism. The actuators are connected to the artificial "bones" of the ornithopter's skeletal structure, functioning as compliant, soft joint actuators. Unlike traditional rigid mechanisms, this approach allows the wing to flap with bio-inspired smoothness and compliance, closely mimicking the joint motion of natural flyers such as bats. Also, both materials are compatible with accessible manufacturing processes, including 3D printing and molding, making this approach practical for research and development in soft robotics and bio-mimetic systems. Pneumatic System The PneuNet actuator serves as a flexible joint in place of traditional rigid components. It is built from soft elastomeric materials that expand and bend when air is pumped into them. These actuators are designed to bend in a controlled way, much like natural joints found in bats. Compressed air is supplied to the actuator via a solenoid valve, while a quick exhaust valve (QEV) is used for rapid deflation. When the ESP32 microcontroller switches on the solenoid valve, compressed air flows into the actuator (Fig.~ fig:Flowchat ). The internal pressure causes the actuator walls to expand, and because the base material resists stretching in one direction, the expansion results in a smooth bending motion. The actuator continues to bend until the air pressure is stopped. Once the solenoid is turned off, the input pressure drops suddenly. The QEV then quickly deflates the PneuNet actuator. This quick release allows the actuator to return to its original shape quickly. By controlling solenoid valves, the bending and relaxing of each joint can be controlled. This can help control the wing joints independently, mimicking the way real bats fly. The materials used are compatible with standard 3D printing and molding techniques, making this design approach efficient and accessible for bio-inspired robotic systems. The entire actuation system is based on pneumatic control rather than rigid mechanics. At the center of this system is a 3/2-way solenoid valve with an air input, an air output, and an exhaust. The input is connected to a diaphragm air pump that draws in ambient air. The Output sends compressed air to the PneuNet actuator and the Quick Exhaust Valve. The exhaust is connected to the atmosphere. This setup allows continuous air pumping, with flow controlled by switching the solenoid. When air is directed into the actuator, the QEV stays closed, and the actuator inflates. When the solenoid turns off, the inlet pressure drops, and the QEV opens immediately, venting the actuator. This rapid inflation-deflation cycle allows the wings to flap at 6–7 Hz. To achieve such fast, responsive motion, the solenoid valves and QEVs must be placed as close as possible to the actuators to minimize dead volume in the tubing. The airflow is drawn from near the body to avoid affecting the wings' aerodynamics. The control sequence is simple: all solenoids are activated to fold the wings during the upstroke. The solenoids are turned off during the downstroke, letting the wings open. A slight delay is added to the solen

title: Multi-quadrotor systems interconnected via structurally unknown forces and moments
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Video available at: https://tinyurl.com/4mzpb9rf
summary: This work addresses the challenge of controlling multi-quadrotor systems subject to tight uncertain couplings. We consider interconnection forces and moments among the quadrotors to be state-dependent functions of the coordination errors, without assuming knowledge of their functional/parametric structures, e.g., no linear-in-parameters assumptions are made. We only rely on general state-dependent quadratic bounds valid for several Euler-Lagrange mechanical systems. We propose a coordination strategy embedding adaptive laws dedicated to compensating for the lack of structural knowledge. Unlike conventional decoupled position-attitude designs, we present a coupled stability analysis accounting for the position-attitude couplings induced by the interconnection forces and moments. The analysis, along with real experiments involving cooperative aerial transportation of rope-interconnected payloads, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed solution in compensating for these complex interconnections. Comparative experiments show that, when a payload drop induces a disturbance propagating through the ropes across the whole formation, the proposed strategy reduces significantly post-disturbance transients.

Introduction Quadrotors have been attracting significant attention in recent years due to their versatility in diverse tasks Mu2017,Lewis2020 . Beyond single-quadrotor operation, multi-quadrotor operation is desirable in scenarios like cooperative transportation, cooperative search and rescue, among others Chung2018,Lin2023,Rezaee2024,Antal2025 . However, designing controllers for multi-quadrotor systems remains challenging not only due to the nonlinear dynamics of each quadrotor, but also due to the complex interconnections arising during cooperative tasks LIU2019179 . As a motivating example, think about a cooperative transportation task, where the cooperatively-transported payload creates interconnection forces and moments affecting the multi-quadrotor system Gabellieri2023 . Quadrotors in close formation affected by rotor downwash and wake phenomena provide another motivating example of complex interconnections Downwash2023 . In these and other examples, it can be difficult to model the functional/parametric structure of the interconnection forces and moments Dong2019outer,Gong2025 . It is also worth noting that the coupled position-attitude dynamics make quadrotors differ from other classical nonlinear multi-agent systems FastFiniteTimeConsensus,GlobalUniformFiniteTime : coordination of multi-quadrotor systems subject to tight couplings under limited structural knowledge remains insufficiently addressed. Uncertain interconnections in multi-quadrotor systems Interconnections affecting multi-quadrotor systems may be subject to large uncertainty. To elaborate on this, let us classify interconnections as virtual or physical Xu2024 . Virtual forces and moments generated by artificial potential fields to modify the shape of a multi-quadrotor system for navigation through obstacles Szczepanski2023,Haoran2025,Hesheng2024,Tayal2026 would depend on the form of obstacles, which can be a priori unknown. Similar virtual interconnections arise in approaches that assign multiple objectives to multi-agent systems Panagou2016,Panagou2020 . Physical interconnections are typical of cooperative manipulation Cortez2023 or cooperative transportation Xu2023,Wu2023,Goodman2023,Xiaozhen2024, su2023robust : uncertainty about the form of the object that is cooperatively manipulated or transported may add to lack of measurements of the forces and moments generated by the interaction with such object Verginis2020 . This work especially considers a cooperative aerial transportation task where physical interconnections are generated through the transported load (see Fig. fig:Pictorial_rep ): nevertheless, the method we propose is general enough to account for other types of interconnections. Its generality comes from not imposing a specific functional/parametric structure on the interconnections. Interconnection forces and moments would depend on position and attitude coordination (synchronization) errors: not only can their functional/parametric structure be unknown Aerial2018 , but state dependence would invalidate a priori boundedness Fridman2022,Fridman20222 . Furthermore, state dependence is intrinsically coupled along position and attitude dynamics, which makes any separation-based approach inapplicable Sankaranarayanan2022,Shiyang2022 . Summarizing, at least three challenges can be identified for interconnection forces and moments in multi-quadrotor systems: they are hard to model to the point that even their structure can be unknown; their dependence on coordination errors makes it impossible to assume a priori boundedness; they are intrinsically coupled along position and attitude. Contributions of this study Motivated by the outlined challenges, this paper considers complex uncertain interconnections arising in multi-quadrotor systems. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We do not assume knowledge of the functional/parametric structure of the interconnection terms, e.g., no linear-in-parameters structure is assumed. We only rely on general state-dependent quadratic bounds valid for several Euler-Lagrange mechanical systems. We take the interconnection forces and moments as functions of all coordination errors (position, attitude and their time derivative), thus taking into account tightly coupled dynamics. To tackle such a tightly coupled system, we propose an adaptive control strategy compensating for the structural uncertainties. Lyapunov-based stability analysis of the closed-loop system is provided, where the effects of the complex interconnections are studied and compensated. Real experiments with a three-quadrotor system cooperatively transporting two rope-interconnected payloads show that the proposed solution successfully achieves coordination despite the uncertain forces and moments generated by the rope-interconnected payloads, even when these forces and moments are excited by external disturbances (see Fig. 1). Section V provides experimental results to validate and compare the proposed method. Stability analysis is in the Appendix. title: Verifying Test-State Identity in Paired Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Simulation-based VLA evaluation often treats matching task, seed, and episode identifiers as sufficient evidence that two policies faced identical test conditions. Under specific vectorized reset and autoreset conditions, different termination timing can change subsequent initial-state assignment, so the same episode index need not mean the same test state. We present an evaluation-integrity framework for paired comparison - invariants I1-I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker - and a controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study with emulated controllers. Four evidence levels are kept separate: (A) mixed-horizon Sync wave-1 IDs [20, 5, 22, 7] vs [4, 5, 6, 7]; (B) homogeneous separate-job Sync control (16 cells, 0 ID/fingerprint mismatches); (C) Async+Freeze batch-size map differences (12 I3 mismatches; bs=8 incomplete; mechanism unisolated); (D) a synthetic McNemar illustration only. Controllers were emulated and no real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. We recommend checking declared/resolved init-state identity and provenance before paired statistics. We do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.
full_text: Verifying Test-State Identity in Paired Evaluation of\\ Vision-Language-Action Models Simulation-based VLA evaluation often treats matching task, seed, and episode identifiers as sufficient evidence that two policies faced identical test conditions. Under specific vectorized reset and autoreset conditions, different termination timing can change subsequent initial-state assignment, so the same episode index need not mean the same test state. We present an evaluation-integrity framework for paired comparison---invariants I1--I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker---and a controlled LeRobot~0.6.1 LIBERO harness study with emulated controllers. Four evidence levels are kept separate: (A)~mixed-horizon Sync wave-1 IDs vs ; (B)~homogeneous separate-job Sync control (16 cells, 0 ID/fingerprint mismatches); (C)~Async+Freeze batch-size map differences (12 I3 mismatches; bs 8 incomplete; mechanism unisolated); (D)~a synthetic McNemar illustration only. Controllers were emulated and no real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. We recommend checking declared/resolved init-state identity and provenance before paired statistics. We do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid. Vision-Language-Action models, evaluation integrity, simulation benchmarks, reproducibility, paired comparisons Introduction Simulation benchmarks are central to robot learning and VLA evaluation. When two policies are compared under a paired protocol, matching task, seed, and episode identifiers is often taken to mean identical test conditions. That assumption can fail. If Policy~A terminates earlier than Policy~B in a vectorized simulator, different reset/autoreset schedules can assign different initial states to later rollouts that still share the same episode index. The labels look paired; the test conditions may not be. Paired tests require genuine pairing---shared resolved test-state identity---not merely shared episode numbers. This paper concerns evaluation integrity for paired VLA comparisons in simulation: check resolved test-state identity and provenance rather than assume that identifiers imply pairing. Case-study term We use Outcome-Dependent Evaluation Sampling (ODES) for the case-study condition in which subsequent test-state assignment depends on prior termination/reset history. The mechanism is execution-condition dependent rather than universal; we do not claim discovery. Relation to prior work Issue~ 4152~ lerobot4152 documents that LIBERO initial state id assignment under vectorized Sync can depend on termination and reset history, not episode index alone. PR~ 2899~ lerobot2899 discusses advancing init state id on reset in LeRobot's LIBERO wrapper. SmolVLA RL notes~ smolvla_rl_repro report related reproduction concerns for paired evaluation. Those sources provide mechanism reports and engineering context; they do not provide reusable paired-comparison integrity invariants, automated checking with explicit PASS/FAIL/SKIPPED reporting, or the bounded emulated cross-mode characterization summarized as Evidence A--D here. Paired-statistics tooling such as robostats~ robostats joins episode records on declared scenario/init state id keys for McNemar-style tests. Joining on declared keys is necessary for paired inference, but does not certify that a vectorized harness assigned those keys consistently across policies or execution settings. Our contribution is operational: (a)~invariants I1--I5 and an automated checker; (b)~provenance logging and optional scene fingerprints; (c)~controlled characterization (emulated controllers only) under mixed Sync, synchronized-horizon separate jobs, and Async batch-size variation. We do not claim that simulation benchmarks are generally broken, that all fast-versus-slow comparisons are mispaired, or that existing VLA papers/leaderboards are invalid. Contributions Evaluation-integrity framework I1--I5 (I1--I3 stressed in particular harness experiments; I4--I5 enforced as checker/protocol requirements). Automated checker with provenance and optional scene fingerprints. Controlled LeRobot/LIBERO characterization (emulated controllers): mixed Sync divergence, synchronized-horizon separate-job control, Async batch-size map differences. Practical protocol: log resolved initial-state identity and run integrity checks before paired statistics. Problem Formulation Pairing (here). Shared declared controls and matching identity under I1---preferring resolved init state index when both logs provide it, otherwise raw initial state id---optionally corroborated by a non-disabled scene fingerprint when both sides log one. Matching episode indices alone are not sufficient. Matching logged init IDs establish declared identity, not necessarily identical complete simulator states; fingerprints add evidence only when their construction is documented and both values are usable. ODES (case-study term). Subsequent test-state assignment depends on prior termination/reset history~ lerobot4152,smolvla_rl_repro,lerobot2899 . Evaluation-Integrity Framework sec:framework We treat evaluation integrity as five checkable invariants implemented by the repository checker (evaluation integrity.checker). I1 (Identity consistency). For every shared key , when both rows log resolved init state index the checker compares those indices; otherwise it falls back to raw initial state id and states the fallback in the detail string. It also reports raw id mismatches and coverage . If both also log a non-empty, non-DISABLED scene fingerprint, those fingerprints must match. Absent fingerprints, I1 still compares resolved (or raw) IDs but cannot corroborate scene content. I2 (Identity consistency under outcome contrast). If termination step or success differs on common keys, I1 must still hold. If outcomes do not differ on common keys, I2 is marked SKIPPED (no outcome contrast; identity-under-contrast not tested). This re-checks declared/resolved identity when outcomes differ; it is not a causal proof of policy independence. I3 (Execution consistency). Caller-labeled condition logs (e.g., batch size or mode) must induce the same map relative to a reference label (--reference LABEL, defaulting to the first --condition label as given on the command line, not lexicographic order). If fewer than two labeled conditions are supplied, I3 is marked SKIPPED. I4 (Execution-mode declaration). Each compared run must log a single non-empty execution mode (or normalized harness mode) on every row. The checker does not validate autoreset enums beyond presence/uniqueness. I5 (Provenance completeness). Every row must contain non-None values for policy id, task id, episode index, initial state id, seed, batch size, slot, termination step, success, reset count, execution mode, harness id. scene fingerprint is optional and not required for I5. Integrity checker sec:checker The checker standardizes join keys, computes pairing fraction, localizes mismatches, checks provenance, and (when conditions are supplied) compares episode init maps across settings---capabilities that manual ID inspection does not package reproducibly. Inputs JSON or JSONL episode logs (list, or object with an episodes array). Required provenance fields are those listed under I5; optional scene fingerprint, n init states, and resolved init state index. I3 needs labeled paths (--condition LABEL=PATH) and optional --reference LABEL. Duplicate keys within a log make I1 FAIL (duplicated keys are listed in the detail message). Outputs and exit status Each invariant returns exactly one status---PASS, FAIL, or SKIPPED---plus a detail string and evidence (I1 includes pairing fraction, coverage, raw id mismatches, and the compare mode; I3 compares labeled conditions to the reference label). Exit code is 0 iff no invariant is FAIL. SKIPPED means incomplete evidence for that invariant (reported as any skipped); it does not by itself make the process exit nonzero. fully checked is true only when there is neither FAIL nor SKIPPED. Example A (homogeneous Sync; I3 not exercised) Early vs late, libero spatial task~0, Sync bs 4, seed~0 (homogeneous sync bs4.stdout.json): I1 pass (pairing fraction=1.0, coverage~ , ; raw-ID fallback when resolved indices are absent); I2 pass under termination contrast; I3 skipped (no conditions) any skipped=true, exit~0 if no FAIL; I4/I5 pass. Example B (I3 exercised; cached CLI-shaped reports) Same-policy Async+Freeze logs with --condition bs1=..., bs2=..., bs4=... (async i3 cli.stdout.json): I3 fail, 12 mismatch records vs reference bs1 (exit nonzero). The analogous Sync conditions (bs1/bs4/bs8) yield I3 pass (sync i3 cli.stdout.json); I2 is SKIPPED in that same-policy exercise (no outcome contrast), so the run is not fully checked, but exit is~0 absent any FAIL. Experimental Setup sec:setup Stack. LeRobot~0.6.1~ lerobot , Gymnasium~1.3.0, LIBERO~ libero2023 ; RTX~2060 6\,GB (as recorded in results/frozen phase2/environment.json, which also records robostats==0.1.0). Modes. Sync with NEXT STEP autoreset (finished slots reset on the next vector step); Async with FreezeAfter in the harness freeze path. Batch sizes were attempted; Async bs~ 8 is N/A in Table~ tab:i3 . Controllers. Emulated early/late (and mixed-horizon) controllers isolate harness assignment behavior; they are not learned VLAs. No real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. Synchronized-horizon control (homogeneous separate jobs). Separate early vs late jobs on task~0 of libero spatial and libero object, seeds , Sync batch sizes , episodes per cell---16 Sync cells (2 suites 2 seeds 4 batch sizes), from results/audit/summary.csv. In these cells all slots share the same horizon within a job, so counters advance in lockstep. Mixed-horizon Sync probe (Fig.~ fig:odes ). One shared Sync vector env on libero spatial task~0, seed~0, bs 4, episodes; even slots truncate early ( ), odd slots late ( ). Wave-1 denotes the second fill of the vector after the first staggered terminations/resets. Evidence levels (not interchangeable): (A)~mixed Sync; (B)~synchronized-horizon control; (C)~Async batch-size maps; (D)~synthetic McNemar. Results Evidence B: Synchronized-horizon control Separate early/late Sync jobs: 16 cells, each with episodes, yield 160 early--late episode pairs. Every pair logged a usable (non-empty, non-DISABLED) scene fingerprint; summary and direct log comparison report 0 fingerprint mismatches and 0 initial state id mismatches (results/audit/summary.csv; Fig.~ fig:contrast , left). This shows declared identity and usable fingerprints can match for homogeneous separate Sync jobs under the tested cells; it does not certify all harnesses, all homogeneous protocols, or complete simulator-state equivalence beyond the logged fingerprint definition.
