title: pico-WAM: Evaluating Counterfactual Prediction and Planning Error in a Compact World Action Model
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures. Code available at https://github.com/keivalya/pico-wam
summary: When a World Action Model fails at control, is the bottleneck proposal generation or trajectory scoring? We introduce pico-WAM, a compact model with supplied physical state for tracing policy-dynamics interactions. Using 206 Push-T demonstrations and 15 training seeds, we compare data regimes and search configurations. Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and enlarges the coverage advantage of policy-restarted over warm-started search by 4.8 percentage points; restart wins under both data regimes. Replacing learned trajectory scores with simulator costs improves coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals. Substituting simulator states in proposal generation alone shows no detected gain. Component diagnostics and a separate door-opening study show why better ranking need not yield better control or outperform imitation. These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models.
full_text: When a World Action Model fails at control, is the bottleneck proposal generation or trajectory scoring? We introduce pico-WAM, a compact model with supplied physical state for tracing policy–dynamics interactions. Using 206 Push-T demonstrations and 15 training seeds, we compare data regimes and search configurations. Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and enlarges the coverage advantage of policy-restarted over warm-started search by 4.8 percentage points; restart wins under both data regimes. Replacing learned trajectory scores with simulator costs improves coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals. Substituting simulator states in proposal generation alone shows no detected gain. Component diagnostics and a separate door-opening study show why better ranking need not yield better control or outperform imitation. These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models. Code Introduction pico-WAM is a compact architecture for isolating how a World Action Model predicts outcomes and selects actions. A single shared representation feeds the policy, transition model, and an explicit state readout, making every decision step traceable: observe, propose actions, imagine consequences, score, and execute. We use this transparent setup to study how training data coverage and search choices govern closed-loop behavior. A world model trained strictly on demonstrations only observes the actions experts chose, yet a planner must evaluate counterfactual actions they did not choose. Can a compact model score these off-manifold proposals accurately enough to guide control? Figure~ fig:task illustrates this gap between predicting state transitions and selecting the best action sequence. We investigate two controlled questions under strictly matched action labels, initial parameters, and training updates. First, does adding counterfactual simulator branches change the benefit of restarting search from the policy versus warm-starting from the previous plan? Second, does replacing learned trajectory scoring with ground-truth simulator costs improve control when retaining learned policy proposals? We find that branch data sharpens cost ranking and favors policy-restarted search, while exact simulator scoring substantially boosts task coverage using the learned proposals. These paired interventions form our core contribution. Component ablations explain the behavior of our shared representation, a supplementary door-opening study extends our ranking findings, and imitation baselines demonstrate why better trajectory ranking alone does not guarantee stronger closed-loop control. Related Work PETS and MBPO address model error through uncertainty-aware search and restricted model rollouts chua2018pets,janner2019mbpo . Our added transitions instead come from the true simulator. DINO-WM plans in visual features, PILOT starts from a policy, and SufficientPlan reduces search cost zhou2025dinowm,liu2026pilot,li2026sufficientplan . Generative Predictive Control ranks diffusion-policy proposals with a learned model qi2025gpc . These establish policy-guided planning; we study its components using supervised state and a known geometric objective. AD-WM and Action--Consequence Alignment train models for action discrimination qiu2026adwm,wang2026aca ; AD-WM already measures ranking and selection regret. Decision-relevant error, model exploitation and planning-horizon effects are established concerns wang2026errors,bhamidipaty2026exploitable,alrasheed2026limits . DreamTrue expands action coverage using generated videos li2026dreamtrue ; our simulator supplies paired ground-truth outcomes. Our paired experiments measure how branch data changes the warm/restart gap and how exact scoring helps while retaining learned proposals. These results explain interactions among existing components. Diffusion Policy supplies an imitation reference chi2023diffusion ; our adapted task does not reproduce published visual-goal benchmark scores. Model and Planner sec:method The policy answers ``what action should I imitate?'' The dynamics answers ``what happens if I take this action?'' A state readout exposes the prediction, and an external planner uses it to compare actions (Fig.~ fig:architecture ). Shared Representation Inputs are a image, a fixed instruction and an eight-dimensional state: agent position/velocity and block position/orientation . A three-layer CNN with 16 spatial-softmax keypoints, a GRU and a state MLP feed a fusion MLP, producing . The policy has three 512-unit hidden layers and predicts eight two-dimensional actions. Residual dynamics with two 256-unit hidden layers advance the latent: A linear readout maps latents to standardized physical state. Applying the policy to imagined latents supplies an initial plan. The optional image decoder is disabled; full state is available at inference and the instruction is constant. This isolates policy/dynamics interaction rather than visual perception or language generalization. Training For a window of transitions, Each term is squared error averaged over its batch and all output coordinates; future losses also average over . BC regresses eight-action expert chunks. State targets use training-demonstration means and standard deviations, floored at . Future latent targets are observation encodings with gradients stopped; prediction gradients reach the dynamics, readout and initial encoder. Action and auxiliary batches are sampled separately (Sec.~4.1). A branch perturbs eight demonstration actions from every fourth recorded state with Gaussian noise (SD 0.3), clipped to . The 6,013 branches yield 48,104 transitions, inherit their source episode's split and supply prediction targets only. Branching changes both state and action coverage. Planning The policy rolls forward for 12 steps to form a proposal. The 256 candidates comprise the policy proposal, a search center and 254 noisy perturbations (SD 0.1), clipped to . We score them using Here , increases linearly from 0.5 to 1.5, and averages distances between corresponding block and target corners in pixels. With agent position and block center of mass , subtracts the agent radius. One search iteration selects the cheapest plan's first action before replanning. Restart centers search on the current policy proposal (duplicated in the bank); warm uses the shifted previous plan, appending the proposal's final action. The first call uses the proposal in both cases. Experimental Protocol Data and Matched Training Push-T requires pushing a T-shaped block onto a target. The 206 LeRobot demonstrations lerobotpusht provide 25,444 transitions at 10\,Hz, with keypoints supplying block pose and controller replay recovering agent velocity. We retain the original geometry and 100\,Hz physics, but use relative actions (up to 100\,px per axis) and rebuild physics each step for exact replay; replayed block transitions agree within \,px at the 99th percentile. Coverage measures maximum target overlap during an episode (including reset), and success requires exceeding 95 . Because the recordings contain no successes under this threshold (Appendix~ sec:reproduction ), control success requires completion beyond recorded outcomes. sec:matched BC learns actions only, Current adds current-state reconstruction, and WAM optimizes all losses at horizon . Current and WAM train on either demonstration-only windows or equal mixtures of demonstrations and counterfactual branches. Within each training run, all five conditions share initial parameters, action minibatches, Adam updates, and batch size 64. Demonstration-only conditions resample windows to match auxiliary sample counts, matching updates and labels rather than compute. Lacking trained dynamics, BC and Current act reactively. Episodes split into training, validation, and test demonstrations. Each of the 15 training runs uses development and final evaluation starts shared across conditions, with warm and restart search sharing checkpoints. Our predeclared primary contrast tests whether branch training increases the advantage of restart over warm search: where is mean coverage and denote branch and demonstration-only training. Four additional coverage contrasts and all success contrasts are secondary. All checkpoints were frozen before final evaluation. Measurements and Interventions sec:followups Prediction tests roll forward from one encoded observation under recorded or random actions. Normalized mean squared error ( ) divides each state-coordinate error by its training standard deviation before squaring and averaging. Random-action tests sample eight sequences in from starts spaced five steps apart, using zero-action outcomes as a reference. Every ten control steps, a non-intervening diagnostic replay compares predicted and true progress of the selected 12-step plan. For candidate ranking, every model scores the same 256 candidates across states: recorded states and states from 50 fresh noisy-expert episodes (action noise 0.2). Half the candidates are uniform in , while half perturb recorded actions (noise 0.1). Selection regret is the chosen sequence's true cost minus the best true cost in the pool. The proposal/scoring study crosses learned (L) and exact (E) components—LL, LE, EL, and EE (proposals first)—reusing 15 frozen branch-trained checkpoints across 256 candidates, a 12-step horizon, and 100 fresh starts per run, with coverage as primary. Exact scoring evaluates candidate actions in the simulator via Eq.~ eq:cost , whereas learned scoring uses predicted states. Exact proposals render and re-encode simulator states before querying the policy, replacing the full latent pipeline. Candidate random streams are paired per episode, though closed-loop states naturally diverge. Secondary tests substitute a two-layer, 256-unit state MLP or simulator dynamics while retaining policy and search settings. Architecture ablations retrain five runs with a single modification: blocked auxiliary encoder gradients, masked image or state inputs (retaining parameter counts), removed instructions, or omitted individual prediction losses. Blocked-gradient minus full-model reactive coverage is primary; gradient blocking tests representation shaping rather than separate encoders. Additional checks repeat training at with 16-step branches, evaluate frozen models in original gym-pusht 0.1.8 via an action adapter, and compare imitation baselines. Tuned BC sweeps 16 configurations of learning rate, head width, history, and chunk length on separate starts. Diffusion Policy follows its state-based recipe (two observations, 16 predicted/eight executed actions, 100 denoising steps, 5,000 epochs, and EMA weights) across five runs. Comparisons on the dynamics study's starts were selected post-hoc and are exploratory. Door Opening A separate study on Meta-World door-open-v3 yu2021metaworld (39-D state, 4-D actions) trains two-layer, 256-unit state-space dynamics models on 80 scripted-expert episodes alone or mixed equally with 80 noisy-expert episodes (noise 0.3), totaling 5,840 five-step windows per condition. Models share initialization, expert-data normalization, and 10,000 updates at batch size 128, paired with a separate BC policy. Primary regret is evaluated across 60 states from 20 fresh expert episodes using 64 shared five-step candidates, with cost defined as handle-to-goal distance plus hand-to-handle distance. Planners perturb a repeated BC action and execute the best sequence's first step. Secondary control tests use 50 shared starts and 150-step limits across ten runs. Fixed data and evaluation banks mean intervals reflect training-run variance rather than dataset sampling, testing the data-to-ranking mechanism rather than pico-WAM architecture transfer. title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models
summary: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
full_text: 0pt 5pt Introduction sec:introduction X-World~1.0~ xworld2026 established controllable, action-conditioned multi-camera generation as a practical component of autonomous-driving development~ gaia12023,gaia22025,m4world2026,hu2026zyt . Its streaming autoregressive interface already supported closed-loop simulation, online reinforcement learning, and synthetic data generation in XPENG's VLA~2.0 workflow. The starting point for X-World~1.6 is therefore an existing interactive simulator, with controls over ego motion, traffic participants, road geometry, and global appearance. X-World~1.6 advances this foundation through stronger base-model controllability, more effective long-horizon post-training, and a more complete evaluation and iteration pipeline. Together, these developments support Virtual City: recorded real-world locations become configurable interactive environments for the established closed-loop evaluation and policy-training workflows. Stronger and broader scene control. We strengthen existing controls, add traffic-light positions and colors and road-surface markings, and improve geometric association across camera views. The principal extension beyond element-level control is absolute static scene control. Scene references from 3D Gaussian representations~ gaussiansplatting2023,chen2026quantifying,zhang2024gaussian , point clouds, and visual observations constrain persistent geometry and appearance while ego trajectories and supported traffic conditions change. This provides evidence for buildings, roadside structures, and location-specific details that sparse road annotations do not determine. The objective is to preserve a specified place within the available reference coverage, while allowing scenario-dependent content to evolve. These conditioning paths use independently trained models; the common interface does not imply a single model accepting every reference modality. More effective long-horizon post-training. The two-stage training organization is retained: a bidirectional base model learns controllable generation, and post-training develops causal, few-step interaction~ selfforcing2025,causalforcingpp2026 . Connected Self Forcing (CSF) restores feedback from later predictions through the history on which they depend~ csf2026 . Longer teacher supervision and student rollouts extend this optimization to longer temporal contexts. Reward-guided refinement further targets visual quality and ego-motion adherence. The emphasis is on maintaining useful observations during continued interaction, where errors from earlier predictions can affect subsequent generation. Evaluation as part of model iteration. The human annotation pipeline provides a shared taxonomy and localized annotations of generation failures. VLM-assisted pre-labeling and human correction make this process more efficient, while automated benchmarks compare temporal and cross-view consistency across versions and training variants. We report both the annotation-efficiency benefit and the model comparisons. Scene-reference fidelity, internal consistency, and downstream behavior reproduction are kept distinct so that each result supports the capability it actually measures. Together with the model and training changes, this evaluation infrastructure supports the improvements in existing closed-loop applications reported in this work. Data sec:data X-World~1.6 expands and curates real-world driving recordings to support controllable multi-camera generation and interaction-rich training. As illustated in Figure.~ fig:data (a), the data pipeline combines capture-quality screening, scenario tagging, and targeted selection for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Data Scaling sec:data_scaling Compared with X-World~1.0~ xworld2026 , the candidate recording pool is four times as large and the selected training dataset is twice as large. The distinction between candidate and training data matters: the larger pool allows stricter selection while retaining more usable clips and a wider range of driving situations. Both versions construct their training datasets by selecting clips from the available recordings. Quality Screening sec:data_cleaning We exclude video segments affected by capture defects, including abrupt luminance flicker, horizontal color stripes, lens contamination or obstruction, strong color casts, and overexposure. Detection thresholds are calibrated through manual review of flagged samples and samples close to each threshold. Screening degraded camera streams uses both absolute image-quality signals and comparisons with other cameras. This helps distinguish a faulty view from environmental conditions such as fog, rain, or low light that can affect several cameras together. Candidate screening is followed by VLM verification. Scenario Tags sec:tag_expansion The annotation taxonomy now contains more than 150 tags, with additions covering data quality, fine-grained agent behavior, and corner cases. Quality tags identify potential capture issues, finer behavior labels distinguish maneuvers previously grouped together, and corner-case tags make uncommon situations retrievable. These tags support targeted retrieval and control of the selected scenario mix. We also refine the tagging algorithms to reduce incorrect and missed labels. The same annotations provide the behavioral context used in SFT selection. SFT Construction and Distribution sec:sft_data Routine lane keeping and steady cruising dominate the natural recording distribution. We increase the representation of less common maneuvers through two complementary selection strategies. Kinematics-based selection identifies sustained high-curvature motion and deceleration to a complete stop directly from ego trajectories. Behavior-based selection uses tags to identify contextual events such as intersection turns, merges, and overtaking. A clip may contain several occurrences of a behavior, so each tag instance serves as a sampling unit. Category-specific resampling ratios favor scenarios with richer interactions. Combining motion-based selection with behavior tags retains both the executed maneuver and its driving context, without assuming that one is a substitute for the other. Figure~ fig:data (b) organizes selected SFT tag distributions into three families: ego behavior, environment, and conditions. Ego behavior covers intersection maneuvers, lane changes, split and merge events, lane keeping, and ego status; environment covers traffic, road type, lighting, and weather; conditions cover dynamic objects, road markings, and traffic lights. Percentages are normalized within each labeled category. They describe the selected SFT data, not the full training corpus or real-world occurrence frequencies. Behavior distribution. Within the Intersection category, left turns, right turns, and U-turns account for 41.5 , 40.3 , and 18.2 , respectively. Other behavior panels describe lane transitions and changes in ego motion, including starting, stopping, and acceleration or deceleration. These breakdowns complement the two selection mechanisms: trajectories identify the motion, while behavior tags provide its event context. Environmental context. Urban roads account for 58.4 within Road Type, while rainy conditions account for 9.5 within Weather. The environment panels also distinguish traffic conditions and lighting, showing the context accompanying selected maneuvers. Scene conditions. Red and green signals account for 36.0 and 32.2 within Traffic Light. The Road Marking panel covers crosswalks, directional arrows, and stop lines; Dynamic Objects distinguishes vehicle classes and pedestrians. These distributions describe the elements represented by the selected condition tags. Together, the three families connect SFT sampling to actions, their environmental context, and condition following. The signal and marking categories are particularly relevant to the traffic-light and road-surface-marking control interfaces added in X-World 1.6. Method: Controllable Base Model sec:method X-World 1.6 strengthens existing controls over ego motion, traffic participants, road geometry, and appearance; adds traffic-light and road-marker conditions; and introduces absolute static scene control. The base-model phase learns these conditioning interfaces through bidirectional video training. Subsequent post-training improves their use during sustained autoregressive interaction. Task and Architecture sec:city_formulation The model generates synchronized seven-camera video from scenario controls , target camera configurations , and, where available, location-specific scene evidence : Here contains ego motion, traffic participants, road geometry, traffic-light states, road markers, and environmental text. Camera poses must agree with the requested ego motion. The distinction between scene evidence and controls allows the same location to support different driving scenarios: persistent structures remain constrained by the reference, while supported traffic and appearance conditions can change. Figure~ fig:virtual_city_architecture shows the conditioning paths around the multi-camera video backbone. All model variants share the same backbone architecture and are fine-tuned separately for their respective conditioning modalities and tasks. Scene evidence is encoded as geometry-aware scene tokens and fused with target-video tokens through joint self-attention; temporal and cross-view attention model the generated video. The model family also supports initialization from a single image and synchronized dashcam-to-surround completion. The latter follows the source video's recorded evolution and does not provide independently editable future dynamics. Shared geometric representation. Geometry-aware positional encoding (GeoPE) associates image patches with viewing rays in a common scene coordinate system~ li2025cameras,wu2026rayrope . Each descriptor combines ray direction, a symlog-scaled Pl\"ucker moment, and horizontal and vertical angular extent. It relates reference observations to target viewpoints without requiring surface depth. To account for temporal compression by the WAN2.2 VAE~ wan2025 , GeoPE constructs a geometry embedding for each latent from the ordered geometric descriptors of its corresponding frames: a still image or the first video latent has one-frame support, while subsequent latents have four-frame support. A shared encoder adds these geometry embeddings to reference and target tokens. Figure~ fig:geope in Appendix~ app:method illustrates the spatial descriptor, ordered temporal support, and geometry--visual fusion; the corresponding definitions and masking details accompany the diagram. Enhanced Basic Control sec:basic_control Ego actions retain the velocity, curvature, roll, and pitch representation of X-World 1.0~ xworld2026 , encoded with symlog normalization, Fourier features, and an MLP before action-dependent modulation. Dynamic participants combine semantic features with spatial states; lanes and road boundaries describe continuous road geometry. Environmental text continues to control weather, illumination, and appearance. The action embedding is combined with the diffusion-timestep embedding to parameterize AdaLN-Zero. Dynamic-object category features originate from the text encoder and are combined with Fourier-encoded coordinates. These inherited interfaces remain distinct from absolute static control: specifying an object or lane constrains a selected element, whereas a scene reference supplies the surrounding environment. A traffic light is static in position even though its state changes over time. Road markers and shared structured conditioning. X-World 1.6 adds discrete road-surface markings represented by category features, sampled geometry, and adjacent-point offsets. Dynamic objects, road markers, and lanes use separate encoders, preserving the representation appropriate to each condition type while mapping their outputs to the same DiT width.

title: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification
comment: Accepted version. Published in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems, vol. 62, pp. 9706-9717, 2026. 13 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/Y-Z3IN--_Vc
summary: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety_checker library, takes approximately 500-520 ms to verify its safety for the next 4 s into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time (~300-500 ms).
full_text: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety checker library, takes approximately to verify its safety for the next into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time ( ). Autonomous Aerial Vehicles, Formal Verification, Swarm Robotics Introduction sec:introduction Many of the emergent strategies in the verification community have only been exercised either in numerical simulation or, in the case of robotics, indoor conditions in which localization is accomplished by a high-precision motion capture (MoCap) system, and communication occurs via a local WiFi setup. These conditions enhance the ability to isolate the performance of the verification strategy and algorithm but also remove two of the most significant complicating factors of outdoor, real-world deployments where uncertainty and disturbances in the environment, as well as much less capable communication and localization systems may dominate design decisions and algorithm performance. Furthermore, when it comes to robotic swarms the vast majority of research only validates in either simulation or indoor testbeds, which, we argue, is significantly holding back technological advancement in this space by widening the gap between theory and practice. In a survey of 330 research papers Selection chosen by papers tagged with ``multi-robot'' or ``swarm'' in the last 5 years of IEEE IROS, ICCPS, ICRA, and CDC conferences. presenting novel swarm control, verification, or task management, only 8 performed any outdoor experimentation, and only 1 on swarms of more than 3 Unmanned Aircraft Vehicles (UAVs). Simulation results can be insightful, but limitations in vehicle hardware can break design-time assumptions, leaving the usefulness of methods without experimental results in question, particularly those motivated by real-world applications (i.e., search and rescue in disaster areas or contested and dynamic spaces). Aircraft, to some extent, rely on the large-sky, small-plane paradigm to limit collisions. This breaks down near airports and congested flight corridors, and completely falls apart in swarm arnold2019what operations where mission objectives are furthered by close proximity flight. Crewed aircraft rely on see-and-avoid kephart2008comparison , Traffic Collision Avoidance Systems (TCAS) williamson1989developmenta , and separation by air traffic controllers brooker1983aircraft to remain safe, but these solutions are not suited for autonomous, small UAVs due to their Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP)-constrained nature. Moreover, those solutions attempt to maximize separation distance within constraints, while swarms often attempt to fly in close formation to accomplish particular goals. Formal-method-based verification strategies offer promise in this regard as they provide more precise spatial and timing limits for vehicles. However, such strategies are also traditionally computationally complex, and may require accurate dynamic models of the collective swarm to ensure collision-free trajectories zhou2015reachable . Decentralized verification strategies are scarce and, when available, may require highly reliable, high-rate communication, complex models, or abundant computation, all of which are poorly suited to SWaP-constrained UAVs. The objective in this work is to examine the adaptations needed to implement a reachability-based verification strategy onboard a modern robotic swarm fleet, as well as to provide extensive experimental data and analysis to inform future research into assured autonomy strategies. In this paper we focus narrowly on a swarm anti-collision strategy, though our analysis can be generalized since we capture computational and communication resource limitations. The goal is to implement, integrate, and deploy the verification strategy and obtain data about: 1) what simplifications and optimizations must be made to obtain suitable online, runtime performance on a common small UAV platform, and 2) what unforeseen challenges exist in a real-world deployment, and how the deployment data can be used to further improve the system. To do this, we enhance, and adapt the reachability-based approach described in tran2019decentralized for implementation due to its decentralized nature and suitability for a swarm deployment in which the desired global safety property is to prevent potential collisions between the agents in the swarm. This work bridges the gap between theoretical formal verification and deployment in a representative environment. While the core mathematical reachability analysis builds upon the face-lifting method established in tran2019decentralized , our contribution lies in the system-level architectural synthesis and rigorous characterization required to deploy these guarantees on hardware. Specifically, this paper contributes: The synthesis of a runtime verification framework that adapts formal reachability analysis to the specific timing, network, and SWaP constraints of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) UAV hardware. Extensive outdoor evaluation (140 flights across 6 swarm deployments) demonstrating the efficacy of decentralized verification in environments with realistic disturbances and communication loss, exceeding the scale of prior experimental work (e.g., gillula2011applications ). A detailed decomposition of Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) and network broadcast delays, providing design guidelines for the trade-offs between swarm size, safety horizons, and verification periods Related Work sec:related-work Reachability-based verification. Reachability analysis is the heart of many verification tools for cyber-physical systems (CPS). It involves the construction of exact or overapproximate reachable sets containing all possible trajectories of the systems. Many verification tools based on reachability algorithms have been proposed for CPS modeled as hybrid linear/nonlinear systems, such as SpaceEx frehse2011spaceex , d/dt asarin2002d , JuliaReach bogomolov2019juliareach , Hylla bak2017hylaa , CORA althoff2015introduction , Hypro schupp2022recent , Flow* chen2013flow , DReach kong2015dreach , C2E2 duggirala2015c2e2 , DryVR fan2017dryvr , Hamilton-Jacobi bansal2017hamilton . Distinguished from the reachability-based verification approach, Keymaera platzer2008keymaera is the well-known theorem prover for CPS. Recently, there has been an emerging research area in reachability-based verification for deep neural networks tran2019star,yang2021reachability,zhang2020verification , and learning-enabled CPS tran2020verification . Although there has been rigorous research on CPS verification, only a few approaches focus on verifying distributed CPS kumar2012hybrid,loos2011adaptive,li2023verse,duggirala2012static . Importantly, these methods require explicit modeling of distributed CPS as a hybrid system and perform the verification in a centralized manner. We seek a simpler, decentralized verification approach as it enhances robustness of the distributed system and is more suitable for field-based drone swarm operations where centralized strategies may be impossible (i.e., due to range). Particularly, we use the reachability-based face-lifting method dang1998reachability to compute the reachable set of each autonomous agent to a time horizon in the future. Importantly, this method does not require explicit modeling of the distributed CPS, and instead we perform distributed reachability analysis via reachable set communication between the agents tran2019decentralized . The face-lifting method can be more efficient for real-time verification on small embedded platforms as it does not require complicated data structures/libraries or extensive computational resources bak2014sfl . UAV Collision Avoidance. In the broader aviation context, the Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS II) williamson1989developmenta and the next-generation Airborne Collision Avoidance System (ACAS Xu) owen2019acasxu for uncrewed systems represent the gold standards for mid-air de-confliction. While TCAS II relies on rule-based logic to issue vertical resolution advisories, ACAS Xu utilizes probabilistic models (Markov Decision Processes) to optimize avoidance logic mueller2016multi . However, these centralized or pairwise standards are primarily designed for "detect-and-avoid" operations to ensure large separation minima in civil airspace. This design philosophy often proves too conservative for robotic swarms, where mission objectives frequently require close-proximity formation flight that would trigger constant false alarms in separation-based systems. Furthermore, standard ACAS implementations typically rely on pre-computed lookup tables or heavy centralized computation, which may not align with the dynamic, fully decentralized, and SWaP-constrained architecture required for scalable autonomous swarms. In contrast, our reachability-based approach provides formal set-based safety guarantees that allow agents to operate safely within tighter spatial margins. Collision avoidance for UAVs has been extensively studied as the platform has gained popularity over the past two decades. Towards integrating UAVs into the national airspace, the vast majority of the work is focused on the ability of a single UAV to detect and avoid collisions with other air traffic yasin2020unmanned or obstacles gageik2015obstacle . In this context, perception zsedrovits2011collision,mcfadyen2016survey is responsible for detection and identification of the obstacle and some combination of an estimator luo2013uav , path planner lin2017samplingbased,tony2017avoidance , and controller herbert2017fastrack generates and guides the vehicle through safe trajectories. Aerial swarm collision avoidance has received comparatively less attention, in part due to the need to deliberately fly near friendly agents in the swarm to accomplish mission objectives. This is most typically researched as cooperative formation flying that incorporates collision avoidance into the controller either by a combined controller sharma2009collision,bai2020hierarchical , potential fields abeywickrama2017algorithm , machine learning wang2007cooperative , or model predictive control Jin2022 . Of particular relevance is the work by Gillula et al. gillula2011applications , which applied hybrid reachability analysis to a 4-vehicle swarm (STARMAC). title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$
comment: Accepted to the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop at CoRL 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.

title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
summary:
Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks.
  Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga
full_text: Introduction ``Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.'' In physical manipulation, a failed attempt changes the scene, often irreversibly. Unlike simulated settings where an agent can call repeatedly on a target task to tune coordinate offsets, control scripts, or failure notes before evaluation~ hexashell2026,embodiedevo2026,physicalrsi2026,sear2026 , a deployed robot must complete an unseen task within a single episode. Tuning procedures across repeated trials on a fixed scene also fits to that scene's layout, and performance drops when object positions are randomized or the task changes. Generalization in manipulation therefore separates two problems: across tasks during development, using failures to improve the shared perception, control, and verification tools rather than task-specific scripts; and during execution on an unseen task, completing the task in one episode without prior trials, demonstrations, or resets ( ). On a 210-episode diagnostic across all 42 tasks of the RoboDojo benchmark~ robodojo2026 , the main bottleneck is physical execution rather than task reasoning ( ). When GPT-6 Astra is given a privileged action that moves objects along chosen waypoints without the robot arm, it succeeds in 76.2 of episodes; when it drives the arm through the benchmark's reference end-effector interface (RoboProbe~ unexpected2026 ), it succeeds in 22.5 . The model usually identifies the right object and destination, but the arm misses a grasp by a few millimeters, loses the object in flight, or hits a container rim during transport. Common control interfaces do not catch these errors in time. Step-wise and chunked action interfaces~ pi052025,xvla2025,unexpected2026 issue motions from the latest frames without showing the full route in advance, so collisions appear only after the arm has moved. Program generation~ liang2023code,capx2026 hands execution to a script that cannot see the scene, where normal program exit does not mean the intended contact succeeded. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that narrows this planning--execution gap within a single zero-shot episode ( ). In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions, while the harness measures the scene, checks and executes motions, and reports what happened: Task-agnostic harness and explicit task belief ( ). Auriga contains no task-specific code, prompts, or heuristics, and exposes no privileged simulator state. One persistent model session plans the task, chooses actions, and recovers from errors. As an episode grows long, the model records its current plan, open questions, and task premises ( , , , or ) in a concise task belief , while full interaction logs stay in an off-context evidence record retrieved on demand. Preview and verification through a single admission gateway ( ). Every physical motion, whether called directly or from a model-written program, passes through the admission gateway in a preview--execute--verify loop. While simulation is paused, plans a multi-stage dual-arm sequence into a trajectory preview showing the path, step cost, and clearance warnings. During execution, the previewed trajectory runs while checks model-set arrival tolerances , gripper openings, and observation checkpoints. If a stage misses its tolerance, stops the robot and returns a receipt with the completed stages, measured deviations, unexecuted stages, and fresh camera views so the model can recover from the current state ( ). 3D geometric measurements and finger-referenced actions ( ). On the input side, camera calibration, VGGT-Omega~ wang2026vggt depth, and SAM~3.1~ carion2026sam segmentation provide 3D object estimates, ray--plane intersection with height sensitivity, and two-view triangulation, together with in-hand slip measurements and warnings when a motion re-enters a past failure region. On the output side, the model sets goals at the finger contact region rather than the wrist, chooses tolerances per stage, and coordinates both arms on a shared timeline. Auriga separates cross-task tool development from single-episode execution ( ). Over 13 development iterations ( ), manipulation failures were used to identify missing capabilities in 3D localization, contact checking, and state tracking, raising zero-shot performance across all 42 RoboDojo tasks from 36.2 SR (45.5 Score) at iteration~ 4 to 57.7 SR (64.0 Score) in the final harness. During evaluation, the harness is frozen and runs under the single-episode zero-shot protocol ( ), with no target-task exploration, demonstrations, or resets: RoboDojo~ robodojo2026 . Across all 42 tasks and five dimensions (6,300 episodes over three seeds), Auriga with GPT-6 Astra reaches an average Score of 64.0 and SR of 57.7 , ranking first overall on the leaderboard across learned policies and agent methods, more than doubling the GPT-6 Astra reference harness (29.0 Score, 22.5 SR), and leading all 12 columns of the agent block ( ). On the 210-episode diagnostic set, Auriga closes 68.3 of the gap between reference arm control and arm-free object motion ( ). Scene randomization. Across the 12 Generalization tasks ( ), learned policies drop by up to 33.9 in SR on randomized layouts, whereas Auriga ranks first on both standard scenes (52.3 SR) and random scenes (45.6 SR) and achieves the highest generalization score ( ). RoboCasa365~ robocasa3652026 . On the 50 Target50 mobile manipulation tasks in unseen kitchens (250 episodes), Auriga reaches 73.2 Overall SR (92.2 Atomic-Seen, 67.5 Composite-Seen, 57.5 Composite-Unseen) without a learned policy or cross-episode memory, outperforming VLA-assisted agents RPent~ harnessvla2026 (59.2 ) and PyRUA-Lean~ pyrua2026 (56.4 ) by 19.4 and 23.1 on composite tasks ( ). Problem Setting and Positioning We study zero-shot manipulation, in which a general-purpose model uses a shared robot harness to construct and execute a task procedure from the task specification and interaction feedback. We first define the single-episode zero-shot evaluation protocol ( ), then quantify the planning--execution gap that motivates our harness ( ), and finally position cross-task harness evolution relative to within-task trial search ( ). Zero-Shot Single-Episode Protocol sec:problem_setting Task and interaction. The unit of evaluation is a case, defined by a task instruction and a specified scene variant, random seed, and layout. Each case starts from an initial scene and is evaluated under the benchmark's execution budget and success criteria. The agent receives the task specification and accesses observations and robot actions through the shared harness. It uses the available observations and interaction history to choose subsequent tool calls or programs, then receives feedback from their execution. This interaction continues until success, termination, or budget exhaustion. The benchmark's evaluator determines task success from the resulting execution. Zero-shot protocol. We define zero-shot evaluation through three conditions: No target-task exploration or development before evaluation. Evaluation starts with a pretrained model, a fixed shared harness, and task-independent operating guidance. No preparatory exploration or trials are conducted on the target task, including its other layouts, to develop or select task-specific prompts, programs, skills, or policies. Model parameters remain fixed throughout evaluation. No demonstrations at evaluation time. The agent receives the task specification and permitted observations, without additional solution examples or expert demonstrations. For memory tasks, the benchmark-defined event sequence forms part of the case's observation input. One execution per case. Each case is initialized and executed once, without a reset or rerun. Its outcome is recorded whether the episode succeeds or fails. Within-episode adaptation. An episode comprises successive model decisions, observations, and physical actions. During this interaction, the agent may inspect the scene, write and revise programs, preview motions, revisit its history, and recover from a failed grasp or placement. Recovery continues from the physical state left by earlier actions under the remaining execution budget, rather than resetting the scene to start over. Plans, generated code, and interaction memory evolve within the current episode and are not transferred to subsequent evaluation cases. compares six aspects of target-task preparation and information available to the test agent across representative manipulation settings (scope and per-setting qualifications are detailed in ). The Planning--Execution Gap sec:gap Deciding without the arm. To separate what a vision-language model decides from how the robot arm executes it, we run the same harness with one additional privileged action, which moves an object along waypoints given by the model without using the arm. The model still chooses the object and every target pose from its own perception. The object moves under simulated physics, stops at a collision, and settles under gravity at the end, after which the action reports where the object came to rest. Success under this action therefore estimates what the model's own decisions achieve when execution by the arm is taken out of the loop. We compare it with two executed systems on the same 210 episodes, five for each of the 42 RoboDojo tasks ( ). The first is RoboProbe~ unexpected2026 , the reference harness released with the evaluation of GPT-6 Astra on RoboDojo~ robodojo2026 , and the second is . Averaged over the five dimensions, the success rate is 76.2 with the privileged action, 22.5 for RoboProbe, and 59.2 for . The model therefore decides considerably better than it executes, and recovers 68.3 of this planning--execution gap in SR (70.6 in Score). Why common paradigms leave the gap open. Two common ways of placing a general model on a robot address execution only indirectly. In step-wise action output, as in the reference harness and in VLA policies~ pi052025,xvla2025,unexpected2026 , the model emits one motion step or chunk per call from the latest frames. It never sees the route of a motion before committing to it, and a failed motion is noticed only when the model reads the next frame, by which time the arm has already moved. In code as policy~ liang2023code,capx2026 , the model writes a program that commands the control interface directly. Execution judgment then moves into a program that cannot see the scene. A failure is detected only if the program was written to check for it, and a program may exit normally even after the motions it requested have failed. keeps the judgment with the model, which describes a complete action sequence in each call rather than a single step. Before execution, the model can see the whole trajectory, its cost, and its projection on the camera image ( ), and the harness checks the measured outcome after every movement ( ). General-Purpose Harness Evolution sec:rsi_positioning sec:exp-rsi Improvement in embodied agents can target either a procedure for a particular task or the shared capabilities used across many tasks~ duan2026lastai,zhou2026physicalrsi . Within-task trial search versus cross-task tool evolution. Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI) groups autonomous improvement into six levels from L0 to L5~ duan2026lastai : L0--L2 (within-task search and refinement): Under a single-task objective, the system repeats trials to adjust a trajectory, script, or task note, so the resulting gains stay mainly on the practiced task. L3--L4 (cross-task experience and tool evolution): The system turns recurring failures across different tasks into reusable tools, interfaces, and verification steps that apply to unseen tasks. L5 (meta-improvement): The system revises its own perception, control, and verification mechanisms so that later tasks are solved more reliably. title: ClothDojo: Learned Data Generation and Benchmarking for Bimanual Garment Flattening and Folding
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://clothdojo.github.io/
summary: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.
full_text: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge. Introduction sec:introduction Garment flattening and folding require visual understanding and bimanual control throughout long sequences of interaction. Garments differ in structure and appearance. Wrinkles and self-occlusion hide relevant parts, and each contact changes the cloth configuration and the conditions for subsequent actions. Policies must continually adjust to the outcomes of their actions. Training across garments therefore requires continuous trajectories covering many initial states. Collecting these trajectories on real robots is time-consuming and requires repeatedly setting up complex configurations that are difficult to reproduce. Differences in robots and scenes further limit the reuse of data and experiments, making training and evaluation at scale costly. Simulation allows initial states to be reused and rollouts to run in batches, but successful trajectories must still be designed or collected. Task-specific primitives, keypoint planners, and prescribed scripts can execute fixed procedures at scale, but cannot readily capture the state-dependent action transitions in long-horizon garment manipulation. Fig.~ fig:folding-trajectories illustrates such behaviors: flattening involves midair regrasping, dynamic unfolding, and local adjustment, while folding involves hand switching, rotation, and post-fold refinement. Their timing, arm assignment, and subsequent adjustments depend on the cloth state produced by preceding actions and are difficult to prescribe as a uniform procedure. Human teleoperation naturally produces such trajectories, but its cost scales with the number collected. We therefore study how to extend adaptive garment manipulation to more garments and initial states. Real-robot laundry systems show that demonstrations, human corrections, and autonomous experience can form an effective data collection and learning cycle~ pistar06,chi0,demavla . Inspired by these systems, ClothDojo trains a closed-loop data-generation policy to collect trajectories from new states. We first train the policy on human demonstrations with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then perform batched rollouts. Task metrics automatically retain successful trajectories. For failed executions, a human selects states and provides human-in-the-loop (HIL) corrections to update the policy. Simulation also allows normalized object coordinate space (NOCS) to be encoded as the garment texture. Through the standard image interface of a vision-language-action model (VLA), these coordinates provide canonical surface-position cues for learning cloth interaction. Successful trajectories are then re-rendered with randomized appearances to train downstream RGB policies without NOCS. Human effort is thus concentrated on demonstrations and necessary corrections, while the data-generation policy scales trajectory collection through autonomous rollouts. As shown in Fig.~ fig:framework , ClothDojo connects learned trajectory generation, data expansion, and closed-loop evaluation through dynamic interaction between bimanual robots and cloth. Our contributions are: A simulation and evaluation platform. A simulation platform for continuous bimanual garment manipulation, with shared interfaces for human teleoperation, policy rollouts, and closed-loop evaluation. Learned data generation. A data-generation pipeline that learns from human demonstrations and corrections, uses NOCS through a VLA's image interface, and autonomously collects trajectories without task-specific primitives. Trajectory data and training value. Nearly 8,000 successful trajectories across hundreds of garments. Under the same human supervision budget, RGB policies trained on generated data outperform those trained directly on human data across all evaluated garment and appearance conditions. Related Work sec:related-work Garment manipulation policies Many methods define a set of task-specific primitives for garment flattening and folding. A policy selects a primitive or predicts parameters such as grasp locations from visual observations, while a predefined controller executes the continuous motion~ flingbot,clothmate,clothfunnels,speedfolding,unifolding . The policy can observe the cloth again between primitives, and some primitives also use feedback during operations such as stretching. These action priors reduce the learning space and have been used for flattening multiple garment types and for structured folding. Another approach learns continuous actions from data. Recent VLAs directly predict action chunks and perform long sequences of picking up, flattening, folding, and stacking garments on real robots~ pistar06,chi0,demavla . These systems establish initial behavior with human demonstrations, expose failures through autonomous rollouts, and use human corrections to cover states encountered by the policy. This learning cycle also lets the policy learn action ordering, bimanual coordination, and adjustments during execution. Simulation environments and data generation Existing garment simulation platforms provide diverse garment assets and dynamic robot--cloth interaction for tasks including flattening and folding~ garmentlab,dexgarmentlab,lehome,simweaver . Their publicly described trajectories primarily come from task primitives, demonstration transfer, or limited teleoperation. Automatic trajectory expansion largely follows two approaches. Programmatic methods construct trajectories using keypoints, task stages, or folding patterns~ foldnet,instantfold . Demonstration transfer adapts segmented behaviors to new assets and initial states, then executes them to obtain new physical trajectories~ softmimicgen,sim1 . Existing large-scale results mainly concern folding tasks with well-defined steps. For severely crumpled garments, however, the course of flattening changes with the cloth state, making fixed procedures and segmented demonstrations difficult to reuse directly. ClothDojo brings the demonstration--rollout--correction cycle used in real-robot garment manipulation to simulation trajectory generation. The data-generation policy learns from human interaction and then runs autonomously on diverse garments and complex initial states; Fig.~ fig:folding-trajectories shows examples of the resulting behavior. Method sec:method ClothDojo separates physical trajectory generation from RGB training-data construction (Fig.~ fig:method-framework ). We first train NOCS-conditioned data-generation policies from human demonstrations and corrections, then deploy them on a broader set of garments and initial states. Task metrics automatically retain successful rollouts. We sample one appearance for each retained trajectory and replay its states to render RGB observations for downstream policy training. Interaction environment and tasks ClothDojo combines MuJoCo robot dynamics~ todorov2012mujoco with Newton's SolverStyle3D cloth solver~ newton to support continuous bimanual control. Virtual reality (VR) teleoperation and policy execution use the same physics, so human demonstrations, corrections, and autonomous rollouts share the same robot--cloth interaction. We convert more than 10,000 garments from the large-scale parametric GarmentCodeData dataset~ GarmentCodeData into simulation assets and select 500 structurally diverse garments as a core pool for trajectory generation and evaluation. Human demonstrations and corrections are not restricted to this pool. As shown in Fig.~ fig:garment-assets , this set spans large variations in garment length, body width, sleeve length, and sleeve width, and includes sleeveless, hooded, low-cut, open-back, asymmetric, and unconventional designs. Flattening starts from a crumpled state produced by randomly hanging, releasing, and settling a garment. The goal is a naturally flat, face-up configuration. All four cardinal orientations on the table are accepted, and its position within the tabletop is unconstrained. Folding starts from a preconstructed state that satisfies the flattening criterion. Depending on data availability, these states come from human-demonstration endpoints, successful rollouts from the data-generation policy, or standard flattened configurations. The goal is a compact, flat rectangular bundle with little protruding material. We prescribe no aspect ratio, crease pattern, or action order. Initial states for both tasks are saved in advance so that policies can run from identical states; the quantitative success criteria are given in Sec.~ sec:success-criteria . NOCS-conditioned data-generation policies We encode normalized object coordinate space (NOCS)~ wang2019nocs as the garment texture to provide a consistent surface-position reference as the cloth deforms. Let denote a vertex of the canonical mesh, with component-wise bounds and . Its normalized coordinate is whose three components form the RGB channels. Each color is assigned in the canonical configuration and remains attached to the corresponding vertex as the garment deforms. Similar relative positions across garments therefore receive similar colors. This exposes canonical surface-position cues through the model's existing image interface. The policy still observes only visible surfaces, and matching colors do not imply exact semantic correspondence across garments. We use the pretrained model~ pi05 as the base and separately fine-tune data-generation policies for flattening and folding. Each policy receives NOCS images through the model's original visual interface, together with the robot state and task instruction, and predicts joint targets and gripper commands for both arms. During execution, the policy applies only a prefix of each predicted action sequence and then replans from the latest observation, producing a closed-loop trajectory. Learning from demonstrations and corrections sec:experience-corrections We collect separate flattening and folding demonstrations through VR teleoperation. To collect a folding demonstration, we restore the final state of its corresponding flattening demonstration and continue from that state. The demonstrations for each task are recorded separately and used to fine-tune the respective data-generation policies with the base model's action-prediction objective. Sec.~ sec:trajectory-agent-eval reports the garment coverage and number of demonstrations. To cover states visited by the data-generation policies, we collect one round of human corrections in a DAgger-like manner~ DAgger . For each task, we first generate a candidate pool of 800 autonomous rollouts. A human collector selects executions

title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
summary: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.
full_text: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions.
