At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, thereby its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67 , the highest among the evaluated -based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with . Introduction Early vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla build on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and generate actions through next-token prediction. However, such autoregressive prediction suffers from slow inference and limited action precision. Along another line of research, diffusion policy~ chi2025diffusion produces multimodal actions with higher speed and precision. Motivated by these complementary strengths, recent works combine the understanding capability of pretrained VLMs with the multimodal modeling capability of diffusion or flow action experts~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2504pi0,bjorck2025gr00t . In these models, the VLM typically serves only as a static condition during both training and inference, while the action expert performs the entire denoising process. This design can be sufficient for in-domain tasks, where the model mainly learns relatively simple mappings from visual and language inputs to actions. However, it decouples perception from control. When facing out-of-distribution tasks, the action expert cannot effectively leverage the perception and reasoning capabilities of the VLM, which often leads to characteristic failure modes~ chen2026robodojo,nasiriany2026robocasa365 . In addition, the VLM learns about actions only through gradients passed back from the action expert. The VLM should therefore dynamically participate in action generation rather than only provide a static condition. As mentioned above, given the current visual state and a language instruction, pretrained VLMs can plan actions and be adapted into strong action generation models. Furthermore, prior work~ cen2025worldvla shows that given the current clean action as a condition, the model can inversely predict the next visual state. In image generation, RepFusion~ pan2026repfusion also lets the semantic condition change with the current noisy state during denoising. Here, we take these observations as a design principle for action generation. If a VLM can perceive clean action representations, can it also process their noisy counterparts during denoising? Answering this question requires noisy actions to be represented in a form that is compatible with the VLM and has meaningful semantic structure, which recent action tokenizers~ pertsch2025fast,zhou2026beast,dong2026actioncodec,liu2026oat,liu2026g0 make possible. Based on this idea, we propose (Joint Action DEnoiser), a VLA model in which a pretrained VLM denoises actions jointly with the action expert, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser . Our approach consists of three key designs. (1) In addition to visual and textual inputs, we feed compact latents of the current noisy action into the pretrained VLM. At every denoising step, the resulting VLM features condition the action expert, which denoises the action in its native action space. This design lets the VLM apply its strength in understanding structured representations to action generation. (2) To further unify perception and control, we supervise the VLM to predict clean action latents from noisy ones, which provides it with a direct action-learning signal from demonstrations. (3) Because each denoising step is better informed, can use far fewer steps, which largely offsets the extra latency of joint denoising, and an adaptive step-size schedule further balances performance and efficiency. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*] We propose , a VLA framework in which the VLM reads the current noisy action at every denoising step and guides the action expert. This lets the VLM provide dynamic denoising priors beyond static vision-language conditioning. We find that joint denoising makes action generation easier, so ~can use far fewer denoising steps than conventional flow-based VLAs. With an adaptive step-size schedule, ~further balances performance and efficiency. We show that ~consistently improves over its ~ intelligence2504pi0 base on RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo , and four real-world bimanual tasks, and ablations verify the effectiveness of its key designs. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Early VLAs discretize continuous controls and predict action tokens within the language-model sequence~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla . More recent VLAs use diffusion or flow action generators, where features from a pretrained vision-language backbone condition a continuous action expert~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2504pi0,bjorck2025gr00t . We follow this paradigm but enable the VLM to dynamically participate in the iterative refinement of the evolving action. Action Tokenizers. Action tokenizers connect continuous control with sequence modeling. Early approaches quantize each action dimension independently~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla , and later methods exploit temporal structure through frequency-domain compression, learned discrete codes, or structured latent representations~ pertsch2025fast,wang2025vq,dong2026actioncodec,liu2026oat . JADE builds on OAT~ liu2026oat and uses its compact latents to let the VLM read the current noisy action. Integration of Language Models and Denoisers Multimodal generative models increasingly combine pretrained semantic models with diffusion or flow generators, through learned queries~ pan2025transfer,chen2025blip3 , through shared attention, Mixture-of-Transformers, and unified architectures~ shi2026lmfusion,deng2025emerging,zhou2025transfusion,ma2025janusflow , or through conditions that change with the current noisy state~ pan2026repfusion . Robot learning shows a similar trend, where VLMs are coupled with continuous action generators through attention, shared representations, or intermediate action abstractions~ black2024pi_0,bjorck2025gr00t,bi2025motus,agarwal2026cosmos,li2026rotvla . However, in many modular diffusion and flow VLAs, the vision-language features used for action generation do not depend on the evolving noisy action. JADE instead contextualizes the current noisy action with vision and language in the VLM and feeds the resulting features to the action expert at every denoising step. Method Preliminaries Flow-based VLA Policies. Given a multimodal observation consisting of images, a language instruction, and robot state, a flow-based VLA policy couples a pretrained VLM of hidden width with a continuous action expert to predict a future action chunk ~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2504pi0 . The width includes padded dimensions, and the superscript keeps the valid physical dimensions of any action-shaped tensor, such as . Training uses conditional flow matching, interpolating clean actions with Gaussian noise as The action expert predicts a velocity that regresses , and at inference this velocity is integrated from Gaussian noise at toward clean actions at . Ordered Action Tokenization. OAT~ liu2026oat uses a transformer encoder with learnable registers to aggregate information across an action chunk into compact continuous latents . Through nested dropout, its training encourages an ordered representation, with earlier registers capturing coarse action structure and later registers encoding finer details. The original OAT framework discretizes these latents using finite scalar quantization (FSQ), while uses their continuous values before rounding as the action interface to the VLM. We pretrain OAT through action reconstruction in the same normalized action space as the policy and keep it frozen, and we write for the latents of a noisy action and for those of the clean action. We choose OAT because its few compact registers keep the per-step VLM cost low and it performs best among the action representations we tested. Other representations also improve over , as Section~ sec:ablation shows, so the benefit of joint denoising does not hinge on this choice. Appendices~ app:flow_preliminaries and~ app:oat_preliminaries give more details. Noisy Action Representations for VLM sec:encoding_noisy_action As shown in Figure~ fig:jade_architecture (b), uses the VLM to transform the current noisy action into observation-conditioned register features at each denoising step. Given a noisy action , the frozen OAT encoder produces continuous latents , and a trainable input adapter maps them to the VLM input . The same VLM that encodes the observation prefix then processes these registers, and we denote the layer-wise keys and values of the prefix by . At each layer, the registers attend to valid prefix tokens and bidirectionally to one another, while the prefix does not attend to them, so is computed once per observation and reused across denoising steps. Each register hidden state further passes through a bottleneck residual adapter shared across layers, which preserves the compact register sequence while adapting its features. We write the resulting register features at each of the layers and at the final output as where denotes the VLM computation together with the shared adapter, which Appendix~ app:semantic_adapter describes in detail. To give the VLM a direct action-learning signal, a linear head predicts the clean OAT latents from the final register features with averaged over registers and latent dimensions. The VLM thus learns to recover clean action latents from the observation and a noisy action. Because the adapter is shared across layers, the structure it learns under this supervision also shapes the layer-wise features , which guide the action expert as described in Section~ sec:joint_denoising . Joint Denoising with the VLM sec:joint_denoising We incorporate the action-state-dependent VLM features from Section~ sec:encoding_noisy_action into the action expert, allowing both pathways to contribute to velocity prediction. In each native expert layer, action queries attend to the valid observation prefix and all action positions, with attention weights normalized over the combined key set. The observation prefix does not attend to actions. title: Same Path, Less Time: Training-Free Fast Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models under Inference Latency
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, yet deployed robots waste time in two ways that are independent of model capability: they halt while the next chunk is inferred, and they move at the speed of slow, cautious demonstrations. Existing remedies remove one loss each, and stacking them fails, because asynchrony and speed-up each change the correspondence between planned progress and executed motion. We present Path-preserving Time Scaling (PTS), a training-free execution layer for frozen action-chunking policies built on one principle: the robot's motion is a time reparameterization of a reference path, and the path changes only in response to new observations. A path layer decodes every replan deterministically in one step and enters it at the progress consumed during inference. A time layer sums the planned increments, keeps the arm at 1x while the gripper moves, and caps the rate by the actuator's linear range and by chunk feasibility under latency. We show that misaligned entry and stochastic sampling add a bias and a variance to the continuation error, and derive a break-even success rate that states when speeding up pays off. On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs under injected inference latency, PTS raises task throughput over the strongest deployable baseline by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA while matching or improving the success rate, is best on all six model-suite combinations, and exceeds zero-latency 1x execution. Against asynchronous 1x execution with the same one-step decoder, the time layer alone adds 28% and 38%. On LIBERO-Dynamic it improves on stop-and-wait execution by 38% and is comparable to asynchronous 1x execution.

Existing remedies remove one loss each, and stacking them fails, because asynchrony and speed-up each change the correspondence between planned progress and executed motion. We present Path-preserving Time Scaling ( ), a training-free execution layer for frozen action-chunking policies built on one principle: the robot's motion is a time reparameterization of a reference path, and the path changes only in response to new observations. A path layer decodes every replan deterministically in one step and enters it at the progress consumed during inference. A time layer sums the planned increments, keeps the arm at 1 while the gripper moves, and caps the rate by the actuator's linear range and by chunk feasibility under latency. We show that misaligned entry and stochastic sampling add a bias and a variance to the continuation error, and derive a break-even success rate that states when speeding up pays off. On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs under injected inference latency, raises task throughput over the strongest deployable baseline by 33 for and 104 for while matching or improving the success rate, is best on all six model--suite combinations, and exceeds zero-latency 1 execution. Against asynchronous 1 execution with the same one-step decoder, the time layer alone adds 28 and 38 . On LIBERO-Dynamic it improves on stop-and-wait execution by 38 and is comparable to asynchronous 1 execution. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs) brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,pi2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla predict action chunks, short sequences of future actions zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion . The default deployment is synchronous: infer a chunk, execute part of it, stop, and infer again. This wastes time in two ways that do not depend on how capable the model is. First, the robot stands still during every inference: if one inference takes about 150\,ms, a 20\,Hz robot pauses for three steps after every eight it executes. Second, execution is locked to the speed of the demonstrations, which are typically slow, cautious teleoperation. a shows both losses in one episode. This paper removes both for a frozen policy, without any training. Why the two fixes do not compose Each loss has a known remedy. Asynchronous execution, e.g., real-time chunking (RTC) black2025rtc , keeps the robot moving during inference but executes at 1 . Training-free speed-up such as FreeSpeed hu2026freespeed amplifies the actions but assumes synchronous execution. Stacking the two fails: run asynchronously, FreeSpeed drops the success rate of on our LIBERO-Spatial development set from 45/50 to 20/50, even with the same gripper handling as our method; keeping its speed profile but summing the planned increments instead of resampling them restores 47/50. The cause is bookkeeping. A chunk is a plan that starts at the moment its image was taken, and by the time it arrives the robot has already consumed part of it; speed-up changes how much. If the executor loses track of how much of the plan has actually been executed, the robot repeats or skips motion and leaves the planned path ( c). Key idea: separate the path from its timing An action chunk defines a planned path. If execution changes only the timing along that path, i.e., the robot follows the path the model planned but traverses it faster and never stops during inference, then speeding up reduces to shortening time inside a feasible set. This separation of path and time underlies time-optimal path parameterization (TOPP) in robotics bobrow1985time,shin1985minimum,pham2018toppra . Learned policies add two ingredients that classical TOPP lacks: closed-loop replanning makes the path a concatenation of chunks, and inference latency means the robot has moved on by the time a new chunk arrives. Execution therefore has to answer two questions. Which path should the robot follow at each instant? Our answer is that the path should change only because of new information: decode the plan for the newest observation deterministically, and enter it at the progress actually consumed during inference. How fast should it traverse that path? As fast as the actuator's linear range and the chunk's lifetime allow, but at 1 while the gripper moves, with commands formed by summing the planned increments. Results We call the resulting method Path-preserving Time Scaling ( , ). On the four LIBERO suites with frozen and under injected inference latency, raises the pooled task throughput by 33 and 104 over the strongest deployable baseline, matching the success rate on and raising it on , and is best on all six model--suite combinations ( b,c). Both layers contribute: with the same one-step decoder chen2026simple , the time layer adds 28 and 38 over asynchronous 1 execution, and deterministic decoding raises 's success rate from 0.53 to 0.805 under the same timing rules. Contributions Method. , a training-free execution layer for frozen VLAs that output relative-increment chunks. It consists of one path-layer rule (rolling continuation with deterministic one-step decoding) and three time-layer rules (incremental summation, gripper synchronization, rate limit), and has one tuned hyperparameter, the rate cap . For flow-matching policies it also makes inference cheaper than -step sampling. Analysis. A decomposition of the continuation error showing that misaligned entry adds a bias and stochastic sampling a variance ( ), and a break-even success rate that states when speeding up pays off ( ). Evaluation. Two VLAs, four LIBERO suites, six baselines, layer and rule ablations, and a dynamic benchmark (6 , 160 test episodes), plus studies of rate selection, actuator strength, and latency. Related Work sec:related Inference latency and asynchronous execution Predicting chunks reduces compounding error zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion , and most VLAs adopt this output, generated by flow matching black2024pi0,pi2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla or decoded from action tokens pertsch2025fast . Asynchronous execution keeps executing the old chunk during inference, at the price of seams between chunks and of plans conditioned on outdated observations. Training-free methods make the new chunk agree with the old one: BID selects the most consistent of several samples liu2025bid , RTC freezes the executed prefix by guided inpainting black2025rtc , FreeBar replaces guidance by a closed-form barrier yu2026freebar , PACT-VLA verifies candidates speculatively zhu2026pact , and PICES adapts the number of executed steps lee2026pices ; ships a queue-based asynchronous stack shukor2025smolvla . Training-based methods condition on the executed prefix black2025ttrtc , on future states tang2025vlash , or on the newest observation through a correction head sendai2025a2c2 , or add adapters, preference learning, or streaming decoding jiang2026futurertc,zhu2026deflect,lu2026faster,li2026flashvla,yang2026eaglevla ; agouzoul2026async compares them under one protocol. Apart from VLASH, which also speeds up execution (discussed below), these methods execute at 1 . The path layer of approaches inter-chunk consistency differently: instead of steering a random sample toward the old chunk, it removes sampling randomness that carries no new information and enters the new plan at the consumed progress. It needs no guidance (RTC guidance multiplies inference time by about 1.8 in our implementation), and one-step decoding makes inference faster. title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
summary: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.

Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key--value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78\,s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0\,s. Under a 0.25\,s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1 starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0\,s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24--2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00--5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets. Introduction sec:intro The computing architecture of a robot is changing. A capable vision--language model (VLM) can serve as a brain: it observes the scene, reasons about task progress, and selects tools. A vision--language--action (VLA) policy such as ~ pi05 transforms an instruction into a short sequence of motor actions. A coding-agent-style harness connects the two: the brain chooses a tool, receives its result, extends its context, and chooses the next action. Serving these brains from a shared graphics processing unit (GPU) cluster introduces long-lived conversational key--value (KV) cache state into robotic fleet scheduling. Robotics serving research has established deadline-aware action-model scheduling, multi-model execution, and resource sharing~ rosa,robion,beyondllm . Agent serving research has established the importance of KV retention, tool-return timing, and thrashing under concurrent workloads~ continuum,concur,cachewise,efficientagent,tao . Their combination raises a new fleet-capacity question: how do the deadline of an action chunk and the working set of a frequently invoked, tool-driven brain jointly bound the number of robots a shared cluster can serve? We answer with an empirical study of the robot programs and of the serving resources they consume. We collect 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes from GPT-6-Astra running the RPent harness with . The traces contain 1,862 brain turns, 216 VLA-tool invocations, and 1,582 VLA inference chunks. We profile VLA latency and deadline-limited capacity, measure the compute cost of a Qwen3.6-27B brain proxy on H800 GPUs, and replay the measured growing-context request sequences on a real vLLM large language model (LLM) serving engine. summarizes the two resource constraints and the measurement design. 1: the brain is a frequent, long-lived participant in control. The median brain context is 78k tokens and the maximum reaches 215k. Brain turns occur 8.6 as often as VLA-tool entry points. The measured Astra request latency is 7.78\,s at the median, while the median intervening environment-step gap is 1.0\,s. A high-level agent can therefore spend substantially more time reasoning than its robot spends advancing between calls. This creates frequent reuse opportunities for growing KV states. 2: robot capacity moves between deadline and KV constraints. At a five-step, 20\,Hz action deadline of 0.25\,s, the measured one-GPU VLA capacity under a 1 starvation service-level objective (SLO) is one robot. At a 1.0\,s deadline, the tested capacity reaches at least 32. Meanwhile, retaining a 130k-token brain prefix reduces the modeled 150-token call time from about 6.8\,s to 1.7\,s. The deployment envelope depends on both action deadlines and brain KV residency. 3: sustained fleet demand exposes KV thrashing and the value of admission. With a continuously replenished fleet, brain serving throughput falls from approximately 2.40 requests/s at 20 virtual robots to 0.60 requests/s at 32, while computed prompt tokens rise to about 1.5 million/min. Applying established working-set admission at episode boundaries restores 2.24--2.25 requests/s and raises complete trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00--5.55 episodes/min. Finite-job comparison and transient overload tests further characterize how load duration and cache-recovery behavior shape this operating regime. The contributions are (1) a turn-resolved characterization of embodied agents' context growth, tool timing, and brain latency; (2) an experimentally grounded two-layer fleet-capacity envelope; and (3) a sustained-fleet KV-thrashing analysis with admission benefits measured at both server-request and complete-program levels. Together these findings establish the resource model and telemetry required to serve long-running agentic robot fleets. Background and Related Work sec:background Embodied brain--VLA systems. RPent exposes perception, geometric motion primitives, and VLA skills through an agent-style tool interface~ rpent . The brain repeatedly inspects intermediate results and maintains a cumulative multimodal conversation. In this system, the VLA is one tool in a richer program that also includes perception and geometry. The high-level model's invocation pattern follows task progress and tool results. Robotic model serving. ROSA~ rosa coordinates GPU resources for multi-model robot pipelines involving planning, safety, and action models. Robion~ robion optimizes multi-robot VLA serving through GPU resource coordination, while VLA workload characterization~ beyondllm measures deadline-constrained inference and overlap between action and computation. Our study complements these systems by measuring the persistent context state and tool-return timing of a general-purpose agent brain alongside action-model deadline capacity. Agent serving and KV-cache management. Continuum~ continuum optimizes KV preservation across tool gaps. CacheWise~ cachewise characterizes coding-agent prefixes and designs reuse-aware KV policies. EfficientAgent~ efficientagent models reuse working sets for concurrent agents. TAO~ tao incorporates tool readiness and cache value into scheduling; ScaleSim~ scalesim estimates invocation distance for multi-agent memory management. CONCUR~ concur shows KV-cache thrashing and congestion-aware agent admission. Our contribution measures how embodied agent timing, action deadlines, and continuously replenished robot programs interact with these established mechanisms. Working sets and recovery. Denning's working-set model~ denning1968 explains cyclic cache replacement and admission-based relief. Research on metastable failures~ bronson2021,huang2022 motivates testing whether a low-throughput state persists after a trigger has been withdrawn. We quantify delayed cache thrashing under sustained load and evaluate recovery following overload retraction. positions the present evaluation among robotic model-serving and agent-cache systems. The central measured interaction is between a robot's control deadline and its brain's long-lived cache working set. Methodology sec:method We combine traced embodied-agent programs, separate GPU profiling of the action and brain layers, and sustained replay of growing-context brain requests on a real serving engine. This design connects each model's measured serving cost to the dependency and timing structure of the original robot program. Task traces and timing conventions Collection. The brain is GPT-6-Astra (low reasoning effort), invoked through Codex in RPent~ rpent . The tools include rendering, geometric reasoning, scripted movement, and a LIBERO-tuned policy. A small paired no-SAM3 check produced 19/20 successes in each arm; the study uses the no-SAM3 setting. We execute ten tasks with two seeds in each of four LIBERO-PRO suites: 80 episodes, including 74 successes. Response-level logs record token use, brain elapsed time, per-tool environment steps, and VLA inference chunks. Responses are deduplicated by response ID. What an inter-turn second measures. We distinguish three clocks. Brain request latency is the recorded duration of one hosted Astra call, including the request's observed turnaround. Environment-step gap is the number of steps advanced between consecutive brain calls divided by the 20\,Hz simulation control frequency. Simulator tool gap is the corresponding original wall-clock gap, inflated by software rendering and inverse kinematics. These clocks describe complementary parts of a single robot program: the environment-step gap measures physical progression, and brain latency measures the time spent awaiting high-level decisions. draws on all 1,862 brain request records and 1,782 within-episode gaps. For the paired intervals, we compute a sum per call before taking percentiles; medians of the separate components are not added. The hosted-brain request latency has a 48.26\,s maximum. Environment-step gaps are the timing inputs to the serving replay, where the local proxy's own measured response time replaces Astra request latency. The simulator wall-clock gap quantifies execution overhead; the environment-step gap determines the replay schedule. Hardware and two-layer profiling Our node has eight H800 80\,GB GPUs connected by NVLink, with GPUs 4--7 reserved for brain measurements. The brain proxy is Qwen3.6-27B in bfloat16 (BF16) at tensor parallelism four (TP=4), served by vLLM 0.17.1 with automatic prefix caching~ vllm . The NVIDIA driver is 535.161.08; nvidia-smi reports CUDA 12.3, while the Stage 6 user-space installation is PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128 (torch.version.cuda=12.8). A four-GPU all-reduce benchmark measured about 359\,GB/s bus bandwidth. The VLA uses five denoising steps per chunk. collects the evaluated configuration and its measurement conventions. Behavior and compute cost. Hosted Astra supplies the program's call sequence, context growth, token lengths, and tool gaps. Qwen3.6-27B supplies per-call compute cost on a controllable local serving engine. Re-tokenized length estimates had a median Astra/Qwen input-token ratio near 1.03. The replay uses random token IDs preserving input lengths and exact prefixes, isolating the cost and cache dynamics of the observed request pattern. Sustained and finite replay sec:method:replay Each virtual robot issues dependent requests to the vLLM server using its previous turn's exact token prefix, the newly observed input length, and the trace's requested output length. After each response, the client advances by the recorded environment-step gap. In sustained replay, each robot immediately draws a fresh episode upon completion. In the finite comparison, every robot runs two episodes and finishes. We record full-prefix cache hits, completed request throughput, five-second Prometheus metrics, and client-side waiting. The full-prefix hit metric is conditioned on calls after the first turn of an episode. The onset measure is the first 120-second window with full-prefix hit rate below 80 ; runs without such a window contribute right-censored observations. Robot-level episode completion requires the final brain call in that episode's trace to finish; unfinished instances are recorded as censored. title: Dual Path Following for an Aerial Manipulator Under State and Input Constraints via Transverse Feedback Linearization
summary: This paper studies dual path following for a quadrotor carrying a three-degree-of-freedom arm. The center of mass of the combined system must follow a vehicle path and the end effector must follow a second path, while the arm respects its joint limits and avoids its singular postures. The vehicle and the arm are mechanically coupled, so one controller must handle both paths. With the center of mass and the end-effector path coordinates as outputs, and a dynamic extension of the thrust, the system admits a normal form without internal dynamics. We characterize the states where this normal form fails. We formulate the transverse feedback linearizing controller as a quadratic program that relaxes only the speed of the end effector along its path and imposes safety and actuator limits as inequality constraints. The program reduces to a scalar problem with a closed-form solution. If it remains strictly feasible for all time, the feedback is locally Lipschitz, both paths are invariant and attractive, and every constraint holds. In the physics engine Drake, the controller resolves a conflict between the two speed references by slowing the end effector while both paths remain invariant. By contrast, a cascade with a safety filter leaves both paths. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/am_dual_pf-/
full_text: Dual Path Following for an Aerial Manipulator Under State and Input Constraints via Transverse Feedback Linearization Hamza Tariq and Adeel Akhtar Hamza Tariq and Adeel Akhtar are with the Department of Mechanical Industrial Engineering at the New Jersey Institute of Technology, Newark, NJ 07102, USA. \ ht299, adeel.akhtar\ @njit.edu =-1 This paper studies dual path following for a quadrotor carrying a three-degree-of-freedom arm. The center of mass of the combined system must follow a vehicle path and the end effector must follow a second path, while the arm respects its joint limits and avoids its singular postures. The vehicle and the arm are mechanically coupled, so one controller must handle both paths. With the center of mass and the end-effector path coordinates as outputs, and a dynamic extension of the thrust, the system admits a normal form without internal dynamics. We characterize the states where this normal form fails. We formulate the transverse feedback linearizing controller as a quadratic program that relaxes only the speed of the end effector along its path and imposes safety and actuator limits as inequality constraints. The program reduces to a scalar problem with a closed-form solution. If it remains strictly feasible for all time, the feedback is locally Lipschitz, both paths are invariant and attractive, and every constraint holds. In the physics engine Drake, the controller resolves a conflict between the two speed references by slowing the end effector while both paths remain invariant. By contrast, a cascade with a safety filter leaves both paths. Code and animations are available at . Introduction =-1 Aerial manipulators, that is, multirotors carrying a robotic arm, are used for the inspection and maintenance of structures such as bridges, pipes and tanks~ ollero2021past . These tasks may require the end effector to trace a prescribed route along the structure while the vehicle follows a second route that keeps its rotors clear of the structure. The end effector and the vehicle must stay on their routes. The speed along them is secondary, and it may be reduced when the arm approaches a joint limit or a singular posture~ siciliano2009robotics , a configuration at which the joints can no longer move the end effector in every direction relative to the center of mass. =-1 In this work we study the dual path-following problem. Its objective is convergence of the vehicle and the end effector to their paths together with path invariance, that is, once they reach their paths they remain on them for all future time. Transverse feedback linearization (TFL)~ nielsen2008local achieves this by rendering the dynamics transverse to the path linear and controllable, so that a linear feedback makes the path invariant and attractive~ akhtar2015path . Path invariance via TFL has been shown for a single quadrotor~ akhtar2012path, allawati2026qstfl . A partial feedback linearization gives it for a manipulator on a wheeled mobile base~ gill2017path . There, only the end effector is assigned a path, and the dynamics of the base and of the arm are assumed to be decoupled. In li2016synchronized , a differential drive robot and a serial manipulator, two separate systems, are synchronized while each follows its own path. An aerial manipulator allows neither simplification. The vehicle and the arm form one mechanically coupled system. The arm moves the center of mass and the inertia of the vehicle, while the attitude moves the end effector. One system must therefore follow both paths. =-1 Control of aerial manipulators is surveyed in~ ollero2021past . Differential-flatness-based controllers and planners take the center of mass, or its momentum, with the yaw and the joint angles as flat outputs welde2021dynamically, wei2021differential . These outputs have a well-defined vector relative degree after a dynamic extension of the thrust wei2021differential . The end-effector pose is flat only for designs whose center of mass is fixed in the end-effector frame welde2020coordinate . Kinematic controllers make the end effector of a hexarotor with a three-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) arm follow a path carvajal2023path, carvajal2024multitask , but without path invariance or safety constraints. A feedback linearizing controller tracks trajectories of the base and the end effector together~ mirnajafizadeh2025unified , again without constraints. A quadratic program (QP) with actuator bounds and joint limits tracks the base position, the yaw and the end effector simultaneously laribi2026qp , but without asymptotic tracking guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, no existing controller for an aerial manipulator renders both a vehicle path and an end-effector path invariant under safety constraints. =-1 In~ tariq2026relaxed we formulate the feedback linearizing controller of a unicycle as a QP with relaxed equality constraints. In~ tariq2026decentralized we present the TFL controller of a quadrotor as a QP and relax only its along-path speed constraint, just as the stability constraint is relaxed in~ ames2016control . This preserves the path and heading dynamics exactly, while control barrier function (CBF) inequalities enforce safety. In this work we extend the relaxed QP-based TFL to a quadrotor carrying a 3-DOF arm~( ). The arm moves the center of mass and brings joint limits and singular postures that the quadrotor alone does not have. The main contributions are the following. [leftmargin=*,nosep] We propose an output, built on the flat outputs of welde2021dynamically, wei2021differential , for which the dynamically extended aerial manipulator model admits a normal form without internal dynamics, and we give its singular set in closed form ( ). We propose the TFL controller as a QP that imposes safety and actuator limits and relaxes only the speed of the end effector along its path. We show that this QP has a closed-form, locally Lipschitz solution ( ). We prove that, under strict feasibility, both paths are invariant and attractive and every constraint holds. On closed paths at low vehicle speed, a feasibility margin along the solution extends these guarantees to all time ( ). We evaluate the controller against the nominal controller and a safety-filtered cascade in Drake drake , on a Skydio X2 with an OpenMANIPULATOR-X arm. title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
summary: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.
full_text: 2 Introduction sec:introduction Recent breakthroughs in frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026astra , Opus 5.5~ opus ) have shown surprising zero-shot performance in robotic manipulation, highlighting robot-use agents (RUAs)~ isola2026robotuse as a promising approach for robotics~ rua1,rua2,rua3 . This approach effectively transfers the models' generic problem-solving capabilities, such as task decomposition and failure recovery, which are hard to learn from limited robotics data alone, yet extremely useful for robotics~ isola2026robotuse,chu2026openrua,jia2026agent . However, because these frontier foundation models are proprietary, research on RUAs has been limited to using the models as-is, such as harness design~ li2026roboharness,rua2,harness3 . Without access to their weights, researchers cannot directly explore how further training of these models can advance RUA capabilities. Moreover, API dependence makes large-scale interaction costly~ openai2026astra and restricts model-level optimization, such as efficient caching, despite inference speed being a major bottleneck for RUA~ isola2026robotuse . The main challenge in adapting open-weight models for robot use is the capability gap between open-weight and closed-weight foundation models. Robot use demands strong spatial understanding and agentic capabilities, which existing open-weight models often lack. Consequently, prior work has focused on ad-hoc improvements, including leveraging privileged information such as ground-truth simulator states or oracle task-success feedback~ fu2026cap,zhang2026harnessvla , or incorporating task-specific skills~ lu2026aspire . Before attributing these limitations to the models themselves and pursuing ad-hoc improvements, we argue that we must first establish a generalizable and effective robot-use harness to systematically understand and maximize their existing capabilities, laying the foundation for future RUA training. In this paper, we take a first step toward democratizing robot-use agent research by laying this foundation for both competitive open-weight agents and future robot-specific training. We introduce , a general-purpose RUA harness. It provides Unified tool interfaces and feedback formats across models, embodiments, tasks, and environments, supporting joint training on simulation and real-world interaction data. For future large-scale training, we emphasize Efficiency by overlapping model reasoning with tool execution to accelerate interaction, and Modularity through interchangeable agent runtimes, tools, and robot backends. Together, these designs provide a scalable, extensible foundation for RUA research. The proposed enables competitive manipulation performance with open-weight models, including Qwen and DeepSeek, in both simulation and physical environments. A key finding is that well-structured information, such as camera calibration and robot descriptions, together with reliable tool interfaces that provide informative feedback, are sufficient for effective robot use. As a result, without privileged inputs, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with achieves a Score of 31.39, surpassing GPT-6 Astra's result (28.97) on RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo from the RoboDojo team~ zhang2026unexpected . To the best of our knowledge, this is the first system to outperform closed-weight foundation models on RoboDojo using open-weight models, without privileged informations or distillation from those closed-weight models. In real-world experiments on 19 tabletop manipulation tasks, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with achieves a Score of 49.50, outperforming Dream-1 (35.50; ) and matching fine-tuned (47.75; ). Having established the competitiveness of open-weight RUAs, we further compare models across generations, families, and sizes to investigate the capabilities underlying robot use. Trajectory analysis reveals four common failure patterns involving visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning. Based on these findings, we posit that current robot-use capability emerges from a combination of these general-purpose capabilities and identify them as key areas for improvement in future RUA training. Finally, we provide an analysis of the effect of privileged information, cost, and execution efficiency. : A Unified and Modular Harness sec:harness In this section, we introduce the key mechanisms of . We describe how the harness connects diverse agents, robot environments, and embodiments through shared tools and supports interaction based on information only available in real-world deployments. System Overview sec:system-overview connects different agent runtimes to a shared toolkit for simulation and physical robots. The agent selects operations using task instructions and observations, while the harness executes them and returns feedback. We organize this interaction around four principles: Unified. Shared tools give operations and feedback a common meaning across environments, with adapters handling native APIs (Section~ sec:unified-interface ). The resulting interaction records can also be combined for subsequent training. Efficient. Reasoning should overlap physical execution, while operations that share a resource retain their required order (Section~ sec:efficient-execution ). Realistic. Agents and tools should rely on information available in physical deployments, without simulator-provided depth or task-verifier feedback (Section~ sec:realistic-inputs ). Modular. Explicit interfaces should allow researchers to replace runtimes, tools, and perception models independently. We introduce this architecture below. These principles guide how we organize the system, but reliable interaction also requires care in how observations, actions, and feedback are handled. We first describe the architecture, then examine these practical design choices in Section~ sec:key-design-choices . Modular Architecture. A tool call passes through five layers with explicit interfaces (Figure~ fig:architecture ). The agent layer manages model interaction and context, passing tool requests to the orchestration layer for scheduling and dispatch. The tool layer implements shared robot operations and accesses environment, perception, and action-model capabilities through the service layer, which manages their runtime resources. The backend layer supplies the concrete simulator, robot, and model implementations used by these services. Results return through these interfaces to the agent, completing the interaction. Unified Interaction Interface sec:unified-interface [t] 0.49 Moving a gripper to a target pose should mean the same thing in simulation and on a physical robot, even when their control APIs differ. We give agents a shared set of tools for motion, perception, skills, and episode control, with common arguments, units, and feedback formats. Environment descriptions identify the available arms, cameras, and optional capabilities. This lets the agent use familiar operations while accounting for the robot and sensors available in each environment. [t] 0.48 Tool reuse across environments. Shared tools avoid implementations. : tool; : adapter; : environment. fig:tool-reuse To make these operations work across environments, shared tools access observations, robot state, and primitive actions through a common interface implemented by environment adapters. For example, the shared move tool generates intermediate targets and monitors progress; the adapter translates those targets into native commands and returns the resulting state. Adding an environment therefore requires an adapter and its configuration rather than a separate implementation of every tool. As Figure~ fig:tool-reuse illustrates, tools can share their logic across adapters, avoiding tool--environment implementations. The common request and feedback formats also make the experience collected across environments easier to combine for subsequent training. Efficient Execution sec:efficient-execution The orchestration layer determines how agent interaction proceeds while tools are running. Waiting for every movement to finish delays reasoning that could proceed independently, yet successive movements may still need to execute in order. We combine background tool calls with resource-aware scheduling to satisfy both requirements, forming a pipeline between agent reasoning and tool execution. Two Levels of Concurrency. The agent need not wait for every tool, but its next call may still need to wait for a resource: [topsep=3pt,itemsep=2pt,parsep=0pt] Between agent and tools. A background call returns a job handle, allowing the agent to continue independent reasoning and retrieve the result later; an immediate call waits for completion. Decisions that depend on the result must still wait. Among tool calls. Calls sharing an exclusive resource execute in submission order; parallel calls run outside that queue. Two move calls on the same resource therefore run sequentially, while reading an existing snapshot can overlap movement. [t] 0.49 Two-Stage Pipelining. These mechanisms enable a two-stage pipeline comprising agent reasoning and tool execution (Figure~ fig:agent-tool-pipeline ). The agent can submit successive calls while previously submitted calls execute in resource order. Reasoning and execution thus overlap even when the tools themselves execute sequentially. When observations or execution feedback require a change of plan, the agent can use flush queue to cancel calls that have not started for a specified resource. Where supported, a single model response can submit multiple tool requests, and a batched wait can retrieve multiple results. [t] 0.48 Serial interaction and pipelining. Reasoning ( ) overlaps sequential tools ( ); queues while runs. Solid/dashed arrows show submissions/results; shading marks overlap. Timings are schematic. fig:agent-tool-pipeline Interaction Without Privileged Inputs sec:realistic-inputs Efficient execution alone does not ensure that simulation performance carries over to physical robots: the information supporting each action also matters. Existing systems provide depth-based geometry and completion checks~ li2026roboharness , or construct object models to maintain a virtual scene~ wang2026spatialharness . In physical settings, depth measurements can vary or be missing even in a static scene, and simulator task-verifier feedback is unavailable. These differences motivate testing whether agents can infer spatial relationships and assess progress from more limited observations. Key Design Choices sec:key-design-choices Effective robot use requires careful design of how observations reach the agent, how commands are executed, and how outcomes inform subsequent decisions. We introduce six practical design choices spanning observation and execution consistency, coordinated motion control, progress monitoring, actionable feedback, and visual context management. Keeping Observations and State Consistent. When a robot moves after an image is captured, interpreting a selected pixel using a newer camera pose mixes two physical states. We bind images, camera calibration, and robot state to an immutable snapshot and use that snapshot for localization (Figure~ fig:design-snapshot-consistency ). The agent and tools thus work from the same recorded state. Preventing Repeated Actions After Communication Failures. The agent must also know which actions have occurred: a missing reply may mean lost feedback, so retrying could repeat a physical action. We record request identities and execution status to reject duplicates (Figure~ fig:design-uncertain-execution ). If completion is uncertain, further actions are blocked while the session attempts to recover the execution record; unresolved requests remain explicitly marked as uncertain. title: AegisBench: Auditing Aerial Search-and-Rescue Person Detection Under the Conditions It Is Deployed In
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Accepted at the Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD) workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code and results: https://github.com/Altis-2026/SentinelBench
summary: Drone-based person detection is being adopted by emergency-management agencies to find missing people faster than ground teams can. The benchmarks behind that adoption were collected in calm, clear daylight, while the missions that trigger deployment happen in floods, wildfires, storms, and at night. AegisBench measures that gap. It applies nine physically motivated corruptions from four disaster families, each at three severities monotone in a declared image statistic or physical quantity, to two aerial search-and-rescue datasets, HERIDAL and SARD. Three architecturally distinct detectors (Faster R-CNN, YOLOv11, RT-DETR) are scored across 168 conditions by one shared evaluator, at confidence thresholds frozen on clean validation data as a fielded system would run. Robustness is highly uneven. Low light is the extreme case: a 4.5-stop exposure loss drives recall to exactly zero for all three detectors on both datasets, a result that holds under threshold-free mAP and across three training seeds, and is mirrored on 300 real night drone images, where 2 of 759 people are found. Surviving detections largely stay on target, so the failure is silent: an empty frame looks the same as one whose occupants the system cannot see. Fine-tuning on milder low-light levels recovers 0.06 to 0.19 recall at the held-out severity, at an architecture-dependent cost on other conditions, and does not transfer to real night imagery. Spatial corruptions rank differently on the two datasets, which we cannot attribute to altitude alone because their parameters scale with frame size rather than person size. We release the corruption engine, evaluation pipeline, and all per-condition results as an audit instrument for anyone evaluating these systems.
full_text: Drone-based person detection is being adopted by emergency-management agencies to find missing people faster than ground teams can. The benchmarks behind that adoption were collected in calm, clear daylight, while the missions that trigger deployment happen in floods, wildfires, storms, and at night. AegisBench measures that gap. It applies nine physically motivated corruptions from four disaster families, each at three severities monotone in a declared image statistic or physical quantity, to two aerial search-and-rescue datasets, HERIDAL and SARD. Three architecturally distinct detectors (Faster R-CNN, YOLOv11, RT-DETR) are scored across 168 conditions by one shared evaluator, at confidence thresholds frozen on clean validation data as a fielded system would run. Robustness is highly uneven. Low light is the extreme case: a 4.5-stop exposure loss drives recall to exactly zero for all three detectors on both datasets, a result that holds under threshold-free mAP and across three training seeds, and is mirrored on 300 real night drone images, where 2 of 759 people are found. Surviving detections largely stay on target, so the failure is silent: an empty frame looks the same as one whose occupants the system cannot see. Fine-tuning on milder low-light levels recovers 0.06 to 0.19 recall at the held-out severity, at an architecture-dependent cost on other conditions, and does not transfer to real night imagery. Spatial corruptions rank differently on the two datasets, which we cannot attribute to altitude alone because their parameters scale with frame size rather than person size. We release the corruption engine, evaluation pipeline, and all per-condition results as an audit instrument for anyone evaluating these systems. Introduction sec:intro Automated person detection in drone imagery is moving out of the literature and into public emergency management. Agencies fly aerial search patterns and run detectors over the footage, letting one operator review coverage that would take a ground team days to walk. The appeal is straightforward: time is the dominant factor in survival, and incident data show that most missing subjects are found within the first day, with the odds of a good outcome falling as the search lengthens~ koester2008lost . The evidence behind that adoption has a gap in it. Published results on the two standard benchmarks for this task, HERIDAL~ bozic2019heridal and SARD~ sambolek2021sard , report strong detection performance, and both datasets were collected in calm, clear, well-lit conditions. Real missions are launched because something has gone wrong: after a flood, during a wildfire, in a storm, or at night, when visibility is worst and the need for automated coverage is greatest. No existing benchmark systematically measures how these detectors behave under the visual conditions of the disasters that trigger their deployment. An agency comparing systems and a vendor reporting accuracy are both working from numbers collected in conditions the system will rarely operate in. This is a familiar pattern in applied machine learning: a model performs well on the distribution that justified its adoption and worse on the one it is deployed against~ koh2021wilds . What makes the aerial search case unusually tractable is that the deployment conditions are physically characterizable. Haze, smoke, rain, muddy water, and darkness have documented optical models, so the missing evaluation can be built rather than only argued for. AegisBench builds it. Nine physically motivated corruptions, spanning four disaster families (flood, wildfire, storm, and earthquake), are applied to the HERIDAL and SARD test sets, and three architecturally distinct detectors are evaluated across all resulting conditions. Three design choices make the result usable as an audit rather than only as a research finding. First, each corruption is built on a documented optical model of a disaster condition, such as the Koschmieder scattering model for smoke and dust, so a result maps onto a named condition an operator can recognize. Second, each corruption's three severities are calibrated against a declared, machine-checked image statistic rather than chosen by eye, so severity claims are falsifiable. Third, every detector's confidence threshold is selected once on clean validation data and frozen across all corrupted conditions, matching how a system is fielded rather than a best case that is unavailable mid-mission. Robustness turns out to be highly uneven (Figure~ fig:headline ). Low light is the extreme case: it drives recall to exactly zero on both datasets for all three architectures, a result that holds independently of the confidence threshold and across training seeds, and that has a close counterpart on real night drone imagery. The detections a model does retain largely stay on the person, so the dominant failure is a detector ceasing to find someone rather than misplacing the box. That makes it an oversight problem as well as an accuracy problem: a misplaced box is a visible error an operator can catch, while a frame with no detections is indistinguishable from a correctly searched empty one. Contributions. [leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt] A disaster-grounded corruption benchmark. Nine corruptions across four disaster families, each at three severities monotone in a declared physical or image statistic, deterministically seeded so the corrupted test sets regenerate bit-identically from the public source data (Section~ sec:design ). A deployment-realistic audit protocol and its results. Frozen operating points, one shared evaluator, bootstrap intervals, and a localization-stability axis, applied to three detectors across 168 conditions. Every per-condition number is released (Sections~ sec:protocol -- sec:results , Appendix~ app:full ). A cross-architecture low-light collapse, checked against the obvious alternative explanations (operating point, training seed, synthetic optics) and against a targeted augmentation, which moves the synthetic floor at an architecture-dependent cost elsewhere (Section~ sec:lowlight ). Evidence that the failure is silent, and a concrete condition-stratified reporting practice for systems used in disaster response (Sections~ sec:locstab and~ sec:deployment ). A low-cost, reusable audit instrument. The corruption engine, evaluator and all results are public under an MIT license, run on a single 8~GB GPU, and accept any detector behind a common interface, so agencies and other groups can audit their own systems under the same 168 conditions. Related Work sec:related Aerial search-and-rescue person detection. This task is most often benchmarked on HERIDAL~ bozic2019heridal , high-altitude imagery of wilderness terrain, and SARD~ sambolek2021sard , lower-altitude drone video of staged rescue scenarios. Both report strong accuracy from CNN detectors trained and evaluated under calm, clear conditions~ bachir2024yolov5sar . Adjacent benchmarks extend the small-person-in-large-scene setting to other domains~ yu2020tinyperson,varga2022seadronessee . The closest prior robustness evaluation on this data is the corrupted supplement released with SARD itself~ sambolek2021sard , which adds fog, snow, ice, and motion-blur variants: generic weather effects without a calibrated severity structure, reported as a single check rather than a systematic sweep. Outside that supplement, evaluation in this literature is conducted under clear conditions. Corruption-robustness benchmarking. ImageNet-C established the practice of evaluating models under a fixed suite of synthetic corruptions at graded severities~ hendrycks2019imagenetc . Michaelis et al.~ michaelis2019benchmarking carried it into object detection for driving scenes and remain the closest methodological antecedent, and 3D Common Corruptions~ kar20223dcc showed that corruptions which respect scene geometry expose failures that flat image filters miss. Our domain, our disaster-specific and statistically calibrated corruptions, and our localization-stability axis all differ. In remote sensing, Mei et al.~ mei2024robustness benchmark the natural and adversarial robustness of many classifiers and detectors on overhead imagery, using generic perturbations rather than condition-specific physical models. Robustness benchmarking for drone imagery has become active only recently: UAV-C~ liu2024uavc benchmarks UAV tracking against generic corruptions, HazyDet~ feng2024hazydet pairs synthetic haze with real foggy drone photographs for general object detection, and WRRT-DETR~ liu2025wrrtdetr builds a weather-robust detector around a maritime dataset. Each targets a different task, a narrower corruption scope, or a different domain than the sweep presented here, and most pair the benchmark with a proposed architecture. We propose no detector, so the measurement stands on its own as an audit instrument. Adverse weather and low-light vision. Our corruption models draw on the Koschmieder scattering model as formalized by Narasimhan and Nayar~ narasimhan2002vision , the linear-domain treatment of low light of Chen et al.~ chen2018dark , and the rain-streak model of Garg and Nayar~ garg2007rain . Sakaridis et al.~ sakaridis2018foggy apply synthetic fog to real driving imagery, the closest precedent for corrupting a real dataset with a physical model, and later contribute real adverse-condition data~ sakaridis2021acdc . Dehazing~ he2011dark and low-light datasets and enhancement~ loh2019exdark aim to restore images or train for darkness rather than to measure how a fielded detector degrades. Small persons in HERIDAL-scale frames motivate the tiled inference we adopt~ akyon2022sahi . Documentation for deployed systems. Our framing follows the model- and dataset-documentation literature, which argues that systems entering consequential use need standardized statements of intended use and of the conditions under which performance was measured~ gebru2021datasheets,mitchell2019modelcards . Model cards in particular call for results disaggregated by relevant conditions. For this task the relevant conditions are environmental, and the disaggregated number has never been measured, so there has been nothing to put in the card. We supply the measurement and release the instrument that produced it. Benchmark Design sec:design Nine corruptions are organized into four disaster families: flood ( , , ), wildfire ( , ), storm ( , , ), and earthquake and post-disaster ( ). Each models a documented optical signature of its disaster family rather than a generic image-processing filter (Figure~ fig:taxonomy , Table~ tab:taxonomy ). Grouping by family lets a result read as ``this system loses of detections in wildfire smoke,'' which is the form an operational decision needs. Earthquakes have no optical signature of their own; what degrades post-collapse imagery is suspended dust, so the family is represented by one physically distinct corruption rather than padded with relabelled copies of others. Optical models. The three haze-family corruptions ( , , ) use the Koschmieder atmospheric scattering model~ koschmieder1924theorie,narasimhan2002vision , , with a spatially varying transmission field . They differ in the chromaticity of the airlight (neutral gray for combustion smoke, brown for mineral dust, warm for firelit haze), in the spatial frequency of the transmission field, and, for dust, in coarse near-lens grain; the smoke and dust chromaticity difference is enforced by a unit test on the red-to-blue ratio.
