title: SCOUT: Planning under Occlusion via Object-Centric World Model Rollouts
summary: Robots manipulating in cluttered spaces must often plan from partial views where foreground objects occlude the target, surrounding geometry, and usable free space. Reactive policies often miss these hidden constraints, while exhaustive search becomes computationally prohibitive in dense clutter. We present SCOUT, an occlusion-aware planning framework that bridges high-level deliberation with grounded physical rollouts. SCOUT leverages an object-centric scene representation to reconstruct hidden geometry and derive a relational planning state capturing blocker hierarchies and accessibility corridors. To navigate the vast action space in clutter, an LLM proposes structured action candidates which are then rigorously evaluated via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) using a learned action-conditioned world model. Evaluations on 'Reveal' and 'Placement' tasks show that SCOUT outperforms Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, embodied agents, and 3D world models, with significant gains in long-horizon tasks requiring reasoning over occluded geometry. We further validate the framework's robustness through real-world robotic manipulation in a cluttered shelf environment.
full_text: Robots manipulating in cluttered spaces must often plan from partial views where foreground objects occlude the target, surrounding geometry, and usable free space. Reactive policies often miss these hidden constraints, while exhaustive search becomes computationally prohibitive in dense clutter. We present , an occlusion-aware planning framework that bridges high-level deliberation with grounded physical rollouts. leverages an object-centric scene representation to reconstruct hidden geometry and derive a relational planning state capturing blocker hierarchies and accessibility corridors. To navigate the vast action space in clutter, an LLM proposes structured action candidates which are then rigorously evaluated via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) using a learned action-conditioned world model. Evaluations on `Reveal' and `Placement' tasks show that outperforms Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, embodied agents, and 3D world models, with significant gains in long-horizon tasks requiring reasoning over occluded geometry. We further validate the framework’s robustness through real-world robotic manipulation in a cluttered shelf environment. Introduction Manipulation in cluttered, occluded spaces is fundamentally difficult because the objects and free space that matter most are often not directly visible dogar2012nonprehensile,wong2013activeoccluded . A target may be buried behind front-row blockers in a shelf, reachable only through a narrow corridor that is itself occluded or only after several intermediate rearrangements danielczuk2019mechanical,bejjani2021occlusion . Reasoning about these unobservable spaces to manipulate in clutter requires a robot to move beyond purely reactive visual feedback, necessitating deliberation across possible environment and object layouts and their intricate relationships among each other. A natural way to enable such deliberation is to plan in belief space, where the robot represents unobserved scene structure and reasons over possible hidden configurations kaelbling2013beliefspace . For occluded manipulation, such a belief must capture more than the mere existence of hidden objects. The planner must also reason about which object is likely to block the target and where free space may exist around it. This suggests an explicit scene representation that captures object-level geometry and spatial structure, rather than only symbolic hidden-state hypotheses. Moreover, representing the hidden scene is only part of the problem. To manipulate in clutter, the robot must also reason about how that scene representation will evolve under candidate actions. It therefore needs a world model that predicts how an action reveals the target, creates free space, or simply changes the occlusion pattern hafner2019planet . Recent progress in vision-language and foundation-model-based robotics has improved action selection from observed images and led to strong results in semantic grounding, skill selection, program synthesis, and visually guided planning ichter2023saycan, liang2023codeaspolicies, singh2023progprompt, huang2023voxposer, nasiriany2024pivot, liu2024okrobot . These methods are effective when the relevant objects and affordances are visible, showing that large models can provide useful high-level structure for robotic decision making. World models and search offer a complementary route by supporting imagination-based planning over candidate futures schrittwieser2020muzero, hafner2023dreamerv3, wu2022daydreamer, yang2024unisim, bar2025nwm , and recent language-guided search methods combine Large Language Models (LLMs) with search to improve long-horizon decision making chang2024lgmcts, dainese2024gifmcts . However, these approaches still largely operate over the currently observed scene or over abstract state representations that do not explicitly capture the hidden 3D structure created by physical clutter, which are essential for occluded manipulation. We therefore present , a planning framework for manipulation under occlusion that combines hidden-scene reconstruction, action-conditioned prediction, and LLM-based deliberation. Given a small number of RGB-D observations from the frontal viewpoints, our reconstruction module, GHOST (Geometry-aware Hallucination for Occluded Scene Topology), produces an object-centric scene representation capturing geometry and occupancy beyond the observed view. A learned world model predicts how this representation evolves under discrete object-level actions hafner2019planet . An LLM proposes structured action candidates, and a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)~ browne2012survey module evaluates simulated rollouts under the learned world model. The next primitive is selected via grounded search, and planning repeats from the updated state. We evaluate the method on cluttered manipulation tasks in which targets are initially occluded, partially observable, and require multi-step rearrangement to access dogar2012nonprehensile, wong2013activeoccluded . In these settings, we find that planning over reconstructed scene structure and simulated futures is more effective than relying on visible-only reasoning or one-shot language predictions alone. Our contributions are: 0.25em A structured hidden-scene representation for occluded manipulation from sparse frontal RGB-D views. A planning method that reasons over this representation using a learned world model and LLM-guided search. Simulation and real-robot validation on cluttered multi-step rearrangement tasks. Related Work Planning under Occlusion with Hidden-Scene Models. Planning under occlusion is classically a belief-space problem kaelbling1998planning . In embodied AI, recent work has addressed hidden targets and incomplete maps through semantic priors, diffusion-based planning, and uncertainty-aware task-and-motion planning. PONI predicts potential locations of unseen targets from partial semantic maps ramakrishnan2022poni , while value-guided diffusion planning explicitly targets navigation under partial observability through multi-step candidate generation and best-plan selection zhang2024valueguided . TAMPURA and related partially observable TAMP methods reason under action uncertainty using symbolic belief representations and information-gathering strategies curtis2024tampura, kaelbling1998planning , with extensions incorporating LLM-guided state estimation over hidden objects kim2026cocotamp . Occluded planning further depends on reconstructing hidden 3D structure from limited observations. Prior work in semantic scene completion and open-world 3D scene understanding reconstructs geometry and semantics beyond the field of view cao2022monoscene, li2023voxformer, nguyen2024open3dis, agarwal2024scenecomplete . Spatially aware robot foundation models show that explicit geometric alignment improves manipulation quality and generalization qu2025spatialvla, li2025spatialforcing , while recent work leverages robot trajectories and test-time adaptation to improve action semantics and value estimation chen2025robo2vlm, ziakas2026vita . In contrast, we address planning under occlusion in cluttered 3D scenes by reasoning over a reconstructed hidden scene and using an action-conditioned world model to evaluate how different actions reveal previously unobserved structure. Language and vision foundation models for robotics. Foundation-model approaches have enabled robots to select skills, synthesize code, and plan trajectories from language and images ichter2023saycan, liang2023codeaspolicies, singh2023progprompt, huang2023voxposer . PIVOT shows that iterative visual prompting can substantially improve spatial decision-making by repeatedly refining proposals rather than committing to one-shot predictions nasiriany2024pivot . OK-Robot demonstrates how open-knowledge components can be composed into a robust mobile-manipulation pipeline, while recent analysis highlights the importance of spatial grounding and operational detail when integrating such modules liu2024okrobot . Our method differs from these works in two key respects: it explicitly reasons over a hidden-scene belief rather than only visible observations, and it uses the language model as a search prior, while the world model and MCTS perform physical evaluation and final action selection. World models and search for embodied planning. Learned world models have proved effective for planning and policy improvement in games and control, including MuZero, Dreamer, and DayDreamer schrittwieser2020muzero, hafner2023dreamerv3, wu2022daydreamer . More recent simulators and generative world models expand this perspective to real-world video and navigation yang2024unisim, bar2025nwm . Language-guided search has also been explored for object rearrangement and code world-model generation chang2024lgmcts, dainese2024gifmcts . Our goal is not to simply attach an LLM to search. Instead, the LLM narrows the object-action space using the relational planning state, while MCTS and the learned world model evaluate candidate futures and select the final plan from grounded rollout evidence. Method We address long-horizon manipulation under partial observability by combining an object-centric scene representation, a learned world model, and an LLM that generates structured action proposals for planning. Our formulation explicitly separates (i) action proposal generation from the relational planning state, from (ii) physical feasibility and multi-step outcome prediction, handled by the learned world model. Fig.~ fig:overview provides an overview of , from hidden-scene reconstruction and LLM-guided action proposals to world-model rollouts and final plan selection. The complete execution flow of the system is detailed in Algorithm~ alg:scout . Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulatio We consider manipulation under partial observability, where an agent must plan a sequence of object-level actions from a limited set of observations. Each instance is defined by a hidden scene state , a goal specification , and a finite action budget . The agent receives a set of RGB-D observations captured from frontal viewpoints, providing partial visibility of objects, free space, and access corridors. The objective is to compute a finite-horizon action sequence , where , that achieves the task goal. The action space consists of object-centric manipulation primitives , where indexes the manipulated object and . In the initial-view protocol, the scene is reconstructed once from , and subsequent planning states are updated using the world model without re-observation. We consider four task families instantiated from a shared distribution of cluttered shelf scenes: Reveal, Reveal Multi, Place, and Place Multi. Each task defines a binary success condition evaluated at the end of the sequence. Reveal tasks require the target to be visible and accessible, while placement tasks require the object to lie within a goal region, with Reveal Multi and Place Multi being the counterparts over multiple objects. The system operates over a reconstructed scene representation obtained from observations, and a derived planning state capturing task-relevant structure (Sec.~3.2). A learned world model predicts state transitions (Sec.~3.3), enabling simulation of action-conditioned future states. The planner can be viewed as a mapping , which uses the reconstructed scene representation, LLM action proposals, and world-model predictions to evaluate candidate action sequences up to horizon . title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
summary: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9$\times$ the success, 5.4$\times$ the generalization, and 3.9$\times$ the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8$\times$ faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Natura non facit saltus. \\ (Nature does not make jumps.) \\[2pt] --- , 1704 Robot learning has advanced rapidly in the past few years. In imitation learning (IL), visuomotor policies~ dp,zhao2023learning , vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t , and world action models (WAMs)~ zhang2026imagewam, an2026feedback, hou2026world now perform a wide range of manipulation tasks. In reinforcement learning (RL), actors trained in massively parallel simulation let legged and humanoid robots walk and track human motions~ rudin2022learning,mittal2023orbit,liao2026beyondmimic . Despite their differences, most of these policies follow the same paradigm. They encode the history of observations and the proprioceptive state, and map it directly to future actions at discrete time steps. This paradigm has limits in both settings. In IL, it relies on large-scale data and compute to generalize. Yet robot data are heterogeneous in embodiment, quality, and control interface, and cannot be collected at the scale of internet data. Training large foundation policies is also costly. Generative policies~ dp,black2024pi_0 further need multiple network evaluations for each chunk. They react to new observations only after the whole chunk is produced, which limits real-time execution~ black2026real,bai2026flash,jia2026action . In RL, the policy must gather experience from a large number of interactions~ rudin2022learning . Without explicit regularization, its actions often oscillate at high frequency. This wastes control effort, wears the actuators, and hurts the transfer from simulation to reality~ mysore2021caps,raffin2022smooth,peng2020learning . A novel robot policy paradigm that is efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, and especially amenable to scaling, is therefore needed. A robot is a macroscopic classical system that moves continuously in time. The actions that command it, e.g., those teleoperated by humans, are largely continuous as well. A demonstration is therefore largely a sampling of a continuous action trajectory at the control frequency. Direct-action policies must learn this continuity implicitly from data. At chunk boundaries, it is not even guaranteed, and the commands jump~ black2026real . An ordinary differential equation (ODE)~ chen2018neural naturally describes such continuous change. Applied to the action, an ODE can model its dynamics, a law of motion shared by every step. Integrating it yields a continuous action trajectory by construction. Notably, animal motor cortex is thought to generate movement through such dynamics rather than by encoding its target~ churchland2012neural,shenoy2013cortical . ODEs have long described robot motion~ ijspeert2013dmp,bahl2020ndp . However, they fix the form of the vector field or force it to converge to an attractor. Each model is thus limited to a few motions. In this work, we propose ~policy . It learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself, i.e., it models the policy directly as an ODE (Fig.~ fig:concept ). Concretely, a neural ODE~ chen2018neural learns the vector field of the action, conditioned on the observation. The action is then integrated over the physical time of the robot. Integrating over a whole demonstration accumulates drift and requires the costly adjoint method. In IL, we therefore integrate over action chunks~ dp,zhao2023learning , a key to current direct-action policies~ pan2025much,lazzati2026 , and supervise the integrated path without any derivative of the actions. A contractive perturbation shifts the start of each training chunk and teaches the field to return, which improves robustness. In RL, we integrate over single control steps. At inference, each action is integrated from the previous one, across chunk boundaries in IL and across control steps in RL. Direct-action policies, in contrast, often jump or pause at chunk boundaries in IL and oscillate between steps in RL. Finally, a lightweight diversity head adds a sampled offset to the vector field to retain multi-modal behavior~ dp,jia2026mars . We validate ~policy across the mainstream IL models and in RL (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). We instantiate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action expert of the VLA~ intelligence2025pi05 , as the action head of the ImageWAM~ zhang2026imagewam WAM, and as the actor of SuperMimic~ liao2026supermimic for whole-body motion tracking of a humanoid. We further deploy it on a real single-arm robot, a dual-arm robot, a robot with dexterous hands, and a humanoid, where it replaces the action head of GR00T N1.7~ bjorck2025gr00t . The real-robot tasks include high-precision, long-horizon, deformable, multi-modal, dexterous, and loco-manipulation tasks. We compare with 14 state-of-the-art baselines, including generative and regression-based IL methods. Within each setting, all methods share the same backbone, data, and training schedule. Experiments show that ~policy learns remarkably fast. After one epoch, it succeeds in 79.2 of the LIBERO episodes, against at most 43.2 for the baselines. As the action head of , it succeeds in 96.0 against 75.5 for its flow matching expert. As that of ImageWAM, it succeeds in 82.6 against 24.6 for the original head. It matches flow matching with less than half of the demonstrations. As the actor of SuperMimic, it reaches a higher return early in training. On 14 tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate on every task. It also generates actions fast and smoothly. A chunk takes 10.8 times less time than with flow matching in simulation, and 3.5 to 27 times less than with the diffusion and flow matching baselines on real robots. On real robots, its motion is smoother than the human demonstrations in most cases. Moreover, it generalizes robustly to unseen perturbations in simulation, and it transfers dexterous skills learned from public data of another lab to our real robot. It also keeps multi-modal behavior, both on a navigation task and on a real bimanual task, where it uses both arm assignments. Finally, the learned field supports data without action labels and arbitrary control rates. Related Work sec:related ODE in Robot Policies sec:related_ds Action dynamics as ODEs. Representing robot motion as a dynamical system has a long history, from dynamical movement primitives~ ijspeert2013dmp and stable dynamical systems~ khansari2011seds to neural vector fields with contraction or stability guarantees~ beikmohammadi2024ncds,sochopoulos2024stable . Neural dynamic policies~ bahl2020ndp,totsila2023andp further predict the parameters of such systems from images. However, the fixed form or the stability constraint limits each system to a few motions toward an attractor, mostly on single tasks. ~policy instead places no structural constraint on the vector field and learns one field for large-scale tasks. State dynamics as ODEs. A conventional paradigm in robot learning is to learn the state dynamics of the robot or its environment and then design a policy or analytical controller upon it. Learned dynamics, often in the form of neural ODEs, are used for model-based reinforcement learning~ yildiz2021continuous and for feedback controllers that compensate for model uncertainty~ jia2024feedback,jia2025FORESEERR,jia2026physics . Continuous-time networks~ hasani2022cfc likewise evolve the hidden state of a policy by an ODE. In these works, the ODE describes the state of the system or of the network, and the action is still produced by a separate controller or output layer. ~policy instead learns the ODE of the action itself. Generative processes as ODEs. Diffusion and flow matching policies~ dp,black2024pi_0 integrate over a generation time without physical meaning. Streaming flow policy~ jiang2025streaming aligns the flow time with the execution time, but it is still trained by regressing velocities derived from the demonstrations and regenerates each chunk over a rescaled time interval. Chronos policy~ wang2026chronos encodes the physical times of observations and actions in a diffusion transformer, but time remains an input, and actions are still generated at a fixed rate. In contrast, ~policy integrates over physical time itself, is trained through the integrated path without velocity labels, and continues each chunk from the previous one. Action Chunking sec:related_chunk Predicting a chunk of actions per observation was popularized by action chunking transformer (ACT)~ zhao2023learning and diffusion policy~ dp , and is now standard in large foundation models~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t . Recent analyses show that chunking is a key factor in the performance of current IL policies~ lazzati2026,pan2025much . Executing a chunk open-loop often outperforms updating the action at every observation~ park2026bcmystery , which contrasts with the classical control experience that a higher closed-loop rate is better. However, independently predicted chunks may be inconsistent at their boundaries, which is mitigated by temporal ensembling~ zhao2023learning or by conditioning each chunk on the committed actions of the previous one~ black2026real . ~policy also builds on chunking for IL, but uses the chunk as the unit of integration. During training, it integrates the vector field over one chunk, so the gradient passes through a few solver steps without the adjoint method. At inference, it integrates each action from the previous one, which keeps the actions continuous across chunks and executes each action without waiting for a whole chunk. Some policies predict actions relative to the current pose~ chi2024universal , but still output each action of a chunk as a separate value. In ~policy, all actions of a chunk follow from one vector field evaluated along the path. Efficient Policies sec:related_efficient Efficient IL policies. Generative policies require multiple network evaluations per chunk. Consistency models~ Consistency,zhang2025flowpolicy , self-distillation~ li2026ofp , and mean flows~ geng2026mean,fang2025omp reduce the sampling to one or a few steps, and informed source distributions shorten the transport path~ warmstarts,dai2026where . VITA~ gao2025vita , action-to-action flow matching (A2A)~ jia2026action,zuo2026deltaflow , and FLASH~ bai2026flash further replace the flow source with image observations or historical actions, which improves both learning efficiency and inference speed. These methods improve the efficiency of IL within the conventional direct-action paradigm. ~policy instead changes the paradigm to an ODE, which exploits the inherent continuity of physical motion to improve efficiency. Efficient RL policies. In RL, sample efficiency is mostly improved on the side of the critic and the update, e.g., by high update-to-data ratios with ensembled or regularized critics~ chen2021redq,hiraoka2022droq,bhatt2024crossq , scaled networks~ lee2025simba,kim2026flashsac , or learned world models~ hansen2024tdmpc2 . SuperMimic~ liao2026supermimic learns a differentiable world model and trains the actor by backpropagating analytic gradients through short imagined rollouts. It surpasses a state-of-the-art motion tracker after 3 hours on one GPU with more than 1000 times fewer GPU hours. These methods keep the actor as a direct map from states to actions. ~policy instead changes the actor itself, and further speeds up SuperMimic as a drop-in replacement of its actor. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries This section first formalizes the direct-action policies that ~policy replaces, in both IL and RL, and then introduces the neural ODE on which ~policy is built. Direct-Action Policy sec:prelim_il Let denote the visual observation in the image space , the proprioceptive state, and the action sent to the low-level controller at control step , where are the state and action dimensions. title: OpenNWM: A Generalist Navigation World Model with Latent Action Pretraining
summary: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.
full_text: NavAnywhere Dataset Details app:navanywhere We introduce NavAnywhere, a large-scale, action-free visual navigation dataset assembled from 15 sources, including public datasets and our in-house recordings. The collection consists of RGB videos and sampled image sequences without action annotations, comprising 70,756 sequences, 17,496,570 sampled frames, and 1,188.65 hours of source video. NavAnywhere covers a broad spectrum of environments encountered in everyday life, ranging from residential and public indoor spaces to urban streets, parks, and natural outdoor environments. (see Figure~ fig:NavAnywhere ) Dataset Composition app:navanywhere_composition NavAnywhere brings together 15 sources, including public datasets and in-house recordings, covering a broad range of navigation environments, camera viewpoints, and motion patterns. Below, we briefly describe each source and its main characteristics to provide an overview of the dataset’s composition: BotanicGarden~ botanicgarden : Robot-mounted observations of botanical gardens, featuring vegetation, pathways, and other outdoor structures. CityWalker~ liu2025citywalker : Urban navigation sequences featuring sidewalks, intersections, pedestrians, and vehicles. DL3DV-10K~ ling2024dl3dv : Scene-exploration videos spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, viewpoints, and camera motions. Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d : A navigation-related subset of egocentric videos depicting everyday activities and movement through indoor and outdoor environments. EgoWalk~ akhtyamov2025egowalk : First-person walking videos covering urban, residential, public, and recreational environments. KrishnaCam~ krishnacam : Long-term egocentric recordings of daily activities, including walking, commuting, and visits to indoor and outdoor spaces. LAVN~ lavn : A collection combining real-world recordings with simulated navigation sequences. ROVER~ rover : Robot navigation recordings collected in gardens, parks, and campus environments across different seasons and illumination conditions. RealEstate10K~ realestate10k : Real-estate video clips of residential interiors, exteriors, and surroundings, including drone footage. SANPO~ sanpo : Real and synthetic egocentric navigation sequences covering sidewalks, roads, parks, and other outdoor environments. The Great Outdoors~ go : Robot-mounted observations of natural and off-road environments, including forests, unpaved trails, and uneven terrain. Walking Tours~ walkingtour : Long-form internet videos depicting walking tours and outdoor exploration. i2Nav-Robot~ i2nav : Robot navigation sequences covering campus buildings, streets, parking areas, and transitions between indoor and outdoor spaces. uB-VisioGeoloc~ ub : Pedestrian-view urban sequences covering streets, public spaces, and parks, together with synthetic sequences. In-house collected data: Our in-house collection of nine RGB videos, covering offices, residential neighborhoods, and public landmarks across indoor and outdoor environments under daytime and nighttime conditions. Table~ tab:navanywhere_statistics and Figure~ fig:navanywhere_composition reports the complete NavAnywhere dataset statistics. Scene and Environment Diversity app:navanywhere_scene NavAnywhere covers a wide range of indoor and outdoor environments, reflecting the diversity of scenes encountered in everyday navigation. We organize these environments into five broad scene categories, each characterized by distinct spatial layouts and environmental features, as described below: Residential environments: Homes, residential buildings, and surrounding neighborhoods. Public and commercial environments: Offices, schools, shops, restaurants, and cultural facilities. Urban and transportation environments: Streets, sidewalks, intersections, parking areas, and transit spaces. Parks and managed outdoor environments: Gardens, campuses, recreational areas, and maintained green spaces. Natural and off-road environments: Forests, trails, uneven terrain, and unstructured outdoor spaces. Across these categories, the constituent sources exhibit substantial variation in viewpoints, illumination conditions, scene layouts, and motion patterns. Dataset Details and Preprocessing app:dataset_details_preprocessing In addition to NavAnywhere, we use five action-annotated navigation datasets and three complementary out-of-domain evaluation sets. These datasets are not part of NavAnywhere and are excluded from its corpus statistics. This section describes these datasets, the preprocessing procedures applied to all data sources, and their respective roles in OpenNWM training and evaluation. title: Appointed-Time Fault-Tolerant Fast Terminal Sliding Control for UAVs with a Tracking Error-Based Disturbance Observer
summary: This paper addresses the critical challenge of high-performance fault-tolerant tracking control for quadrotor UAVs under complex conditions including external disturbances, parameter uncertainties, and actuator faults. A synergistic control framework is proposed by decoupling the system into position and attitude loops, each governed by the following three innovations. First, an Appointed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (AT-PPF) is developed to strictly constrain the tracking error within a predefined funnel boundary, ensuring convergence within a fixed time regardless of initial conditions. Second, a Tracking Error-Based Fixed-Time Composite Disturbance Observer (TFxTCDO) is developed to enable fast and accurate estimation of lumped disturbances without requiring full-state information or precise system modeling. This observer directly couples disturbance estimation with the control objective, thereby enhancing robustness and convergence. Third, a Fast Second-Order Terminal Sliding Mode Controller (NFSO-TSMC) is designed to achieve faster convergence and effective chattering mitigation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed control strategy significantly outperforms conventional methods in terms of tracking accuracy, fault recovery speed, and robustness against uncertainties.

Fault-Tolerant Control (FTC), Prescribed Performance Control (PPC), Sliding Mode Control (SMC), Tracking error Observer, UAV Introduction he low-altitude economy is rapidly emerging as a strategic emerging sector with tremendous potential. intro_low_altitude_economy_potential . Within the low-altitude economy platform, quadrotor Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have found the most widespread application due to their excellent maneuverability and broad application prospects intro_uav_cornerstone . However, as the application scenarios expand, quadrotor UAVs are increasingly confronted with complex operational environments. A host of challenges, including external disturbances, parameter uncertainties, input saturation, and actuator faults, invariably arise, posing significant threats to flight stability and mission reliability. For instance, dense urban environments characterized by high-rise buildings can generate complex turbulence, subjecting the UAV to severe and unpredictable disturbances. Prolonged operation may lead to the gradual performance degradation of critical components, thereby amplifying parameter uncertainties. Furthermore, during high-payload transportation or aggressive maneuvers, the issue of input saturation frequently occurs, constraining the vehicle's control authority. More critically, the occurrence of an actuator fault directly compromises flight safety and mission execution. Therefore, investigating fault-tolerant tracking control with prescribed performance for quadrotor UAVs operating in complex environments is of paramount importance. Such research holds significant theoretical value in advancing control theory and, more pressingly, addresses an urgent practical need to ensure the safe and efficient development of the low-altitude economy. This paper is dedicated to tackling these challenges by proposing a robust and unified control framework. In the domain of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) control, Prescribed Performance Control (PPC) has been widely adopted as a powerful technique to enhance system robustness and convergence speed. A significant body of research has evolved around the design and application of various types of Prescribed Performance Functions (PPFs), prominently including the Finite-Time Prescribed Performance Function (FTPPF), the Fixed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (FxTPPF), and the Appointed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (AxTPPF). The FTPPF method ensures that the system converges within a finite time, with the convergence duration being dependent on the initial conditions of the system. A study successfully employed an FTPPF to achieve rapid trajectory tracking for a UAV ppc_ftppf_example . However, a notable limitation of this approach is that the convergence time remains susceptible to the initial error magnitude; a large initial error can lead to a comparatively slower convergence process. To overcome this dependency, the FxTPPF method was developed, which guarantees system convergence within a fixed-time upper bound, irrespective of the initial conditions. The work in ppc_fxtppf_example utilized a fixed-time control strategy, demonstrating improved rapid response capabilities and enhanced resilience against external disturbances in UAVs. Nevertheless, under conditions of high nonlinearity and strong uncertainties, the convergence rate of FxTPPF might degrade, and it can potentially demand excessive control energy. More recently, the AxTPPF has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the distinct advantage of allowing the user to pre-specify the convergence time, which is independent of both initial conditions and system parameters. This feature renders AxTPPF particularly advantageous for tasks with stringent temporal requirements, such as navigation in dynamic environments or cooperative control, when compared to FTPPF and FxTPPF. Recent studies have substantiated the high efficiency of the AxTPPF methodology in managing uncertain systems ppc_axtppf_example . In the context of complex low-altitude environments, where quadrotor UAVs are subjected to a confluence of challenges including external disturbances, input saturation, and actuator faults, conventional finite-time or fixed-time approaches may struggle to meet the demanding requirements for high timeliness and strict performance constraints. Therefore, this paper adopts an Appointed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (AxTPPF). By leveraging AxTPPF, we ensure that the tracking error converges within a pre-assigned time interval, independent of the initial state. Sliding Mode Control (SMC) has garnered significant research interest for quadrotor applications. Depending on the design of the sliding surface and the control law, SMC methodologies can be categorized into several prominent variants, including Terminal Sliding Mode Control (TSMC), Finite-Time Sliding Mode Control (FTSMC), Fixed-Time Sliding Mode Control (FxTSMC), Integral Sliding Mode Control (ISMC), and Recursive Sliding Mode Control (RSMC). Terminal Sliding Mode Control (TSMC) is designed to drive system states to the equilibrium in finite time. TSMC is proposed for quadrotor trajectory tracking smc_tsmc_example , which successfully enhanced the convergence rate. However, a persistent challenge with conventional TSMC is the pronounced chattering phenomenon, which can compromise the execution of high-precision tasks smc_chattering_issue . To address this, Finite-Time Sliding Mode Control (FTSMC) was developed, offering robust performance against disturbances while ensuring finite-time convergence smc_ftsmc_example . Nonetheless, the convergence time of FTSMC is contingent upon the initial system states, rendering it less suitable for missions with strict temporal constraints smc_ftsmc_limitation . Subsequently, Fixed-Time Sliding Mode Control (FxTSMC) emerged, which, through the construction of an appropriate control law, guarantees convergence within a fixed time independent of the initial conditions smc_fxtsmc_example . However, a notable drawback is its potentially high computational complexity, particularly when implemented in higher-order or strongly nonlinear systems smc_fxtsmc_limitation . On another front, Integral Sliding Mode Control (ISMC) enhances robustness against external disturbances by incorporating an integral term into the sliding surface. Its application to UAV attitude control, as demonstrated in smc_ismc_example , has shown superior disturbance rejection capabilities. However, a possible limitation of this approach is the introduction of additional dynamic errors due to the integral action, which may compromise control precision and degrade overall performance smc_ismc_limitation . Lastly, Recursive Sliding Mode Control (RSMC) employs a multi-layered, nested sliding surface design to achieve recursive-like approximation control for complex systems smc_rsmc_example . This method, however, is often computationally intensive and relies heavily on high-precision state observation smc_rsmc_limitation . Addressing the limitations of the aforementioned methods, this paper presents a Fast Second-Order Terminal Sliding Mode Control (NFSO-TSMC). This innovative approach synergizes the chattering-suppression characteristics of second-order SMC with the efficient convergence properties of TSMC. The proposed NFSO-TSMC ensures global convergence within a prescribed time while simultaneously mitigating chattering, thereby enhancing both the tracking precision and dynamic response performance of the quadrotor in complex environments.To overcome these challenges, we put forth a Fast Second-Order Terminal Sliding Mode Control (NFSO-TSMC), which artfully blends the merits of second-order and terminal SMC to refine tracking precision and dynamic responsiveness. To ensure the stable and fault-tolerant control of quadrotor UAVs in complex environments, researchers have developed a variety of Fault-Tolerant Control (FTC) strategies to counteract issues such as actuator faults, sensor failures, and external disturbances. FTC approaches can be broadly classified into Passive FTC, Active FTC, Reconfigurable FTC, Data-Driven FTC, and Hybrid FTC ftc_overview . Passive FTC methods are designed to be inherently robust by considering system uncertainties and potential fault effects during the initial controller design phase. This allows the controller to maintain system stability upon fault occurrence without requiring online parameter adjustments. For instance, robust techniques like Sliding Mode Control (SMC) ftc_passive_smc and H-infinity control ftc_passive_hinf have been employed to enhance a UAV's resilience to actuator faults. However, the adaptability of passive methods is limited; they may still suffer from performance degradation when faced with severe actuator faults or significant variations in system parameters. In contrast, Active FTC relies on a Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) module to dynamically compensate for fault effects by adjusting the control law in real-time. Adaptive Control ftc_active_adaptive and Model Reference Adaptive Control (MRAC) ftc_active_mrac are widely utilized within this paradigm ftc_active_adaptive_example , thereby improving flight stability. A drawback of adaptive control, however, is the potential for estimation delays of system parameters, which can affect the response speed. Model Predictive Control (MPC) has also been applied to UAV fault tolerance ftc_active_mpc , offering the ability to optimize control inputs by considering future states, but its high computational complexity often hinders real-time implementation. Reconfigurable FTC achieves fault tolerance through control law adaptation or Control Allocation (CA), as demonstrated in ftc_reconfigurable_ca , where stable flight is maintained despite the complete failure of a single actuator. Nevertheless, such methods typically necessitate redundant actuators or sophisticated thrust allocation schemes, which increases system complexity and hardware costs. More recently, data-driven approaches have been introduced to the FTC landscape, leveraging Reinforcement Learning (RL) ftc_datadriven_rl and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) ftc_datadriven_dnn for fault compensation, enabling UAV to maintain stability under unknown fault conditions ftc_datadriven_drl_example . The performance of these methods, however, is highly dependent on the quality of the training data, and their generalization capabilities require further enhancement. In comparing these paradigms, Active FTC demonstrates superior adaptability and real-time performance by promptly detecting and compensating for faults without relying on hardware

title: Robust Reward Machine Learning and Execution in Noisy Environments
comment: 44 pages, 21 figures, 5 tables. Published in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research. Code: https://github.com/rparac/Prob-IRM
summary:
Background: Reward machines (RMs) represent non-Markovian reward functions as finite-state machines over high-level propositional events. Traditionally, these events are generated by a deterministic labelling function that maps environment states to proposition sets. However, real-world labelling functions are inherently noisy.
  Objectives: Design and implement a method that learns RMs in the presence of noisy labelling functions and exploits them for policy learning in both discrete and continuous environments.
  Methods: We propose Prob-IRM, a method that learns RMs from noisy proposition histories using inductive logic programming (ILP) and exploits them for policy learning. Noisy proposition histories are represented as training examples for ILP, which learns an RM that maximises coverage of low-uncertainty histories. RM learning is interleaved with policy optimisation. Prob-IRM uses a belief over RM states to determine when to relearn the RM and to provide additional guiding rewards.
  Results: Prob-IRM is evaluated on environments with discrete and continuous state spaces under varying levels of labelling noise. Prob-IRM performs comparably to baselines using handcrafted RMs and outperforms approaches that use recurrent neural networks to encode history, despite operating with noisy labels.
  Conclusions: Prob-IRM represents a step towards deploying reward machines in noisy, real-world environments.

title: W2A: Distilling World Priors into Action Models for Real-Time Robotic Control
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate competitive success rates while significantly improving inference efficiency. On LIBERO, W2A achieves a 95.9% average success rate. More importantly, W2A achieves about 21x faster inference than the representative WAM baseline.

Introduction sec:introduction Building general robotic policies is a central goal on the path toward artificial general intelligence. Built upon internet-scale pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic control, offering strong semantic grounding and generalization~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,gr00tn1_2025,song2025reconvla . However, because VLAs are largely trained on static image-text pretraining, they still have limited understanding of physical dynamics and procedures, both of which are crucial for long-horizon and contact-rich robotic manipulation. To address this limitation, recent works~ hu2024video,pai2025mimicvideo,li2025unified,ma2026dit4dit,yuan2026fastwam have begun to integrate video-based world modeling into robot policy learning, giving rise to World Action Models (WAMs). By leveraging future visual prediction or latent representations, WAMs incorporate richer temporal and physical structure. Existing WAMs can be broadly categorized into two classes: (1) video-conditioned action modeling and (2) joint modeling of future states and actions. The former injects predicted future observations or latent representations as conditions into an action expert for action generation~ hu2024video,pai2025mimicvideo . The latter, in contrast, jointly models future observations and actions during training, generating both within a unified framework~ bi2025motusunifiedlatentaction,kim2026cosmos . However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at inference time, incurring substantial computational overhead and inference latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we refer to world priors as the latent knowledge of video models about how scenes evolve over time. We focus on two questions: (1) what world priors in the video models used by WAMs are truly important for action generation, and whether they can be captured by a low-dimensional latent subspace? (2) Can such essential world priors be distilled into an action model, thereby eliminating the additional inference overhead and enabling real-time robotic control? Our key insight is that the latent representations of video models contain much information that is not directly useful for action generation, such as static scene content and task-irrelevant visual details, while only a small subset of features truly captures action-relevant dynamics. If this critical knowledge can be distilled into an action model, the video model can be removed at inference time. Motivated by this insight, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework that transfers world priors from video models into action models for real-time robotic control. Specifically, in the first stage of training, we adapt a pretrained language-conditioned video diffusion transformer (DiT)~ Peebles2022DiT to robotic video data. We then apply principal component analysis (PCA)~ hotelling1933analysis to the latent representations of the video DiT, projecting them into a lower-dimensional latent space. In the second stage, we train an action DiT from scratch as our action model. For action DiT training, in addition to a flow matching objective~ lipman2022flow , we introduce a Q-Former~ li2023blip to read out features from the action DiT. These queried features are then aligned with the projected video latents through a similarity-based distillation loss. At test time, our framework removes the video DiT entirely, retaining only the action DiT. We believe that although video latents and action latents are not directly causal variables, they share the same action-conditioned dynamics: one captures the resulting world evolution, while the other must encode the control patterns that induce it. This shared structure makes distilling world priors from video models into action models both practically and conceptually plausible. Figure~ fig:overview shows the differences between W2A and the existing WAMs. Our experimental results suggest that world priors useful for action generation can be effectively distilled into action models. This allows W2A to preserve the benefits of WAMs and improve the performance of action models, while avoiding the deployment overhead of video models. Related Work sec:related_works Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action models extend large VLMs from semantic understanding to embodied control, and have become a major direction for generalist robotic policies~ zhao2025cot,shukor2025smolvla,team2025gemini,liu2024rdt,jiang2025galaxea,zhaozhang2025vla2,zhong2026acot,wu2026pragmatic,intelligence2026pi . Early milestones such as RT-1~ brohan2022rt and RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt established the paradigm of mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, while demonstrating that large-scale internet pretraining can significantly improve semantic grounding and task generalization in manipulation. Subsequent work shifted from task-specific instantiations toward more general and scalable policy learning. In particular, Octo~ octo_2023 explored large-scale multi-task robot pretraining, and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla further advanced this line by providing an open and reproducible VLA framework for general-purpose manipulation. More recent robot foundation models, including ~ intelligence2025pi_ , ~ intelligence2025pi , and GR00T N1~ gr00tn1_2025 , continue to push the frontier by scaling data diversity, improving cross-embodiment transfer, and strengthening real-world adaptability~ team2025gemini . Despite these advances, VLAs are still largely rooted in static image-text pretraining, which limits their ability to reason about how actions change the world over time. World Action Models and Video Generation for Policy Learning. Recent progress in video generation has motivated new training paradigms that bring pretrained video world models into robotic control~ yuan2026fastwam,du2023learning,wu2023unleashing,feng2025vidarembodiedvideodiffusion,zheng2026video,zhu2025uwm,team2026motubrain,guo2026unified,zhang2026world . An early representative work is Video Prediction Policy (VPP)~ hu2024video , which showed that video diffusion models pretrained for future prediction can provide predictive visual representations that substantially improve downstream policy learning. Mimic-video~ pai2025mimicvideo retains the two-stage recipe of first adapting a video model and then training an action decoder, further demonstrating that video models can serve as strong spatio-temporal backbones for robot action generation. A different line pushes this integration further by reducing or removing the gap between world modeling and policy learning. Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos directly adapts a pretrained video model into a robot policy with minimal architectural changes, jointly modeling actions, future states, and values within the latent diffusion process. More recent works such as LingBot-VA~ lingbot-va2026 , DreamZero~ ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot , and GigaWorld-Policy~ ye2026gigaworld further strengthen this trend by unifying future-state prediction and action generation within autoregressive or joint-denoising formulations. However, most WAMs still retain a video backbone or world-modeling branch at test time, introducing additional computational overhead and inference latency for real-time control. W2A addresses this issue by using the video model only as a training-time teacher, distilling its world priors into an action model and discarding the video model entirely during deployment. title: Spatial Uncertainty Analytics for Budget-Limited Inspection of Hyperspectral Scenes
summary: Land-cover maps classified from wide-area hyperspectral surveys are least reliable along class boundaries and in ambiguous regions, so their errors are spatially structured. We study how this structure can direct a limited verification budget: when a low-altitude UAV or a ground crew can visit only a handful of sites, where it should go depends on how classifier uncertainty is arranged across the scene and how a fixed sensor footprint tiles that arrangement. We estimate a per-pixel uncertainty surface from the disagreement of an ensemble of spectral classifiers and select sites by greedy, field-of-view-aware coverage of the uncertainty mass. On seven benchmark scenes, the highest-uncertainty decile of pixels is 2.6 to 7.9 times richer in errors than the scene as a whole, and the coverage greedy covers up to 57% of the classifier's errors with 15 sites, 1.7 to 18 times as many as uncertainty-agnostic sampling of the same labelled region. A non-overlapping selection of the footprints richest in uncertainty does equally well, so the gain comes from scoring whole footprints by uncertainty mass. The advantage persists under spatially blocked evaluation and with a spectral-spatial classifier, although disagreement then ranks errors less well. It requires restricting the surface to labelled land cover: over the whole scene, disagreement peaks on unlabelled ground, where inspections cannot be scored. The best policy for covering connected high-uncertainty regions depends on the scene and on the threshold that defines them, and Gaussian-process selection covers less uncertainty than the coverage greedy on every scene. The pipeline runs on commodity CPUs.

The pipeline runs on commodity CPUs. <ccs2012> <concept> <concept_id>10010147.10010257.10010293</concept_id> <concept_desc>Computing methodologies~Machine learning approaches</concept_desc> <concept_significance>500</concept_significance> </concept> <concept> <concept_id>10002951.10003227.10003236.10003237</concept_id> <concept_desc>Information systems~Geographic information systems</concept_desc> <concept_significance>500</concept_significance> </concept> <concept> <concept_id>10010405.10010432.10010437</concept_id> <concept_desc>Applied computing~Earth and atmospheric sciences</concept_desc> <concept_significance>300</concept_significance> </concept> </ccs2012> Introduction Scientific remote-sensing workflows increasingly use machine learning to turn high-dimensional observations into spatially distributed maps of land cover, vegetation state, and other environmental phenomena. A less-studied question is how to allocate limited physical-verification effort once the map is produced, because its reliability is spatially heterogeneous: a model's errors are not distributed uniformly but concentrate along class boundaries, in mixed or transitional land cover, and in regions whose signatures the training set under-represents. A map of where the model is uncertain therefore has spatial structure: it concentrates in particular fields and along their edges rather than spreading evenly across the scene. This paper is about turning that structure into action. When a scientific or operational workflow can afford to verify only a handful of locations, for example with a low-altitude UAV revisiting a farm or a field crew sampling a wetland, where that effort is spent is a spatial-analytics question. The answer depends on how uncertainty is arranged across the scene and on how a fixed sensor footprint tiles that arrangement. We show that exploiting this structure lets a fixed verification budget cover substantially more of the model's genuine errors than uncertainty-agnostic alternatives, and we characterize how the best strategy shifts with the scene. We instantiate this on hyperspectral imagery. Hyperspectral sensors record reflectance across hundreds of contiguous spectral bands, allowing materials and vegetation states to be distinguished by their spectral signatures. This underpins applications in precision agriculture, environmental monitoring, and resource management, where the goal is often to locate and characterize anomalous or ambiguous regions (stressed crops, contaminated water, unexpected land cover) within a large scene. The follow-up verification our method plans supports a downstream scientific decision: targeted crop or land-cover confirmation in agriculture, ecological sampling in wetlands, and field inspection of uncertain map regions in earth observation more broadly. Operational remote-sensing pipelines for these applications are frequently two-stage. A first stage performs a wide-area airborne survey, for example with a fixed-wing aircraft or a high-altitude UAV carrying a hyperspectral sensor, and produces a classified map of the scene. This stage is cheap per unit area and covers everything, but its output is only a set of model predictions whose reliability varies across the scene. A second stage therefore dispatches a far more expensive resource, a low-altitude UAV for close-range inspection or a ground crew for in-situ sampling, to verify selected locations. This survey-then-target structure is a recurring design pattern in precision agriculture~ pretto2021flourish , and ground-truthing is routinely used to validate airborne hyperspectral classifications. Representative low-altitude platforms carry lightweight hyperspectral payloads at a few tens of metres above ground, for example to \,m~ guo2021maize,barbedo2022viticulture , and their endurance is capped by battery capacity, which limits how much area a single sortie can inspect at close range~ popovic2020ipp . The second stage is therefore budget-limited, and the operator must decide where to spend scarce verification effort. This paper addresses that second-stage decision. We assume a hyperspectral survey has already been acquired and classified, and ask: given a spatial map of where the classifier is most uncertain, and a UAV that can inspect only a limited number of sites, where should it go? This is an error-targeted inspection prioritization problem over an already-surveyed scene, not robotic exploration of an unknown environment or the selection of new training labels; re-surveying or ground-truthing everything is precisely what is too expensive. The naive answer, repeatedly visiting the single most uncertain pixel, ignores both the sensor's footprint and the fact that uncertainty concentrates in particular parts of the scene. The right place to inspect depends not only on where uncertainty is high but also on how it is arranged (scattered into many small fragments or concentrated into a few large regions) and on how a fixed footprint tiles that arrangement. We quantify uncertainty without requiring calibrated probabilities: an ensemble of spectral classifiers is trained on a random subset of the labelled, dimensionality-reduced pixel spectra, and the disagreement among its members gives a normalized uncertainty surface over the scene. We then select inspection sites greedily over this surface under an explicit field-of-view model and compare three scores: a peak-uncertainty policy that targets the most ambiguous remaining pixel, a coverage policy that maximizes the mean uncertainty of a footprint's unvisited pixels, and a dispersion policy that weights that mean by the footprint's unvisited fraction. The dispersion score equals the uncertainty mass a footprint newly covers divided by the constant footprint area, so it is exactly the classical greedy algorithm for our coverage objective and inherits its guarantee; the other two are heuristics. To test whether uncertainty guidance is doing real work, we compare against uncertainty-agnostic baselines (a systematic lawnmower sweep and uniform random sampling), both over the whole scene and restricted to the labelled region where errors are counted. To test whether the greedy rule itself matters, we also compare against two simpler uses of the same surface: non-maximum suppression over footprint uncertainty mass, and stratified sampling that places one high-mass footprint in each part of the scene. We evaluate on seven hyperspectral benchmarks. Four are standard archival airborne scenes spanning agricultural, wetland, and urban land cover (Indian Pines, Salinas, Kennedy Space Center, and Pavia University); three are UAV-borne scenes at centimetre-to-decimetre resolution (WHU-Hi LongKou, HanChuan, and HongHu~ zhong2020whuhi ). We validate against ground-truth error and report spatial metrics: uncertainty covered, coverage of high-uncertainty pixels, coverage of connected high-uncertainty components, and the spatial dispersion of the chosen sites. This lets us characterize the trade-off between depth (concentrating the budget where uncertainty mass is densest) and breadth (reaching as many separate high-uncertainty regions as possible). We make three contributions: [noitemsep,topsep=2pt] A formulation of post-classification inspection as maximum coverage of footprint uncertainty mass over an ensemble-disagreement uncertainty surface, implemented in a CPU-only pipeline. The greedy algorithm we use for it is classical; the contribution is the formulation and the evidence that footprint uncertainty mass is a useful objective for spatial verification. A ground-truth-anchored comparison against uncertainty-agnostic baselines, scene-wide and restricted to the labelled region, and against simpler samplings of the same surface. Scoring whole footprints by uncertainty mass, with the coverage greedy or a non-overlapping top-mass selection, which perform alike, covers to times as many errors as the best region-matched baseline when the surface is restricted to labelled land cover. An empirical characterization of the depth-versus-breadth trade-off: the best policy for covering uncertainty is the same on every scene, but the best policy for covering connected high-uncertainty regions depends on the scene, and, in an exploratory analysis over seven scenes, that dependence is not predicted by a single scalar measure of uncertainty concentration. Section~ sec:limitations discusses implications and limitations, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes. Related Work sec:related Spatial Analytics for Scientific Decision-Making sec:rw_spatial A growing body of work treats spatial structure (dependency, heterogeneity, and autocorrelation) as the central object of analysis rather than a nuisance, using it to drive decisions over geospatial data. Within this journal, representative examples include modeling the spatio-temporal evolution of remote-sensing imagery for prediction~ das2020sardine , estimating environmental fields such as air pollution from spatial covariates~ steininger2020maplur , interpolating sparsely sampled sensing data across space~ middya2021interpolation , and building tooling that brings deep learning to geospatial raster data~ stewart2025torchgeo . Our work is in this spirit but addresses a decision that follows classification rather than classification itself: given a spatial surface of classifier uncertainty and a budget to physically verify only a few locations, we ask where verification should be spent. The analytics we exploit are the spatial arrangement of uncertainty, whether it is scattered or concentrated, and how a fixed sensor footprint tiles that arrangement. title: DexArena: A Unified Benchmark for Long-Horizon Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental challenge for robot learning, requiring the composition of multiple skills, precise bimanual coordination, generalizable visual understanding, and robust skill transitions. Yet existing manipulation benchmarks largely emphasize isolated skills or support only a limited range of end-effectors, making these capabilities difficult to evaluate systematically. We introduce DexArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate learning and generalization in long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation. DexArena features 10 long-horizon tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning diverse household and industrial scenarios. Each long-horizon task is composed of explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling reliable evaluation of both intermediate progress and end-to-end task completion. A unified benchmark interface and verified human-teleoperated demonstrations enable testing different policy learning algorithms, with standardized simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation. Through extensive baseline experiments, we identify substantial challenges in precise manipulation, generalization to scene variation, and skill composition. DexArena establishes a challenging and reproducible benchmark for developing robot learning methods that move toward generalizable long-horizon dexterous behavior.

Long-horizon dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental challenge for robot learning, requiring the composition of multiple skills, precise bimanual coordination, generalizable visual understanding, and robust skill transitions. Yet existing manipulation benchmarks largely emphasize isolated skills or support only a limited range of end-effectors, making these capabilities difficult to evaluate systematically. We introduce DexArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate learning and generalization in long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation. DexArena features 10 long-horizon tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning diverse household and industrial scenarios. Each long-horizon task is composed of explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling reliable evaluation of both intermediate progress and end-to-end task completion. A unified benchmark interface and verified human-teleoperated demonstrations enable testing different policy learning algorithms, with standardized simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation. Through extensive baseline experiments, we identify substantial challenges in precise manipulation, generalization to scene variation, and skill composition. DexArena establishes a challenging and reproducible benchmark for developing robot learning methods that move toward generalizable long-horizon dexterous behavior. Introduction Data-driven robot learning has made gripper-based manipulation increasingly capable. By learning from expert demonstrations, imitation learning methods zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion can acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, such as grasping, placing, and plugging. However, much of this progress has focused on parallel-jaw end-effectors and short, isolated tasks. Dexterous hands substantially expand the space of behaviors that robots can perform: multiple fingers can regrasp, twist objects, and manipulate tools. These contact-rich, in-hand interactions are often beyond the capabilities of a parallel-jaw gripper. At the same time, dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional action space and complex contact dynamics, making learning robust policies for long-horizon tasks particularly challenging. Recent progress in this area also requires an efficient and reproducible evaluation infrastructure. Real-robot experiments are costly, time-consuming to reset, and difficult to reproduce across hardware platforms. These challenges are especially pronounced for dexterous hands, whose complex mechanisms and precise actuation can limit the duration and scale of repeated experiments. Physics-based simulators provide an attractive alternative by enabling controlled randomization, scalable interaction, and exact state reset. However, beyond individual simulated tasks, there is a need for a benchmark that systematically evaluates whether a learned policy can execute dexterous skills, compose them across multiple dependent stages, and generalize across different scene configurations. The existing benchmark landscape leaves this problem only partially addressed. RLBench james2019rlbench , Meta-World yu2020metaworld , ManiSkill2 gu2023maniskill2 , RoboCasa nasiriany2024robocasa , and RoboTwin robotwin2025 provide broad coverage of manipulation skills, household scenarios, or dual-arm settings, but primarily emphasize gripper-based manipulation. Dexterous benchmarks, including Adroit rajeswaran2018learningcomplexdexterousmanipulation , DexArt Bao_2023_CVPR , DexMimicGen jiang2025dexmimicgenautomateddatageneration , and DexJoCo dexjoco2026 , have begun to address dexterous hand manipulation, even for bimanual tasks. However, long-horizon composition across dependent stages is rarely evaluated under a shared task definition. Consequently, it remains difficult to disentangle whether a method has learned a dexterous skill itself, can reliably compose skills over long horizons, or is specialized to a particular visual configuration. We introduce DexArena, a unified benchmark designed to make these capabilities measurable within a common physical framework. DexArena contains 10 multi-stage tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning household and industrial-style scenarios. Each multi-stage task consists of two to five stages, while each stage corresponds to an exact slice of its parent sequence: the multi-stage task and its stages share the same workstation, dynamics, and randomization ranges, with identical success conditions for each corresponding stage. This design enables controlled evaluation of isolated skill execution and skill composition without changing the underlying physical setting. Task completion is determined by explicit criteria, including articulated-object angles, relative poses, and insertion depths. Success must persist for a specified duration, preventing transient contacts or unstable configurations from being counted as successful completion. DexArena further separates skill learning from embodiment and rendering choices. The benchmark provides a common interface across a parallel-jaw gripper and three dexterous hands (Sharpa Hand, Wuji Hand, and XHand), and supports both single-arm and bimanual manipulation. All environments use standardized physical parameterizations and workstation configurations. Every recorded frame stores the scene state, so an episode can be restored frame by frame for re-rendering, and its recorded actions can be replayed from the recorded initial state. Importantly, recorded trajectories can also be rendered under different camera configurations and background scenes after collection, enabling controlled evaluation of visual generalization without changing the underlying physical interaction. To support data-driven learning, we collect human-teleoperated demonstrations for every stage-level task, providing physically valid trajectories for later evaluations. Using this infrastructure, we evaluate three representative policy families: demonstration-guided reinforcement learning, single-task imitation learning, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. We measure stage-level task success, generalization to scene variations, and end-to-end completion under sequential stage execution. These evaluations expose different failure modes, distinguishing failures in contact-rich skill execution, visual generalization, and long-horizon skill composition. Together, DexArena provides a common empirical framework for studying the transition from isolated manipulation skills to robust, compositional, and long-horizon dexterous behavior. We summarize our contributions as follows: We introduce DexArena, a unified benchmark for long-horizon, bimanual dexterous manipulation, with 10 multi-stage tasks and 30 physically grounded stage-level tasks that support evaluation of skill execution, generalization and composition. We provide a reproducible benchmark infrastructure with four heterogeneous end-effectors, standardized simulation and randomization configurations, trajectory replay, and stage-level/task-level success criteria. In particular, we invest substantial effort in collecting and validating physically valid, replayable demonstrations, enabling consistent reproduction of the demonstrated interactions and providing high-quality data for policy learning. We establish representative baselines spanning imitation learning, demonstration-guided reinforcement learning, and vision-language-action models, and evaluate them on stage-level task performance, scenario generalization, and long-horizon composition to provide a common reference point for future methods. Related Work Most existing manipulation benchmarks focus on gripper-based manipulation and have established the foundations for systematic evaluation of robot manipulation. RLBench ~ james2019rlbench provides procedurally generated vision-based tasks and demonstrations. Meta-World ~ yu2020metaworld evaluates multi-task and meta-reinforcement learning across a family of tabletop skills. ManiSkill2 ~ gu2023maniskill2 provides GPU-parallel simulation, diverse assets, and standardized interfaces for large-scale manipulation experiments. RoboCasa ~ nasiriany2024robocasa extends evaluation to household manipulation through procedurally generated scenes and language-conditioned tasks. More recent benchmarks, including RoboTwin~ robotwin2025 and RoboDojo~ robodojo2026 , further explore scalable data generation and evaluation for bimanual and gripper-based manipulation. Together, these benchmarks demonstrate the value of standardized simulation for studying visual generalization, multi-task learning, and manipulation policy performance. Dexterous hands introduce additional challenges including underactuated or high-dimensional control, contact-rich interactions, and coordination across multiple fingers. Adroit ~ rajeswaran2018learningcomplexdexterousmanipulation studies object relocation, in-hand manipulation, tool use, and door opening with a dexterous hand, using human demonstrations to support policy learning. DexArt ~ Bao_2023_CVPR focuses on articulated-object manipulation with dexterous hands. DexMimicGen ~ jiang2025dexmimicgenautomateddatageneration presents nine bimanual dexterous-manipulation environments across three embodiments and synthesizes demonstrations from a small set of human teleoperation demonstrations. DexJoCo ~ dexjoco2026 studies 11 dexterous manipulation tasks based on MuJoCo simulation todorov2012mujoco . These efforts motivate benchmark designs that evaluate more dexterous manipulation tasks and consider the ability to compose skills. Despite this progress, existing benchmarks provide different combinations of task diversity, horizon, embodiment coverage, and evaluation granularity. DexArena complements these efforts by providing a unified benchmark for long-horizon dexterous manipulation across heterogeneous end-effectors. It features explicitly staged tasks with physically grounded success conditions and supports evaluation of both intermediate progress and full-task completion. By combining multi-stage task composition and embodiment variation within a common simulation framework, DexArena enables systematic evaluation of the capabilities required for complex dexterous manipulation. DexArena Benchmark DexArena is a physics-based simulation benchmark for long-horizon dexterous manipulation built on the SAPIEN simulator Xiang_2020_CVPR . This simulator allows us to run multiple environments in parallel for fast inference while maintaining high fidelity scene rendering. DexArena comprises 10 multi-stage manipulation tasks and 30 stage-level tasks, spanning scenarios from household activities to industrial-style manipulation, with both single-arm and bimanual settings. Each multi-stage task is decomposed into explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling a policy to be evaluated both on individual skills and on their composition into a complete task. The benchmark supports four end-effector types: a parallel-jaw gripper and three dexterous hands (Sharpa Hand, Wuji Hand, and XHand). By combining long-horizon task composition, contact-rich dexterous interaction, multiple embodiments, and standardized evaluation, DexArena provides a unified testbed for studying the capabilities and limitations of modern robot learning methods.
