title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation
comment: 32 pages, 14 figures, including supplementary material. Project page: https://kimspacehuni.github.io/HeLM/
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human `inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78 subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5 less memory and running 2.5 faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons. Introduction The rise of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has revolutionized robotic control by enabling generalization across diverse language instructions and embodiments~ kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel, pi0 . Built on large-scale pretrained vision-language models, VLA models generate robot actions based on visual observations and natural language instructions. This approach has led to widespread deployment, with variants focusing on visual grounding~ zheng2025tracevlavisualtraceprompting, li2025fastmemorybaseddataefficientvisionlanguage , complex reasoning capabilities~ zawalski2025roboticcontrolembodiedchainofthought, huang2025thinkactvisionlanguageactionreasoningreinforced, huang2022innermonologueembodiedreasoning , or subtask planning~ shi2025hirobotopenendedinstruction . While recent advancements in robot policies have enhanced fine manipulation capabilities, tasks requiring working memory remain a key challenge for real-world deployment. When wiping the window, the robot cannot determine whether the surface has already been wiped and ends up wiping the same area repeatedly. Such tasks are fundamentally non-Markovian, meaning that the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the optimal action. Yet most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, treating manipulation as a sequence of independent decisions. These structural limitations cause failure in memory-intensive tasks (see Fig. ~ fig:motivation ). Recently, various approaches have been proposed to address such limitations~ pomdpkaelbling1998planning . One line of work extracts latent embeddings from historical observations~ liberomem, fang2025sam2actintegratingvisualfoundation or compresses tokens into a memory module~ memoryvla . While these approaches are effective to some extent, relying on latent representations makes it difficult to identify causes of failure due to limited interpretability. Another line of work directly leverages visual history by stacking past frames~ torne2025learninglongcontextdiffusionpolicies or using keyframe annotations~ memer . A drawback of these approaches is computational overhead caused by accumulating image tokens, which limits long-horizon scalability. To overcome these limitations, we draw inspiration from how humans utilize an `inner monologue'. Just as humans manage complex tasks by internally keeping track of their progress (e.g., ``I pressed the button twice; one more to go") or spatial data (e.g., ``The cup was originally on the left"), we suggest that natural language can serve as an efficient and interpretable representation for robotic memory. By nature, this compact form preserves critical information (e.g., counts, locations) across long-horizon tasks. More fundamentally, language is a natural memory representation for VLM-based policies: it is the native modality of vision-language reasoning, scales compactly across long horizons, and exposes inspectable memory states for analysis. Building on this insight, we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), which incorporates language memory into robotic manipulation. HeLM separates high-level memory management from low-level action generation. Specifically, a VLM-based high-level policy (HLP) maintains the task relevant history in language form and generates action commands, while a VLA-based low-level policy (LLP) executes actions. Memory updates are event-triggered and occur only after task-relevant events or instruction changes. The language memory is organized into working and episodic fields according to whether information is needed within or across instructions. Together, these design choices support non-Markovian reasoning both within and across episodes. We evaluate HeLM on diverse non-Markovian tasks, including newly formulated inter-episode tasks. HeLM improves intra-episode subtask success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78 on compositional HLP generalization tasks. As task length grows, HeLM uses up to 4.5 less memory and runs 2.5 faster than the visual-memory baseline at long horizons. Contributions. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: [topsep=2pt, itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt, leftmargin=*] We propose HeLM, a hierarchical framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. Across 10 real-world tasks, HeLM outperforms memory-augmented and visual memory baselines, supported by component-level failure analysis. We formulate inter-episode persistence as an underexplored axis of robotic memory and introduce a task suite of 10 non-Markovian tasks (56 variants). Related Work sec:related_work Memory-Augmented and Hierarchical VLA Models VLA models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and map current visual-language observations to robot actions~ brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,pi0,kim2026rldx1technicalreport . Recent works extend these models with richer reasoning capabilities ~ geminiroboticsteam2025geminiroboticsbringingai,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,onetwovla,foreact , while hierarchical VLA frameworks decompose complex tasks into high-level instructions executed by low-level policies~ shi2025hirobotopenendedinstruction . However, these approaches do not necessarily maintain explicit task-relevant history over long horizons. Prior memory-augmented policies retrieve latent features or historical tokens~ memoryvla,mapvla,lin2025echovlaroboticvisionlanguageactionmodel,pragmabot,liberomem , while others preserve visual history through feature traces or multi-frame observations~ zheng2025tracevlavisualtraceprompting,chen2025historyawarevisuomotorpolicylearning,hu2025resolvingstateambiguityrobot,jang2025contextvlavisionlanguageactionmodelamortized,memer . These representations can retain historical information, but provide limited access to the explicit task state required for counting, sequencing, or cross-episode recall. Language has also been used to support temporal reasoning. Inner Monologue~ huang2022innermonologueembodiedreasoning provides language feedback such as success signals and scene descriptions to support closed-loop replanning, whereas HeLM explicitly keeps task-relevant history in language over the sequence. MEM~ mem combines short-horizon visual context with long-horizon textual memory, whereas HeLM separates event detection from memory updates, updating language memory only when task-relevant events are detected or instructions change. HeLM further evaluates inter-episode tasks, where completing a later instruction requires information acquired during an earlier episode. RoboMemory~ robomemory stores and retrieves past experience to support future interactions, whereas HeLM focuses on maintaining task-relevant history for the current non-Markovian task. Chameleon~ chameleon also uses a two-part memory but operates over latent multimodal tokens rather than explicit language. Overall, HeLM studies explicit language memory as a compact and interpretable way to carry task-relevant information over time and across instructions. Non-Markovian Manipulation Tasks in Robotics Manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO and RLBench evaluate episodes independently, with environment resets and no requirement to retain information across task boundaries~ rlbench, liu2023liberobenchmarkingknowledgetransfer, robocasa, mikasarobo, li2024evaluatingrealworldrobotmanipulation . Recent memory-focused benchmarks such as MemoryBench, LIBERO-Mem, RMBench, and RoboMME~ fang2025sam2actintegratingvisualfoundation, liberomem, rmbench, robomme introduce historical dependencies such as object occlusion, action history, and sequential progress. However, these benchmarks primarily evaluate memory within individual task episodes. In contrast, our task suite includes inter-episode tasks, where completing a later instruction requires information acquired during an earlier episode that cannot be recovered from the current observation alone. HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory sec:method HeLM's design follows a single principle: language can serve as a memory representation for VLA-based manipulation. This section formalizes the non-Markovian problem (Sec.~ subsec:problem_formulation ), hierarchical decomposition (Sec.~ subsec:overview ), structured memory (Sec.~ subsec:structured_memory ), and event-triggered inference (Sec.~ subsec:two_phase ). Standard VLA policies model the action distribution as , implicitly assuming that provides sufficient state information. However, identical observations can correspond to different underlying states depending on past events: A memoryless policy conditioned only on cannot distinguish histories that yield the same current observation but require different actions (see Fig.~ fig:motivation ). To address this gap, we introduce an explicit, structured textual memory that captures task-relevant history, reformulating the policy as . title: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair for Safe Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.
full_text: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair for\ Vision-Language-Action Models Chan Park , Sunwoo Hong , Kirak Kim , Yoonjeong Park ,\\ Alexander W. Olson , Ali Pesaranghader Sungkyunkwan University KAIST University of Toronto LG Electronics, Toronto AI Lab \\ pchan1018@g.skku.edu ali.pesaranghader@lge.com Corresponding Author Industry Advisor Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub . Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 . They are effective for task-oriented manipulation, but they do not guarantee safe execution~ safevla,hu2025vlsa . In obstacle-rich scenes, an action that moves the robot toward the target object can still pass through an unsafe region~ hu2025vlsa . This safety gap becomes critical in manipulation tasks. A small collision can move an obstacle, disturb the target object, or push the robot into an unfamiliar state. In such cases, the policy may still understand the task, but the execution path becomes difficult to recover. Prior work has addressed this issue by adding a post-hoc safety layer after the VLA policy~ hu2025vlsa . AEGIS follows this direction by applying a control barrier function quadratic program (CBF-QP) to the VLA action~ hu2025vlsa . The QP solver finds an action close to the original VLA output while satisfying a hard safety constraint~ ames2017cbf,hu2025vlsa . This local projection is effective for avoiding immediate collisions~ hu2025vlsa . However, local safety projection does not provide trajectory recovery. A CBF-QP filter can push the robot away from an obstacle, but importantly it does not decide how the robot should move around the obstacle or return to the task trajectory. Once the robot is pushed off this trajectory, the VLA policy may enter an unfamiliar state region and fail to recover the intended behavior~ ross2011dagger,mehta2024stablebc . We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module for safe VLA execution. Our method uses short-horizon action chunks predicted by the VLA policy to estimate the nominal path. If this path is blocked by an ellipsoidal unsafe region, we generate route candidates with entry, exit, and rejoin waypoints. The selected route is added to the QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard~ ames2017cbf . We evaluate the method on SafeLIBERO, where a robot must complete language-conditioned manipulation tasks while avoiding obstacles~ hu2025vlsa,libero . Raw VLA policies often fail because they have no explicit obstacle-avoidance mechanism~ safevla,hu2025vlsa . AEGIS improves collision avoidance through local CBF-QP repair, but can still lose task progress after safety intervention~ hu2025vlsa . Our route-guided repair improves the average collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess rates over the evaluated baselines, indicating that route-level guidance helps connect local safety correction with successful task execution. Our contributions are: We identify a trajectory-recovery failure mode of local CBF-QP safety projection in VLA robot execution. We introduce a route-guided CBF-QP repair method that detects blocked short-horizon VLA trajectories and generates entry-exit-rejoin guidance. We show that route guidance improves safe task execution on SafeLIBERO, when compared with raw VLA policies and AEGIS-style local safety repair. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models and Safety Repair VLA models extend vision-language and embodied multimodal models to robot action generation. Earlier language-conditioned robot systems grounded language-model reasoning in robot affordances or embodied observations~ saycan,palme . More recent generalist robot policies have benefited from large-scale robot datasets and cross-embodiment training~ openx,octo,rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 . These models have improved language-conditioned manipulation through web-scale VLM transfer, open-source robot demonstration training, flow-based action generation, and heterogeneous co-training. In parallel, diffusion-based action generation has become an effective paradigm for visuomotor policy learning, and discrete-diffusion-based VLAs have begun to study action decoding as iterative refinement over discretized action chunks~ diffusionpolicy,ddvla . Despite these advances, VLA policies are still mainly optimized for task completion rather than explicit safety~ safevla,hu2025vlsa . Post-hoc safety repair addresses this limitation by modifying the action after it is predicted~ hu2025vlsa . AEGIS is a representative example that adds a plug-and-play safety constraint layer after the VLA output and uses CBF-QP repair to project unsafe actions into a safe set~ hu2025vlsa . This design preserves the pretrained VLA policy and avoids retraining. However, existing repair layers mainly focus on whether the immediate action is safe. In contrast, our work focuses on whether the repaired action remains recoverable for future task execution. CBF-QP Safety Filtering and Trajectory Recovery Control barrier functions provide a principled way to keep a controlled system inside a safe set~ ames2017cbf,ames2019cbf . In a CBF-QP formulation, the controller optimizes for a nominal action while enforcing a barrier constraint that prevents unsafe state evolution~ ames2017cbf,rauscher2016constrained . This makes CBF-QP useful as a safety filter~ wabersich2023data . Safe nominal actions remain nearly unchanged, while unsafe actions are minimally corrected~ ames2017cbf,rauscher2016constrained,hu2025vlsa . This closest-safe-action principle becomes limited when the nominal controller is a VLA policy~ wabersich2021predictive,wabersich2023data . Closeness to the current VLA action does not necessarily imply recoverability of the future trajectory~ wabersich2022predictive . If an obstacle blocks the nominal path, repeated local projections may keep the robot safe near the obstacle boundary, but they do not provide a route around the obstacle or back to the task trajectory. Our method preserves the hard CBF safety constraint, but adds route-level guidance as a soft objective term so that the solver favors safe actions that support obstacle bypass and trajectory rejoin. Method sec:method We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc safety repair module for VLA robot execution. Given an action predicted by a pretrained VLA policy, the module repairs the action before execution. The key idea is to keep the CBF safety constraint hard while adding route-level guidance as a soft objective term when the nominal VLA trajectory is blocked by an obstacle. This allows the repair module to select an action that is not only safe, but directed toward a recoverable route. AEGIS applies a post-hoc CBF-QP safety layer to the VLA action and projects unsafe actions into the safe set. Since the VLA backbone is fixed, this comparison isolates the effect of adding route guidance for obstacle bypass and trajectory rejoin. Benchmark and Metrics We evaluate on the SafeLIBERO benchmark~ hu2025vlsa . SafeLIBERO extends LIBERO-style language-conditioned manipulation tasks with obstacle constraints. A policy must therefore complete the task while avoiding collisions. We report results on four suites: Spatial, Goal, Object, and Long. title: Swarm Choreography Made Simple: Superposed Guiding Vector Fields for Rigid Formation Path Following
summary: This paper presents a decentralized guiding vector field framework for rigid formation path following in multi- UAV systems based on the superposition of simple rule-driven vector fields. Each control objective is encoded as a dedicated vector-field component: a normalized tangential term to ensure progression along a prescribed geometric path at a desired speed, a convergence term driving the formation toward the path, a local coordination term that preserves the desired formation shape through a pseudo-path parameter, and a local separation term for inter-agent collision avoidance. The coordination mechanism requires the exchange of only a single scalar per agent, resulting in low communication bandwidth. Partial theoretical results establish convergence of the swarm to the desired path and formation in the absence of the sepa- ration term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed. The approach is experimentally validated using a swarm of five quadrotors executing two 3D choreographies. The first experiment involves tracking a helical path while maintaining a rigid V-shaped formation. The second demonstrates a spiral- like motion obtained by a rotating circular formation tracking a vertical line. The experimental results support the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed framework.
full_text: Swarm Choreography Made Simple: \ Guiding Vector Fields for Rigid Formation Path Following João Machado , Matthieu Verdoucq , Christophe Jouffrais , and Murat Bronz João Machado is a PhD Candidate at ENAC Email: joao.machado@enac.fr Matthieu Verdoucq is a Post-Doctoral Researcher at ENAC Email: matthieu.verdoucq@enac.fr Christophe Jouffrais is a Professor at CNRS, IPAL, IRIT Email: christophe.jouffrais@cnrs.fr Murat Bronz is an assistant professor at ENAC Email: murat.bronz@enac.fr This paper presents a decentralized guiding vector field framework for rigid formation path following in multi-UAV systems based on the superposition of simple rule-driven vector fields. Each control objective is encoded as a dedicated vector-field component: a normalized tangential term to ensure progression along a prescribed geometric path at a desired speed, a convergence term driving the formation toward the path, a local coordination term that preserves the desired formation shape through a pseudo-path parameter, and a local separation term for inter-agent collision avoidance. The coordination mechanism requires the exchange of only a single scalar per agent, resulting in low communication bandwidth. Partial theoretical results establish convergence of the swarm to the desired path and formation in the absence of the separation term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed. The approach is experimentally validated using a swarm of five quadrotors executing two 3D choreographies. The first experiment involves tracking a helical path while maintaining a rigid V-shaped formation. The second demonstrates a spiral-like motion obtained by a rotating circular formation tracking a vertical line. The experimental results support the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed framework. multi-UAV systems, guiding vector fields, decentralized control, rigid formation control, path following, collision avoidance, drone swarms Introduction Coordinated motion of mobile robots is of significant interest, with applications across domains including drone light shows, environmental monitoring, wildfire detection, search-and-rescue operations, and defence systems. Multiple autonomous agents must coordinate to achieve shared objectives such as area coverage, target tracking, formation control, and obstacle avoidance alqudsi_uav_2025 . Recent research has increasingly focused on decentralized coordination algorithms, in which each robot makes decisions based on local information and limited communication with neighbouring agents. Such approaches improve scalability, robustness, and adaptability, enabling multi-robot systems to operate effectively in dynamic and unpredictable environments without dependence on a central controller. A key challenge is ensuring that locally computed control actions, based only on partial state information and local interactions, collectively induce globally convergent behaviour of the swarm ProrokRobustnessTaxonomy2021 . Despite the significant advances in the field, coordinated drone motion still faces challenges in terms of efficiency, scalability, and robustness, including when multiple objectives such as path following, formation keeping, and collision avoidance must be satisfied simultaneously ames_control_2019, abdel-nasser_decentralized_2025 . This paper proposes a decentralized guiding vector field (GVF) framework based on vector field superposition. Each swarm objective is decomposed into one or more “rules”, each represented by a vector field enforcing the corresponding behaviour. The overall guiding vector field is obtained by superimposing these rule-based vector fields. The results are validated experimentally with a swarm of 5 DJI Mini 3 drones, presented in Figure. fig:djis . Some theoretical analysis and proofs are also provided. Related Work The unification of multiple objectives such as path following, formation control, and obstacle avoidance into a single control law poses challenges for guaranteeing global convergence. Existing approaches typically increase complexity through online optimization, hierarchical architectures, or switching strategies. Simple superposition of independent control laws may lead to instability, conflicting directions, or undesired equilibria, as control actions associated with different objectives may generate conflicting vector directions tanner_relaxed_2014, ames_control_2019 . However, if such a superposition were feasible, each objective could be designed independently, significantly simplifying the problem. This work explores this idea through the superposition of vector fields into a single GVF. A related approach is abdel-nasser_decentralized_2025 , where superposition is restricted to gradients of artificial potentials, whereas this work allows a more general formulation beyond potential fields. Agent path following has been extensively studied in the literature SujitUnmannedAerial2014 . Common approaches include error-regulated methods EbrahimpourFaultTolerantRobust2025, LiErrorConstrainedFormation2024 , optimal control methods ReinhardtFixedWingUAV2023, Hirst3DPathFollowing2025 , virtual target tracking methods JiangEnhancedPure2025, MacenskiRegulatedPure2023 , and vector-field-based methods Kapitanyukguidingvector2018, LuVersatileDistributed2025, YaoSingularityfreeGuiding2021, YaoGuidingvector2022, ZhouInverseKinematics2025 . Guiding vector field methods generate control commands by defining a continuous vector field whose integral curves converge to a desired path. These methods offer several advantages over alternative approaches. In particular, they do not require the agent to start near the path and often achieve high path-following accuracy with relatively low control effort. A known limitation is the presence of critical points where the vector field vanishes or is undefined SujitUnmannedAerial2014, YaoTopologicalAnalysis2022 . These sets are typically measure zero and unstable, and can often be mitigated via suitable extensions or virtual coordinates YaoSingularityfreeGuiding2021 . Additionally, system inertia and disturbances make convergence to these points unlikely. GVFs are commonly decomposed into tangential and convergence components. The former enforces motion along the path, while the latter reduces tracking error. In Kapitanyukguidingvector2018 , convergence is based on a gradient term scaled by the path error, whereas ZhouInverseKinematics2025 employs an inverse-kinematics formulation. This work adopts the structure of Kapitanyukguidingvector2018 and normalizes both components following ZhouInverseKinematics2025 to achieve a desired constant speed tracking and smoother error-dependent convergence. Formation control in multi-agent systems oh_survey_2015, chen_survey_2023 may refer either to task-driven emergent configurations or to rigid formations with predefined geometry lau_co-operative_2015, marina_distributed_2016 . This work focuses on rigid formations. Some GVF-based formation control approaches have been proposed. In YaoGuidingvector2022 , convergence of a drone swarm to a manifold defined by the intersection of up to surfaces in is established, enabling path following and rigid formation within that manifold. This approach could be extended to include the full space, requiring virtual coordinates for agent coordination. In this paper, the coordination in is done with only 1 scalar parameter reducing the necessary bandwidth. In LuVersatileDistributed2025 , higher-level abstraction using parametric coordinates and virtual references allows agents to coordinate around closed paths and achieve arbitrary shapes. While flexible, this strategy drastically complicates explicit geometric formation specification for non-circular shapes. No other work addressing rigid formation assignment under GVF-based path following was found. Collision avoidance in multi-robot systems can be achieved through barrier-function–based methods, artificial potential fields, or learning-based techniques ames_control_2019, khargharia_collision_2026, merei_survey_2025 . Among these, artificial potential fields are well suited to the present framework, as they naturally generate repulsive vector fields that can be directly superimposed with vector fields arising from other control objectives pavle_obstacle_2025, khatib_real-time_1985, abdel-nasser_decentralized_2025 . A typical approach is to consider a potential field whose gradient results in a polynomial or an hyperbolic term. The polynomial term keeps the total vector field smooth while the hyperbolic term ensures the agents can never collide gonzalez-sierra_smooth_2023, khatib_real-time_1985 . In this paper a combination of both is used to try to achieve smoothness and guaranteed repulsion. Contributions This paper proposes a decentralized guiding vector field framework based on the superposition of simpler vector fields to achieve global asymptotic convergence of a drone swarm to an arbitrarily specified rigid formation in while tracking a prescribed path. Unlike approaches relying on implicit manifold descriptions or high-dimensional parametric coordination, the proposed method assigns explicit relative positions to each agent in the formation. Coordination requires sharing only a single scalar parameter per agent, thereby significantly reducing communication bandwidth. The main contributions are: A novel GVF-based strategy for simultaneous path following and rigid formation keeping in multi-agent systems; An explicit and low-complexity method for enforcing arbitrary rigid formations via prescribed relative positions with respect to a common formation reference; A decentralized coordination mechanism that reduces inter-agent communicated information from dimension to , per agent; A unified framework based on vector field superposition that simultaneously addresses path following, path convergence, formation maintenance, and collision avoidance; Rigorous theoretical results for key components of the framework, supported by analysis of subsystem convergence; Experimental validation using a real-world swarm of five quadrotors. title: VLALagBench: Understanding When and Why VLA Inference Latency Matters
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.
full_text: 20pt Introduction sec:introduction Physical AI has the potential to enable robots to perform diverse tasks autonomously in the real world. Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models have brought this goal closer by predicting robot actions via visual observations and natural-language instructions. These models have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of manipulation tasks, highlighting their potential for general-purpose robotics~ intelligence2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00tn1,fang2026molmoact2 . Although VLA models need to respond in real time to keep up with changes in the physical world, the inference latency required for successful task execution remains poorly understood. From a systems perspective, VLA-Perf~ jiang2026vlaperf uses 10\,Hz and 100\,Hz as reference points for acceptable and high-performance inference, respectively, without evaluating how these rates translate into task success. Similarly, Realtime-VLA~ ma2025realtimevla,yang2026realtimevlav2,niu2026realtimevlaflash improves inference and execution speed, but demonstrates the benefits on a limited set of tasks, such as catching a falling pen. From a benchmarking perspective, popular robotic manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO~ liu2023libero and RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa primarily evaluate model generalization across tasks and scenes, but their static environments provide limited insight into how inference latency affects task success in evolving physical environments. While recent benchmarks such as DynamicVLA's DOM, MoveBench, and ReflexBench~ xie2026dynamicvla,zhang2026ppc,chen2026reflex support manipulation tasks with moving objects, these benchmarks do not systematically evaluate how inference latency affects task success: their evaluations either omit latency, use latencies tied to specific hardware, or cover only a limited set of policies and tasks. In this paper, we present , a benchmark for systematically studying how VLA inference latency affects task success , which provides the foundation for future robotic system design. As shown in Figure~ fig:overview , examines five factors related to latency sensitivity. (1) Task type: grasping a moving object, releasing an object into a moving receptacle, placing an object on a moving surface, and manipulating a moving articulated object. (2) Object speed: different target speeds within each task. (3) VLA policy: popular models including , GR00T N1.7, and MolmoAct2~ intelligence2025pi05,nvidia2026gr00tlibero,fang2026molmoact2 . (4) Execution mode: synchronous and various asynchronous execution methods. (5) Inference latency: controlled latency levels. Beyond our primary benchmark built on the MuJoCo simulator~ todorov2012mujoco , we also conduct experiments in Isaac Sim (another widely-used simulator) and on real robots to verify our findings. Our evaluation with yields four key findings, each addressing a research question: 0pt 4pt Q1. How does inference latency affect task success across different manipulation tasks? Latency sensitivity varies substantially across tasks ( sec:eval-tasks ). For objects moving at \,m/s, a moderate inference latency of 100\,ms nearly halves success in one task (from 71.5 to 40.5 ), while another retains more (86 ) of its zero-latency success rate (from 86.5 to 74.0 ). Q2. What factors determine a task's sensitivity to inference latency? Latency reduces task success through (1) stale observations (the target has moved by the time inference completes) and (2) robot pauses during synchronous inference. Their impact varies by task: stale observations affect tasks that particularly require precise manipulation, while pauses disrupt tasks requiring continuous motion ( sec:eval-tasks ). These factors motivate our next study of asynchronous execution. Q3. What are the trade-offs between synchronous and asynchronous execution as inference latency increases? Asynchronous execution overlaps inference with robot actions, keeping the robot moving and benefiting tasks that require continuous motion. When inference latency is sufficiently short, continuous asynchronous execution also reduces observation staleness through more frequent action updates, improving precision. These benefits come at the cost of more frequent inference requests ( sec:eval-async ). Q4. Do different VLA models exhibit the same latency sensitivity? VLA policies differ in their sensitivity to stale observations and robot pauses, thus benefiting to different extents from asynchronous execution. Additionally, the best-performing policy at a given inference latency depends on both the task and target speed ( sec:eval-policies ). Building on these findings, we further develop an empirical model that guides the selection of algorithm configurations for a given inference system ( sec:eval-deployment ). Different combinations of GPUs, networks, and software runtimes result in different inference latencies and per-robot throughput. Consequently, the VLA configuration, including the execution mode and action execution horizon, that maximizes task success may differ across systems. Because exhaustively evaluating this configuration space is prohibitively expensive, we develop a model that estimates task success across latencies, execution modes, and execution horizons, using only a small set of measurements. Given a system's latency and throughput constraints, we thus use these predictions to select the feasible algorithm configuration with the highest predicted task success. This paper makes three main contributions, which together provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm--system co-designs: 2pt 0pt We introduce to comprehensively benchmark how VLA latency affects task success. We present findings on latency sensitivity across tasks, target speeds, execution modes, and VLA policies. We develop an empirical model that predicts task success rate and use it to guide algorithm configuration choice given a user-provided system specification. Background and Motivation sec:background In this section, we introduce VLA models and review existing benchmarks for evaluating their manipulation performance. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into how inference latency affects task success, motivating our systematic investigation on this important topic. Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent an important step toward physical AI by using visual observations and natural-language instructions to generate robot actions for continuous control~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00tn1 . As shown in Figure~ fig:vla-architecture , a VLA model combines a vision-language model (VLM) backbone that encodes camera images and language instructions with an action expert that predicts the robot's next sequence of actions. Models such as , , GR00T N1, and MolmoAct2 use diffusion transformers (DiT) as action experts, transforming sampled noise into continuous action sequences through multiple refinement iterations~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00tn1,fang2026molmoact2 . OpenVLA and the original MolmoAct instead generate discrete action tokens autoregressively, which are then decoded into robot actions~ kim2024openvla,lee2025molmoact . Modern VLA policies commonly predict an action chunk, a sequence of future actions generated in one inference call~ zhao2023act,black2024pi0,nvidia2025gr00tn1,fang2026molmoact2 . We denote the number of predicted actions by , the action chunk size, and the number executed before switching to an updated chunk by , the execution horizon~ black2025rtc . Predicting multiple actions together helps maintain consistent motion, while executing only a shorter prefix ( ) lets the robot incorporate new observations and adjust its actions sooner~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2025rtc . Figure~ fig:action-chunking shows an example of two chunks generated by separate inference calls (assuming zero inference latency): the robot executes the first actions of chunk A ( ), then switches to chunk B, replacing A's remaining actions. Robot Manipulation Benchmarks Widely used robotic manipulation benchmarks evaluate how well policies perform diverse tasks and generalize across objects, goals, and scenes. For example, LIBERO provides task suites that vary spatial relationships, object identities, and task goals, together with a long-horizon suite that requires executing sequences of manipulation skills~ liu2023libero . RoboCasa expands evaluation to diverse kitchen environments, covering individual skills such as pick-and-place and opening drawers, as well as composite activities that combine multiple skills~ nasiriany2024robocasa . RoboLab evaluates generalist policies on household manipulation tasks organized around visual recognition, spatial relationships, and procedural skills, and measures their robustness to changes in scene appearance and camera configuration~ yang2026robolab . These benchmarks provide valuable measures of task competence and generalization, but limited insight into the consequences of inference latency. Due to the static physical environments in these benchmarks, a longer inference latency increases task completion time without directly affecting the task outcome~ chen2026reflex . Consequently, these benchmarks do not reflect whether a policy can react quickly enough to succeed when the physical world continues to evolve during inference. Dynamic Manipulation Benchmarks Recent dynamic manipulation benchmarks introduce moving objects to test policy reactivity, but they do not systematically isolate how inference latency degrades task success. For example, MoveBench tests grasping under constant, accelerating, and irregular object velocities~ zhang2026ppc , DynamicVLA's Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark evaluates grasping and placing with moving targets~ xie2026dynamicvla , and ReflexBench introduces time-critical tasks such as conveyor picking and ball catching~ chen2026reflex . However, MoveBench does not account for inference latency during simulation~ zhang2026ppc . DOM runs the simulator during inference, but its latencies are tied to the policy and GPU used for evaluation, without a controlled sweep showing how task success changes with inference latency~ xie2026dynamicvla . ReflexBench explicitly varies inference latency under synchronous and asynchronous execution, but studies its effect using a single policy (SmolVLA) on only two tasks~ chen2026reflex . Research gap. Because neither existing benchmarks nor latency-aware model papers (Appendix~ app:related ) jointly vary task types, object speeds, execution modes, and generalist VLA policies under controlled inference latency, the systematic relationship between VLA latency and robot task success rate remains uncharacterized. Benchmark and Execution Modes sec:benchmark We present , a benchmark for systematically studying how VLA inference latency affects task success. As summarized in Figure~ fig:overview , we vary five factors: (1) manipulation task type, (2) target object speed, (3) VLA policy, (4) execution mode, and (5) inference latency. We hope the insights from the systematic evaluation of ( sec:evaluation ) will guide future robotic system and architecture designs. Design Principles sec:design To ensure that performance drops reflect latency sensitivity rather than baseline policy failures or simulator artifacts, is built around four design principles. First, evaluated policies must achieve high success rate in static scenes at zero latency so that accuracy degradation with added latency is attributable to latency. Second, the tasks should cover diverse interactions with moving targets, such as grasping a moving object or placing an object at a moving destination. Third, object moving trajectories must be precisely controllable without altering the simulator's underlying contact physics. Fourth, multiple widely adopted VLA models must provide public checkpoints on the exact same tas

title: A Tightly Coupled Magnetic-Inertial SLAM System for Field Robots
summary: Field robots operating in mines, tunnels, and disaster areas require reliable localization despite GNSS denial and degraded camera and LiDAR measurements caused by dust, smoke, or poor illumination. Missions involving both ground and aerial robots further motivate complementary sensing modalities that do not depend on visibility, preinstalled infrastructure, or wheel contact. This letter presents MISLAM, a tightly coupled magnetic-inertial simultaneous localization and mapping system using an IMU and a nine-magnetometer array, without relying on external odometry or platform-specific motion assumptions. The system combines the inertial navigation model with local polynomial magnetic-field models for short-term motion estimation and a global Gaussian process model for drift correction using an error-state Kalman filter. Offline evaluation on three indoor datasets collected with a handheld rig shows reductions in total endpoint closure error of 45.7% - 78.0% relative to magnetic-inertial odometry. Under poor illumination, MISLAM maintains tracking after visual-inertial odometry fails, achieving a horizontal closure error of 0.332 m, although vertical drift remains a limitation. These results support magnetic-inertial SLAM as a complementary localization modality for robotic sensor suites operating under degraded visual conditions.
full_text: Field robots operating in mines, tunnels, and disaster areas require reliable localization despite GNSS denial and degraded camera and LiDAR measurements caused by dust, smoke, or poor illumination. Missions involving both ground and aerial robots further motivate complementary sensing modalities that do not depend on visibility, preinstalled infrastructure, or wheel contact. This letter presents MISLAM, a tightly coupled magnetic-inertial simultaneous localization and mapping system using an IMU and a nine-magnetometer array, without relying on external odometry or platform-specific motion assumptions. The system combines the inertial navigation model with local polynomial magnetic-field models for short-term motion estimation and a global Gaussian process model for drift correction using an error-state Kalman filter. Offline evaluation on three indoor datasets collected with a handheld rig shows reductions in total endpoint closure error of 45.7 –78.0 relative to magnetic-inertial odometry. Under poor illumination, MISLAM maintains tracking after visual-inertial odometry fails, achieving a horizontal closure error of 0.332 m, although vertical drift remains a limitation. These results support magnetic-inertial SLAM as a complementary localization modality for robotic sensor suites operating under degraded visual conditions. Introduction Reliable localization is a prerequisite for field robots exploring mines, tunnels, and disaster areas. These environments often deny access to global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), while poor illumination, dust, and smoke can degrade camera- and LiDAR-based localization~ Ebadi2024Present . These challenges motivate complementary sensing modalities that provide motion information without relying on visibility, preinstalled infrastructure, or wheel contact. Such capabilities are relevant to both ground and aerial robots and can support localization when other sensors become unreliable. Indoor magnetic fields have been recognized as a promising environmental feature for localization because of their spatial inhomogeneity and temporal stability. Ferromagnetic structures and objects create spatial variations that can remain sufficiently stable to serve as location-dependent signatures~ Li2012Magnetic . Furthermore, magnetic-field-based localization does not require capturing identifiable visual information, avoiding the associated image-privacy concerns. These properties have motivated sustained research over the past two decades, spanning magnetic-field fingerprinting and model-based localization methods~ Vissiere2007magnetometers,Vallivaara2010Simultaneous,Kok2018MagSlam,zmitri2019improving,Viset2022EKF,pavlasek2023magnetic, huang2023mains,ZHANG2023MagODO,Kok2024Online,Shen2024IDFMFL,Kuang2025CrowdMagMap,huang2026inertialmagneticslamsystems,Vallivaara2026Saying,Tongxing2026MAVIS . Magnetic fingerprinting typically matches measurements to locations within a pre-surveyed map. However, surveying an unknown environment in advance can be time-consuming and is often infeasible prior to a field robotics mission. Magnetic-field SLAM addresses this issue by estimating the trajectory and field map jointly. Representative methods~ Kok2018MagSlam,Viset2022EKF,Vallivaara2026Saying use Gaussian processes (GPs) to model the magnetic field along the trajectory and constrain the drift accumulated during pose propagation. Despite these advances, existing magnetic SLAM methods still rely on accurate external odometry---typically from visual-inertial odometry (VIO) or pedestrian dead reckoning---which limits their applicability when primary odometry sensors degrade or the platform's motion pattern is incompatible with the assumptions of the odometry method. Achieving self-contained magnetic-field SLAM without external odometry or restrictive motion assumptions presents two main challenges: 1) High computational complexity: Extracting odometry directly from magnetic field measurements requires high-resolution field models capable of capturing sub-meter spatial variations. As reported in~ skog2025OnTheConnection , 50 to 500 basis functions per square meter are needed to support accurate localization. 2) Degenerate spatial sampling: Spatially proximate measurements often yield overconfident predictions of the magnetic field at nearby locations, particularly when entering unexplored areas~ Vallivaara2010Simultaneous,lee2020magslam . Mitigating this issue requires enforcing a minimum guard distance or time interval between map updates, which further complicates high-resolution modeling. Magnetometer arrays enable an alternative, local modeling of the magnetic fields across the array. Because the array covers a relatively small volume, accurate yet computationally efficient local field models can be constructed. Moreover, because the relative positions of the magnetometers are fixed and known, the local field model can be fitted and evaluated from a single multi-sensor snapshot with lower uncertainty than fitting single-magnetometer measurements along an estimated trajectory. This type of modeling enables magnetic odometry inspired by optical flow~ skog2021magnetic . Magnetic-inertial odometry (MIO) systems, including MAINS~ huang2023mains and other array-based methods~ Vissiere2007magnetometers,zmitri2020magnetic,Li2025SCEKF,liu2026fss , fuse array measurements with inertial measurements to bound velocity and position drift. Although these methods are self-contained and require neither external odometry nor motion constraints, existing MIO systems do not maintain a persistent global field map. Consequently, they cannot exploit loop closures when revisiting mapped areas, leaving long-term navigation drift uncorrected. Building on these developments, this letter presents MISLAM, a tightly coupled magnetic-inertial SLAM system that combines the complementary strengths of local polynomial field modeling and global GP mapping using a single error-state Kalman filter (ESKF). The main contributions of this letter are as follows: We develop a self-contained magnetic-inertial SLAM system using an IMU and a nine-magnetometer array that operates without external odometry or restrictive motion constraints. We develop an ESKF update strategy that validates local field references using chi-square tests, retires each reference after one update attempt, and selects global GP keyframes based on the number of accepted local updates. We evaluate MISLAM against a state-of-the-art MIO system (MAINS~ huang2023mains ) and a VIO system (OpenVINS~ Geneva2020ICRA ) across three indoor datasets collected with a handheld sensor rig under varying revisit topologies and lighting conditions. Overview The proposed MISLAM system fuses inertial and magnetic measurements to jointly estimate the trajectory and the magnetic-field map. The system uses a sensor rig that consists of an array of magnetometers and an IMU. The processing stages---sensor calibration, stationary initialization, inertial propagation, and local and global magnetic updates---are shown in Fig.~ fig:system-overview and detailed in Sections~ sec:initialization and~ sec:magnetic inertial slam . Here, we present the main concepts and notation. After proper sensor calibration and filter initialization, IMU measurements propagate the position, velocity, and attitude. Magnetic measurements from two disjoint groups—the local group \(L\) and the global group \(G\)—reduce the propagation error through the local and global field representations, respectively. A local model captures the spatial field variation around a recent reference pose and provides short-term relative motion information. A global model retains magnetic information across the explored environment, allowing measurements in previously mapped regions to reduce accumulated navigation drift. title: Seeing Through the Illusion: Test-Time Scaling for World Action Models
comment: Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on From Generative Models to Robot Actions (G2A)
summary: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.
full_text: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce (World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0 to 24.0 on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1 to 78.3 mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision. Introduction sec:introduction World action models (WAMs) jointly generate robot actions and predictions of how the observed world may evolve~ kim2026cosmospolicy,li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero,wang2026wamsurvey . This creates a natural opportunity for test-time scaling: sample several complete world-action rollouts from a frozen WAM, evaluate them before execution, and execute the strongest candidate. Sampling and verification have improved action-only policies~ kwok2025robomonkey,zhao2026tapsampling , while recent WAM systems use predicted value, future consensus, geometric consistency, action-distribution consistency, or action-conditioned simulation as decision-time signals~ kim2026cosmospolicy,ruan2026futurecompatible,zhao2026geobon,zhou2026tau0wm . These signals judge the imagined future alone or the action alone, or require an external simulator; none checks whether a single candidate's action and future describe the same motion. The central challenge is therefore how to judge a coupled action-future proposal using only information available before physical execution. A WAM's imagined future can diverge from execution, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:dream_execution_divergence . In the banana-grasp example, the imagined object remains near the gripper while execution displaces it away from the predicted interaction. In the yogurt-motion example, the imagined object moves substantially while execution shows little corresponding motion. Visual plausibility alone does not guarantee that an action will realize the predicted transition. We hypothesize that candidates whose proposed action and imagined future disagree are the ones most likely to diverge in execution, and that this disagreement is measurable before acting. We introduce , a pre-execution selector for frozen WAMs. WISE scores each candidate on three properties: whether its action chunk is valid and temporally regular, whether the motion an inverse dynamics model (IDM) recovers from its imagined future agrees with its proposed action, and how much task progress its imagined future represents. The three bounded scores are summed, and the highest-scoring action chunk is executed. The IDM is trained once per embodiment; the WAM is never updated. We evaluate WISE with Cosmos~3 Edge on RoboLab and DreamZero on LIBERO against Future Consensus, GeoBoN, and Robometer at a matched budget of four candidates. WISE raises success from 6.0 to 24.0 on RoboLab and from 75.1 to 78.3 on LIBERO, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt] A pre-execution selector that combines action validity, cross-output consistency, and task progress in one bounded score, with the WAM frozen. An inverse-dynamics consistency score that tests whether a candidate's co-generated action supports the motion in its own imagined future. Closed-loop evaluation on two WAM and embodiment pairs at a matched budget, with component ablations and agreement analyses. Related work sec:related_work World action models and test-time scaling. Recent WAMs couple visual dynamics prediction with action generation, including PAD, Cosmos Policy, DreamZero, LingBot-VA, GR-2, Unified World Models, and VideoVLA~ guo2024pad,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva,cheang2024gr2,zhu2025uwm,shen2025videovla . WISE is agnostic to their architecture and training objective; it requires only temporally aligned action and future predictions available before execution. Test-time sampling and verification have improved action-only robot policies~ kwok2025robomonkey,zhao2026tapsampling . In WAMs, candidate selection has used predicted value, agreement among imagined futures, cross-view geometry, re-denoising consistency, and action-conditioned simulation~ kim2026cosmospolicy,ruan2026futurecompatible,zhao2026geobon,zhou2026tau0wm . WISE focuses on how to evaluate the native joint rollout itself as a complete control process. Physical action quality and consistency. Robot-action quality has been assessed through smoothness, embodiment constraints, collision/continuity checks, and inverse-dynamics-derived motion rewards~ liu2026evalactions,yang2026vista,wang2026eva,nguyen2026sdn,yang2026physreflect . These signals operate at different stages: some diagnose completed trajectories, others filter training data or post-train world models, and Selected Diffusion Noise uses a kinematic smoothness criterion directly for inference-time action selection~ nguyen2026sdn . WISE uses a lightweight version of this idea as one component of its rollout score: it checks the native WAM action against interface constraints and temporal regularity. Different decision-time methods also use different consistency relations: agreement among alternative futures~ ruan2026futurecompatible , cross-view geometry~ zhao2026geobon , compatibility with a learned conditional action distribution~ zhou2026tau0wm , or recovery of an action supplied to an action-conditioned world model~ seo2026acid . WISE targets a distinct relation exposed by native WAMs: whether the action and imagined future co-generated within the same candidate describe compatible robot motion. Table~ tab:consistency_criteria summarizes the quantities compared by each criterion. In particular, ACID tests whether an IDM recovers the action supplied to an action-conditioned world model~ seo2026acid . WISE applies this comparison to the action and future co-generated within a native WAM candidate. Progress and value. Task-progress and value models provide a complementary semantic signal. TapSampling uses an action-conditioned progress verifier~ zhao2026tapsampling ; Cosmos Policy and -WM use predicted value or progress in planning~ kim2026cosmospolicy,zhou2026tau0wm ; Robometer learns frame-level progress and trajectory preferences~ liang2026robometer ; and RISE uses imagined progress values for policy improvement~ yang2026rise . WISE leaves the task evaluator model-agnostic and uses its frozen judgment as one component of the rollout score. Problem Formulation sec:problem We formulate test-time scaling for world action models as an online selection problem over multiple candidate rollouts. At each control step, the frozen WAM generates several possible future-action trajectories, from which a selector chooses one for execution using only pre-execution information. At control step , let denote the current observation, robot state, and instruction. The frozen WAM samples candidate rollouts where \[ _t^ (i) = ( _ t+1 ^ (i) , , _ t+H_v ^ (i) ) \] denotes the imagined future rollout and \[ A_t^ (i) = ( a_t^ (i) , , a_ t+H_a-1 ^ (i) ) \] denotes its co-generated action chunk. Before execution, the candidates are scored and the highest-ranked rollout is selected: The selected action chunk is then executed, after which the robot observes the resulting state and replans. The WAM remains frozen throughout; test-time scaling acts only through candidate generation and pre-execution selection. WISE: Selecting WAM Rollouts sec:method Rollout scoring sec:process_reward For candidate , WISE defines where the components score action suitability, agreement between the co-generated action and imagined motion, and predicted task progress. They address different potential failures: smooth actions may make no task progress, and apparently useful futures may be incompatible with their proposed actions. Action validity and temporal regularity sec:executability The execution component evaluates whether a candidate proposes an action sequence that is physically plausible to execute. A candidate may predict a desirable future while containing commands that violate the robot's operating constraints or imply implausible motion. We therefore assess the proposed action chunk directly using validity checks defined by the corresponding control interface. For candidate , let , , denote the continuous control components of the -th action in the chunk of Equation~ eq:candidate . Executability is assessed through complementary validity checks. At the most direct level, commanded values should remain within their admissible ranges. When the control representation admits a physical interpretation across time, additional checks can be derived from consecutive commands. We map this violation to a soft score where is the tolerance of check in the same units. Satisfied constraints receive , while increasingly severe violations smoothly reduce the score toward zero rather than causing a hard rejection. The execution score combines the checks supported by the control interface: Higher values indicate action chunks that better respect the robot's physical and control constraints. World-action consistency sec:consistency A WAM candidate jointly predicts an action trajectory and an imagined future. WISE evaluates whether the co-generated action agrees with the robot motion inferred from that imagined future. Let denote an inverse dynamics model (IDM) trained on embodiment-specific demonstration trajectories. Applied to the imagined future , the IDM predicts a continuous action trajectory together with any discrete control predictions required by the embodiment. The IDM outputs normalized coordinates , which are mapped back to the WAM action space using the IDM training-set statistics: Continuous-action consistency. Let denote the continuous channels of the WAM-generated action chunk . We compute the mean absolute discrepancy in standardized training-set units: The discrepancy is converted to a consistency score Discrete-action consistency. For discrete control channels such as the gripper, we compare the command inferred from the imagined rollout with the command proposed by the WAM. After mapping both predictions to discrete states using a decision threshold, the consistency score is defined as The final world-action consistency score combines continuous-motion and discrete-control agreement: A high consistency score indicates that the co-generated action and imagined future provide compatible descriptions of the candidate robot motion. This is an internal property of the generated rollout; correspondence between the imagined future and the subsequently realized environment remains a separate source of uncertainty. title: Pixel-UMI: Learning Environment-Aware Whole-Body Manipulation from Sensorized Human Demonstrations
comment: Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi
summary: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi

We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0 average task progress. Video results are available at Introduction Mobile manipulation requires coordinated motion of the arms, torso, head, and base. Imitation learning provides a way to acquire these behaviors from demonstrations. Teleoperation is a widely used approach to collecting high-quality demonstrations~ fu2024mobile,jiang2025behavior , but is challenging for mobile manipulation: operators must coordinate many degrees of freedom, and collection across environments requires deploying a robot at each site. Sensorized human data collection offers a more direct way to gather demonstrations by giving people a manipulation interface matched to the robot's~ chi2024universal,sunday2025act1 . The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), for example, records images and motion through handheld grippers that the demonstrator uses to interact with objects. This allows people to coordinate their own bodies and receive physical feedback from contact, making demonstration more intuitive than teleoperation while allowing collection across environments without transporting a robot. Extensions to mobile manipulation complement the grippers with a head-mounted camera, providing the broader visual context needed for navigation and whole-body coordination~ xu2026hommi,zeng2025activeumi . Transferring these demonstrations to a robot requires aligning the demonstrated gripper and camera frames with their robot counterparts so that the manipulation and visual observations remain consistent across embodiments~ chi2024universal,xu2026hommi . Although task-frame matching can suffice for tabletop manipulation with limited redundancy, it leaves the posture of a whole-body mobile manipulator underdetermined: many arm, torso, and base configurations can realize similar gripper and head targets. These choices affect whether the robot can continue following the demonstrated motion within the scene. When retrieving a tennis-ball canister from a deep box, for example, the elbow must lift above the rim to allow the gripper to descend. Without an appropriate elbow posture, contact with the rim can obstruct the arm and prevent continued gripper tracking. To support continued task-frame tracking, the robot must choose a body configuration that accommodates the surrounding geometry. To this end, we introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which uses scene geometry to resolve the robot's posture while matching the demonstrated gripper and head motion. EAR reconstructs static scene geometry from the episode's depth sequence, using temporal evidence to separate dynamic objects without requiring a separate scene scan. We then use environment-aware geometric fabrics~ xie2020fabrics to retarget the demonstrated motion against this geometry offline, producing body joint trajectories and base commands. The policy learns these posture choices directly, avoiding the need to combine scene estimation with collision-aware whole-body control during policy rollout. However, fundamental differences in body shape and kinematics between humans and robots can still prevent exact head and gripper tracking, creating viewpoint mismatches between human training images and robot observations~ xu2026hommi . Retargeting alone cannot fully eliminate this mismatch, but we can mitigate its impact during policy training. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM). Because retargeting occurs before policy training, its pose errors reveal when a demonstrated viewpoint is difficult for the robot to reproduce. REAM uses these errors as geometric proxies for visual mismatch in percentile-based camera masking: views with higher-ranked errors are more likely to have their tokens excluded during training. This encourages the policy to draw on other available observations when a view is poorly aligned, while retaining access to all cameras at deployment. Finally, sensorized human data collection without force or tactile sensors records motion states but not the interaction forces underlying human actions~ chi2024universal,liu2025forcemimic,choi2026umift . Motion states alone do not determine the robot commands needed to reproduce these interactions, so policies trained on this supervision can struggle with contact-rich manipulation. Nevertheless, learning from these demonstrations provides a useful policy prior for task motion and whole-body coordination, making on-policy correction practical. We therefore collect on-policy correction data through DAgger~ ross2011dagger to improve performance on contact-rich whole-body tasks. We call our combined pipeline Pixel-UMI and evaluate it on the co-designed platform~ pixel2027system . We summarize our key contributions as follows: =10000 EAR converts head and gripper demonstrations into environment-aware whole-body joint and base supervision. Across three tasks requiring whole-body coordination, it increases average task progress by 64.41~pp. REAM uses percentile-ranked retargeting errors to guide camera masking and reduce dependence on mismatched views. On the same three tasks, adding REAM improves average task progress by 14.05~pp. We evaluate on-policy correction through DAgger to address limitations of state-based UMI supervision. On two challenging, long-horizon, contact-rich bimanual whole-body tasks, two DAgger rounds improve average task progress by 72.95~pp. Hardware Pixel-UMI uses the co-designed robot and sensorized human interface of (Figure~ fig:hardware ). The human-worn grippers match the robot grippers in manipulation geometry, visual appearance, and wrist-camera placement. Together with aligned head RGB cameras, this co-design reduces the physical and visual gaps between embodiments to support the conversion of sensorized human demonstrations into high-quality robot training data. Each human-worn gripper is equipped with an encoder to record gripper width. Meta Quest controllers track the gripper poses relative to the head, while a Meta Quest 3 headset worn by the demonstrator tracks the head pose in the world frame. We refer readers to the Pixel system paper~ pixel2027system for further hardware details. We additionally equip the human headset with a depth camera to record metric depth throughout each demonstration. We use these observations for offline metric 3D reconstruction to support collision-aware retargeting from human demonstrations to robot demonstrations. We note that during robot policy rollout, visual observations come from the head and wrist RGB cameras; the robot-side depth camera is not used. Pixel-UMI sec:method We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning whole-body robot policies from sensorized human demonstrations. Our goal is to address the fundamental human-to-robot gaps involved in converting these demonstrations into high-quality robot training data. Firstly, the recorded head and gripper poses leave the robot's whole-body posture underdetermined due to kinematic redundancy. To address this, we introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR). We reconstruct scene geometry offline and use collision avoidance to guide the robot's whole-body posture while tracking the demonstrated motion. However, the resulting trajectories still only describe robot states, not robot actions. We therefore assign pseudo-actions using calibrated joint tracking delays, so that the training targets better account for the robot's response. Secondly, differences in human and robot kinematics and body geometry can still prevent exact tracking. As a result, the head and wrist camera views during robot policy rollout can differ from those recorded in the human demonstrations. To alleviate this visual gap, we introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses retargeting errors during training to encourage the policy to rely less on poorly matched camera views. Finally, remaining human-to-robot gaps can still limit policy performance on long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation tasks. We therefore collect a small amount of on-policy correction data through DAgger to improve policy performance on these tasks. We use the same indices for task frames, with denoting the pose of frame in a common world frame, obtained from the Meta Quest 3 headset and controller tracking. The left and right gripper states are derived from their encoder readings. An episode contains such samples and a task instruction . We represent the robot configuration as , where is the planar base pose and contains lift, torso, arm, head, and gripper coordinates. The learned action is with planar velocities expressed in the robot base frame and absolute position targets for the body and grippers. Thus, the policy directly specifies joint-space targets, eliminating the need for an online whole-body controller (WBC) to choose motion in the task-space null space. Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR) sec:retarget Our goal is to reconstruct a metric 3D scene for each collected episode, providing the environment geometry for obstacle avoidance during retargeting. The Meta Quest 3 tracking system provides head and gripper trajectories in a common world frame, with synchronized depth images from the head-mounted camera at each timestep. However, potential pose drift or tracking discontinuities can cause depth point clouds to misalign when combined using the recorded poses alone. To address this, we perform offline point-cloud registration and pose refinement, using geometric alignment across observations to refine the head trajectory before fusing the corrected point clouds into a scene. The reconstruction uses observations from the full recording, including a brief floor-calibration observation when needed; a separate scan of the workspace is not required. We convert each depth image into a metric point cloud in the world frame using the calibrated camera intrinsics, head-to-camera transform, and recorded head pose.
