title: Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation
summary: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel
full_text: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present , a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel INTRODUCTION sec:introduction Imagine asking a robot to tidy your bedroom. It might need to collect clothes from the floor, place objects into cabinets at different heights, or operate a vacuum. The robot might also need to understand your instructions, determine where objects belong, plan a sequence of behaviors, and adapt when you rearrange the furniture. Realizing this vision requires integration across a deep robot-learning stack. The hardware must provide the mobility, workspace, strength, compliance, and sensing needed to interact safely in human environments. Its morphology determines where it can reach and how effectively it can leverage different data sources, while its end effectors determine which objects and tools it can operate. Broad capability also requires large, diverse datasets and the interfaces that make such data practical to collect. Yet demonstrations are useful only if the robot's controllers can translate them into safe, physically realizable motions and learning algorithms can extract behaviors that generalize to new situations. Maximizing system-level capability therefore requires co-design across these layers, such that no individual component becomes the bottleneck on the performance of the complete system. Thus far, most robotics work focuses on individual parts of this stack. Open-source hardware platforms have made capable robots and end effectors increasingly accessible, but commonly leave scalable data collection, policy training, and deployment to downstream integration~ shaw2023leap,zorin2025ruka,anjaria2026yor . Conversely, sensorized human interfaces enable demonstrations to be collected at scale without a physical robot, but transfer to a target platform remains constrained by its morphology, sensing, end effectors, and controllers~ chi2024universal,zeng2025activeumi,TaoT-RSS-25 . Other systems connect hardware, teleoperation, and policy training to achieve impressive learned manipulation~ zhao2023learning,fu2024mobile , but use comparatively simple embodiments and rely primarily on demonstrations collected through teleoperation. What remains underexplored is a mobile manipulation system in which the embodiment, data interface, controller, action representation, and learning stack are designed jointly from the start. In this work, we present , a co-designed, open-source mobile robot and learning stack that enables broadly capable mobile manipulation. At the center of the system is a wheeled humanoid robot costing under \ _ 0.7 15,000. Holonomic Mobile Base. is built on a custom holonomic mobile base. Our base has a footprint of , compared with for TidyBot++~ wu2024tidybotopensourceholonomicmobile . This compact footprint allows the robot to navigate cluttered indoor environments and pass through standard doorways. Holonomic mobility enables independent planar translation and rotation, improving maneuverability in confined indoor environments~ wu2024tidybotopensourceholonomicmobile , providing a simple action space for whole-body teleoperation and policy learning, and facilitating the transfer of natural human whole-body motion to the robot in support of goal:alignment . The chassis is constructed from aluminum extrusions, forming a rigid superstructure that houses the batteries, power electronics, drivetrain, lift actuator, and networking hardware. The drivetrain consists of four MK4n swerve modules with Colson wheels from Swerve Drive Specialties~ swerve_drive_specialties . Motivated by our goal of reproducibility in goal:hardware , we exclusively use off-the-shelf parts. Unlike the offset powered-caster design used by TidyBot++, we use zero-offset swerve modules, whose steering axes approximately intersect the wheel contact patches, thus decoupling the steering from chassis motion. This decoupling of steering and chassis translation is particularly important for mobile manipulation, where small steering inputs to the base can cause jerky motions in the end-effector pose and compromise more precise tasks. The resulting drivetrain does not require additional CNC-machined parts wu2024tidybotopensourceholonomicmobile and provides simpler kinematic control. Base control details are available in Appendix~ sec:appendix_base . Vertical Lift. A large vertical workspace is essential for operating in human environments, where tasks may require reaching from the floor to high shelves. An anatomically accurate, multi-joint lower body would more closely match human kinematics and therefore better satisfy goal:alignment , but would substantially increase the robot's mechanical and control complexity and cost. Given the mobility of the base, such additional articulation would provide only limited additional task-relevant workspace compared with a simpler vertical degree of freedom as shown in Figure~ fig:workspace_compare . We therefore design a telescopic lift that provides of travel, a maximum speed of , and a rated payload of . This design preserves the task-relevant vertical motion needed to transfer human demonstrations while substantially expanding the workspace of both arms with a simple and stable mechanism, balancing goal:alignment and goal:hardware . The lift repurposes a commercial electric table column with a custom drivetrain. A Kraken X60 motor drives the column's lead screw through a chain transmission, using a 10-tooth motor sprocket and a 36-tooth screw sprocket for a reduction. Consistent with the safety objective in goal:hardware , the lead-screw mechanism passively holds its position when unpowered, preventing the lift and its payload from falling in the event of power loss. Represented as a single prismatic degree of freedom, the lift also integrates naturally into the whole-body controller described in Section~ sec:control_interfaces . Lift sizing and control details are provided in Appendix~ sec:appendix_lift . Torso, Head, and Arms. To facilitate the transfer of human demonstrations to robot motion, uses a human-proportioned, 17-DoF upper body comprising a torso-pitch joint, two 7-DoF arms, and a 2-DoF head. Compared with mobile manipulators whose arms and cameras are rigidly mounted to the lift structure~ anjaria2026yor,fu2024mobile, i2rt_linearbot , these additional degrees of freedom allow the robot to easily reposition both its manipulation workspace and sensing orientation. In particular, torso articulation extends the forward and downward reach of both arms, while the actuated head enables the robot to maintain task-relevant regions within view during manipulation. These degrees of freedom expand the robot's whole-body manipulation capability ( goal:capability ) while allowing it to reproduce torso pitching and gaze behaviors present in human demonstrations ( goal:alignment ). To avoid unnecessary mechanical and manufacturing complexity, the upper body is built around a simple, rigid torso structure consistent with goal:hardware . The torso is assembled from waterjet-cut, -thick 6061-T6 aluminum plates and is cantilevered from a single torso-pitch joint driven by a MyActuator X10-100 actuator with a rated torque of . Coordinating this joint with the vertical lift and arms allows the robot to reach low or recessed objects while maintaining a stable base configuration. To reduce the kinematic mismatch between human and robot motion ( goal:alignment ), we use two AgileX NERO arms, each with 7 DoFs, a rated payload of \(3\, \), and human-like kinematics. The redundant arm degree of freedom provides additional flexibility for satisfying end-effector targets while avoiding joint limits, self-collisions, and unfavorable configurations in confined bimanual workspaces. The head is actuated in yaw and pitch by two DAMIAO DM-J4310-2EC actuators, allowing the onboard cameras to be oriented independently of the torso. The torso, head, and arms are controlled using joint-space impedance control. For each joint , the commanded torque is \[ _j = k_ p,j (q_j^ -q_j ) + k_ d,j ( _j^ - _j ) + _ g,j ( ) + _j^ , \] where and are the desired joint position and velocity, and are the corresponding stiffness and damping gains, compensates for gravitational torque, and denotes any additional feedforward torque. End Effector. Everyday manipulation requires both precise handling of small objects and secure grasping of large or heavy objects. Although multi-fingered hands provide additional dexterity, they introduce considerable mechanical and control complexity. At the same time, the end effector should enable intuitive and scalable data collection. We therefore co-design a simple, single-DoF pincer gripper and a corresponding human-worn demonstration interface, balancing the simplicity and reproducibility of goal:hardware with the high-fidelity data collection required by goal:alignment . The gripper follows a finger-aligned design resembling the natural pinch motion of the thumb and index finger, making it intuitive for human demonstration while remaining capable of grasping a diverse range of objects during robot deployment~ ohkawa2026yubi . The human-worn interface preserves the task-facing finger geometry and wrist-camera placement of the robot gripper, reducing observation and action mismatch between demonstration and deployment~ chi2024universal . We describe the wearable interface in further detail in Section~ sec:control_interfaces . On the robot side, each gripper is driven by a DAMIAO DM-J4310-2EC actuator through a 14-tooth pinion and two 36-tooth finger gears, yielding a \(2.57 : 1\) reduction. At a motor torque of \(3\, \), the transmission provides a nominal combined torque of \(7.71\, \) across the finger pivots and a measured closing force exceeding \(90\, \). The pincer mechanism provides a maximum aperture of \(240\, \) while maintaining a compact and mechanically simple construction. Each finger consists of a rigid 3D-printed PETG structure, a compliant 95A-TPU membrane, and a Shore-A 30 Dragon Skin silicone contact surface. The distal portion is narrow and comparatively rigid, enabling precise grasps of small and thin objects. The wider, compliant proximal region conforms to larger objects and handles, increasing contact area and resistance to slip. Separating the rigid load-bearing structure from the compliant membrane allows the finger geometry and surface compliance to be tuned independently. Because deformation of the compliant membrane is visible in the wrist-camera image, it also provides visual cues about contact state and grasp force without requiring dedicated tactile sensors, providing additional information to the policy in support of goal:capability . The policy commands the gripper using continuous aperture targets, which are tracked using an impedance controller with variable stiffness, damping, and torque limits. Lo

title: SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose **SHield**, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson $r \geq 0.991$) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of $\leq 0.13$~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across $1{,}600$ wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and $30\%$ opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable.
full_text: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose SHield, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson ) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of ~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable. Introduction sec:intro 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)~ wu20244d,yang2024real achieves real-time dynamic scene rendering by displacing explicit Gaussians via a learned deformation field~ kerbl20233d . Because training these models requires immense data and compute, the resulting parameter files are valuable intellectual property. However, they are also trivially easy to copy and redistribute, creating an urgent need for robust ownership verification. Most Gaussian splatting watermarks operate in the render domain: they fine-tune the scene against a learned decoder until a short bit string survives the rendering process~ chen2025guardsplat,jang20253dgsw,huang2024gaussianmarker . In 4DGS, this introduces a severe temporal challenge. A perturbation that is invisible at one timestamp may become glaringly obvious at the next timestamp as the Gaussians move, this phenomenon is known as ``FVD collapse''~ zhou20264dgsw . Existing methods counter this with heavy, motion-specific machinery. For example, Mark4D~ lee2026mark4d uses trajectory-aligned offsets and a video-text decoder, while 4D-GSW relies on curvature-based gating. This forces thousands of fine-tuning iterations (e.g., steps for Mark4D) just to embed a few dozen bits. While this complexity is necessary if the watermark must be extracted from a rendered video, it is vastly over-engineered if the adversary is simply redistributing the underlying model file. Our approach leverages the fundamental architecture of 4DGS appearance storage. Each Gaussian maintains a single, canonical set of spherical-harmonic (SH) coefficients that the deformation field queries across all timestamps and viewpoints. By writing a perturbation directly into these canonical coefficients, we create a time-invariant watermark. Shifting the verification target from the rendered video back to the redistributed file itself eliminates the need for learned decoders and rendering loops, allowing extraction via deterministic arithmetic while completely sidestepping temporal fragility. We introduce SHield (Figure~ fig:teaser ), the first decoder-free watermarking framework that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS parameter files and recovers them in closed form. SHield operates as a non-blind watermark, meaning verification requires the owner's private key rather than the full original .ply file. The embedding process tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected subset of Gaussians. Because naive tiling ignores whether a Gaussian is actually visible, SHield employs a brief \(T\)-step anchored optimization. This step adapts the perturbation to minimize visual rendering error while tightly anchoring each coefficient to its target value. During verification, the algorithm geometrically re-associates the owner's key with the suspect file using canonical centres (resolving ties via unchanged attributes), subtracts the stored reference coefficients, and averages the redundant copies. Crucially, SHield modifies only the SH coefficients; the scene geometry and deformation network remain strictly frozen. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: [leftmargin=1em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt] First full-resolution image watermark for 4DGS. To our knowledge, SHield is the first method to embed and recover a full-resolution RGB image directly from a 4DGS model file. Prior dynamic scene watermarks rely on learned decoders without reporting image resolution~ liu2025hideinmotion , and full-resolution steganography has previously been restricted to static 3DGS~ meng2026whispersplat . Decoder-free, non-blind verification. Extraction is reduced to closed-form arithmetic on canonical SH coefficients. By introducing centre-based re-association and a coprime stride, the watermark survives adversarial row reordering, opacity pruning, and SH-degree truncation. Anchored optimization. We propose a brief optimization strategy that adapts the tiled perturbation to the renderer's sensitivity. This reduces the visual footprint of plain tiling by \(1.6 \), \(5.6 \), and \(3.0 \) across the three benchmark datasets, trading a modest drop in WM-PSNR for significantly higher rendering fidelity. Rigorous robustness evaluation. We evaluate SHield across models from scenes~ pumarola2021d,park2021hypernerf,li2022neural . We thoroughly map both its capabilities and operational limits, testing against non-adaptive post-processing (e.g., pruning, quantization) as well as adaptive attacks including targeted fine-tuning, duplication, and rigid transformations. Related Work sec:related Image and video watermarking. Classical spread-spectrum watermarking redundantly embeds messages across host coefficients, verifying authenticity by correlating the recovered signal against a registered reference. While blind detectors operate solely on suspect content, informed (non-blind) detectors leverage auxiliary owner-side data~ cox2007digital . Modern deep watermarking subsequently replaced hand-crafted embeddings with neural encoder--decoder pairs trained against synthetic distortions for images~ zhu2018hidden,tancik2020stegastamp,ma2022cin,fernandez2022ssl and video~ zhang2019rivagan,fernandez2024videoseal . SHield adapts this classical informed-correlation approach, shifting the host domain from pixel space to the internal parameter file of a 4DGS asset. Radiance fields and static 3DGS. Neural asset protection initially targeted continuous coordinate fields, where CopyRNeRF~ luo2023copyrnerf and StegaNeRF~ li2023steganerf fine-tune Neural Radiance Fields to allow message recovery from rendered novel views. A similar render-centric paradigm dominates explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting: GuardSplat~ chen2025guardsplat optimizes spherical-harmonic (SH) offsets against a CLIP-guided decoder, 3D-GSW~ jang20253dgsw incorporates frequency-guided densification, and GaussianMarker~ huang2024gaussianmarker anchors watermarks using per-Gaussian uncertainty. To withstand compression, CompMarkGS~ in2025compmarkgs and Robust3DGSW~ wang2026robust3dgsw integrate quantization-aware training into the pipeline. Broader steganographic frameworks extend these ideas to hide complex content, ranging from GS-Hider's~ zhang2024gshider coupled feature substitution and KeySS's~ ren2026keyss optimized key-secured decoders to Splats in Splats~ guo2026splats,guo2026splatspp encrypting secondary scenes into SH attributes. Notably, WhisperSplat~ meng2026whispersplat avoids model modification entirely, learning an SH noise key that renders a secret high-resolution image from a single viewpoint without an explicit decoder. Dynamic Gaussians. Adapting watermarks to 4DGS requires marks to survive continuous motion. Mark4D~ lee2026mark4d learns time-dependent offsets decoded via video encoders, while 4D-GSW~ zhou20264dgsw gates optimization gradients by trajectory curvature. Guard4D~ shi2026guard4d also utilizes SH coefficients with frozen geometry, yet still relies on text-supervised decoders operating on rendered clips. Hide-in-Motion~ liu2025hideinmotion embeds multimodal payloads into composite attributes but requires a private U-Net decoder and omits post-processing evaluation. Splats in Splats++~ guo2026splatspp similarly depends on a render-and-recover framework. Where SHield differs. While prior approaches bind verification to rendering loops or neural decoders, SHield treats the redistributed model file itself as the verification object. Eliminating this overhead enables full-resolution image recovery via direct, closed-form arithmetic. This file-centric reliability requires a non-blind design where the owner matches a registered private key. Method sec:method Background and Threat Model sec:background 3DGS~ kerbl20233d parameterizes a scene using \(N\) Gaussians \( =\ ( _i, _i, _i,o_i, _i)\ _ i=1 ^ N \), defined by their centre, rotation, scale, opacity, and canonical spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \( _i ^ C_ 3 \) (\(C_ = 16\) for degree ). SHield exclusively modifies the SH coefficients, explicitly preserving the geometric and opacity attributes \( _i=(o_i, _i, _i)\) to serve as invariant geometric anchors for key re-association. In 4DGS~ wu20244d , a learned deformation network predicts time-dependent geometric offsets. Crucially, the stored SH coefficients \( _i\) remain canonical and time-invariant; even in architectures like DyNeRF that inject time-dependent SH offsets during rendering, the underlying file parameters remain completely unmodified. The owner embeds an RGB image \( ^ H_0 W_0 3 \) or an \(L\)-bit message \( \ 0,1\ ^ L \) into a trained 4DGS model, distributes the watermarked file, and retains a private key \( \). For non-blind extraction, \( \) stores the selected Gaussian indices, original SH coefficients, canonical centres, static tie-break attributes, and payload metadata. Ownership is verified via Pearson correlation \(r( , ) \) for images, or direct decoding accuracy for bit payloads. We assume the owner registers \( \) and the payload prior to redistribution to establish provenance. We assume a white-box adversary holding the .ply file who can modify any parameter and knows the algorithm, but lacks the private key \( \) (Kerckhoffs' principle~ Kerckhoffs1883 ). We evaluate non-adaptive post-processing (e.g., SH quantization, reordering, pruning, truncation, and noise) alongside adaptive attacks targeting model re-optimization or the key matcher ( ~ sec:attack ). We assume the redistributed file retains its float32 canonical centres in the original coordinate frame. Watermark Embedding sec:embedding SHield embeds the watermark into the canonical SH coefficients (Figure~ fig:overview ). This provides two advantages: a single time-invariant perturbation propagates to all timestamps, and SH coefficients offer a robust carrier with minimal visual sensitivity. title: GatedVLA with Camera-Based Emergency Braking: AlpaSim E2E Closed Loop Challenge Technical Report
summary: This report presents GatedVLA, our entry for the Physical AI AV (PAI-AV) track. Our learned vision-language-action (VLA) policy pairs the driving-pretrained Qwen-Drive-1.0-4B vision-language model with a layer-wise flow-matching action expert that outputs a 2.5 s horizon of acceleration and curvature controls, augmented with a soft visual mask applied to the expert's cross-attention. Compared to an identically trained baseline, the masked policy achieves comparable overall open-loop error while reducing error on left turns. In local closed-loop evaluation across the same 150 scenes (two rollouts per scene), the visual mask increases the mean scene score from 0.479 to 0.517 (paired difference +0.038, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.018, +0.093], wins/losses 37/26, sign test p = 0.21). Incorporating a rule-based automatic emergency braking (AEB) module at deployment further increases the mean score to 0.599 (+0.082, CI [+0.023, +0.143]) and reduces the mean number of scenes with at-fault collisions from 34.0 to 11.0.
full_text: This report presents GatedVLA, our entry for the Physical AI AV (PAI-AV) track. Our learned vision-language-action (VLA) policy pairs the driving-pretrained Qwen-Drive-1.0-4B vision-language model~ qwendrive with a layer-wise flow-matching action expert that outputs a 2.5\,s horizon of acceleration and curvature controls, augmented with a soft visual mask applied to the expert's cross-attention. Compared to an identically trained baseline, the masked policy achieves comparable overall open-loop error while reducing error on left turns. In local closed-loop evaluation across the same scenes (two rollouts per scene), the visual mask increases the mean scene score from to (paired difference , 95 bootstrap CI , wins/losses , sign test ). Incorporating a rule-based automatic emergency braking (AEB) module at deployment further increases the mean score to ( , CI ) and reduces the mean number of scenes with at-fault collisions from to . Introduction Even minor planning errors alter the subsequent observations encountered by a driving policy---a compounding effect that only closed-loop evaluation can reveal. The AlpaSim challenge evaluates policies in closed loop on held-out scenes~ alpasim , where a scene receives a score of zero if the ego vehicle causes an at-fault collision, drives off-road, or exits the recorded driving corridor. In our preliminary experiments, at-fault collisions were the primary source of score loss, predominantly involving slower or stationary lead vehicles when the planned trajectory failed to initiate braking. We therefore introduce (1) a learned visual mask trained to selectively retain image evidence relevant to navigation intent for the action expert, and (2) a detector-based emergency braking module that intervenes when the learned policy fails to decelerate. Related work Vision-language-action driving. Qwen-Drive-1.0~ qwendrive establishes a vision-language foundation model for autonomous driving paired with a planning expert. Alpamayo-R1~ alpamayo couples a reasoning model with a diffusion-based trajectory decoder, while DriveMoE~ drivemoe introduces expert routing to Drive- , an adaptation of ~ pi0 . We train a -style flow-matching expert on top of the Qwen-Drive backbone. Limiting visual evidence. S2~ seeless learns per-token soft masks under a visual evidence budget alongside an ungated pathway. We adopt a similar gating head and budget formulation, but apply the mask directly to the action expert's cross-attention logits, enforce an exact budget by construction, and train the mask via self-distillation (Section~ sec:policy ). Copycat behavior. Imitation learning policies can suffer from causal confusion by over-relying on their own past motion~ causal ; ChauffeurNet~ chauffeurnet mitigates this with history dropout during training. We explored both history dropout and temporal ensembling~ act , but observed no clear gains (Appendix~ app:others ). Method summary Our driving system (Fig.~ fig:system ) comprises an end-to-end learned policy that replans every 0.5\,s and a detector-based AEB module that exclusively decelerates the planned trajectory along its predicted path. We evaluated and submitted three deployment variants derived from a single trained checkpoint: AEB at 10\,Hz, AEB at 5\,Hz, and the policy without AEB. Our implementation builds upon starVLA~ starvla and py123d garage~ garage,py123d , and all evaluations are conducted in AlpaSim~ alpasim . Policy description sec:policy Inputs. Two front wide-angle camera frames (at and \,s) along with the fixed text prompt ``predict trajectory'' are fed into the VLM. Ego-state history and navigation conditioning are provided exclusively to the action expert: five 10\,Hz historical steps of concatenated at each step with a target point and a binary target-presence flag. During training, the target point is the first future ego position at a Euclidean distance of at least 25\,m; at deployment, it is the first such point along AlpaSim's map route (Appendix~ app:driver ). Expert and outputs. The action expert follows a -style layer-wise architecture~ pi0,drivemoe : a 32-block Diffusion Transformer (DiT)~ dit alternates self-attention and cross-attention layers, where each cross-attention block attends to a corresponding VLM layer via a learned linear projection. The expert is trained via conditional flow matching~ flowmatching with a velocity MSE objective and generates trajectories using 10 Euler integration steps at inference. It predicts 25 steps of controls at 10\,Hz, utilizing the kinematic unicycle action space adapted from NVIDIA Alpamayo~1.5~ alpamayocode,alpamayo . Integrating these controls from the current ego speed yields the output poses. Baseline. The baseline shares the same architecture and training protocol but omits the visual mask and Paths B and C (below); as in Path A, the target point is dropped with probability per sample. Visual mask. A gating module takes each visual token's detached final-layer VLM hidden state alongside a conditioning query (which embeds the scaled target point and ego state) and computes a logit score from , following the visual evidence budget formulation of S2~ seeless . The scores are standardized across tokens within each frame to obtain , yielding soft mask values , where the scalar bias is solved via bisection such that the per-frame mean of equals the target budget by construction, eliminating the need for an auxiliary budget loss. We add directly to the expert's cross-attention logits while leaving text tokens and internal VLM representations unmasked. Each training step executes three expert passes sharing a single VLM forward pass, sampled noise, and flow time step: Path A (ungated, target point dropped with ): minimizes the standard flow-matching loss and updates both the VLM and DiT. Path B (stop-gradient mask, target point provided): minimizes to update the DiT; this serves as the inference pathway. Path C (active mask, target point omitted from the DiT state but provided to the gate): minimizes and updates only the gating module. Paths B and C are distilled only on samples where the target point is retained in Path A; consequently, Path C forces the gating module to preserve visual tokens that encode the navigation intent. Emergency brake. An RT-DETRv2-R18 detector~ rtdetrv2,rtdetr pretrained on COCO~ coco processes the current front-camera frame and retains boxes of seven traffic classes with confidence scores exceeding 0.5. The central 40 of each bounding box's bottom edge is projected onto the ego rig's flat ground plane using the nominal - camera calibration. Among detected obstacles within a 1.3\,m lateral corridor of the planned path, the closest obstacle defines the arc-length gap measured from the front bumper along the path; the closing speed is estimated via linear regression over the last 1\,s of (Table~ tab:app_deploy ). With braking margin and required deceleration , the planned speed profile is capped by a linear deceleration ramp from the current speed down to the estimated lead speed at a rate of \,m/s whenever or \,m/s . Under a milder time-to-collision condition ( \,s), the planned speed is constrained not to exceed the current ego speed. Because the trajectory is re-timed along its own path from the ego vehicle's projection, a braked ego will not accelerate to catch up with a stale plan. Upon AEB release, the speed is held for one control tick before an immediate policy replan. Resources and training Data. Models are trained on the NVIDIA PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles dataset~ paiav (NVIDIA Autonomous Vehicle Dataset License Agreement), using only the front wide-angle camera streams and egomotion trajectories from the training split. No LiDAR, radar, or machine-generated perception labels were used. Pretrained weights. We initialize the VLM from Qwen-Drive-1.0-4B~ qwendrive (Apache-2.0) and use off-the-shelf RT-DETRv2-R18 weights (PekingU/rtdetr v2 r18vd, Apache-2.0) for detection. Private resources: None. Training. Both the baseline (W B run ccb412c9) and masked policy (03bdfc50) were trained from the same code commit with random seed 42 for 12 epochs (38 , 400 steps) across 12 Intel Aurora XPU tiles. In the spirit of linear probing then fine-tuning (LP-FT)~ lpft , the VLM backbone remained frozen during the first epoch. Full hyperparameter settings and training curves are provided in the appendix. r 0.56 Open-loop prediction error at step 38 , 400 (baseline / mask). Table~ tab:openloop reports open-loop trajectory prediction performance on a fixed validation subset of 240 samples (80 left turns, 80 right turns, and 80 straight segments). Overall open-loop error is comparable between the two models: the visual mask improves performance on left turns (FDE of 1.100 vs.\ 1.213; miss rate of 0.150 vs.\ 0.200) and yields a slightly lower FDE on right turns, at the cost of higher error on straight segments. Ablating visual inputs degrades FDE substantially more than omitting the navigation target point (masked policy: 1.564 with black frames vs.\ 1.135 with no target and no mask), confirming that visual evidence strongly informs planning in both models (baseline with black frames: FDE 1.408). Appendix~ app:open gives all controls. Closed-loop results. Table~ tab:closedloop summarizes local closed-loop evaluation across the same scenes sampled from the 441-scene curated validation split using the dev challenge preset (40\,m route offset). A rollout without such a failure scores . The first and second rollouts ran on different hosts (NVIDIA Blackwell and Ada), so differences between them reflect both hardware and run-to-run variance. Averaging scores across the two rollouts per scene: mask vs.\ baseline achieves a mean difference of (95 bootstrap CI , wins/losses , sign test ); AEB at 10\,Hz vs.\ mask alone yields (CI , , ); and AEB at 5\,Hz vs.\ 10\,Hz yields (CI , , ). Appendix~ app:closed gives all pairwise comparisons. Runtime and reproducibility Serving. The submission container image is self-contained, operates within the challenge sandbox without external network access, and launches without arguments. Between 0.5\,s replans, it serves poses from the cached plan at 10\,Hz. Latency and memory. The mean Drive latencies reported in Table~ tab:closedloop were recorded locally with driver video recording enabled and up to 12 concurrent rollouts sharing a single driver on multi-tenant hosts, so they are only indicative. In a standalone run with a single rollout per replica and video recording disabled (on a shared NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU), the mean Drive RPC latency was 0.10--0.11\,s for both AEB variants (Appendix~ app:runtime ). The RT-DETRv2 detector requires approximately 0.2\,GiB of VRAM in addition to the policy's 11.6\,GiB footprint. Reproducibility. The deployed inference configuration matches our logged W B training runs. Source code: (branch main, commit 80ab247). Limitations and safety considerations sec:limits Limited generalization evidence for AEB. The AEB decision thresholds were tuned offline by replaying cached detections on the same 150 scenes evaluated in Table~ tab:closedloop , so the observed gains may be optimistic for held-out private test scenes. Remaining collisions. Of the 12 remaining at-fault collisions in the first 10\,Hz AEB rollout (manual inspection, Appendix~ app:closed ), 6 involved obstacles offset by approximately 2\,m laterally that entered the 1.3\,m detection corridor too late or not at all, a trade-off from narrowing the corridor to suppress false-positive braking; the rest involved agents from the side or rear-left (2), low-speed

title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
summary: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD
full_text: Methodology sec:method Based on the trajectory formation analysis in~ , we propose a scene-adaptive framework that jointly selects trajectory representations and decoding depth. Given an input scene , the frozen diffusion VLA performs a single forward sweep, after which layer-specific experts convert representations from the readout band into candidate trajectories, and a scene-conditioned MoE combines them ~ st_moe, switch_transformer_moe, shazeer2017outrageously_moe . The resulting readout draft is either returned directly or refined through adaptive fallback decoding when needed. The proposed framework, as illustrated in~ , adapts inference along two axes: how trajectory predictions from layer-specific representations are combined, and how far iterative decoding should proceed. Instead of applying the same readout configuration and decoding schedule to every scene, it allocates inference computation according to each scene. Early Trajectory Readout sec:method:readout For scene , let denote the hidden state at layer and decoding stage . Following the analysis in~ , we use the trajectory-token representation from the first forward sweep: where indexes the token positions reserved for trajectory prediction, with one position corresponding to each future waypoint. At the same time, we obtain a one-pass draft by selecting, at each trajectory-token position, the vocabulary token with the largest logit during the first forward sweep. The layer-specific readout head, , takes the trajectory-token representation and this draft as input to produce a trajectory prediction: Each readout head is trained with GT trajectory supervision while the backbone remains frozen. The readout path maps the first-sweep representation to continuous waypoints without generating additional reasoning text or trajectory tokens, thereby skipping the remaining native decoding stages. Scene-Adaptive Readout sec:method:adaptive_readout For each layer in the readout band identified in~ , , we construct a trajectory expert with a readout head and a latent editor. Since all experts operate on representations extracted from the same first forward sweep, the expert bank requires no additional backbone forward passes. For layer , the editor is initialized with the corresponding first-sweep representation: where denotes the representation after latent refinement steps. The editor applies residual updates to provide a potential correction to the representation: where is the number of latent refinement steps, and denotes the residual update applied at step for layer , parameterized by learnable parameters . These refinements are intended to compensate for geometric inconsistencies that may arise from direct readout, such as lateral offsets or local curvature. The editor does not directly modify the native decoder output. Instead, its refined representation is converted into a trajectory by the corresponding layer-specific readout head. After latent refinement steps, the layer-specific readout head uses the refined representation and the one-pass draft from the first forward sweep to produce a candidate trajectory, The latent editor refines only the hidden representation, while remains fixed. Each layer-specific expert therefore provides a trajectory candidate based on a different layer representation, while all candidates are computed from a single backbone forward sweep. The candidate trajectories are combined by a scene-conditioned gate. We construct its input by mean-pooling the trajectory-slot and vision-token hidden states, and concatenating these statistics with the ego history, navigation command, one-pass draft, layer-specific candidate trajectories, and their deviations from the candidate mean. The resulting scene representation is denoted by . The gate produces layer-wise mixture weights: outputs one score for each layer in . The softmax converts scores into normalized mixture weights , which sum to one over the candidate layers. Details are provided in the Appendix. The gate is trained with trajectory supervision to optimize planning quality of the fused prediction: where denotes the ground-truth waypoint trajectory. Thus, the gate can emphasize a single layer or combine multiple layer-specific predictions according to the scene representation. To reduce the variance of the MoE prediction, we retain an auxiliary readout branch based on a fixed reference layer . The reference layer is selected during training, and we use in our experiments. This branch applies a sparse mixture over the trajectory-token representation at , followed by a latent editor, to produce an independent trajectory prediction. It is not used to route experts across scenes, but instead serves as a reference branch that stabilizes the MoE output. The final readout draft is obtained by combining the MoE and auxiliary predictions: This trajectory serves as the input to scene-adaptive decoding and the output of the early-exit path. Scene-Adaptive Decoding sec:method:decoding The reliability of the readout draft varies across scenes, making it undesirable to apply native decoding uniformly. Our method therefore uses readout as the default path and invokes native decoding as a fallback only for scenes whose learned decoding gate predicts a benefit from additional refinement. Scenes for which the readout is predicted to be sufficient terminate immediately, while native computation is reserved for scenes predicted to benefit from further refinement. Specifically, the decoding gate forms a scene representation by mean-pooling the pre-decoding trajectory-slot and vision-token states and concatenating these features with the readout confidence, expert disagreement, and navigation context. The complete feature construction is provided in the Appendix. The gate then produces a score representing the benefit of additional decoding, where is a trainable scene-conditioned gate. It is trained on the training split using a binary target indicating whether native refinement reduces the ground-truth trajectory error relative to the readout draft. At inference time, the gate uses only and does not access ground-truth trajectories or evaluator outcomes. If the gate score exceeds a threshold , the scene is sent to the fallback decoding path; otherwise, the readout trajectory is returned directly, Fallback decoding evaluates the native decoder incrementally rather than executing the entire schedule at once. Let denote the total number of decoding stages, and let denote the reference layer used for stage-wise trajectory readout. At each intermediate stage , we extract the trajectory-slot representation and apply a lightweight stage-specific readout probe, Each probe is trained with trajectory supervision using only the hidden state from its decoding stage. The readout draft is withheld from the probe input, so estimates the trajectory recoverable from the native decoder representation at stage rather than copying the initial readout prediction. During fallback decoding, each intermediate trajectory is compared with the readout draft at the prediction horizon. Let denote the number of future waypoints, the trajectory produced by the scene-adaptive readout, and the final future waypoint predicted by the stage- probe. If at least one intermediate stage satisfies the agreementcriterion with threshold , we select the earliest such stage, where defines the agreement criterion. Agreement at the prediction horizon indicates that the trajectory recovered at the current stage is consistent with the initial readout, so further decoding is not performed. The final trajectory is obtained by averaging the readout and stage- predictions: If no intermediate stage agrees with the readout, decoding continues to the native endpoint. Since no probe is used at this endpoint, its native trajectory is combined directly with the readout: Consequently, scenes follow three routes: (1) early termination after readout, (2) termination after a subset of fallback stages, or (3) completion of native decoding. The learned entry gate determines which scenes enter fallback, while the agreement test determines the earliest stopping stage. Together, they allocate a scene-dependent decoding budget without applying the schedule uniformly.

title: AbacusGS: Gaussian Splatting without Per-Splat Sorting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting sorts every splat by depth in every frame. Viewers that draw splats with the hardware rasterizer and sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time in this sort. We present AbacusGS, which stores the blending order of a 3DGS scene in the scene layout. AbacusGS groups the splats into octree boxes of at most 128 splats and stores each box in order along an axis chosen at write time. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs represents a scene with millions of anisotropic Gaussians. A renderer projects each Gaussian to a screen-space ellipse~ zwicker2001ewa , sorts the resulting splats by the depth of their centers, and blends them with the over operator~ porter1984compositing . The depth order changes with the camera. 3DGS recomputes the sort from scratch in every frame. The cost of the sort depends on the platform. On desktop GPUs, a radix sort in CUDA or WebGPU orders millions of splats in well under a millisecond~ higs2026,visionary2025 . Web and mobile viewers draw one instanced quad per splat with the hardware rasterizer and sort the splats in a CPU thread~ kwok2023splat . Web pages and phone browsers show captured scenes with these viewers and download each scene before its first frame. Visionary~ visionary2025 reports 173\,ms for a CPU sort of 6 million splats. In our OpenGL viewer, the CPU sort takes 24.1\,ms of a 26.8\,ms frame. Each new order also uploads an index buffer with one entry per splat. Existing work reduces this cost in three ways. The first way keeps a per-splat order and computes it less often. Neo~ neo2025 and Lumina~ lumina2025 reuse the sorted lists of previous frames and update them per splat. The second way removes the order. Sort-free methods replace the over operator with weighted sums~ hou2025wsr , order-independent transparency~ du2026mobilegs,momentgs2025,sparseoit2026 , or stochastic transparency~ kheradmand2025stochasticsplats,stippling2026 . The new operators differ from the operator that the scene was optimized with, and stochastic estimators add noise at real-time sample counts. The third way orders groups of splats. Duplex-GS~ liu2025duplexgs sorts cells and blends the Gaussians inside a cell with a weighted sum. StreamingGS~ streaminggs2025 sorts voxels and still sorts the Gaussians inside each voxel in every frame. Outside Gaussian splatting, Voxlines~ osman2023voxlines sorts the voxels of a streamline rendering and stores line orders along the coordinate axes inside each voxel. also orders groups of splats and keeps the over operator inside each group. On an abacus, the position of a bead stores a digit and also holds a partial result of the computation. uses the order of its storage in the same way. The splats are grouped into small octree boxes, and the splats of one box usually cover a small patch of surface. The depth order inside a box changes little with the camera, apart from a reversal when the camera moves to the other side of the patch. sorts each box once at write time along an axis that it derives from the training cameras. At render time, sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short fine-tuning adapts the model to the remaining ordering errors. On a hardware rasterizer, each visible box becomes one command of a multi-draw indirect call, and the frame needs no per-splat index buffer. Keeping the over operator has practical value. Existing 3DGS models, training code, and viewers assume this operator. converts an existing model with a short fine-tuning, and a viewer changes only how it orders and draws the splats. Sort-free methods retrain or fine-tune the scene for a new operator. Our paper has three contributions. The first is the task of converting an existing 3DGS model to a blending order stored in the scene layout, together with an evaluation that compares each converted model with a control fine-tuned for the same number of steps and times all methods in one hardware rasterizer with ordering on the CPU. The second is the method, which stores one order per octree box along an axis derived from the training cameras, chooses only the reading direction in every frame, fine-tunes the model with exactly this order, and draws each visible box with one multi-draw command. The third is a set of findings on 13 standard scenes. Fine-tuning reduces the average loss of the two-level order from 1.27 to 0.13\,dB PSNR. An octree BSP order, which is exact for the cells, loses more PSNR than the centroid-depth order for overlapping Gaussians. title: Spend the Bits Where the Tiny Objects Are: Rate-Utility Region Coding for Aerial Detection
summary: Bandwidth-limited aerial cameras must compress their images before a remote detector can find the many tiny objects in them. Threshold-based region-of-interest (ROI) coding sends only confidently detected regions, and because tiny objects provide limited visual evidence and often score low, it can discard the regions that contain them. We propose rate-utility region coding (RUO), which sends a region when its expected detection utility justifies its measured byte cost, choosing to drop it or to send it at low or high quality with one multiplier shared across images. RUO trains no model, uses a standard image codec and decodes in a few milliseconds. On all 1,610 VisDrone-DET test-dev images, RUO uses 42.4% fewer bits than a tuned threshold-based ROI coder, averaged over their shared tiny-object average precision (AP) range. RUO also needs fewer bits for tiny objects than the AV1 Image File Format (AVIF), High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) and three published learned codecs, and its advantage over threshold-based ROI coding persists when the sender and receiver use different detectors. For AP over all object sizes RUO needs 25.4% more bits than the tuned ROI coder, because its allocation drops large regions first at low rates, so it suits tasks that target tiny objects. We plan to release the code.

It therefore also sends small low-confidence regions, so the zoom finds 2 of 4 tiny objects where threshold coding finds none. Grey marks untransmitted regions, and outlines mark matched objects. We plan to release the code. Introduction sec:intro Aerial images often contain many small and tiny objects, whose visual details are easily lost when a bandwidth-limited camera compresses them. For example, a VisDrone test-dev image contains annotated objects on average, with occupying less than pixels and less than pixels~ zhu2021visdrone . At about 0.2 bits per pixel (bpp), full-frame coding with the AV1 Image File Format (AVIF)~ aomedia2025avif reaches an average precision (AP) of for tiny objects (AP ), below the of uncompressed images ( ). A sender under a byte budget therefore has to decide where its bits go. Region-of-interest (ROI) coding is a common answer to this decision, but a confidence threshold can drop the regions that tiny objects need. ROI coders, used in video analytics and in tools for video coding for machines, spend bits where a sender-side detector finds objects, by transmitting the selected regions or giving them higher quality~ du2022accmpeg,roipacking2025,rek2025vcmroi . Threshold-based coders select regions by detection confidence, and tiny objects often receive low scores. At the operating point closest to bpp and a standard threshold of 0.25, selection misses account for of all tiny objects, even more than the sum of compression and receiver misses ( ). Lowering the threshold keeps more candidates but does not weigh what each candidate is worth against what it costs. To address this gap, we propose rate-utility region coding (RUO), which treats region selection as a rate--utility allocation ( ). RUO estimates a region's utility as the sum of calibrated probabilities that its sender detections are correct, and measures its byte cost at two quality levels. A single multiplier shared across images then decides whether each region is dropped or transmitted at low or high quality ( ), so a low-confidence region is sent when its expected utility pays for its bytes. RUO uses a standard image codec and retrains neither detector nor codec. On all VisDrone-DET test-dev images, RUO uses fewer bits than a tuned threshold-based ROI coder and fewer bits than full-frame AVIF, averaged over the respective shared AP ranges, and it needs fewer bits than HEVC and three published learned codecs ( ). The advantage over threshold-based ROI coding persists when the sender and receiver use different detectors, and on UAVDT it is significant with a UAVDT sender but not with a VisDrone sender ( ). For AP over all object sizes RUO needs more bits than tuned threshold coding ( ). Contributions. Our paper has three contributions. First, we propose RUO, a training-free region coder that allocates bytes across regions from calibrated sender utilities and measured byte costs with one multiplier shared across images ( ). Second, we decompose detection misses into selection, compression and receiver misses and show that selection is the largest loss for tiny objects at a standard threshold ( ). Third, we measure rate--accuracy trade-offs on VisDrone and UAVDT, which show gains for tiny objects and costs for detection across object sizes ( ). Related work Remote detection under a byte budget depends on how an image is coded, on where the bits go and on what the detector needs from them, and we review the work on each in turn. Learned and machine-oriented image coding. Image coding for machines changes the representation or objective of a codec that codes the whole frame. Learned image codecs~ balle2018variational,minnen2018joint,cheng2020learned achieve competitive rate--distortion performance for human viewing, and image coding for machines extends their objectives to downstream vision tasks~ le2021image,chen2023transtic,li2024image,shindo2024image , sometimes under constraints on human-perceptual quality~ phamdinh2026seenenough , while MPEG standardizes coding for machine consumption~ duan2020video,eimon2025vcmstandards . RUO instead chooses which regions are sent at all, and we compare it with five such codecs ( ). Task-aware region coding and bit allocation. Task-aware systems send bits according to relevance to the downstream detector, and many choose by a score threshold or a learned policy. Video analytics systems adapt stream configurations to analytics accuracy~ jiang2018chameleon,zhang2018awstream or filter frames before transmission~ li2020reducto . At finer granularity, DDS~ du2020server requests uncertain regions in a second round trip, EAAR~ liu2019edge encodes regions of interest at higher quality and EdgeDuet~ wang2021edgeduet offloads tiles containing small objects. ROI-Packing~ roipacking2025 packs regions selected by a fixed confidence threshold, and the VCM retargeting tool~ rek2025vcmroi simplifies image content around detected objects before standard encoding. Other methods adapt quality spatially, through machine-vision importance in VVC~ huang2021visual , ROI masks in a learned codec~ ahonen2023roi , a two-level mask from a model trained for the server network~ du2022accmpeg , or reinforcement-learned quantization~ gao2026aroie,gadot2025rlrcdot . A UAV telemetry study compares ROI triggering policies under a bitrate constraint~ hybridtelemetry2026 . RUO follows Lagrangian bit allocation~ everett1963generalized,shoham1988efficient,sullivan1998rate , with a calibrated detection utility in place of distortion and with ``do not send'' as an option, so that a region's expected utility is weighed against its bytes rather than compared with a score threshold ( ). Tiny-object detection in aerial images. Methods for tiny aerial objects process selected regions at higher resolution, and those with a budget count patches or computation rather than transmitted bytes. Dedicated benchmarks~ wang2021tiny , including VisDrone~ zhu2021visdrone , have motivated sliced inference~ akyon2022slicing , clustering or querying high-resolution regions~ yang2019clustered,yang2022querydet , and selecting crops~ liu2024esod,densescout2026,afwdnet2026 . DenseScout~ densescout2026 reports weak recall from detector-derived selectors at low patch budgets, and MRU-YOLO~ chen2026mru selects regions by predicted gain under a computation budget. Our budget is bytes, so we give every method the same sliced-inference receiver, which isolates differences in the transmitted information from differences in detection. Method sec:method Overview. RUO decides for every candidate region whether to drop it or to send it at low or high quality, by comparing its expected detection utility with its measured byte cost ( ). A frozen sender detector proposes the candidates, a calibration table turns its scores into utilities, the region codec measures each region's bytes at two qualities, and one multiplier shared across images selects every region's tier. The receiver pastes the decoded regions onto a grey canvas and runs its detector. Setup and candidate regions. The sender builds candidate regions from its own detections, without ground truth or receiver feedback. It holds an image and a detector , and a receiver runs detector , which may differ from , on the decoded image. returns boxes with scores . Every box above a low score floor is padded and snapped to a coarse grid, and overlapping boxes are merged into regions with member sets . The floor is low so that the allocator, not the score, decides. Utility and cost. A region's utility is the sum of calibrated true-detection probabilities of its sender detections, and its cost is the measured size of its coded payload. Calibration is needed because a raw score measures confidence rather than the probability of a true detection, and its meaning depends on object size~ guo2017calibration,kuppers2020multivariate . We calibrate , where is the box area, with a table over score and area bins. A detection of on an uncompressed image counts as true if it matches a ground-truth object of its class at IoU 0.5, and the table is fit on held-out validation images with a Beta prior per bin and made monotone in score within each area bin. The utility of region at tier is the sum of these probabilities, discounted for the low tier, where is a fixed tier weight with , and . The cost is the measured size in bytes of coded with the region codec at the tier's quality , plus the fixed-size region record, and . The sender reuses the coded payload of the selected tier. Allocation. One multiplier shared across all images turns a budgeted allocation into independent per-region decisions. For a region-byte budget after fixed image headers over a set of images, we want to solve the multiple-choice knapsack problem Its Lagrangian relaxation separates over regions, so each region takes the tier with ties broken towards the cheaper tier. title: MMCoT$^3$: Empowering 3D Scene Understanding with 3D-Text Interleaved Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT$^3$, the first 3D-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object-mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. To mitigate this multi-instance ambiguity, we design an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism that uses query-guided cross-attention to fuse candidate object tokens and inject both evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning process. To better equip the model with multi-step reasoning capability, we further develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT instruction tuning dataset with approximately 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue, and planning tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D-text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding.

Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT , the first 3D--Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object--mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D--text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding. <ccs2012> <concept> <concept_id>10010147.10010178.10010224.10010225</concept_id> <concept_desc>Computing methodologies~Computer vision tasks</concept_desc> <concept_significance>500</concept_significance> </concept> </ccs2012> Introduction Understanding 3D visual information is fundamental to numerous emerging technological domains, including autonomous navigation arnold2019survey , augmented and virtual reality xiong2021augmented , robotics huang2023embodied , and intelligent manufacturing systems saimon2025advancing . Recent advances 10981614,hong20233d,xu2024pointllm have enabled large language models (LLMs) to integrate and reason over rich point-cloud geometry, extending them from text-only modeling to multimodal 3D scene understanding. Representative tasks in 3D scene understanding include 3D captioning~ chen2021scan2cap , 3D question answering~ azuma2022scanqa,ma2022sqa3d , 3D dialogue~ huang2023embodied , and scene-aware task planning~ huang2023embodied . These tasks provide an important testbed for evaluating whether models can jointly perceive, ground, and reason over complex 3D scenes under natural-language queries. Existing methods typically employ 3D LLMs he2024segpoint,wang2023chat to encode point clouds and text separately, align them in a shared embedding space, and directly generate outputs with the LLM. Despite the successes, current methods are still facing two critical issues: Firstly, insufficient 3D reasoning capability. The sparse, irregular, and geometry-centric nature of 3D point clouds makes 3D understanding tasks inherently reasoning-intensive. To answer a query, models must jointly reason about object attributes, spatial relations, scene configurations, and task-specific context. However, existing methods still lack the robust reasoning capacity needed for such complex 3D scenes, often leading to incorrect target identification when multiple instances share similar visual characteristics. Secondly, lack of interactions between textual reasoning and visual evidence. Most existing methods only use 3D representations as a static background context, without actively consulting and verifying them during reasoning (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)). Moreover, without effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence, the model cannot properly ground, verify, and revise intermediate conclusions during multi-step inference. Consequently, prior methods are prone to produce hallucinations~ bang2023multitask in multi-step reasoning. For example, the model may hallucinate non-existent objects or produce spatial reasoning inconsistent with the actual scene layout. Recently, researchers attempted to reduce the incorrect target identification by improving the selection and reasoning of scene evidence. For example, TSP3D~ guo2025text introduces a pruning strategy to progressively discard query-irrelevant regions from the 3D scene representation, thereby suppressing redundant scene content and concentrating computation on potentially relevant targets. Another research direction is to incorporate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to enhance the model's capacity for complex 3D inference, enabling it to better organize and integrate multiple cues, such as object attributes, spatial relations, and global scene context, during multi-step reasoning. Nevertheless, existing approaches fall short of fully utilizing visual evidence throughout the reasoning process. As a result, the model cannot effectively revisit 3D evidence to verify intermediate conclusions, refine hypotheses, or resolve ambiguities. On the other hand, to alleviate the issue of lacking interactions between text and visual information, recent 2D multi-modal reasoning studies~ zhang2025vitcot,gao2025interleaved have begun to explore multi-modal CoT paradigms that explicitly interleave textual reasoning with visual evidence during inference. Such a paradigm has shown state-of-the-art performance in purely 2D text-centric inference scenarios. Unfortunately, directly transferring this paradigm to 3D scene understanding remains highly nontrivial: (1) there is a lack of large-scale, high-quality 3D-specific CoT dataset, which hinders the further improvements of 3D understanding tasks. (2) unlike 2D images/videos, 3D point clouds exhibit a sparse, irregular, and large-scale manner, where only a small fraction of the observed content is relevant to the query. Thus, it is considerably more difficult to identify informative 3D evidence compared with 2D multi-modal reasoning tasks. A natural idea of alleviating the above limitations is to explicitly interleave intermediate textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations precisely during multi-step reasoning. A naive solution is to align object-level 3D tokens with object mentions in the textual CoT sequence and inject the matched evidence into the corresponding reasoning steps. However, such a direct interleaving is inherently brittle in the realistic 3D scenes, where multiple instances frequently share the same category label. Thus, a textual entity may match an incorrect token from its associated object tokens, causing subsequent reasoning steps to depend on a mismatched 3D evidence. Even worse, the ambiguity can further propagate through the CoT process, impairing both the faithfulness of intermediate reasoning and the quality of the final prediction. Therefore, effective 3D--Text interleaved reasoning requires not only explicit evidence injection, but also an ambiguity-aware mechanism for identifying relevant candidates, aggregating uncertain evidence, and robustly resolving multi-instance ambiguity. Following the above analysis, we first develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT dataset with 176.2K instances, by enriching the LEO instruction-tuning dataset~ huang2023embodied with high-quality rationales across six representative task settings, including 3D captioning~ chen2021scan2cap , 3D question answering on ScanNet~ azuma2022scanqa , 3D question answering on 3RScan~ huang2023embodied , 3D dialogue~ huang2023embodied , 3D embodied reasoning~ ma2022sqa3d , and scene-aware task planning~ huang2023embodied . To enhance the capability of responding to various queries, we further propose a difficulty-adaptive CoT generation strategy: for complex queries, we explicitly decompose them into progressive multi-step sub-problems to facilitate structured reasoning. For simple queries, we complement them with concise grounding cues that guide the model toward task-relevant visual evidence. By providing explicit CoT supervision for diverse 3D tasks, this dataset enables the model to develop stronger multi-step reasoning capability in complex 3D scenes. To enhance the limited 3D reasoning capability of existing methods and the text-centric inference paradigm, we propose a novel 3D--Text Interleaved Multi-Modal CoT framework MMCoT for 3D scene understanding. By coupling textual CoT reasoning with 3D evidence, our framework not only strengthens the 3D LLM's capacity for grounded multi-step reasoning, but also moves beyond text-centric inference by enabling the model to actively consult and verify scene observations during intermediate reasoning (Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)). To address the brittleness of direct 3D--Text interleaving in realistic 3D scenes, where multiple instances often share the same semantic category, we further develop an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism tailored for 3D scene understanding. Instead of prematurely committing to a single object when multiple candidates match a query mention, we aggregate the matched object tokens into a fused evidence representation through query-guided cross-attention. Meanwhile, we explicitly estimate the ambiguity of the candidate set and encode it as an additional signal, allowing the model to assess the reliability of the injected evidence during reasoning. We then interleave both the task-relevant 3D evidence and its associated ambiguity cue with the textual CoT sequence, enabling the LLM to consult scene observations precisely when intermediate reasoning unfolds, while remaining aware of potential instance-level uncertainty. In this way, our framework not only strengthens compositional reasoning over complex 3D scenes, but also establishes an explicit ambiguity-aware evidence-checking process throughout multi-step inference, improving robustness to instance-level ambiguity and mitigating hallucinations. The contributions of our paper are summarized as follows: We introduce PointCoT, a large-scale, high-quality 3D-specific CoT dataset built upon LEO instruction~ huang2023embodied data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first large-scale 3D-specific CoT dataset for 3D scene understanding, providing explicit supervision for grounded multi-step reasoning across diverse task settings. We propose MMCoT , the first 3D-Text Interleaved Multi-Modal CoT framework for 3D Understanding, which interleaves textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence. We suggest an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation method to mitigate multi-instance ambiguity, enabling more reliable evidence-grounded reasoning for 3D understanding. Extensive experiments on six 3D understanding tasks demonstrate that our framework consistently improves performance across captioning, question answering, dialogue, and scene-aware planning, achieving state-of-the-art results (e.g., absolute gains of +1.9 CIDEr on ScanQA, +10.9 EM@1 on SQA3D, and +2.4 EM@1 on 3RScanQA). title: VLSplat: Vision-Language Guided Object-Centric 3D Gaussian Splatting via Scene Graph
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://vlsplat.github.io/
summary: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.
