However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at . Introduction 1:introduction Understanding 3D scene semantics from multiple 2D views is a fundamental problem in computer vision, enabling object-level understanding and downstream applications such as robotics~ zhang2025openvocabularyfunctional, jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion , AR/VR, scene editing~ zhuang2023dreameditor, chen2024gaussianeditor , and semantic mesh extraction~ chen2026sam, guedon2024sugar . Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Kerbl20233DGS has emerged as a powerful representation for real-time novel-view synthesis, motivating growing interest in learning semantic-aware Gaussian representations for joint rendering and scene understanding. In this setting, the goal is to lift 2D semantic observations, typically segmentation masks, into object-aware 3D Gaussian representations such that 3DGS captures semantic properties of the underlying scene. Existing semantic 3DGS methods can be broadly divided into language-feature lifting and mask-based grouping. Language embedding approaches learn language latent fields or attach vision-language features to Gaussian primitives for open-vocabulary 3D understanding. Language latent-field methods~ zhai2025panogs, qin2024langsplat, li20254d, shi2024language, zuo2025fmgs, zhou2024feature distill CLIP~ radford2021learning features into a continuous 3D feature space for natural-language querying, whereas Gaussian-level embedding methods~ li2025langsplatv2,wu2024opengaussian associate such features with individual primitives for more discrete point-level semantics. However, these methods mainly lift or associate vision-language semantics with reconstructed Gaussians for retrieval and querying, rather than directly optimizing Gaussian features with vision-language guidance for category-aware object representation learning. In contrast, mask-based grouping methods use 2D segmentation masks to learn Gaussian groups at instance-level, often producing more explicit object separation than language-field representations~ ying2024omniseg3d, ye2024gaussian, lyu2024gaga, siddiqui2023panoptic . Recently, codebook-based lifting has been introduced for 3DGS semantic lifting, where Unified-Lift~ zhu2025rethinking associates Gaussian features with a trainable object-level codebook to organize primitives into mask-consistent object regions. However, such methods are induced by local 2D segment masks such as SAM~ kirillov2023segment , whose view-dependent and multi-level predictions can split the same object into multiple parts or merge semantically different regions into one mask, especially in indoor scenes. As a result, the learned Gaussian groups may appear locally consistent in rendered views, but they are not explicitly grounded in category-level object semantics, limiting complete object-centric representation learning. In this work, we propose VLSplat, a vision-language guided framework for category-aware object-centric semantic lifting in 3DGS. Our goal is to extend codebook-based Gaussian lifting from category-agnostic instance grouping to category-aware object representation learning under 3DGS optimization. We first construct hybrid 2D supervision by combining text-prompted object masks for major indoor categories with category-agnostic masks for the remaining regions. This provides semantic object cues while retaining dense mask coverage for the scene. To overcome noise and inconsistency from 2D masks, we reinterpret learned Gaussian-codebook groups as nodes in a scene graph. Each node represents a semantic object candidate or an uncertain fragment, and graph relations provide spatial context for reasoning about whether a group is a meaningful object, noisy component, or candidate region to be reassigned. Based on this graph, VLSplat performs two complementary refinements: intra-group semantic refinement suppresses noisy primitives within object nodes, while inter-group acquisition expands incomplete object support by retrieving structurally plausible candidates from surrounding background regions using vision-language priors. We conduct extensive experiments on 3D semantic and instance segmentation and point-level semantic segmentation. Following the thing--stuff taxonomy~ narita2019panopticfusion , VLSplat targets thing categories, i.e., objects with a well-defined shape such as chairs, desks, and beds. Rather than merely lifting vision-language semantics onto reconstructed Gaussians for retrieval or querying, our method directly optimizes Gaussian features with vision-language guidance through scene-graph structured refinement. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose VLSplat, a vision-language guided semantic lifting framework that extends codebook-based Gaussian grouping from category-agnostic instance clustering to object-centric representation learning. We design an object scene graph that interprets codebook groups as nodes enriched with VLM-derived language priors and spatial adjacency, and use it as an object-level prior for Gaussian refinement. We introduce language-guided Gaussian gating on synthetic object views, enabling intra-node refinement and inter-node acquisition that improve both the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object groups. Related Work 2:related_work 2D-to-3D Semantic and Instance Lifting. 2D-to-3D lifting transfers 2D masks, segments, or semantic features into 3D fields while enforcing multi-view consistency. Neural-field-based methods lift object selections, panoptic masks, or contrastive segments into volumetric representations~ siddiqui2023panoptic, ren2022neuralvolumetric , while related approaches incorporate open-vocabulary semantics, promptable segmentation, or hierarchical grouping into radiance fields~ chen2024panoptic, cen2023segmentanything3d, kim2024garfield . With the rise of 3DGS, later methods lift 2D mask supervision onto explicit Gaussian primitives for object-level instance segmentation~ ying2024omniseg3d, ye2024gaussian, lyu2024gaga, dou2024cosseggaussians, choi2024clickgaussian, piekenbrinck2025opensplat3d . Unified-Lift~ zhu2025rethinking further introduces codebook-based Gaussian semantic lifting, where Gaussian features are associated with a trainable object-level codebook to form mask-consistent object regions. Recent works also revisit the lifting solver itself through structured self-training, global label assignment, or modular segmentation on pre-trained 3DGS scenes~ wang2025plgs, shen2024flashsplat, chacko2025lifting . However, existing lifting methods remain strongly tied to 2D mask quality and cross-view consistency, whereas our proposed VLSplat injects object-level language priors and graph-guided reassignment to refine ambiguous or incomplete Gaussian groups. Vision-Language Gaussian Embedding. Recent works extend 3DGS to language-aware scene understanding by embedding semantic, CLIP~ radford2021learning -aligned, or foundation-model features into Gaussian representations~ qin2024langsplat, shi2024language, zuo2025fmgs, zhou2024feature, dou2024semanticgaussians . These methods distill vision-language features into continuous 3D language fields or Gaussian primitives for open-vocabulary retrieval, natural-language querying, and rendered-view semantic prediction~ qin2024langsplat, li20254d, shi2024language, zuo2025fmgs, zhou2024feature, qiu2024gls, chen2025ovgaussian . Recent SAM~ kirillov2023segment +CLIP~ radford2021learning based approaches improve object-level localization by combining object masks with language features: OpenGaussian~ wu2024opengaussian and LangSplatV2~ li2025langsplatv2 link SAM-derived instance features with CLIP embeddings for point-level open-vocabulary understanding, and PanoGS~ zhai2025panogs uses language-guided graph cuts with SAM-guided affinities for panoptic scene understanding. Beyond per-scene optimization, SceneSplat~ li2025scenesplat and Chorus~ li2026chorus pretrain generalizable 3DGS scene encoders with vision-language or multi-teacher supervision, following self-supervised point representation learning such as Sonata~ wu2025sonata . While effective for queryable semantic fields and transferable scene encoders, these methods mostly treat language features as annotations to be lifted or distilled, whereas VLSplat uses object-level language priors to structurally refine Gaussian object groups. Structured Scene Graph Reasoning. 3D scene graphs provide structured abstractions for objects, regions, agents, and their relations in 3D environments. Early works construct hierarchical scene graphs for indoor scenes and reconstructed environments, linking object-level semantics with indoor-, or scene-level structure~ armeni20193dscenegraph, wald2020learning3dssg, wu2021scenegraphfusion . Later mapping systems extend scene graphs to online spatial perception, dynamic agents, and robot planning through metric-semantic maps and layered graph structures~ ros20213ddynamicscenegraphs, ros2021kimera, hughes2022hydra . Recent language-aware scene graphs further support open-vocabulary scene abstraction, open-set relation prediction, language-guided navigation, and context-aware entity grounding~ gu2024conceptgraphs, deng2024opengraph, werby2024hovsg, koch2024open3dsg, chang2023ovsg, koch2024lang3dsg . While prior works mostly use scene graphs as output abstractions, structured memories, or downstream reasoning substrates~ yan2025dovsg, saxena2025grapheqa, koch2025relationfield, chen2024clip , VLSplat uses graph structure as an optimization scaffold for refining object-centric Gaussian groups during semantic lifting. Proposed Approach 3:proposed_approach VLSplat addresses object-level 3D instance and semantic segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, illustrated in Fig. ~ fig:main_vlsplat . The method first lifts object-aware 2D semantic masks into 3D with Gaussian-level features and an object-level codebook (Sec.~ 3:1 ). It then constructs a 3D scene graph that associates codebook groups with language semantics and spatial context (Sec.~ 3:2 ). Finally, VLSplat uses the scene graph as an object-level prior to refine Gaussian features beyond mask-level supervision, producing more object-consistent semantic representations (Sec.~ 3:3 ). title: SurgStream: A Workflow-Anchored Proactive Streaming Framework and Benchmark for Real-Time Surgical Video Understanding
summary: Surgical video understanding is essential for intraoperative assistance such as workflow monitoring, instrument preparation and procedural documentation. Delivering such assistance in real time requires a model to jointly perceive the ongoing scene, remember past surgical events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming surgical video. In this work, we propose SurgStream, a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding. We first introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record structured instrument-action-target observations and fold them into phase-level summaries, providing compact and queryable surgical memory. Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) is then devised to supervise response states within clinical windows, enabling timely responses before procedural deadlines. We further introduce SurgStream-Bench, comprising 11.7K streaming interactions across various tasks covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory. Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially in memory and forward proactive QA. The source code will be available.

Introduction sec:intro Real-time surgical video understanding plays a crucial role in intraoperative assistance~ maierhein2017sds,maierhein2022sds , such as phase-aware instrument preparation, procedural documentation and progress tracking. Such assistance involves understanding the current scene, recalling past events and delivering responses within relevant procedural windows. Fig.~ fig:teaser illustrates these interaction requirements and the temporal modes considered in this work. Surgical videos are long, visually homogeneous and densely structured by the workflow~ twinanda2017endonet . For time-sensitive assistance, delayed responses may lose their practical value, making real-time surgical interaction challenging. Early surgical video-language models primarily focused on visual question answering on images or complete videos~ seenivasan2022surgicalvqa,yuan2024ssgvqa,he2024pitvqa,li2024llavasurg . Subsequently, general and medical vision-language models~ bai2025qwen3vl,wang2025internvl35,jiang2025hulumed achieved significant progress in visual understanding, and real-time surgical commentary~ he2026surgonair narrated the current frames on the fly. More recently, streaming video large language models (LLMs)~ chen2024videollmonline,wang2024mmduet,qian2025dispider,chen2025livecc,xu2025streamingvlm have enabled causal perception and proactive response on continuous video streams, and OneStreamer~ zeng2026onestreamer further unifies perception, memory and proactive response in a single model. Despite this progress, existing methods are not explicitly designed around surgical workflows. Free-text memory does not explicitly preserve phase boundaries or structured event counts, making retrospective queries difficult to support reliably. Response supervision at a single annotated time~ zeng2026onestreamer also leaves the interval of acceptable responses implicit. These limitations motivate workflow-structured memory, supervision within valid response windows, and evaluation of both answer content and timing. To address these limitations, we propose , a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework that integrates compact surgical memory with response supervision within valid procedural windows. For memory construction, we introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record stable instrument--action--target changes and consolidate each completed phase into a compact Summary, preserving evidence for retrospective queries. We further devise Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) to resample response targets within label-derived clinical windows in each epoch, encouraging early responses once evidence is available and before procedural deadlines. Moreover, we construct , spanning diverse tasks across five clinical scenarios and five temporal modes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that outperforms competing methods, with particularly strong gains in memory and forward proactive QA. Methodology sec:method As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , performs real-time surgical video interaction within a single streaming video LLM. Given a video stream arriving at 1\,fps, the model reads at each step the causal context , consisting of the memory , the recent visual window and the dialogue , and emits a control state , , , , followed by optional text. WAM and DTL anchor memory construction and response timing to the surgical workflow. Workflow-Anchored Memory ssec:wam To provide compact and queryable surgical memory, we propose WAM, which anchors both the write points and the content of memory to the surgical workflow instead of letting the model decide the boundaries of free-text captions. For training-target construction, let denote the structured surgical state at time , i.e., the set of instrument--action--target triplets or present instruments. When changes and the new state remains stable for seconds, the model writes an record at , where denotes the elements newly appearing at time relative to the preceding state. The record lists these elements as ``[mm:ss] instrument verb target''. Let collect the records whose event times fall within phase , . After the phase boundary is confirmed, the model writes a record , where is the phase label and counts the onsets of element in (e.g., clip 3). We replace with and retain the other memory records : WAM retains phase summaries for completed phases and detailed observations for the current phase, reducing the accumulation of historical records. Phase intervals and event counts support retrospective queries, while retained records preserve precise event times. Expert annotations define these training targets. At inference, the model generates memory records solely from causal video context. The memory loss is token-averaged cross-entropy conditioned on the state and causal context. Deadline-aware Transition Learning ssec:dtl To enable timely responses within valid clinical windows, we propose DTL, which extends generic sparse supervision~ zeng2026onestreamer beyond a single annotated response time. Each response target is assigned a clinical window , where is the earliest admissible response time and is the deadline, both derived from annotations and task-specific timing rules (e.g., a preparation reminder is due at the next phase onset). To favour early responses, we resample the target time within the valid window at each epoch using inverse transform sampling. Let and . Here, timestamps are discretized at one-second intervals, and controls the decay of the sampling distribution. We assign , for . Experiments sec:exp Dataset ssec:dataset uses Cholec80 (80 videos, 7 phases and 7 tools) and CholecT50 (50 videos with phase labels and 100 triplet classes), sampled at 1\,fps. The benchmark contains 11 , 667 interaction instances (7 , 315/1 , 320/3 , 032 across the splits), including 1 , 893 FP/PA instances with annotation-derived response windows for evaluating answer content and timing. CM matches phase boundaries and triplet events within 30\,s and requires narration within 10\,s after each phase. Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods Table~ tab:main reports zero-shot and fine-tuned comparisons. Among zero-shot VLMs, MedVLM achieves the best RT accuracy (55.35 ) and Avg (17.59 ), yet all zero-shot models score below 3 on FP and PA and below 7 on CM. Periodic evaluation. It leads on 10 of 12 metrics, raising FP from 21.84 to 27.43 , while fine-tuned Qwen3-VL remains higher on PA and narration (S5). Proactive evaluation. The largest mode gains are on FP (+12.26) and CM (+10.06). Documentation (S4) gains most (+12.96). Compared with its periodic variant, proactive achieves higher BM, CM and Avg without external prompts. Fig.~ fig:qualitative contrasts our accurate recall and timely replies with OneStreamer's premature phase-start response. Overall, achieves the best aggregate scores under both periodic and proactive evaluation, benefiting from workflow anchoring. WAM summarizes completed-phase observations, reducing historical text while retaining the recent visual window. Mean update time is 0.53\,s excluding frame I/O, below the 1\,s input interval. These results show that WAM keeps the context compact over long procedures, enabling to process full-length surgical videos in real time. Ablation Study We ablate WAM and DTL against fine-tuned OneStreamer (Table~ tab:main ), which uses free-caption memory and sparse state supervision (PSTL)~ zeng2026onestreamer , with the same data and training schedule. As shown in Table~ tab:ablation , introducing WAM improves BM by 3.36 and CM by 7.68 percentage points, DTL improves FP by 9.36 and CM by 7.18 points, and combining both performs best overall. WAM brings the larger gain on BM and PA, whereas DTL brings the larger gain on FP. Adding DTL to WAM further improves FP by 8.60 points, while adding WAM to DTL raises BM by 2.16 points. The combination performs best on all modes except PA, where WAM alone is higher (17.58 vs. 16.64 ). Together, WAM strengthens retrospective recall and DTL enables timely responses, confirming that the two modules are complementary for streaming surgical interaction. title: Reconstruction as Spatial Evaluation: Diagnosing Cross-View Spatial Intelligence in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

Introduction sec:introduction A central requirement of spatial reasoning in large vision-language models (LVLMs) is the ability to combine partial, viewpoint-dependent observations into a coherent understanding of three-dimensional space. Although contemporary LVLMs have made substantial progress in visual-semantic understanding ~ bai2025qwen3,comanici2025gemini,achiam2023gpt,fu2025video,fu2026mme , their spatial intelligence remains severely limited, particularly in understanding complex 3D environments~ yang2025thinking,yang2026mmsi,liu2025ir3d . Contemporary spatial benchmarks primarily fall into two main paradigms. Static benchmarks assess individual spatial judgments, such as relative direction and distance~ yang2025thinking, yang2026mmsi, wang2025site,jia2026omnispatial,li2025viewspatial . However, independent queries fail to test whether a model can jointly recover a coherent scene: for instance, knowing which object is closer does not determine whether their 3D positions and extents form a valid layout. Conversely, embodied benchmarks evaluate spatial understanding through interaction in simulated environments~ majumdar2024openeqa,hong2026esi , where outcomes jointly depend on perception, exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. This leaves an unmet need: evaluating whether LVLMs can reason jointly about object geometry across views, independently of interactive execution. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce , a benchmark for evaluating cross-view spatial reasoning in LVLMs through joint prediction of object-level 3D bounding boxes. Given multi-view observations and target object queries, an LVLM is tasked with predicting oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. This joint objective requires models to associate objects across viewpoints, resolve relative camera geometry, and estimate metric extents simultaneously. Providing queried 2D regions controls for open-set detection, isolating spatial reasoning as the primary point of evaluation. We assess each reconstruction along two complementary axes: Structure, which evaluates relative layout and topological arrangement, and Metric, which measures physical scale and camera-anchored 3D placement across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor scenes. organizes evaluation into four levels: Geometric Perception, Spatial Relations, Reconstruction, and Navigation (Figure~ fig:overview ). The first two levels comprise nine spatial QA tasks that probe individual spatial capabilities, including cross-view correspondence, camera pose estimation, and relative distance judgments. Their scores help us examine how these capabilities relate to joint reconstruction performance. Navigation independently evaluates path planning: given multi-view observations, a starting viewpoint, and a visual target, the model predicts a path that reaches the target while avoiding obstacles. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even the top-performing GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4 on Structure but only 58.7 on Metric. Diagnostic analyses connect individual spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality, showing that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection show that replacing self-generated maps with ground-truth geometry boosts navigation success by 55.2 to 69.7 percentage points. This gap indicates that downstream navigation is primarily bounded by perceptual accuracy rather than planning capability. Finally, spatial fine-tuning confers broad performance gains across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: Joint 3D reconstruction for spatial evaluation. We introduce , which establishes a new evaluation paradigm that benchmarks LVLMs on jointly recovering object-level 3D bounding boxes from real multi-view observations. Complementary Structure and Metric scores distinguish relative scene coherence from physical scale and placement. A hierarchical diagnostic suite across diverse domains. Covering indoor, tabletop, and outdoor scenes, unifies atomic items, reconstruction instances, and offline navigation episodes to evaluate local spatial capabilities, joint scene reconstruction, and navigation. Diagnostic insights and transferable supervision. Evaluating eighteen frontier models uncovers a pervasive Structure--Metric disparity. Controlled interventions show that object-level metric depth yields larger Metric gains than relational cues. Downstream map substitution decouples spatial perception from planning competence, and spatial fine-tuning confirms transferable reasoning benefits. Related Work sec:related_work Benchmarking Spatial Reasoning. Spatial reasoning benchmarks have primarily targeted local geometric queries~ yang2025thinking,ma20253dsrbench,wang2025site,jia2026omnispatial,li2025viewspatial,yang2026mmsi or embodied task execution~ majumdar2024openeqa,hong2026esi,zhao2026espire . Recent efforts also explore 3D room generation~ yang2026codeasroom , inverse rendering of synthetic single-image scenes in IR3D-Bench~ liu2025ir3d , top-down metric layouts in Video2Layout~ huang2025video2layout , and 2D floor plans from apartment photographs in Blueprint-Bench~ petersson2025blueprintbench . In contrast, evaluates joint object geometry from real-world multi-view observations, directly scoring predicted 3D bounding boxes against annotated ground truth. Complementary Structure and Metric scores explicitly disentangle relative scene layout from physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Spatial Representations for Reasoning and Planning. Explicit spatial representations provide essential intermediate abstractions between perception and action. Recent agentic approaches support spatial reasoning with intermediate information obtained through code execution, tool calls, or visual sketching~ marsili2025visualagenticaispatial, wu2025vilasr,chen2026spacetools,dai2026sagentspatialtooluseelicits,cho2026spatialclaw , while cognitive-mapping approaches study structured representations that scaffold mental navigation~ yang2025thinking,zhu2026mind_over_space . Complementary work examines data and training strategies for spatial reasoning~ ouyang2025spacer,zhao2026ouroborosspatial,chen2024spatialvlmendowingvisionlanguagemodels,li2026spatialevoselfevolvingspatialintelligence,li2025spatialladderprogressivetrainingspatial . We build upon this insight by treating reconstructed 3D bounding box maps as an explicit spatial reasoning representation, directly probing how their geometric fidelity supports path planning. Reconstruction as Spatial Evaluation sec:benchmark evaluates cross-view spatial reasoning in LVLMs by requiring them to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes from multi-view images and object queries. Spatial QA tasks provide complementary measurements of individual spatial capabilities, while an independent navigation task evaluates path planning (Figure~ fig:task_suite ). Problem formulation Let denote an ordered sequence of multi-view observations, with serving as the reference view. Let denote the target-object queries, where \[ q_k=(u_k,j_k, _k, _k) \] specifies an object identifier , a designated view , its 2D bounding box in that view, and its category label . Given and , the evaluated LVLM is required to output one oriented 3D bounding box for each queried object: where and denote the center and side lengths of the predicted 3D box, and denotes its yaw about the gravity axis. All quantities are expressed in metres in a gravity-aligned frame whose horizontal orientation is anchored to . Its origin is the vertical projection of the reference-camera center onto the support surface. title: Unified Loss-Aware Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: The efficiency and fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting critically depend on adaptive density control, which grows and suppresses Gaussian primitives throughout optimization. However, the standard pipeline still relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets, rather than explicitly assessing the loss-reducing effect of each split, clone, or opacity update. This mismatch can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures, and destabilize training through blanket opacity changes. In this work, we recast adaptive density control as a collection of local loss-reduction decisions. We derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that predict the objective change caused by three primitive-level operations: splitting, cloning, and opacity decay. This yields a unified loss-aware framework with three components. First, we extend second-order splitting to a normalized joint position-scale space, enabling children to adapt not only their locations but also their anisotropic extents. Second, we formulate duplicate cloning as a surrogate minimization problem, selecting only Gaussians whose duplicated contribution is predicted to improve reconstruction and assigning each child a principled opacity. Third, we replace global opacity reset with selective soft opacity decay that weakens harmful primitives while preserving useful ones. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our method produces more targeted primitive allocation and achieves improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets compared to baselines.

Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs has emerged as an effective scene representation for high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. Subsequent studies have improved the reconstruction quality and rendering efficiency of 3DGS through advances in primitive representations~ 2dgs,betasplatting , volumetric rendering~ ever, vol3d , anti-aliasing~ mipsplatting, multigs , and level-of-detail (LOD) strategies for large-scale scenes~ hierarchicalgs . Beyond these advances, reconstruction quality and representation complexity of 3DGS are also influenced by how Gaussian primitives are allocated and refined during training. Adaptive Density Control (ADC) is a key component of this process, progressively refining the scene representation through splitting, cloning, and pruning Gaussians. Despite its effectiveness, ADC still depends heavily on hand-crafted heuristic thresholds and positional gradients. These heuristic strategies can produce redundant Gaussian primitives even in regions where densification is unnecessary~ revising, GDAGS, compact, steep , which increases memory usage and slows rendering as they accumulate. To address this problem, prior works have revisited ADC from various perspectives~ absgs, dc4gs, GDAGS, mcmc, resgs, zhang2024fregs . More recently, SteepGS~ steep mitigates redundant primitive generation by predicting whether splitting each Gaussian locally reduces the reconstruction loss. Despite these advances, two important aspects remain underexplored. In particular, existing loss-based splitting formulations mainly focus on position parameters, while the influence of other Gaussian parameters remains underexplored. Moreover, this loss-aware perspective has not yet been systematically extended to other density-control operations, such as cloning and opacity-based pruning, where conventional heuristic rules are still commonly used. Building on these observations, we propose a loss-aware density control framework for efficient and faithful Gaussian representation. We first revisit splitting. While moving offspring centers refines local geometry, thin or anisotropic structures often require adapting offspring spatial extents in addition to positions. Thus, we extend splitting from a position-only formulation to a joint position-scale space, allowing each split to account for Gaussian extent. As shown in Fig.~ fig:intro ~(a), position-only splitting can leave gaps around thin structures such as a bicycle handle, whereas our scale-aware splitting jointly adjusts offspring positions and scales to form a more faithful local representation. We further extend the loss-aware principle to cloning. Conventional cloning relies on view-space gradient and scale thresholds~ 3dgs , without explicitly estimating whether a duplicate will reduce the photometric objective. Our surrogate-guided cloning instead predicts the loss change induced by each duplicate and clones only primitives whose duplicate contributions are expected to reduce the loss. As shown in Fig.~ fig:intro ~(b), standard 3DGS selects both green and red candidates in the zoom-in boxes. This mixed selection reveals that its heuristic cloning rule is not directly aligned with the loss effect of duplication. The baseline also misses important candidates around under-reconstructed structures such as the wooden frame, leaving these regions inadequately refined. By contrast, our method selects mostly green candidates and places clones in under-reconstructed regions, allowing the proposed surrogate to guide cloning toward primitives that are more likely to improve the objective. A similar objective-agnostic issue appears in opacity-based pruning. Standard 3DGS periodically applies a global opacity reset, reducing the opacity of all Gaussians regardless of whether their current contributions help or harm the objective. To address this, our loss-aware opacity decay predicts which Gaussians currently increase the loss and weakens only those primitives, while preserving useful Gaussians. As shown in Fig.~ fig:intro ~(c), the global opacity reset makes all Gaussian primitives nearly transparent and introduces abrupt changes that can destabilize training~ revising , whereas our opacity decay avoids unnecessary global perturbations and yields a more stable training trajectory. However, directly evaluating the loss change of each candidate operation is computationally expensive, as it requires applying the operation, re-rendering affected views, and recomputing the loss. We therefore derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that approximate the objective change induced by splitting, cloning, and opacity decay~ lecun1989optimal, wu2020firefly, molchanov2016pruning, molchanov2019importance . These surrogates provide a unified criterion for deciding whether each density-control operation is locally expected to reduce the loss. Concretely, as shown in Fig.~ fig:intro ~(d), our framework consists of three loss-aware components: position-scale splitting, surrogate-guided cloning, and surrogate-guided opacity decay. The first adapts both offspring positions and spatial extents, the second selects loss-reducing duplicates and assigns adequate child opacity, and the third weakens Gaussians predicted to increase the objective. Together, these components form a unified loss-aware ADC strategy that allocates primitives more effectively and improves rendering quality with fewer Gaussians on standard 3DGS benchmarks. Related works Novel view synthesis Novel View Synthesis (NVS)~ nvs aims to render images of a 3D scene from previously unseen viewpoints using given multi-view observations. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf have emerged as a major milestone in NVS by representing scenes as continuous volumetric fields. However, their reliance on dense sampling and implicit representations often leads to high rendering costs. In contrast, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs represents a scene explicitly as a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussians and combines this representation with differentiable, visibility-aware rasterization, enabling both efficient rendering and high-quality novel view synthesis. Recent studies have further improved 3DGS through alternative primitive representations~ 2dgs,betasplatting , exact volumetric rendering formulations~ vol3d,ever , anti-aliasing techniques~ mipsplatting,multigs , and hierarchical level-of-detail (LOD) strategies~ hierarchicalgs . As a result of these advances, 3DGS has been actively studied across a wide range of tasks and application domains~ inverserendering,gaussiangrouping,diffusion_based_editing,gsslam,seamless . Adaptive Density Control in 3DGS Adaptive density control (ADC) determines how Gaussian primitives are cloned, split, and pruned during 3DGS training, and therefore strongly affects both reconstruction quality and primitive efficiency. Since the original 3DGS relies on heuristic gradient and scale thresholds, recent works have improved the split and clone operations in ADC by refining densification signals~ absgs, pixelgs, dc4gs, GDAGS , introducing stochastic sampling-based updates~ mcmc, mh , or revising the densification procedure itself~ fang2024mini, revising, dongreframing, resgs . The most relevant work to ours is SteepGS~ steep , which makes Gaussian splitting loss-aware using second-order information. However, its formulation is limited to position-only splitting, while other ADC operations such as cloning and opacity reset also remain heuristic. We extend this loss-aware perspective to the broader ADC pipeline through joint position-scale splitting and local surrogate-based cloning and opacity reduction. Adaptive Density Control sec:prelim_adc Along with standard gradient-based optimization, 3DGS~ 3dgs periodically employs Adaptive Density Control (ADC) to dynamically refine the set of Gaussians during training. ADC determines which Gaussians should be cloned, split, or pruned, and therefore has a direct effect on both reconstruction quality and primitive efficiency. In standard 3DGS, ADC first identifies Gaussians with large average view-space positional gradients as densification candidates. Among these candidates, Gaussians with small scales are cloned to improve local coverage, while Gaussians with large scales are split into smaller offspring. In addition, Gaussians with low opacity are pruned, and opacity values are periodically reset as a heuristic stabilization mechanism. However, these ADC rules do not explicitly assess whether a candidate operation would reduce the training objective. Candidate Gaussians are selected using a hand-crafted threshold on the view-space gradient magnitude, and the choice between cloning and splitting is determined using a scale threshold. As a result, Gaussians may be densified even when they could be refined solely through ordinary gradient-based updates, thereby increasing the number of Gaussians unnecessarily. title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Code available at https://github.com/anoncvlab/svdPrune
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

Code: INTRODUCTION sec:intro Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and their action-oriented extensions such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have emerged as a dominant paradigm for multimodal reasoning and embodied intelligence. By combining visual perception with language understanding, these models enable a broad range of capabilities, from visual question answering to robotic manipulation. Despite their success, visual representations remain a major computational bottleneck. To address this inefficiency, token pruning has become a central direction for efficient multimodal inference. By removing redundant visual tokens, recent methods substantially reduce latency and computational cost. Many existing approaches derive token-wise selection scores from attention statistics, token norms, cross-modal relevance, or related importance signals. Although effective at moderate compression ratios, these criteria do not explicitly measure each token's contribution to the global structure of the full token set. This limitation becomes particularly relevant under aggressive compression, where token-wise scores may fail to reflect the collective structure of the visual representation. We argue that visual token pruning can instead be viewed as a low-rank subspace preservation problem: the objective is to retain a compact subset of tokens that remains representative of the dominant spectral structure of the complete visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free, attention-independent framework that leverages spectral decomposition and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. Our contributions are threefold: We reformulate visual token pruning as a low-rank subspace preservation problem, providing a globally informed alternative to token selection criteria derived from local interactions; We introduce SVD-Prune, a spectral token pruning framework applicable at the encoder side, decoder side, or in a hybrid configuration; Through a unified evaluation across VLMs and VLAs, we demonstrate the robustness of SVD-Prune across multimodal reasoning and embodied decision-making tasks, including under extreme compression, while substantially reducing visual tokens and inference cost. RELATED WORK sec:related_work VLMs typically encode images into hundreds of visual tokens, substantially increasing sequence-dependent computation during multimodal inference. This effect can be further amplified in VLA architectures that employ multiple visual encoders, leading to larger visual token representations~ kim2024openvla, li2026SemanticVLA . Existing visual token reduction methods for VLMs can be broadly categorized according to where pruning is applied. Encoder-side approaches reduce tokens within the vision backbone or immediately after visual encoding. ToMe~ bolya2022token merges redundant tokens directly inside the Vision Transformer, while FasterVLM~ zhang2024cls , HiRED~ arif2025hired , DivPrune~ alvar2025divprune , VisionZip~ yang2025visionzip , and TRIM~ song2025trim operate on encoder outputs. In particular, FasterVLM and HiRED rely on attention-derived importance scores, DivPrune explicitly promotes diversity among retained tokens, VisionZip combines token selection with similarity-based merging, and TRIM exploits cross-modal similarity to identify visually relevant regions. Decoder-side approaches prune visual tokens within the language model during multimodal reasoning. FastV~ chen2024fastv removes tokens after early decoder layers using attention statistics, FitPrune~ ye2025fitprune introduces handcrafted pruning schedules, SparseVLM~ zhang2025sparsevlm performs adaptive text-aware token sparsification with token recycling, and PDrop~ wang2025PDrop progressively increases pruning ratios across decoder depth. Beyond these two categories, hybrid approaches perform token reduction at multiple stages of the vision-language pipeline. IVTP~ huang2024ivtp first removes visually redundant tokens in the vision encoder using attention-rollout-based importance scores, and subsequently prunes instruction-irrelevant visual tokens within the LLM through CLIP-guided text-aware token selection. Recent work has extended visual token reduction to VLA models, initially by adapting pruning strategies developed for VLMs. In particular, FastV~ chen2024fastv and SparseVLM~ zhang2025sparsevlm have been directly applied to VLA architectures, leveraging respectively attention-based saliency scores and text-aware token sparsification. However, these methods do not explicitly incorporate action-specific or temporal signals. EfficientVLA~ yang2026efficientvla addresses this limitation by performing visual token selection on encoder outputs using a combination of instruction-aware relevance scores and feature-diversity measures. More recently, VLA-specific approaches such as SP-VLA~ li2025sp , SpecPrune-VLA~ wang2025specprunevla , VLA-Pruner~ liu2025vlapruner , and ADP~ pei2025action incorporate action-aware or temporal information into the pruning process, exploiting the sequential nature of robotic interaction to better preserve action-critical visual cues. LightVLA~ lightvla introduces a differentiable token pruning framework that learns task-driven visual token importance through dynamic queries to adaptively prune visual tokens. Notably, most VLA-specific methods operate at the encoder level, reducing visual computation without modifying autoregressive action generation. METHODOLOGY sec:methodology Rather than estimating token importance from local interactions, we formulate visual token pruning as the problem of preserving the dominant low-rank structure underlying the full set of visual tokens. To this end, we propose SVD-Prune, a training-free and attention-independent framework that identifies a dominant low-rank spectral subspace and ranks tokens according to their leverage scores within this subspace. This globally informed criterion favors a compact subset of tokens that is representative of the dominant low-rank structure while remaining applicable across encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid pruning configurations. Figure~ fig:svd provides an overview of SVD-Prune. The pipeline consists of four main stages: (1) global pattern extraction, (2) spectral energy truncation, (3) token contribution estimation via leverage scores, and (4) token selection and pruning. Global Pattern Extraction ssec:extraction At a given pruning location, let denote the matrix of visual token representations, where is the number of visual tokens and their feature dimension. Depending on the pruning configuration, may correspond to intermediate encoder features, encoder outputs, or visual-token representations within the language model. Visual token representations often exhibit strong correlations across tokens, motivating the characterization of their dominant low-rank structure. We apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the feature matrix where contains the left singular vectors, contains the singular values on its diagonal, and contains the corresponding right singular vectors. Since the feature matrix is not centered prior to decomposition, the singular values characterize the spectral energy of the representation rather than variance in the PCA sense. Spectral Energy Truncation ssec:var_pattern After decomposition, we identify the dominant spectral components by analyzing the energy associated with the singular values. Specifically, we compute the normalized spectral energy of each component as where denotes the -th singular value. The cumulative retained energy up to rank is then defined as We select the smallest rank such that , where controls the fraction of retained spectral energy and thereby determines the rank of the truncated subspace used for token scoring. According to the Eckart--Young theorem, the resulting rank- approximation is optimal with respect to Frobenius reconstruction error among all rank- approximations of . Importantly, does not directly determine the pruning ratio. The final compression level is instead controlled independently by the token budget during the selection stage. Token Contribution Estimation ssec:leverage Having identified the dominant spectral subspace, we quantify each token's contribution using statistical leverage scores~ mahoney2009cur . In our setting, leverage scores provide a subspace-aware measure of each visual token's influence on the retained low-rank structure. For each token , the standard rank- leverage score is defined as where denotes the standard rank- statistical leverage score of token . Since the columns of are orthonormal, . We use the normalized score such that . This normalization does not affect token ranking. Tokens with higher leverage scores exert greater influence on the retained low-rank subspace and are therefore favored during selection, whereas low-leverage tokens have lower influence on this subspace. Token Selection and Pruning ssec:selection Tokens are ranked according to their leverage scores, and the top- tokens are retained, where denotes the target token budget. The selected token indices are then restored to their original sequence order to preserve positional consistency and maintain compatibility with downstream attention mechanisms. This deterministic top- selection serves as a practical heuristic for identifying representative tokens. While leverage scores provide a subspace-aware ranking criterion, selecting the top- tokens does not guarantee an optimal subset for downstream task performance. Instead, it favors tokens with the largest influence on the retained spectral subspace. Importantly, leverage scores measure token influence with respect to the retained subspace rather than pairwise diversity. Consequently, deterministic top-k selection does not explicitly prevent multiple similar high-leverage tokens from being retained; enforcing explicit diversity would require an additional subset-selection criterion. EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS sec:experiments_analysis Experimental setup ssec:experimental_settings We evaluate SVD-Prune on both VLMs and VLAs. For VLM experiments, we use LLaVA-1.5-7B~ liu2023llava as our primary benchmark and additionally evaluate QwenVL~ bai2023qwenvl to assess generalization across different VLM architectures. Following the standard LLaVA-1.5 configuration, input images are resized to , yielding 576 visual tokens. QwenVL processes images at a higher resolution of , resulting in a larger visual token budget of 1024 tokens. Additional experiment results on LLaVA-1.5-13B are reported in the supplementary materials. Performance is evaluated on a diverse collection of multimodal benchmarks covering visual reasoning, object perception, hallucination robustness, scientific reasoning, and text-centric visual understanding~ lu2022sqa, gurari20

title: Lie Routing Vision Language Models for View-Robust 3D Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) extend visual-language reasoning to scene-level tasks such as object captioning, language-guided localization, and spatial question answering. Early approaches primarily connect language models to explicit 3D representations, including point clouds and object-level scene features~ xu2024pointllm,chen2024ll3da,huang2024chat . These representations provide direct spatial structure, while their reliance on reconstructed scene inputs motivates complementary approaches that learn 3D understanding from RGB observations. Recent 3D MLLMs derive geometry directly from multi-view RGB observations, enabling 3D understanding without requiring preconstructed 3D scene models. Pretrained geometry encoders such as VGGT~ wang2025vggt extract scene structure and cross-view correspondences, and recent methods inject these features into MLLM visual representations for 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning~ zheng2025learning,huang20253drs,zhang2026generalization . This learned geometry injection paradigm preserves the scalability of video-based MLLMs while providing strong spatial context. Despite these advances, geometry is primarily used to augment visual representations, while how it should drive viewpoint-adaptive changes in visual semantics remains underexplored. We observe that a fixed scene entity and query can yield substantially different target-related responses across viewpoints. As camera pose, apparent scale, and visibility change, the response may weaken, become diffuse, or shift toward irrelevant regions, a phenomenon we term viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We visualize it using query-relevant activations, obtained by projecting final visual tokens through the vocabulary head and averaging their positive support over the target-phrase tokens. Viewpoint change between frames and is measured by the geodesic distance ~ hartley2003multiple,huynh2009metrics . Taking the first frame containing the referred target as reference , we define over the remaining views , with both distances reported in degrees. Figure~ fig:teaser (a) varies viewpoint along a fixed camera trajectory while holding the scene, target, query, checkpoint, and reference view constant, showing that Lie routing preserves more localized responses. Figure~ fig:teaser (b) relates task performance to , with LieVLM maintaining stronger performance as viewpoint variation increases. To address this challenge, we introduce LieVLM, which adapts visual semantics through geometry-conditioned Lie routing. Camera rotations are described by , motivating us to use the same structure for feature adaptation across viewpoints. Lie routing applies learned rotations to three-dimensional groups of projected visual features, changing their directions while preserving their lengths. Concretely, geometry tokens predict local generators and channel-wise routing coefficients. A Pad\'e--Cayley realization converts the generators into local rotations, and only the resulting identity-relative corrections are projected back into the MLLM representation. The corrections are gated and fused with the original visual features and direct geometry features before language generation. This design combines structured feature adaptation with retained semantic and spatial-context paths, without requiring relative camera poses as inputs to the routing module. We evaluate LieVLM on 3D captioning, grounding, video object detection, and spatial reasoning~ chen2021scan2cap,chen2020scanrefer,wang2024embodiedscan,yang2025thinking . LieVLM consistently improves over matched additive geometry fusion, with gains that generalize across spatial benchmarks, training scales, and stronger multimodal backbones. Controlled analyses further connect these improvements to structured geometry conditioned transformations and robustness to viewpoint variation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: [itemsep=0.2pt, topsep=1pt, leftmargin=2em] We characterize viewpoint-induced semantic drift in 3D MLLMs through cross-view target-response diagnostics and its association with downstream task performance. We develop Lie Routing Vision Language Models (LieVLM), combining local prediction, rotation-preserving residual transformations, and channel-wise gating to adapt pretrained visual semantics across viewpoints. We demonstrate consistent gains across 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning, with controlled evaluations across training scales and backbones and targeted analyses of routing structure and viewpoint robustness. Related Work sec:related 3D Vision Language Models. 3D VLMs incorporate explicit spatial inputs such as point clouds and object representations~ xu2024pointllm,chen2024ll3da,huang2024chat,zhu2024llava , or derive geometric priors from image sequences~ zheng2025learning,wang2025vggt,wang2024dust3r . Reconstruction-aware models further couple video understanding with 3D reconstruction~ chen2025vid,fan2025vlm,hu2025g , establishing geometry as an important representation for 3D reasoning. Recent RGB-based systems additionally combine semantic and geometry encoders through camera-guided fusion~ zhao2025spacemind . Our work builds on these interfaces and studies geometry-conditioned routing of pretrained visual semantics across viewpoints. 3D Scene Understanding and Spatial Reasoning. Scene understanding benchmarks evaluate localization, grounding, and captioning~ chen2020scanrefer,chen2021scan2cap,wang2024embodiedscan . Spatial reasoning benchmarks assess depth, distance, viewpoint, and multiview relations~ yang2025thinking,tong2024cambrian,fu2024blink,zhang2026generalization , while instruction datasets develop these capabilities from embodied observations~ chen2024spatialvlm,zhang2025flatland,ray2024sat . Multi-view grounding methods further aggregate view-dependent evidence through inter-view attention and learned view prototypes~ guo2023viewrefer . These efforts motivate our focus on semantic stability and task robustness under viewpoint variation. Geometry in Neural Representations. Prior work spans conditional feature modulation through FiLM~ perez2018film , explicit geometry-induced transformations in multi-view attention via GTA~ miyato2024gta , and equivariant representations under or Euclidean symmetries~ deng2021vector,hutchinson2021lietransformer,fuchs2020se,satorras2021en . Orthogonal and Cayley parameterizations further provide structure-preserving learned transformations~ helfrich2018orthogonal . We instead study geometry-conditioned Lie routing in pretrained 3D MLLMs, where learned geometry tokens predict token-wise local actions and channel-wise gates over latent subspaces for viewpoint-adaptive routing without explicit relative pose inputs. title: Gnomon4D: Learning Where and When to Focus for Geometric Motion-Grounded World-Action Modeling
summary: World-action models (WAMs) use video-generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Yet RGB futures entangle physical state changes with appearance, while frame-wise depth and point maps lack temporal correspondence. Existing 4D approaches either keep motion implicit in visual features or translate predicted traces into actions through a separate interface. We present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field encoding the cross-frame image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. By placing embodiment motion and object responses in a shared space, GeoDelta exposes their motion relations to the action expert at inference. Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) uses these relations to focus spatial readout on task-relevant interaction regions, while Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) aggregates evidence around changes in their relative motion, such as grasp and release. GeoDelta describes surface motion independently of embodiment-specific controls, providing a shared human--robot quasi-action for action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H followed by robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms the strongest real-robot baseline by 7.0 and 16.0 percentage points under in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, respectively.

Introduction sec:intro Robot manipulation advances along complementary routes: vision-language-action models (VLAs) map observations and instructions to actions~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation,intelligence2026pi07steerablegeneralistrobotic , world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions~ shen2025videovlavideogeneratorsgeneralizable,zhu2025unifiedworldmodelscoupling,guo2026videopredictionpolicy2,wang2026openwamopenmodularexploration,miao2026internw0deltaworldactionmodel , and agentic recursive self-improvement (RSI) refines skills or generates simulation-ready worlds~ physicalrsi2026,physicalrsiteam2026awomosimdataengineagenticsimulationreadyworldgeneration . All three aim to generate actions that change object states to accomplish a task, and WAMs in particular explicitly predict these changes to guide the action. Most WAMs represent this future as video~ kim2026cosmospolicyfinetuningvideo,wang2026openwamopenmodularexploration,zhao2026rynnworld4d4dembodiedworld , inheriting the visual priors of large video foundation models~ wan2025wanopenadvancedlargescale , which has driven their rapid adoption. RGB futures, however, entangle task-relevant state changes with texture, lighting, and background, leading policies to overfit to appearance and generalize poorly to unseen visual conditions~ yuan2026dreamwamrgbfutureprediction,lou2026maskworldmodelpredicting . As 2D projections of the scene, they further lack the 3D geometry that precise manipulation such as insertion and stacking requires~ qu2025spatialvlaexploringspatialrepresentations . To strengthen geometric perception and reasoning, recent WAMs either predict depth together with video~ guo2026unified4dworldaction,bardhan2026depthworld3dworldmodel or distill depth-aware features during training~ li2026wam4dfast4dworld . Yet depth and point maps remain frame-wise: they locate surfaces but provide no temporal correspondence, and thus do not directly encode embodiment--object motion through approach, manipulation, and release. 4D geometric motion addresses this gap by tracking physical points over time, yielding explicit and temporally coherent dynamics. Existing methods use such 4D cues in two ways. 4D-WAM~ yang20264dwaminfusingspatiotemporalawareness and GEM-4D~ zhou2026gem4dgeometryenhancedvideoworld regularize WAM features with dense trajectory fields during training, but discard the 4D teacher or geometric branch at inference, leaving no explicit motion for the action to read (Fig.~ fig:paradigm a). TraceGen~ Lee_2026_CVPR_C2601 and ~ lee2026mu0scalable3dinteractiontrace predict sparse 3D traces, but translate them into robot control through separate interfaces (Fig.~ fig:paradigm b). Thus, existing methods either keep 4D cues implicit in visual representations or decouple them from control through a separate trace-to-action interface. None of them jointly generates future video, explicit 4D motion, and robot actions as online modalities, nor explicitly uses embodiment--object motion relations and their transitions to organize action readout. What is therefore needed is an efficient 4D geometric motion representation that bridges video and action. It should align with the visual future, be generated jointly with the action, and place embodiment and object motion in a shared spatiotemporal space. Accordingly, we introduce , a WAM built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture~ liang2025mixtureoftransformerssparsescalablearchitecture that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and a video-aligned 4D geometric motion, , (Figs.~ fig:teaser and~ fig:paradigm c). For each foreground pixel on the embodiment and the manipulated object, records the image-plane displacement and depth change of the same physical point over a short interval, forming a video-aligned field of 3D motion. Unlike per-frame depth and point maps, its explicit cross-frame correspondences make motion directly observable and temporally coherent. Unlike 2D optical flow, its depth component captures motion along the line of sight, distinguishing 3D motions that induce similar image-plane displacements. Defined on the video pixel grid, reuses the video VAE while preserving alignment with the visual future and its generative priors. Within this architecture, Video, , and Action experts denoise jointly through shared attention. The and Action experts further share a denoising clock and exchange information at matched stages, making predicted geometric motion directly available to the action expert. Yet explicit 4D geometric motion alone does not tell the action expert where and when to focus. We hypothesize that control-relevant cues concentrate spatially at embodiment--object interaction regions and temporally when contact is established, the object begins to move with the embodiment, or release occurs. Low-dimensional action supervision offers no direct localization among dense video and motion tokens, so the expert may memorize actions from embodiment-centric patterns rather than reason over these interactions~ lin2026breakingvisionactionshortcutlatent . Probe experiments on RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin20scalabledata confirm this tendency: the action attention of existing WAMs favors the embodiment as a whole over embodiment--object interaction regions (see supplementary material). To direct the action expert toward these cues, uses predicted 4D motion for task-adaptive spatiotemporal reweighting. Specifically, employs Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) to emphasize interaction regions from task-conditioned embodiment--object relative motion, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) to emphasize and aggregate frames where this relation changes. The resulting interaction tokens are injected residually into the dense action readout. Returning to the representation itself, is embodiment-agnostic: it describes foreground surface motion without encoding embodiment-specific joints, poses, or control parameters. It can therefore serve as a shared quasi-action across human hands and diverse robot embodiments. Existing human-video pretraining pipelines instead treat estimated hand poses, such as MANO parameters, as actions~ luo2026beingh07latentworldactionmodel,dyna2026dyna2 , learn latent actions from human videos~ yang2026lawm3dlearning3dawarelatent , or align human and robot data through embodiment-specific retargeting and robot rendering~ ma2026humanscaleegocentrichumanvideo,miao2026internw0deltaworldactionmodel . By contrast, defines an explicit, video-aligned motion space shared directly by human and robot videos, without mapping either source into the other's action space. Using this shared representation, we first pretrain the Video and experts on (5,000+ hours of action-free egocentric manipulation video). We then mid-train the full model on Robot-30H (30+ hours of real-robot data) to connect this motion space to robot controls, and finally post-train it on target tasks. Our contributions are threefold: , a WAM that jointly generates future video, actions, and , an explicit 4D geometric motion representation that exposes embodiment--object interaction dynamics to the action expert. InSAttn and TransAgg for task-adaptive spatiotemporal reweighting, focusing the action expert on interaction regions and transition frames. Embodiment-agnostic as a human--robot quasi-action for action-free pretraining on , with state-of-the-art performance on three simulation benchmarks and real-robot validation.
