title: OctreeSplat: Hierarchical Octree-Guided Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown considerable potential for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction. Feed-forward methods avoid costly per-scene optimization, but fixed image or spatial resolutions limit their ability to allocate primitives according to local complexity. We present OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided feed-forward Gaussian splatting. OctreeSplat extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model (VFM), constructs a hierarchical octree, and predicts densification scores. The resulting representation allocates Gaussian primitives at spatially varying densities according to local complexity. Stochastic solids volume rendering improves depth rendering, strengthens geometric supervision, and supports surface reconstruction. When camera parameters are available, an optional test-time optimization (TTO) module improves agreement between predicted and ground-truth parameters. Training updates only 76 million additional parameters and requires 35 GPU-hours. Experiments on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive RGB view synthesis, depth synthesis, and surface reconstruction. OctreeSplat reduces the number of Gaussian primitives while maintaining high reconstruction quality.
full_text: OctreeSplat: Hierarchical Octree-Guided\ -Forward Gaussian Splatting Yibin Zhao , Yihan Pan , Wenli Yang, Jun Nan, and Jianjun Yi : equal contribution. : Corresponding author. Yibin Zhao, Wenli Yang, Jun Nan, and Jianjun Yi: East China University of Science and Technology, Shanghai, China (e-mail: \ Y20230063,Y30260694,Y20240039\ @mail.ecust.edu.cn; jjyi@ecust.edu.cn). fig:toutu 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown considerable potential for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction. Feed-forward methods avoid costly per-scene optimization, but fixed image or spatial resolutions limit their ability to allocate primitives according to local complexity. We present OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided feed-forward Gaussian splatting. OctreeSplat extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model (VFM), constructs a hierarchical octree, and predicts densification scores. The resulting representation allocates Gaussian primitives at spatially varying densities according to local complexity. Stochastic solids volume rendering improves depth rendering, strengthens geometric supervision, and supports surface reconstruction. When camera parameters are available, an optional test-time optimization (TTO) module improves agreement between predicted and ground-truth parameters. Training updates only 76 million additional parameters and requires 35 GPU-hours. Experiments on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive RGB view synthesis, depth synthesis, and surface reconstruction. OctreeSplat reduces the number of Gaussian primitives while maintaining high reconstruction quality. 3D Gaussian splatting, visual foundation model, hierarchical octree, novel view synthesis. Introduction Image-based 3D reconstruction has traditionally relied on structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines, with iterative techniques represented by bundle adjustment (BA) BA for multi-view pose estimation and sparse reconstruction. Common scene representations include point clouds, voxels, and signed distance fields. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl3DGS has combined photorealistic novel view synthesis with high rendering efficiency. Given images and camera parameters, 3DGS iteratively renders the scene and optimizes the parameters of Gaussian primitives. Adaptive density control (ADC) periodically adds and removes primitives during optimization, which typically takes tens of minutes to an hour. Visual foundation models (VFMs) wang2025vggt,wang2025pi3,wang2026vggtomega learn strong priors from large-scale datasets and directly regress 3D information from image collections. Outputs include depth maps, 3D point maps, and camera parameters. These models reduce accumulated errors and iterative computation in conventional reconstruction pipelines while maintaining strong generalization. Feed-forward 3DGS methods ye2025yonosplatneedmodelfeedforward,jiang2025anysplat,depthanything3 similarly predict Gaussian scenes in a single feed-forward pass. However, commonly used pixel-aligned representations chen2024mvsplat,ye2025yonosplatneedmodelfeedforward can introduce overlapping primitives and floating artifacts. Voxel-aligned methods wang2025volsplat,jiang2025anysplat and methods that regress primitives from fixed token sets li2026querysplat,li2026tokensplat produce more compact representations. Nevertheless, their primitive allocation does not explicitly adapt to local scene complexity, limiting density flexibility and geometric accuracy. To address the above problems, we propose OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided feed-forward Gaussian splatting. Given uncalibrated images and optional camera parameters, OctreeSplat predicts a geometrically accurate 3DGS scene with spatially adaptive primitive allocation. Depth maps and camera parameters predicted by a VFM backbone support voxel aggregation at multiple resolutions. A dense prediction transformer (DPT) upsamples the backbone's patch tokens to construct aligned multi-resolution voxel features. A sparse-convolutional U-Net (SPUNet) processes these features and predicts Gaussian parameters at each level, together with densification scores between adjacent levels. During inference, subdivision starts from the coarsest voxels and selects a fixed fraction for refinement according to the predicted scores. Gaussian primitives associated with the selected octree nodes form the final octree-aligned scene. We initialize the backbone with pretrained VFM weights and introduce an optional test-time optimization (TTO) module. When camera parameters are supplied, TTO improves alignment between the predicted parameters and the ground-truth. Stochastic-solid volume rendering provides more accurate geometric supervision by representing Gaussian primitives as equivalent stochastic solids and volume rendering along viewing rays. This formulation improves depth rendering and geometric accuracy while supporting surface reconstruction. The backbone remains frozen during training. Only the feature-upsampling DPT, SPUNet, densification-score heads, and Gaussian prediction heads are optimized, totaling 76 million parameters. This design allows OctreeSplat to be trained in 35 GPU-hours on RTX PRO 6000. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided method that reconstructs geometrically accurate Gaussian scenes from uncalibrated images and optional camera parameters. Predicted densification scores guide adaptive octree subdivision and allocate Gaussian primitives according to local scene complexity. A frozen VFM backbone limits training to 76 million additional parameters and 35 GPU-hours. Optional TTO aligns camera predictions with ground-truth without updating backbone weights. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive RGB view synthesis and geometric reconstruction across multiple datasets and settings. Related Work 3D Scene Representations Conventional reconstruction methods represent scenes using point clouds colmapsfm , voxels seitz1999photorealistic , signed distance fields (SDFs) curless1996volumetric , or triangle meshes labatut2009robust . Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) mildenhall2020nerf instead use multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) to represent scenes as continuous implicit radiance fields, which map 3D positions and viewing directions to volume densities and colors. Differentiable image rendering optimizes radiance fields' parameters to produce photorealistic NVS. Subsequent work has improved reconstruction speed mueller2022instantngp,yu2022plenoxels , rendering quality barron2022mipnerf360,barron2021mipnerf , and surface reconstruction wang2021neus,neus2 . Despite NeRF's reconstruction accuracy, implicit representations require repeated field inferences along each ray during volume rendering. This computational cost limits rendering efficiency and transferability. 3DGS kerbl3DGS addresses this bottleneck by explicitly storing scenes as 3D Gaussian primitives. These primitives are initialized from sparse point clouds, typically obtained through SfM colmapsfm , and optimized by iteratively rendering the input images. ADC splits, clones, and prunes primitives using photometric gradients kerbl3DGS or alternative criteria kim2024color,lyu2025resgs . The optimization process typically takes tens of minutes to an hour. Later methods accelerate optimization chen2025dashgaussian,mallick2024taming3dgs,meuleman2025fly by controlling the primitive count. However, they still require precomputed camera poses and sparse point clouds, and optimization generally takes at least several minutes. ADC strategies have also received sustained attention ye2024absgs,ren2026fastgs . Vanilla 3DGS primarily optimizes RGB rendering and lacks explicit surface supervision. Subsequent studies improve geometric accuracy through surface-alignment regularization guedon2023sugar . Depth-distortion, normal-consistency, and multi-view-consistency constraints further reduce geometric ambiguities arising from photometric supervision Huang2DGS2024,chen2024pgsr . GOF Yu2024GOF constructs an opacity field from Gaussian primitives and extracts its isosurface for surface reconstruction. GGGS zhang2026gggs and GW gw further improve surface reconstruction by representing Gaussian primitives as equivalent stochastic solids. Feed-Forward Reconstruction Another line of research predicts Gaussian scenes through a single feed-forward based on neural-network. Feed-forward methods such as pixelSplat charatan2024pixelsplat take images and camera parameters as input. They aggregate multi-view features, estimate per-pixel depth, back-project pixels into world coordinates, and regress Gaussian parameters. Multi-view cost volumes chen2024mvsplat and pretrained depth priors xu2024depthsplat improve reconstruction quality in challenging scenes. VolSplat wang2025volsplat replaces pixel alignment with voxel alignment, reducing the dependence of primitives on individual input views. VFMs extend reconstruction to uncalibrated images without requiring camera parameters as input. DUSt3R dust3r_cvpr24 formulates image-pair reconstruction as 3D point-map regression, allowing dense geometry prediction without camera parameters. MUSt3R cabon2025must3r extends DUSt3R to multiple views and predicts geometry directly in a common coordinate system. VGGT wang2025vggt alternates single-view and multi-view self-attention to aggregate information across a variable number of views. A shared backbone and separate prediction heads jointly estimate camera parameters, depth maps, 3D point maps, and point tracks. Subsequent work improves robustness wang2025pi3 , long-sequence processing liu2025vggtx , and model scalability wang2026vggtomega . VFMs have also advanced feed-forward 3DGS.Some approaches build directly upon VFM backbones by adding prediction heads for pixel-aligned Gaussian attributes depthanything3,smart2024splatt3r . As more views are added, overlapping observations and the one-to-one pixel-to-primitive correspondence introduce redundant, overlapping primitives that can blur the rendered images. AnySplat jiang2025anysplat uses pretrained VGGT geometry for pseudo-geometric supervision and differentiable voxelization for multi-view aggregation, reducing redundancy and overlap artifacts. Other methods li2026querysplat,li2026tokensplat regress Gaussian primitives directly from backbone tokens, removing the one-to-one correspondence with pixels. Nevertheless, increasing the number of input views can still introduce blur, and geometric accuracy remains limited. Some methods have explored Gaussian self-splitting during the feed-forward process kim2026f4splat . However, they remain focused on the pixel coordinate system, which leads to the overlapping of primitives. Method OctreeSplat reconstructs a geometrically accurate 3DGS scene from uncalibrated images and optional camera parameters, as shown in . The network predicts Gaussian primitives at multiple octree levels and uses densification scores to guide subdivision. The hierarchical representation improves geometric accuracy and NVS quality while controlling the total number of Gaussian primitives. title: GaussFlaw: Fine-Grained Perceptual Diagnosis for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel- view synthesis with real-time rendering, yet fine-grained di- agnosis of its rendering artifacts remains challenging. These artifacts are typically spatially localized and exhibit diverse degradation patterns, making them difficult to character- ize using global quality metrics and image-level assessment benchmarks, which provide no explicit indication of where they occur or what types of artifacts they represent. To ad- dress this limitation, we introduce GaussFlaw-80K, the first large-scale dataset for fine-grained perceptual diagnosis in 3DGS. Constructed through a model-assisted human-in-the- loop pipeline, GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 artifact re- gions across 14,289 rendered images, each annotated with a pixel-level mask and one of eight flaw labels spanning ge- ometric, blending, and photometric degradations. These an- notations turn 3DGS artifact diagnosis into an explicit and measurable task. Building on this dataset, we propose Ge- oCritic, a geometry-guided multi-task model that integrates RGB appearance with depth-derived cues to jointly localize artifacts and classify their flaw types. Beyond evaluation, we further demonstrate the downstream benefits of fine-grained diagnosis through three complementary targeted operations: Gaussian densification, attribute correction, and outlier prun- ing. Experiments show that GeoCritic achieves an AUC-J of 0.9507 and an Acc@1 of 80.08%, while diagnosis-guided re- finement improves all reported global and crop-level metrics across diverse datasets and 3DGS backbones.
full_text: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel-view synthesis with real-time rendering, yet fine-grained diagnosis of its rendering artifacts remains challenging. These artifacts are typically spatially localized and exhibit diverse degradation patterns, making them difficult to characterize using global quality metrics and image-level assessment benchmarks, which provide no explicit indication of where they occur or what types of artifacts they represent. To address this limitation, we introduce GaussFlaw-80K, the first large-scale dataset for fine-grained perceptual diagnosis in 3DGS. Constructed through a model-assisted human-in-the-loop pipeline, GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 artifact regions across 14,289 rendered images, each annotated with a pixel-level mask and one of eight flaw labels spanning geometric, blending, and photometric degradations. These annotations turn 3DGS artifact diagnosis into an explicit and measurable task. Building on this dataset, we propose GeoCritic, a geometry-guided multi-task model that integrates RGB appearance with depth-derived cues to jointly localize artifacts and classify their flaw types. Beyond evaluation, we further demonstrate the downstream benefits of fine-grained diagnosis through three complementary targeted operations: Gaussian densification, attribute correction, and outlier pruning. Experiments show that GeoCritic achieves an AUC-J of 0.9507 and an Acc@1 of 80.08 , while diagnosis-guided refinement improves all reported global and crop-level metrics across diverse datasets and 3DGS backbones. Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d and its variants~ feng2025flashgs,navaneet2023compact3d,hu20254dgc,NEURIPS2025_923285de have emerged as powerful representations for novel-view synthesis, offering photorealistic rendering with real-time efficiency. Despite its impressive global quality, 3DGS renderings often remain locally unreliable: perceptually salient artifacts such as floaters, ghosting, needle-like stretching, and over-smoothed details can persist within otherwise realistic novel views. Importantly, these artifacts exhibit distinct spatial patterns and degradation characteristics, reflecting different failures in geometry, opacity and blending, or texture representation. Since such flaws are typically spatially localized, their perceptual impact can be easily obscured by the overall rendering quality. A reliable assessment of 3DGS therefore requires fine-grained perceptual diagnosis that explicitly answers two questions: where does an artifact occur, and what type of flaw does it represent? Conventional full-reference metrics, such as PSNR, SSIM~ 1284395 , and LPIPS~ Zhang_2018_CVPR , aggregate spatially varying errors into a single score, merely reflecting the global rendering quality. Recent 3DGS quality assessment datasets, including NVS-QA~ zhang2025evaluatinghumanperceptionnovel , GS-QA~ 11219925 , 3DGS-QA~ wan2026perceptual , 3DGS-IEval-15K~ 10.1145/3746027.3758206 , and MUGSQA~ chen2026mugsqa , broaden the evaluated scenes and perceptual dimensions, yet still rely primarily on image- or sequence-level quality annotations. Consequently, they cannot expose localized flaws hidden within otherwise high-quality renderings, nor do they provide the region masks and labels of artifacts for targeted refinement. General-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer richer semantic descriptions, but their lack of 3DGS-specific artifact priors makes dense spatial grounding and fine-grained artifact discrimination unreliable. Existing approaches therefore remain limited to global quality prediction, leaving fine-grained diagnosis largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce GaussFlaw-80K, the first large-scale dataset for fine-grained perceptual diagnosis in 3DGS with joint spatial and categorical annotations. Its pixel-level masks identify where perceptually significant artifacts occur, while its fine-grained labels characterize what type of flaw each region exhibits. Together, these annotations extend prior assessment from global score prediction to explicit flaw localization and classification (Table~ tab:dataset_comparison ). GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 annotated artifact regions from 14,289 rendered images and organizes common 3DGS artifacts into a hierarchical taxonomy of eight categories spanning geometric, blending, and photometric degradations. The annotations are collected through a model-assisted human-in-the-loop pipeline to ensure an optimal trade-off between pixel-level precision and scalable annotation costs. By moving beyond image-level quality scores, GaussFlaw-80K establishes fine-grained artifact diagnosis as a measurable and reproducible task for 3DGS. Building on the pixel-level supervision provided by GaussFlaw-80K, we propose GeoCritic, a geometry-guided multi-task perception model that jointly localizes 3DGS rendering artifacts and classifies their fine-grained flaw types. GeoCritic integrates RGB appearance with depth- derived geometric cues to improve spatial grounding and distinguish visually ambiguous artifacts. Beyond evaluation, we demonstrate the downstream benefit of fine-grained diagnosis for 3DGS refinement. Specifically, we translate GeoCritic's class-aware regional diagnosis into three complementary operations: Gaussian densification for underrepresented content, attribute correction for unreliable primitives, and outlier pruning for detached Gaussians. Extensive experiments show that GeoCritic achieves state-of-the-art performance in both artifact localization and fine-grained classification (yielding an AUC-J of 0.9507 and an Acc@1 of 80.08 ). Furthermore, our targeted refinement significantly improves affected Gaussian representations across diverse datasets and backbones while minimizing unnecessary changes to well-reconstructed regions, demonstrating the practical value of region-level diagnosis for 3DGS refinement. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce GaussFlaw-80K, the first dataset for fine-grained diagnosis of 3DGS rendering artifacts, providing 80,049 pixel-level artifact masks with category labels and enabling explicit region-level diagnosis beyond conventional global quality assessment. We propose GeoCritic, a geometry-guided diagnostic expert that synergizes visual semantics with physical depth priors, enabling fine-grained spatial grounding and explicit topological reasoning of rendering artifacts. We demonstrate the downstream benefit of fine-grained diagnosis by translating class-aware regional predictions into three targeted Gaussian operations, which consistently improve local perceptual quality across multiple 3DGS backbones. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of our proposed GeoCritic in accurately localizing and classifying 3DGS artifacts. Additionally, our empirical results demonstrate that the targeted refinement effectively rectifies local flaws, achieving noticeable perceptual improvements over existing baselines. GaussFlaw-80K Construction We construct GaussFlaw-80K, a large-scale dataset specifically designed for fine-grained diagnosis of 3DGS rendering artifacts. It provides precise pixel-level region masks and fine-grained flaw type annotations for over 80K flaw regions across 8 artifact categories. Artifact Taxonomy As shown in Table~ tab:dataset_comparison , existing 3DGS evaluation datasets are primarily restricted to global quality scores (e.g., MOS) at a limited scale. To overcome this, we advance the annotation format from traditional holistic scoring to pixel-level diagnosis. Supported by an unprecedented volume of 80K annotations, this fine-grained paradigm enables precise spatial location and categorization of specific rendering flaws. Central to this pixel-level assessment is a hierarchical taxonomy, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:1 , which organizes common 3DGS artifacts into eight specific categories across three high-level dimensions. Specifically, Geometric and Topological Distortions encompass Floater, characterized by detached or foreground-like blobs; Needle Stretch, manifested as thin and elongated spike-like structures; and Structure Missing, referring to absent or incomplete scene structures. Opacity and Blending Artifacts include Transparent Haze, which appears as veil-like opacity accumulation over otherwise valid content, and Ghosting, characterized by duplicated, trailing, or semi-transparent structures. Lastly, Texture and Photometric Flaws comprise Over-smooth, characterized by excessively smoothed structures and appearance; High-frequency Blur, referring to the loss of fine textures and edge details; and Specular Collapse, manifested as spurious, unstable, or distorted view-dependent highlights. At a high level, these artifacts reflect insufficient representation coverage, unreliable Gaussian attributes, and inadequate geometric support. This taxonomy provides a structured and interpretable foundation for fine-grained perceptual diagnosis. Data Collection and Annotation Rendering Sources and Diversity. To ensure a comprehensive and generalizable data distribution, we curate rendering outputs from three representative 3DGS methods: vanilla 3DGS~ kerbl20233d , FastGS~ Ren_2026_CVPR , and HAC++~ 11106187 . Specifically, we train models using three methods across 26 scenes sourced from five widely used datasets (Mip-NeRF 360~ barron2022mip , DeepBlending~ 10.1145/3272127.3275084 , LERF~ lerf2023 , TandT~ kerbl20233d , and Tanks Temples~ knapitsch2017tanks ). Recognizing that rendering artifacts dynamically evolve and manifest distinct visual characteristics at different training stages, we extract rendered images at six distinct checkpoints for each model, starting from 5K steps with a 5K-step interval. This temporal sampling yields a total of 468 intermediate checkpoint models. Furthermore, we comprehensively sample multiple novel views for each scene. Human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline. We design a four-stage model-assisted human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline. (1) Annotators first align with the established taxonomy through a pre-annotation phase. Subsequently, a small initial subset of rendered images is precisely annotated manually, providing pixel-level boundary masks and corresponding fine-grained topological labels for each distorted region. (2) We pre-train a preliminary artifact perception model GeoCritic-v1 (detailed in Sec. 3) on this initial subset, and apply it to the remaining unannotated renderings to automatically generate candidate masks and topological pseudo-labels. (3) Annotators manually adjust inaccurate mask boundaries, correct misclassified labels, filter out false-positive predictions, and add artifact regions missed by the model. (4) Final annotations are reconciled through majority voting and cross-validation by experts to eliminate subjective biases. Consequently, each sample in GaussFlaw comprises a 3DGS rendering, precise artifact region masks, and fine-grained artifact labels. This paradigm significantly reduces annotation cost compared with fully manual annotation. Quality Control. To ensure annotation quality, all GeoCritic-v1 proposals were manually reviewed and corrected. Starting from 17,444 manually annotated seed regions, GeoCritic-v1 generated 62,510 candidate regions, of which annotators retained 52,359. Among the retained masks, annotators refined the boundaries of 92.9 , changed the areas of 39.99 by more than 10 , and corrected the category labels of 15.3 . Annotators also added 10,246 missed regions. Finally, we obtained 80,049 pixel-level artifact regions with categorie labels across 14,289 rendered images, averaging 5.6 regions per image. title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
summary: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro You don't know what you don't know.\\[2pt] --- Socrates, Philosopher Recent advances in robot learning are shifting the field from policies tailored to individual tasks and platforms toward general-purpose models~ fang2026molmoact2,team2025gemini,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,gr00tn1_2025,lee2025molmoactactionreasoningmodels trained across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments~ 10611477,khazatsky2024droid . Although compelling demonstrations from leading robotics companies highlight the potential of these models~ dyna2026dyna2,sunday2025act1,skild2025roboticbrain,generalist2026gen1 , establishing their reliability under real-world deployment conditions remains a fundamental challenge. In language and vision, large-scale benchmarks incorporating human preferences on real-world tasks have helped drive progress by providing a shared basis for assessing model capabilities relevant to end users~ zheng2023judging,chiang2024chatbot,huang2024vbench . Robot policies, by contrast, operate through closed-loop interactions with the physical world, where each action shapes the conditions for what follows. Evaluating them reliably is therefore difficult, especially at scale and in the varied, uncontrolled settings of the real world. Measuring progress requires understanding what robots can consistently accomplish across these conditions. Such assessments are difficult to standardize because outcomes depend jointly on the policy, robot setup, initial conditions, and surrounding environment~ vincent2024generalizable . Even nominally identical tasks can differ in object placement, camera configuration, lighting, and physical properties, making it difficult to attribute performance differences to policy capability. Physical evaluation must therefore reconcile two requirements: sufficient control to support meaningful comparisons and sufficient environmental diversity to assess robustness beyond a particular setup. Simulation supports scalable evaluation through repeatable resets and controlled variation in tasks and environments~ 9001253,tao2025maniskill3 . However, differences in sensing, calibration, dynamics, and visual appearance can limit how well simulated performance predicts real-world outcomes, making physical validation essential~ li24simpler,pumacay2024colosseum,kim2026molmospaces . Achieving comparable scale with physical robots requires substantial labor for setup, resets, hardware maintenance, and trial execution. Consequently, real-world studies often rely on relatively few rollouts, leaving performance estimates sensitive to trial selection and experimental variability~ kress2024robot,vincent2024generalizable . Distributing evaluation across sites broadens environmental coverage~ khazatsky2024droid,atreya2025roboarena , but efforts that depend on students and volunteers are difficult to sustain and scale. Running physical trials requires continued staffing, equipment maintenance, and coordination across sites, often alongside competing research commitments. Sustained evaluation therefore requires dedicated operators and shared physical infrastructure, supported by protocols for repeating trials, matching local conditions, and verifying whether measured performance can be reproduced. We introduce , a distributed, multi-embodiment benchmark for evaluating general-purpose robot policies in the wild. It connects geographically distributed sites through unified evaluation and policy-serving infrastructure, with standardized hardware configurations, task definitions, and evaluation protocols. The benchmark initially supports four embodiments Bimanual-YAM, SO-101, Franka, and Unitree G1 and evaluates eight foundation models: five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier LLMs. Two complementary tracks assess adaptation and generalization. The Fine-tune Track measures performance on predefined semantic tasks after adaptation using a fixed budget of task-specific demonstrations. The Open Track evaluates zero-shot generalization across diverse real-world tasks and environments without task-specific adaptation. Together, they enable systematic assessment of physical intelligence across heterogeneous embodiments. With a growing fleet of over 100 robots across the United States, United Kingdom, Singapore, Malaysia, and China, operated by full-time evaluators, aims to make real-world evaluation scalable and sustainable. This shared infrastructure provides a lens into the capabilities and limitations of robot foundation models, enabling the research community to investigate fundamental scientific questions through systematic physical trials. To broaden access, we pledge 10,000 hours of free evaluation to academic labs and partners. Our initial study includes 5,699 Open Track pairwise comparisons across 124 sites and Fine-tune Track evaluations on 20 tasks across four embodiments. Frontier AI agents achieve manipulation performance competitive with specialized VLA policies, while reliable task completion remains challenging as task difficulty increases. With the same 100-demonstration adaptation budget, policies exhibit strongly task- and embodiment-dependent performance, with weak agreement in rankings across embodiments ( ) and substantial rank reversals between the Open and Fine-tune Tracks. Finally, leaderboard stability improves with evaluation scale, while active matchmaking reaches approximately 90 agreement with the full-data ranking after 400--500 evaluations, compared with roughly 1,000 under uniform sampling. These findings demonstrate the importance of evaluating physical intelligence across diverse tasks, embodiments, and environments, while showing that large-scale real-world evaluation can be made statistically reliable and sample-efficient. Related Work sec:related Simulated and Real-World Benchmarking sec:robot_benchmarks Real-world robot benchmarks aim to make physical policy evaluation more reproducible despite variation in hardware, calibration, object placement, and scene reset. These factors can substantially affect measured performance, motivating standardized hardware, task definitions, initial conditions, and success criteria~ kress2024robot . Early benchmarks such as FurnitureBench improve comparability by prescribing a common robot platform, workspace, objects, and task protocols~ furniturebench2025 , while SceneReplica further studies reproducibility by reconstructing physical scenes using reference images and calibrated setups~ SceneReplica2024 . Remote testbeds such as TOTO and the Real Robot Challenge instead centralize physical hardware and allow researchers to submit policies for evaluation on a shared robot platform, reducing variation caused by independently constructed setups~ toto2023, pmlr-v176-bauer22a . More recent benchmarks extend these ideas toward broader policy and embodiment coverage~ pumacay2024colosseum,wang2025roboeval,kim2026molmospaces,wang2026roboplaygrounddemocratizingroboticevaluation . RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo evaluates 18 real-world tasks across three bimanual robot platforms using standardized workspaces, reset procedures, and sub-step scoring, while VLA-REPLICA provides a low-cost SO-101 setup designed to be reconstructed at different locations~ chen2026robodojo, huang2026vlareplica . RoboColosseum builds on this line of work while targeting broader physical coverage across multiple embodiments and sites under shared evaluation protocols. Generalist Robot Policies sec:rfm Generalist robot policies seek to transfer learned skills across tasks, environments, and embodiments. RT-X models demonstrate that pooling demonstrations from different robots can improve performance through transfer across platforms~ 10611477 . Octo provides a pretrained policy that can be adapted to new observation and action spaces~ octomodel2024 . Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA combine pretrained vision-language representations with robot demonstrations to predict actions from visual observations and language instructions, while supporting fine-tuning on demonstrations from a target setting~ kim2024openvla . Recent models extend these capabilities through diverse training data and different approaches to action generation. combines data from multiple robots with web data and semantic supervision to support manipulation in previously unseen homes~ black25p05 . GR00T combines vision-language processing with a dedicated action-generation module~ bjorck2025gr00t , while MolmoAct2 connects a backbone trained for embodied reasoning to a continuous-action expert~ fang2026molmoact2 . These models provide different approaches to combining semantic knowledge with physical control. General-purpose language models can also guide robot behavior through skill selection or program generation. SayCan selects learned robot skills using both language-model predictions and estimates of execution success~ ahn2022can , while Code as Policies generates programs that process perception outputs and call robot control APIs~ liang2022code . RoboColosseum compares VLA policies and frontier AI agents across physical environments and embodiments without task-specific adaptation, and separately measures how VLA policies adapt using a common budget of task demonstrations. Distributed Robotics Evaluation sec:arena_style_eval Distributed evaluation provides an alternative to tightly centralized robot benchmarks by allowing policies to be tested across heterogeneous physical environments while aggregating results into a common comparison. RB2 is an early example, distributing manipulation evaluation across multiple laboratories while controlling task definitions and aggregating site-specific rankings rather than directly comparing raw scores across different physical setups~ dasari2021rb . More recently, RoboArena extends this idea to generalist robot policies through a decentralized evaluation network spanning seven academic institutions. Evaluators freely select tasks and environments, while each local comparison evaluates two anonymously assigned policies back-to-back under matched scene conditions. Across 612 pairwise comparisons, RoboArena showed that rankings derived from distributed evaluations correlate more strongly with an exhaustive oracle ranking than conventional fixed single-site evaluation~ atreya2025roboarena . However, RoboArena is instantiated on a single DROID/Franka embodiment, and its open-ended decentralized design makes controlled single-factor experiments difficult. Pairwise comparison has also been widely used for arena-style evaluation. Chatbot Arena ranks anonymized models from human pairwise preferences using Bradley--Terry-based estimation chiang2024chatbotarena , while active-ranking methods show that comparisons can be allocated toward more informative model pairs rather than sampled uniformly heckel2018approximate . These ideas provide methodological precedent for RoboColosseum’s Open Track, where pairwise physical evaluations are aggregated into a global ranking and costly robot trials can be prioritized toward uncertain model pairs. RoboColosseum Benchmark sec:robocolosseum_benchmark We present RoboColosseum, a distributed real-world benchmarking framework for systematically evaluating the generalization and adaptation capabilities of general-purpose robot policies across heterogeneous embodiments. A central contribution is the design of the physical infrastructure and operational protocols required to sustain large-scale, distributed robot evaluation. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:framework , the framework integrates geographically distributed robot evaluation sites, shared policy-serving infrastructure, and standardized evaluation protocols into a unified benchmarking system. title: 3D Gaussian Splatting within Self-Learned Neural View-Dependent Color Fields
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a vital tool in novel view synthesis. 3D Gaussian functions with attributes like color, opacity, and scale are stacked together to explicitly model a radiance field. However, discrete 3D Gaussians usually produce poor depth with few geometry details but lots of floaters, which hinders the effective modeling of smooth radiance fields. To address this issue, we propose to learn a radiance field within a continuous view-dependent color field parameterized by neural networks. With continuous constraints in color, the bias on low-frequency signals of neural networks can highly encourage the geometry modeling to contribute to high-frequency color variations on images, getting rid of solely relying on the color attribute itself. Moreover, we impose a constraint to improve the Lipschitz continuity of the neural color field, making large changes of each Gaussian's color also match with large changes of its position in terms of a ratio. To this end, we additionally introduce novel self-learning strategies to improve the learning of the neural view-dependent color field without any external knowledge or priors, aiming for better generalization on unseen scenes. Our numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks justify our idea and show better ability of high fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS. Project page: https://github.com/yangyixi21/Neural-Color-Fields-3DGS.
full_text: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a vital tool in novel view synthesis. 3D Gaussian functions with attributes like color, opacity, and scale are stacked together to explicitly model a radiance field. However, discrete 3D Gaussians usually produce poor depth with few geometry details but lots of floaters, which hinders the effective modeling of smooth radiance fields. To address this issue, we propose to learn a radiance field within a continuous view-dependent color field parameterized by neural networks. With continuous constraints in color, the bias on low-frequency signals of neural networks can highly encourage the geometry modeling to contribute to high-frequency color variations on images, getting rid of solely relying on the color attribute itself. Moreover, we impose a constraint to improve the Lipschitz continuity of the neural color field, making large changes of each Gaussian's color also match with large changes of its position in terms of a ratio. To this end, we additionally introduce novel self-learning strategies to improve the learning of the neural view-dependent color field without any external knowledge or priors, aiming for better generalization on unseen scenes. Our numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks justify our idea and show better ability of high fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS. Project page: . Introduction 3DGS~ 3dgs has become a crucial representation for radiance fields due to its high efficiency and good quality in rendering. 3DGS employs discrete 3D Gaussians with additional attributes like color, scale, and opacity to approximate a continuous and smooth radiance field, which can be rendered into RGB, depth, and normal images. While the approximation does not make up the discrete essence of 3D Gaussians, which usually struggles to fit high-frequency color change, resulting in rough and incomplete geometry recovery. Recent effort focuses on constraints that can directly get imposed on geometry. These methods usually employ various strategies such as continuous distance fields~ gspull , multi-view consistency~ pgsr , and monocular or geometry consistent priors~ monosdf,zhang2025monoinstance , leading to better surface inference. However, these strategies suffer from sensitive mappings from signed/unsigned distances to density, extensive verification of consistency across multiple views in iterative optimization, or limited generalization ability of external knowledge or priors, respectively. Thus, more general solutions are still expected for smoother radiance fields represented through 3DGS. To overcome this obstacle, we instead impose constraints on 3D Gaussian color within a neural view-dependent color field that can be learned without a need of any external prior or data-driven strategy. During a splatting procedure, each Gaussian first gets a color estimation from an implicit neural network, and then use it along with other learnable attributes like scale and opacity for alpha blending. Our motivation is two fold, both of which significantly improve the geometry inference of 3DGS within a smoother color field. First, the inherent spectral bias of the neural network towards low-frequency color signals encourages the geometry modeling to explain high-frequency color variations in images. Second, we impose a constraint to improve the Lipschitz continuity of this neural color field, which ensures that significant changes in a Gaussian's color must correspond to significant shifts in its position. To this end, we parameterize a view-dependent color field using a neural network and introduce novel strategies to improve the learning of the neural view-dependent color field along with the learning of 3D Gaussians, without a need of external priors or data-driven strategies, leading to better generalization on various unseen scenes. We justify our idea on widely used benchmarks in numerical and visual evaluations, which shows our superiority over the latest 3DGS variations as well. Our contributions are listed below. We introduce 3DGS within a neural view-dependent color field and novel self-supervision to learn the color field along with the learning of Gaussians with 3DGS. We introduce a novel perspective of improving geometry inference with 3DGS by imposing continuous constraints on color, which encourages high-frequency geometry recovery. We report the state-of-the-art performance on the widely used benchmarks and show advantages over other 3DGS variations. Related Work Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting NeRF~ nerf achieves photorealistic view synthesis with an implicit MLP representation, but suffers from high training and rendering costs. Subsequent works therefore explored hybrid grid-based and point-based representations~ fridovich2022plenoxels,InstanceNgp,pointnerf . Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs has emerged as an efficient explicit scene representation. It models scenes with anisotropic 3D Gaussians and uses spherical harmonics to capture view-dependent colors, enabling real-time rendering with high fidelity. However, 3DGS often struggles within textureless regions and recover high-frequency geometry details, leading to incomplete geometry and noisy depth. Our method builds on 3DGS and improves its attribute representation for better geometry reconstruction. Geometry Reconstruction and Regularization in 3DGS Since the geometric inference through 3DGS~ 3dgs is usually unsatisfactory, a significant body of work has focused on improving its geometric reconstruction capabilities, typically by introducing geometric constraints or modifying the representation. For example, 2DGS~ 2dgs considers view-dependent effects as a source of noise and proposes to model the scene using 2D Gaussians embedded in 3D space. By flattening 3D ellipsoids into 2D planes, these primitives adhere more closely to object surfaces, achieving clearer surfaces and fewer floating artifacts. Similarly, PGSR~ pgsr also improves depth rendered by 3DGS~ 3dgs . It proposes a novel geometry modeling with depth and enhances the smoothness and multi-view consistency by introducing various constraints. GSPrior~ noda20263d derives self-constrained geometric priors from a TSDF grid fused from rendered depths. For sparse-view surface reconstruction, DP-GS~ han2026sparse propagates high-confidence depths with normal priors, while VGGS~ xiang2026vggs uses VGGT-derived geometric priors with anchor-calibrated depth estimation and relative depth consistency. MaterialRefGS~ zhang2025materialrefgs uses multi-view material consistency for reflective scenes. Another line of work integrates geometric priors. For instance, SuGaR~ sugar regularizes the 3D Gaussians to align with the underlying surface and extracts a mesh from the Gaussian representation, thereby improving geometric consistency. Moreover, Anysplat~ anysplat learns priors to generate Gaussians. Neural Implicit Fields and Regularization Neural implicit fields~ ma2021neuralpull represent continuous signals with networks that favor low frequencies~ rahaman2019spectralbiasneuralnetworks . Frequency consolidation priors~ chen2025sharpening recover high-frequency geometry. While positional encoding~ tancik2020fourierfeaturesletnetworks typically counters this bias in NeRFs, we argue this inherent smoothness can serve as a geometric regularizer for explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting. NeRFPrior~ zhang2025nerfprior and VRP-UDF~ zhang2026vrpudf use radiance-field and volume-rendering priors for reconstruction, respectively; SparseRecon~ han2025sparserecon enforces feature and depth consistency. Moreover, recent methods like Splatfields~ splatfields , GOF~ yu2024gof , and NeRF-GS~ fang2025nerf utilize networks to model Gaussian attributes, while others~ martins2024feature,qiu2024feature,zhou2024feature,li2024spacetime incorporate high-dimensional feature fields. To improve stability, Lipschitz continuity prevents disproportionate output changes. For 3D geometry, constraining the Lipschitz constant aids learning from noisy data~ liu2022learning , with recent works constructing 1-Lipschitz neural distance fields for robust estimation~ 1lipschitz . Level-set alignment~ ma2023gradient improves SDF gradient consistency. Crucially, Lipschitz constraints can link geometry and appearance. PermutoSDF~ permutosdf limits color field variation to force high-frequency signals into geometric structures. Distinct from these methods, we propose a direct approach that constrains the neural color field's Lipschitz constant, forcing large color variations to correspond to significant geometric changes and preventing overfitting to high-frequency noise. Methods Overview and Background . As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , we learn 3D Gaussians (with center , opacity , scale , color ) from RGB images via 3DGS. We also learn a neural implicit function that maps a feature and a ray direction pointing to a Gaussian to a view-dependent color . During splatting, each Gaussian queries for its color before alpha blending. The color field is learned with rendering supervision and a novel self-supervision, leading to smoother radiance fields and better geometry. with 3DGS. We can learn 3D Gaussians by minimizing the discrepancy in Eq.~ between the rendered and the observed , where the depth rendering is optional, Neural View-dependent Color Fields We use an implicit function to represent the view-dependent color field using a neural network. For each Gaussian , we first employ a hash feature grid to model the spatial feature in 3D. We use its center to interpolate a feature from the grid , which is then used to predict a color through the neural network, where is the normalized direction from the camera center to the Gaussian center . The MLP is queried once per camera--Gaussian pair, and the predicted color is shared across its projected footprint, To improve the efficiency of feature interpolation from , we do not follow INGP~ InstanceNgp which uses a cubical grid and linearly interpolate features from the hashed eight corners of the containing cell. Instead, we adopt a tetrahedral lattice~ permutosdf,learningdeformabletetrahedralmeshes which only needs four corners in each cell in interpolation. It reduces both of the storage and the computation complexity by a factor of two. title: KAUSTics-Net: Diffusion-Based Through-Water UAV Restoration with a Semi-Synthetic Dataset
summary: Accurate mapping of shallow-water environments using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is challenged by water-induced distortions, including refraction, caustics, and wavelength-dependent attenuation. The scarcity of paired distorted and reference imagery further limits the development of supervised restoration methods. To address this challenge, we introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset combining 1,280 reference patches derived from 32 high-resolution UAV images with 12,800 degraded observations generated through Blender-based water-surface rendering and empirical color and blur augmentations. We further propose KAUSTics-Net, a pixel-space conditional diffusion framework integrating a multi-scale conditional encoder, feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), cross-attention, and a composite reconstruction objective to restore shallow-water imagery. We evaluated the framework against eight image-restoration methods, complemented by architectural ablations and cross-dataset experiments. On KAUSTics, KAUSTics-Net achieved a mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 31.715 +/- 0.439 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.849 +/- 0.002, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) of 0.145 +/- 0.007 across three training seeds. On the independent Sea-Undistort dataset, sampler-aware fine-tuning improved restoration fidelity, reaching 19.469 +/- 0.332 dB PSNR and 0.554 +/- 0.005 SSIM under combined water-surface distortions, although perceptual trade-offs remained. Additional experiments on real UAV imagery examined feature preservation and segmentation behavior. These findings demonstrate the potential of semi-synthetic training and conditional diffusion for shallow-water image restoration while highlighting the importance of evaluating both reconstruction fidelity and downstream remote-sensing utility.

Accurate mapping of shallow-water environments using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is challenged by water-induced distortions, including refraction, caustics, and wavelength-dependent attenuation. The scarcity of paired distorted and reference imagery further limits the development of supervised restoration methods. To address this challenge, we introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset combining 1,280 reference patches derived from 32 high-resolution UAV images with 12,800 degraded observations generated through Blender-based water-surface rendering and empirical color and blur augmentations. We further propose KAUSTics-Net, a pixel-space conditional diffusion framework integrating a multi-scale conditional encoder, feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), cross-attention, and a composite reconstruction objective to restore shallow-water imagery. We evaluated the framework against eight image-restoration methods, complemented by architectural ablations and cross-dataset experiments. On KAUSTics, KAUSTics-Net achieved a mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of ~dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) of , and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) of across three training seeds. On the independent Sea-Undistort dataset, sampler-aware fine-tuning improved restoration fidelity, reaching ~dB PSNR and SSIM under combined water-surface distortions, although perceptual trade-offs remained. Additional experiments on real UAV imagery examined feature preservation and segmentation behavior. These findings demonstrate the potential of semi-synthetic training and conditional diffusion for shallow-water image restoration while highlighting the importance of evaluating both reconstruction fidelity and downstream remote-sensing utility. Caustics, Conditional Diffusion, Image Restoration, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Remote Sensing, Shallow Water. Introduction oastal regions support critical ecosystems, including coral reefs, seagrass meadows, mangroves, and tidal flats, while also hosting substantial populations and infrastructure. Their monitoring is essential for ecosystem assessment, coastal management, restoration, and climate adaptation jmse12030386,MOTTAZANIN2024120667,deguenon_sea-level_2024,CHOWDHURY202575 . Although in situ surveys provide detailed observations, they are spatially limited, logistically demanding, and often unable to capture rapid changes in dynamic coastal environments holzner_analyzing_2025,rs9070653,TSAI2024107136 . Satellite and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) remote sensing provide broader and more frequent coverage, enabling shallow-water mapping at scales impractical for field surveys alone app15094771,YANG2022155939,KUJAWA2025104604 . Extracting reliable information from optical imagery over shallow coastal waters nevertheless remains challenging. Surface waves focus and defocus sunlight, producing dynamic, high-frequency caustic patterns unrelated to actual seabed variability 8391752,scilla2025computer . Specular reflection at the air--water interface generates sun glint that can saturate parts of the image and obscure the underlying scene QIN2024298,rs11202422 . Refraction displaces apparent object locations and distorts submerged shapes, while wavelength-dependent absorption and scattering alter the signal returning from the seafloor. Together, these effects degrade contrast and color, distort geometry, and complicate applications such as benthic habitat mapping rs13214452 , bathymetry agrafiotis2020correcting , and photogrammetry Partama_photogrammetry . Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate water-induced distortions. Physics-based methods invert simplified radiative-transfer models but often require estimates of water depth, optical properties, and atmospheric conditions maritorena_diffuse_1994,dierssen_ocean_2003,rs12111861 . Image-processing approaches apply deglinting, dehazing, contrast enhancement, or multi-view corrections Hedley01052005,agrafiotis2020correcting,scilla2025computer . More recently, deep learning has enabled data-driven mappings between distorted and reference imagery. GAN-based methods have been applied to underwater enhancement and coastal water removal 9570386,QIN2024298,10720144 , while diffusion-based image-to-image models have demonstrated capabilities for removing complex degradations while preserving scene structure 10.1145/3588432.3591513,Xia_2023_ICCV . However, learning-based restoration of shallow-water UAV imagery is constrained by the scarcity of large, high-resolution paired datasets containing observations of the same scene with and without water-surface distortions 10720144,kromer2025sea . Repeated acquisitions under different sea states and illumination rarely provide aligned pairs and make it difficult to separate water-surface effects from genuine scene changes KUJAWA2025104604 . Purely synthetic data, in contrast, may not capture the spatial complexity and variability of real coastal environments. This motivates semi-synthetic approaches that combine real UAV imagery with physically based simulations of water-induced distortions. To address this gap, we introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset for high-resolution UAV water-distortion removal, together with KAUSTics-Net, a conditional diffusion-based restoration framework. We evaluated the proposed approach on KAUSTics and the independent Sea-Undistort benchmark kromer2025sea , complemented by an exploratory assessment on real UAV imagery. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: We introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset comprising 1,280 high-resolution UAV reference patches and 12,800 degraded observations generated through physically based water-surface rendering and empirical color and blur augmentations. We propose KAUSTics-Net, a pixel-space conditional diffusion framework combining multi-scale conditioning, FiLM-modulated residual blocks, cross-attention, and a composite restoration objective for through-water UAV imagery. We evaluate KAUSTics-Net against eight restoration methods using source-image-disjoint partitions, architectural ablations, cross-dataset experiments, and real-UAV assessments of downstream image-processing utility. Related Work sec:related_work Image restoration has been extensively studied across computer vision and remote sensing, including dehazing, deblurring, deraining, and underwater image enhancement. However, methods explicitly targeting water-surface distortions such as caustics, sun glint, and refraction in high-resolution UAV imagery remain comparatively limited. In practice, many approaches applied to this problem were originally developed for generic image restoration or underwater cameras rather than through-water aerial observations fabbri2018enhancing,10720144,guan2023diffwater . Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into statistical and physics-based corrections, generative adversarial networks (GANs), and diffusion-based restoration models. Statistical and Physics-Based Approaches In UAV-based shallow-water imaging, refraction at the air--water interface displaces apparent object locations and distorts submerged shapes, while wave-induced caustics and sun glint introduce strong spatially varying radiometric artifacts Chong03082022,scilla2025computer . Early correction methods primarily focused on geometric effects by applying empirical refraction factors derived from Snell's law. Partama et al. proposed a correction of apparent depths from UAV structure-from-motion reconstructions, while related studies incorporated refraction correction into shallow-water bathymetric inversion schemes partama2017simple,lambert2023refraction . Reviews of UAV-based shallow-water bathymetry have highlighted the effectiveness of these approaches, but also their dependence on acquisition geometry, water depth, seabed properties, and assumptions regarding the water surface luis2015synoptic,specht2022analysis . A complementary family of methods exploits temporal redundancy in high-frame-rate imagery. Fluid lensing uses repeated observations of the same scene to model the dynamic water surface as a time-varying optical lens and reconstruct refraction-corrected, caustic-reduced imagery chirayath2016drones,chirayath2019fluid . More recently, Scilla et al. showed that frame-wise temporal aggregation combined with color-transfer correction can reduce caustics, refraction-induced shape variations, and sun glint in UAV video while improving the consistency of submerged features scilla2025computer . Although effective, these approaches generally rely on explicit physical assumptions, hand-crafted corrections, or repeated observations of the same scene. They therefore do not directly learn a single-image mapping from a distorted observation to a clean seabed representation, motivating the use of data-driven generative models. Generative Adversarial Networks Generative adversarial networks learn image distributions through competition between a generator and discriminator goodfellow2014generative , and have been widely adopted for image enhancement and restoration. In image-to-image translation, CycleGAN introduced cycle consistency for learning mappings between unpaired image domains zhu2017unpaired , a particularly useful property when paired distorted and clean observations are difficult to acquire. Underwater enhancement models such as UGAN, FUnIE-GAN, MLFcGAN, and UWGAN use adversarial learning to improve color balance, contrast, local structure, and, in some cases, downstream robotic perception fabbri2018enhancing,islam2020fast,liu2019mlfcgan,wang2019uwgan . These approaches have demonstrated substantial improvements for imagery acquired by underwater cameras. However, their target domain differs from through-water UAV imagery, where wave-induced refraction, dynamic caustics, and sun glint introduce stronger spatially varying geometric and radiometric distortions. Only a limited number of GAN-based methods have directly addressed aerial water removal. DeWaterGAN is a physics-guided unsupervised framework for UAV coastal imagery that combines a CycleGAN backbone with a light-transport-inspired attention mechanism 10720144 . The model can reduce water interference while preserving color and texture, but it primarily targets appearance restoration and does not rely on pixel-aligned distorted/undistorted training pairs. Overall, GAN-based methods demonstrate the potential of learned restoration, but their application to through-water UAV imagery remains challenging, as these images belong to substantially different domains, containing stronger refraction induced distortions, and complex caustic patterns that are not fully captured in classical underwater datasets. title: When Delay Meets Drift: Physical Safety of Robot Foundation Models Is a Cross-Layer Problem
summary: Robot foundation models now act in a closed loop, yet their safety is evaluated one variation at a time: robustness benchmarks perturb the scene while assuming instantaneous inference, and real-time execution methods study inference delay in nominal scenes. We argue that physical safety is not a property of the model alone, but emerges from how variations in the physical environment, the model, the computing platform, and execution interact in closed loop. We formalize this as cross-layer variation propagation across these system layers and use an interaction contrast to measure when joint variation creates more risk than the sum of its parts. In 4,000 paired closed-loop episodes of the pi0.5 vision-language-action model on LIBERO, a 400 ms inference delay raises the safety-violation rate by 3.5 percentage points under the training viewpoint but by 37 percentage points under a 60-degree camera shift: 33.5 percentage points (95% CI: 25-43) more than the two effects combined. We close with a research agenda toward predictable physical intelligence: predicting when variation becomes risk, and adapting compute, power, and control accordingly.

Introduction sec:intro A language model that thinks longer gives a slower answer. A robot that thinks longer acts on an older world. Consider the vision-language-action (VLA) model ~ pi2025pi05 asked to pick up a black bowl next to a ramekin and place it on a plate (Fig.~ fig:concept ). Under its training viewpoint it succeeds safely, and 400\,ms of inference delay does not change that. With the camera rotated by , it still succeeds safely. With both, it sweeps across the table, knocking an identical, uninvolved bowl 19\,cm and pressing on the table with 201\,N: a failure that neither condition causes alone. This is not an anecdote: across 4,000 paired episodes, the effect of delay on safety grows sharply with viewpoint shift (Sec.~ sec:evidence ). This example exposes two properties of physical AI safety. First, thresholds make additive effects non-additive: physical shift and delay each consume safety margin, but harm occurs only when the margin is exhausted, so conditions that are individually benign can be jointly unsafe. Second, the layers are coupled: physical shift destabilizes the policy's actions, and the conditions with the least stable actions are those in which staleness costs the most. Existing evaluations nonetheless examine these variations in isolation. Robustness benchmarks perturb viewpoint, lighting, and layout while assuming instantaneous inference~ fei2025liberoplus ; real-time execution methods mitigate inference delay under nominal scenes~ black2025rtc,tang2025vlash,agouzoul2026async ; and safety benchmarks separate success from safety while holding compute fixed~ fan2026safevlabench,cui2026liberosafety . r 0.41 Layers of the robot system, not of a network. Sec.~ sec:evidence varies the bold factors and measures the italic ones. fig:stack We argue that physical safety is an emergent, cross-layer property: it cannot be certified by testing the scene and the hardware separately, and it should be studied as the propagation of variation from the physical world, through the model and the computing platform, into execution. We make three contributions: (1)~a formulation of cross-layer variation propagation with an explicit interaction term (Sec.~ sec:formulation ); (2)~preliminary evidence: a joint safety surface over camera-viewpoint shift inference delay for in 4,000 paired episodes, showing a super-additive interaction (Sec.~ sec:evidence ); and (3)~a research agenda for predicting and controlling variation-induced risk (Sec.~ sec:agenda ). Cross-Layer Variation Propagation sec:formulation Safety outcomes---collisions, excessive contact force, disturbance of non-target objects---emerge from how these interact in closed loop, and execution feeds back into the next observation. A cross-layer analysis locates such regimes and the pathways that produce them, e.g., shift representation drift action instability stale execution unsafe contact; this pathway is hypothesized, and Sec.~ sec:evidence measures only its action-instability step. Related work. VLA robustness benchmarks show large drops under modest camera shifts~ fei2025liberoplus but assume instantaneous inference. Real-time execution methods compensate for inference delay in chunked policies~ black2025rtc,tang2025vlash,agouzoul2026async , and adaptive test-time compute trades decision quality against latency~ li2026elastic ; both are evaluated in nominal scenes and by task success. Safety benchmarks measure violations beyond success~ fan2026safevlabench,cui2026liberosafety , and failure detectors monitor model-internal signals~ seligmann2026vlafail,gu2025safe , but compute is held fixed. Perturbing the reasoning stage exposes architecture-specific fragility~ trinh2026doubleedged . We connect these threads: the variations they study separately interact. Preliminary Evidence sec:evidence Setup. We evaluate ~ pi2025pi05 fine-tuned on LIBERO~ liu2023libero on all 10 LIBERO-Spatial tasks in closed-loop simulation (20\,Hz control; 50-step action chunks, replanned every 10 steps). Physical variation: the agent-view camera is orbited about the workspace by , , , and ( -- ). The levels were chosen on held-out initial states so that zero-delay success spans 0.93 to 0.53 . Compute variation: inference latency \,ms. For reference, one chunk takes 221\,ms on an RTX~3080, so this range brackets consumer-GPU latency. Because simulation pauses during inference, we emulate latency in simulation time. Each chunk is computed from the observation steps old ( \,ms) and executed from the index for the current step, so every executed action is at least steps stale; one inference is in flight at a time. This is the naive asynchronous setting of~ black2025rtc,tang2025vlash . Metrics: task success, and a safety violation when the robot displaces a non-target object by more than 2\,cm or presses on a non-target object, fixture, or the table with more than 150\,N (cf.~ fan2026safevlabench ). Delay is benign in distribution, not under shift. Under the training viewpoint, even 400\,ms of delay barely changes the outcome: success falls from 0.97 to 0.92 and the violation rate rises from 0.045 to 0.080 (Fig.~ fig:surface a,b). Under a shift, the same delay drops success from 0.57 to 0.06 and raises the violation rate from 0.215 to 0.585. Physical and compute variation interact super-additively. Delay makes failures more dangerous, not just more frequent. Violations concentrate in failed episodes. The successful-but-unsafe rate stays at in every cell, so a success-only benchmark misses little unsafe success, but it cannot see how policies fail. Among failures, the share a violation rises with delay, from 0.17 to 0.43 at and from 0.44 to 0.62 at (0 vs.\ 400\,ms). Viewpoint shift destabilizes the policy. Within a viewpoint, however, an episode's zero-delay instability does not predict its harm from delay , so instability alone is not a sufficient early-warning signal. Research Agenda: Toward Predictable Physical Intelligence sec:agenda Where does variation amplify? Instrumenting every layer---representation drift, action variance, latency, action staleness, and contact---turns a failure into a traceable pathway. The scientific target is to identify where along the stack variation is amplified, and which layer gives the earliest warning. When does variation become risk? Most variation is harmless: a distribution shift or a latency spike is not a failure. Rather than detecting anomalies, a runtime monitor should predict propagation, , from cross-layer evidence , extending model-internal failure detectors~ seligmann2026vlafail , such as SAFE~ gu2025safe , with compute and execution state. Our pathway result suggests why: action instability alone does not identify which episodes a delay will harm. When should a robot think longer, and when should it act sooner? More test-time compute can improve a decision while making it staler~ li2026elastic , so risk may be non-monotonic in compute. The balance depends on scene dynamics, proximity to hazards, the precision the task requires, and uncertainty: a difficult but slow-changing scene rewards deliberation, whereas a dynamic one rewards fast, frequent updates. Compute and power as safety variables. A power cap or thermal throttling lowers GPU frequency, lengthens inference, and makes every action staler. Compute and power should therefore be allocated by physical risk rather than for efficiency alone---for instance, minimizing energy subject to ---with responses ranging from more compute to shorter action horizons, re-observation, slowing down, or stopping. Together, these questions define predictable physical intelligence: embodied AI predictable and safe despite variation across its environment, model, compute, and execution. Conclusion and Limitations sec:conclusion Physical safety of robot foundation models is a cross-layer property: the conditions that matter most are combinations, not isolated perturbations. In 4,000 paired episodes, inference delay that is nearly harmless under the training viewpoint becomes a major source of unsafe behavior under viewpoint shift. Our evidence is preliminary: one policy, one task suite, one perturbation pair, and emulated delay in simulation. Extending to more policies and perturbations, to hardware-induced delay (contention, power caps, thermal throttling), and to real robots is future work . Layers, Action Age, and the Interaction Contrast app:notation Layers. Variation arises at every layer of the embodied stack: the physical environment (lighting, clutter, viewpoint, object pose, dynamics), the embodiment (calibration, payload, actuator response), the model (representation shift, action instability, uncertainty), the compute platform (latency, jitter, contention, power caps, thermal throttling), and execution (stale actions, missed control updates, trajectory deviation). Throughout, a layer is a level of the robot system, never a layer of the policy network. Action age. Let be the physical state and the environment condition.
